I'm the production controller, so if the packaging isn't signed off, we can't  make  anything. Sounds like a right pickle. Sounds like ‘e needs a bit of a… nudge. A firm one, by the sound of it. You gotta be assertive, love. Don't let ‘im walk all over you. You've got a good ‘ead on your shoulders, and a fancy degree to prove it! I  have  been assertive! I sent a very polite but firm email yesterday. And this morning, just a quick message saying, “Any update on the packaging?” Nothing. I’m starting to feel like I’m talking to a brick wall. Maybe I should just go and find him and corner him in the kitchen. That’s what I used to do with Mr. Henderson down at the bakery, when I worked there. Always “forgetting” to order the flour. A quick little chat, face-to-face, usually did the trick.

Right, so I’m tellin’ ya, tryin’ to explain rugby league to Madame Dubois was…an experience. She kept askin’ if it was like American football, and I just kept sayin’ “Nah, it’s… different.” Different doesn’t really cover it, does it? She was convinced they stopped to have a cuppa halfway through. Oh my god, that’s brilliant. Madame Dubois sounds delightfully clueless. Honestly, trying to explain cricket to anyone not British is a lost cause. They just stare at you blankly when you mention leg before wicket. It’s a whole other dimension of confusion. How’s the French course going otherwise? Still struggling with the subjunctive? Strugglin’ is an understatement. It feels like they made it up just to torture language learners. And the grammar! Don't even get me started. It's not logical, is it? Like, why  that  ending and not  this  one? Back home, things are a lot more straightforward. Though, I am slowly gettin' better at orderin' a pain au chocolat without soundin' like a complete idiot. Small victories, eh? Honestly, French grammar is designed to break you. I'm finding the vocabulary surprisingly difficult too. It's not necessarily  learning  the words, it's remembering which one to use when. Like, there are five different ways to say ‘to know’! And don't even think about the false friends. I accidentally asked for a condom instead of a preserve the other day… mortifying. No way! You didn't! Oh, that's… that's amazing! See, this is why I stick to askin' for ‘un croissant, s’il vous plaît’. Safe option, that. Speaking of safe, are you still thinkin’ about applyin’ for that internship at the science museum in London? Yeah, I am, but I’m getting increasingly anxious about the interview. It feels like everyone else applying has already done a PhD in astrophysics or something. I mean, I’m good at the core science, the methodology and stuff, but I worry I’ll stumble over the more niche questions. What about you? Still thinking about a gap year before uni? Aye, I am. Thinkin' I'll pick up some work, maybe try and save some proper money. Dad's been on at me to get a trade, like plumbing or electrics. Says it’s a ‘proper job’ with good prospects. But I'm not sure I can face spendin’ all day under someone’s sink.

… honestly, I just about jumped out of my skin. It was  huge . Not one of those little house spiders, oh no. This thing was… substantial. Like a tarantula, but, you know, British. Oh, you and your spiders, Brenda! Always a drama. I swear, you’d think they were venomous when half the time they're just lost and lookin' for a bit of warmth. Warmth? Brenda, it was clinging to the lampshade! The  lampshade , Doreen! It wasn’t seeking warmth, it was plotting world domination, I’m sure of it. Richard had to come and deal with it, armed with a magazine and a look of profound disgust. Richard ain't keen on the creepy crawlies neither, is he? Mine would just shriek for me to sort it. Men. Honestly. Although, speaking of unwelcome guests, I had a mouse in my airing cupboard last week.  That  was stressful. A mouse! Oh, heavens. Worse than a spider, I think. Something about the scurrying… it’s just so unsettling. Did it cause any damage? Thankfully, no. Just a few little droppings. I laid down some of them sticky traps. Got it the next morning. Felt a bit bad, mind you. Little thing. But it had to be done, didn't it? Can’t have them nesting. Absolutely. Hygiene is key. It’s amazing what turns up, isn’t it? I had a bird fly  into  the house last autumn. Through the open kitchen window. Absolute chaos. No! A whole bird? What sort? A robin, tiny little thing, flitting about like a feathered missile. It kept bumping into everything. Richard was trying to coax it out with a tea towel, and I was trying to close all the other doors so it wouldn't get lost in the house. It ended up perching on top of the grandfather clock for a good hour. Oh, that’s brilliant! A robin on the grandfather clock! I can just picture it. Birds are lovely, though. I put up a feeder in the garden, you know. Gets all sorts visiting. Blue tits, robins, even a great spotted woodpecker once. Really? A woodpecker? That’s amazing! I’ve tried with a feeder, but I mostly just attract pigeons. They’re like feathered hooligans, aren’t they? Always squabbling and making a mess. Pigeons are greedy, that’s their problem. You need a proper feeder, one of them ones with little cages around it, so only small birds can get in.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork after Mum died was just… relentless. Probate, informing everyone, going through  everything  she owned. It was exhausting, even with David helping. Though he’s brilliant with the practical side of things, bless him, he doesn’t really  do  emotions. Which is fine, someone has to be the steady one, I suppose. It’s just… I found a box of old photos, and that’s really got me thinking about the family. Are you much into family history, Bronwen? I know you taught history for years, but did you ever delve into your own roots? Oh, love, don’t I just! Though my methods were probably less… formal than what you’re doing now. I never really had the time or the funds for proper genealogy research, but my Nan, she was  obsessed . She could tell you about every single Jones, Williams, or Davies back to the 1700s, and usually with a scandal attached! Being Welsh, family is… everything. It clings to you, you know? It’s woven into the landscape. I grew up hearing stories, mostly around the kitchen table fuelled by strong tea and bara brith. That sounds lovely. Mum… Mum wasn’t really a storyteller. More of a keeper of things. Boxes and boxes of things. Which is how I ended up with this tangled mess of half-finished family trees. She started it years ago, when Grandad passed, but never really got very far. I think it upset her too much, to be honest. The idea of things ending, people disappearing… It resonated with her, especially towards the end. You know, the Lewy Body Dementia. It just… stole her, bit by bit. Oh, that’s awful, Sarah. Dreadful disease. My sister’s husband, Gareth, had something similar, vascular dementia. It’s just heartbreaking to watch someone you love fade away like that. The person is still  there , but… not really. It’s a cruel kind of loss. It’s good you’re trying to keep her memory alive, though, even through the family tree. It's a lovely tribute. Was she born in Dorchester then, your Mum? I seem to recall something… She was! Born and bred. Her father, my grandfather, was a stonemason, worked on quite a few of the buildings around the county town. Very proud man, apparently. He’s the one I’m really struggling with in this tree.

Honestly, this is exactly what I needed. Just… green. And quiet. London feels like a constant thrum, even when you’re trying to  find  quiet. Did you see that kestrel hovering over the field back there? Absolutely beautiful. I did! Magnificent. Bit of a contrast to the pigeons vying for chips outside the university, isn’t it? Though, to be fair, they’re pretty tenacious little things. Reminds me of Mabel trying to steal sausages off the barbeque last summer. Oh, Mabel. The audacity. She really thought she’d get away with it, didn’t she? A tiny sausage bandit. You know, watching those hot air balloons drifting over those fields yesterday… it just made me think about how ridiculously  expensive  everything is becoming. To even  go  up in one of those, must cost a fortune. It does. I looked into it, ages ago, as a potential ‘big’ birthday present for you. Quickly realised a weekend camping with proper kit was significantly more achievable, financially speaking. And less likely to end in a panicked descent into a farmer’s field. Sensible man. Seriously though, it feels like we work and work, and for what? To essentially be able to afford… slightly less stressful versions of existing experiences. Like trading a cramped city flat for slightly more space in the countryside, but with the added anxiety of oil tank refills. That’s a bit bleak, even for you, love. We're doing alright. We've got a roof over our heads, a ridiculously fluffy dog, and access to ridiculously lovely countryside like this. And, let's not forget, stable jobs. Lecturing isn’t going to make us millionaires, but it’s comfortable. Comfortable, yes. But ‘comfortable’ feels a long way from building any real security, you know? Especially with everything going on. I was reading about the cost of energy spiking again. And look at those power lines marching across the landscape. They feel… ominous. A constant reminder of how reliant we are on things we don’t truly control. They are a bit grim, aren't they? Breaching the landscape like that. But honestly, I find the wildlife more fascinating. Did you notice that hare darting into the hedgerow? I swear they look like they're perpetually surprised to be alive. They do, don't they? Little fluffy question marks. You're good at shifting the perspective. It's one of the things I… well, you know.

…and honestly, the humidity today is just  suffocating . Not like a nice, warm summer humidity, but a thick, cloying sort. Did you feel it on the court, David? It was sticking to me almost immediately. Aye, felt it alright. Proper sticky, it was. Yorkshire weather prepares you for a bit of damp, but this… this is different. It’s almost… Mediterranean in its weight, isn’t it? Though thankfully without the sunshine to go with it. Still, good workout though, wasn't it? Malcolm’s really pushing us this season. It was good, yes. Brutal, but good. I'm feeling it in my calves already. I think he’s secretly training us all for the over-50s circuit. Speaking of which, how’s work going? Still travelling all over the Midlands with the gyms? You’ve hit the nail on the head! Seems like I spend more time  in  the car than  at  the gyms sometimes. Got a new one opened in Birmingham last month, though, which is doing well. Lots of young professionals wanting to look good, apparently. It’s a relentless cycle, this fitness industry. Wanting to be healthier while simultaneously working themselves into the ground. It’s true. It’s the same with language learning, in a way. People desperately want to connect with other cultures, but they often don’t have the time, or the motivation, to put in the consistent effort required. I’m teaching a particularly… enthusiastic group of beginners at the moment. Lovely people, but their pronunciation is… interesting. Oh, are you still doing the evening classes? Always admired that, teaching. Seems a world away from spreadsheets and profit margins, doesn’t it? I left school at sixteen, mind. Sixth form, then straight into work. Never really got the bug for academia. Though, I do enjoy a good book. Just finished a thriller by Lee Child, good bit of escapism. It is a different world, yes. Very rewarding, though. Though challenging, particularly getting people to move beyond just memorising vocabulary. It's about mindset, and confidence. I’ve been reading a lot about coaching techniques – not just in the language learning context, actually. It’s fascinating how transferable the principles are. You use them in gyms, with people reaching their fitness goals, and I use them with students trying to master a new language. Now that  is  interesting. I’ve seen a few personal trainers using similar techniques, breaking down goals into tiny steps, positive reinforcement, that sort of thing.

Now then, lad, are you sure you’ve packed enough for your trip to London with school? It’s a long way to go and you don't want to be borrowing socks from your mates, do you? Your Gran and Grandad are proper worriers, you know. Yeah, Mum, I’ve got everything. Checked the list three times. Jacket, trainers, phone charger… the essentials. Honestly, you’d think I was going to the Amazon, not a museum. He’s right, love. You're spoiling the boy rotten. When  I  went on school trips, a packed lunch and a good pair of shoes were all I needed. And a prayer it didn't rain! Remember the trip to Whitby, Arthur? Whitby? Aye, I remember Whitby. Got soaked to the bone, we did. And young Brenda – that was your cousin, wasn’t she, Elsie? – she lost her new cardigan right off her back. Blown straight into the North Sea, it was. That  was  Brenda. Always a bit of a drama queen, she was. And you, Arthur, were always more concerned about the fish and chips than Brenda’s cardigan. Fish and chips sound good actually. Are we having tea soon? I’m starving. Always thinking about your stomach, aren’t you? We can have something substantial after, but I brought those little Yorkshire Curd tarts. They’re fresh from Mrs. Higgins down the road. She makes ‘em just like me mam used to. Oh, lovely! I haven't had a proper Yorkshire Curd tart in ages. Elsie, you are a treasure. Though, I still think you should be putting your feet up, not baking. Nonsense, Margaret. Keeps me busy. What else would I do? Watch daytime television? No thank you. Though, Arthur  does  insist on watching that gardening show with that bloke who shouts at plants. He’s giving them encouragement! It’s a perfectly reasonable method. You need firm guidance, plants do. Just like…well, never mind. You shouting at plants, Grandad? That's brilliant. Can I record that next time? Don't you dare, young man! He'd never forgive you. Now, about the house. I’ve been meaning to ask, Elsie, did you manage to get someone to look at the leaking gutter? It’s driving me mad, the dripping. Oh, that. Young Gary promised he’d come Tuesday. Said he’d squeeze us in between jobs. Don’t hold your breath, pet.

Right, are you  absolutely  sure this is the right way, love? Because this looks suspiciously like…well, like the road to Old Man Hemmings’ sheep farm. And last time we ended up having to reverse out of a muddy field while he shouted at us about disturbing Bess. Relax, Brenda. The satnav says this is the scenic route. I told it to avoid motorways, didn't I? You wanted to see a bit of the countryside before the gig. Besides, Hemmings’ sheep are remarkably unimpressed by reversing cars. I think he enjoys the drama. Scenic is one thing, practically off-roading is another! And I’m starting to think this 'state-of-the-art' satnav of yours is about as useful as a chocolate teapot. Remember when we used to just use a proper map? None of this digital nonsense. I swear, technology's made us all daft. Now, now, don't go blaming the technology. It's a very sophisticated piece of kit. It's just…interpreting “scenic” a little liberally, perhaps. And you were the one moaning about me constantly asking for directions! Besides, maps require unfolding. And folding. A complete waste of valuable gig-going time. Unfolding and folding builds character, Arthur! And hand-eye coordination. Something I suspect you’re losing rapidly, judging by your attempts at knitting last winter. That scarf still looks like a particularly disgruntled badger. It was…abstract! A textural exploration of the Northumbrian landscape, if you will. And I was rather proud of the wonky bits. Anyway, more important matters. Are you still on for helping Auntie Mabel choose flowers for the wedding? She’s panicking, apparently. Said she’s dreamt three times about hydrangeas wilting. Oh, dear Mabel. Always prone to a bit of melodrama. Yes, I’ve promised to go with her on Saturday. Though honestly, choosing flowers feels incredibly frivolous when the council’s threatening to close the library again. Honestly, Arthur, it's a disgrace. They’re prioritizing a new car park over literacy! I heard. It’s appalling. I've written to the local paper, you know. A strongly worded letter. Though I suspect it'll end up lining someone’s budgie cage. Speaking of which, did you see old Mrs. Higgins' prize-winning budgie escaped yesterday? Flew right over the village green, apparently. Caused absolute chaos. No! Goodness me. That little Winston is a character. Always thought he had ambitions beyond a cage.

…and honestly, the sheer audacity of cladding a brutalist building in  rose gold  panels. It's just…wrong. Utterly, fundamentally wrong. Did you see Ben’s face? He looked like he’d swallowed a lemon whole. Ben’s expression is always good for a laugh. Though I have to admit, even I winced. Rose gold? On the concrete monolith that is the old Poly? Someone’s been spending too much time on Pinterest. What did Professor Davies say? She actually tried to defend it! Said it was ‘a commentary on the juxtaposition of industrial and feminine aesthetics’. Honestly, I nearly choked on my coffee during the site visit. I mean, it's a student project, right? We’re supposed to be thinking about context, materiality, function…not just slapping on whatever’s trendy. Exactly! It’s the principle of the thing. Though, thinking about principles… how’s your communal living experiment going? Last I heard you were still negotiating dishwasher schedules. Don't even  start . It's…evolving. The dishwasher situation has stabilized, surprisingly. Turns out a colour-coded rota and passive-aggressive post-it notes work wonders. It’s Maisie who’s the problem now. She’s been incredibly down since…well, since the breakup. Barely leaves her room. Oh, no. Still? That’s awful. Is she eating? She’s forcing herself to, I think. I leave little care packages outside her door - soup, biscuits, the occasional ridiculous magazine. I tried to get her to come to that lecture on biophilic design with me yesterday, thought it might cheer her up. No luck. Poor thing. She needs a distraction. You’re a good friend for looking out for her. Speaking of distractions, have you decided what you're doing for the university brief? I’m still kicking around ideas. I was thinking a vertical farm integrated into a social housing project. Something practical, you know? That actually sounds brilliant. I'm leaning towards a regenerative community space, focusing on brownfield sites. I’m obsessed with the idea of reclaiming derelict land and turning it into something truly sustainable and beneficial. It’s ambitious, I know, but… I feel passionately about it. Ambitious is good! We need ambitious. Plus, you’re genuinely gifted at that stuff, Amelia. Remember that renovation you did of that old warehouse in Watford when you were still studying? It was incredible. The way you played with the light and space… Oh, stop it.

…and honestly, the A1 was  gridlock . Absolutely dreadful. Took me nearly an hour to get from Stamford to here, and that's only twenty-odd miles! You wouldn’t believe the tailbacks. Ugh, seriously? That sounds awful, Mum. Did something happen? There wasn’t anything on the radio when I was driving back from Lucy’s. Apparently, a lorry shed its load – a whole load of… well, I don’t even know  what  it was, just a huge mess across all three lanes. They were trying to clear it up, but it was taking ages. Honestly, the drivers! No spatial awareness. Leaving gaps big enough to let people merge properly, just… stop-start, stop-start. It’s infuriating. People are terrible at merging, aren't they? Always trying to sneak in at the very last second. Lucy was moaning about someone tailgating her on the A46 earlier. She said it completely stressed her out. Oh, that’s dreadful. Honestly, it’s a wonder there aren't more accidents. Speaking of Lucy, how was your afternoon with her? Did you finally manage to sort out the tickets for that concert? Yeah, we did! Got the last two standing tickets, can you believe it? It's going to be chaos, but it’ll be worth it. She’s buzzing about it. We went to that new vegan cafe afterwards, "Green Haven", near the market. It was actually really good, even for me, and you know I’m a bit of a meat-and-potatoes girl. Oh, good! I’ve been meaning to try that place. I’ve heard good things. Standing tickets, though? Your knees will be killing you! Remember what happened at that festival a few years back? Oh, don’t remind me! But honestly, it’s the only way to get to see them. They’re massively popular. Anyway, enough about my aching feet. How was your day at work? Did you manage to close that deal with Harrison Chemicals? It's… complicated. They’re being very cautious. The new CEO is a bit of a stickler for detail, keeps asking for endless revisions to the proposal. It’s exhausting, frankly. But I think I’m slowly winning him over. I had him on a Zoom call for over an hour this afternoon, outlining all the projected ROI. I think he finally started to see the value. Good. You’re brilliant at that stuff, Mum, don’t doubt yourself.

…and honestly, the ‘dynamic team player’ bit just feels so… hollow, doesn’t it? Like everyone  says  that. I’ve rewritten it three times now and it still reads like corporate jargon vomit. Corporate jargon vomit is a brilliant phrase, honestly. You’re right, though. It’s the most overused thing in job applications. What’s the actual job, remind me again? Beyond “something in media”? It’s a Content Creator role at that digital marketing agency, ‘Bright Sparks’. They specialise in social media campaigns for local businesses. It’s a step down, maybe, from the teaching side of things, pay-wise, probably, but…it’s  different . And, frankly, a bit less soul-crushing than marking GCSE essays on the passive voice for the rest of my life. I get it. A change of scenery. And content creation plays to your strengths, surely? You’re always sending me brilliantly witty stuff you’ve found online. Way better than what most agencies churn out. So, ditch the ‘dynamic team player’. What  specifically  makes you good at this? That’s what I’m struggling with! I feel like I’m underselling myself. Should I mention my language skills? Obviously, it’s not a language teaching job, but I could talk about adaptability, understanding different audiences… that kind of thing? Absolutely! Highlight the transferable skills. Being able to break down complex information into something easily digestible – that's huge for content creation. You do that  all  the time when explaining grammar to teenagers. Frame it as ‘ability to tailor communication to specific demographics’ or something equally buzzwordy, but meaningful. They love that. Right, okay. ‘Tailor communication’. I can work with that. It feels less… fake. What about the ‘experience’ section? I've got the teaching, obviously, but I did that tiny stint volunteering at the local radio station a few years ago, didn’t I? Is that worth mentioning? Definitely! Even if it was just helping with the playlist, it shows initiative and some understanding of the media landscape. Don't downplay it. Think about what you  did  there. Did you write any scripts? Even little promotional bits? Did you use any editing software? Any of that stuff. It all adds up. I did write a few short ad reads, yeah. Awful ones, probably, looking back. And I learned the basics of their editing software, Audacity, I think it was. Ok, okay, I'm making notes.

…Honestly, I’m still turning it over in my head. Leaving the tech world feels… enormous. After twenty years building that business, it’s a huge part of my identity, you know? It's not just a job, it's  what  I did. Of course it does. It’s absolutely massive. But you were looking… strained, Ben. Positively grey around the temples. That much stress isn’t healthy. And you always said you regretted not pursuing the woodworking properly after uni. This feels less like abandoning ship and more like… finally steering towards something you genuinely want. That’s a lovely way of putting it, love. Steering. I like that. But going from multi-six figure revenue to… building bespoke coffee tables? It’s a bit of a jump, isn't it? Especially with the market being what it is. Everyone and their dog is a ‘maker’ these days. Right, but  your  work is different. I’ve seen it. It’s not just ‘rustic chic’ – there’s real artistry there. And you’ve got the business acumen to actually make it sustainable. That’s what sets you apart. Remember old Mr. Henderson, the cabinet maker back in Wellington? He didn’t know a balance sheet from a biscuit tin, and he struggled. You won’t. True. Henderson was a brilliant craftsman, completely hopeless at the business side of things. Alright, so let’s say I commit. What's Phase One? Beyond, you know, acquiring a shed and a decent lathe? Okay, well, I've been doing some preliminary research. There's a couple of makers' markets fairly regularly in Byron Bay. They aren’t huge, but they’re a good way to test the waters, get feedback, build a local profile. We could start small, just a couple of tables, a few smaller pieces. Then, a simple website. Etsy is an option, but feels a bit… crowded. Website definitely. I can handle the coding side, obviously. But the marketing… that's where I always relied on Sarah back at the company. I’m hopeless at Instagram. That’s where  I  come in. Honestly, as a teacher, I practically live on social media, keeping up with parents! I can handle the marketing, the photos, the whole shebang. We can even tie it into the house-sitting, you know? "Australian timber, crafted with New Zealand flair…" It has a ring to it, doesn't it?

Honestly, this is lovely, Margaret, but I feel like I’ve spent the entire day negotiating with a tiny human about five different shades of green. It’s exhausting. And then Leo decides  now  is the time to practice his throwing… with mashed potato.      Thwo! Good thwow!      Oh, the joys of toddlerhood, dear. You’ll blink and he’ll be a teenager, rolling his eyes at everything you say. Remember when young Hamish decided the living room wall needed redecorating with crayon? A very… modern abstract piece, he called it.      Ah, yes, the artistry of youth. Though I suspect Hamish's wall was less damaging than some of the manuscripts  I  had to deal with. Editors, you know, often have, shall we say,  strong  opinions. Speaking of strong, have you noticed young men are suddenly obsessed with growing beards? It’s a veritable forest out there these days.      It  is  a bit of a trend, isn’t it? Leo’s father is attempting one. It’s… patchy, to be polite. He says it makes him look distinguished. I told him he looks like he’s lost a fight with a badger.      Dada’s face… fuzzy!      Careful now, wee one! Grandad’s face is off-limits. Though I agree with your mother, dear. A wispy beard doesn’t exactly scream ‘distinguished.’ It’s more ‘trying too hard.’ Now, this discussion about toddlers… it reminds me. The school situation in Cambridge is utterly dire. I was volunteering at the library this morning, and a mother was in tears because she’s been put on a waiting list for  three  different primary schools.      The housing shortage fuels it, doesn’t it? Everyone wants to live here, drawn by the university, the tech companies… and naturally, the charming streets. But the infrastructure simply hasn’t kept pace. It's a tragedy. When  I  was a young man, getting a place in a good school was a matter of course.      It’s terrifying. We’re lucky Leo’s father has a job with the university, which gives us some priority, but even then… I'm already worrying about secondary school. It feels like you have to start planning from birth. And then there’s the whole influx of families from abroad, which I’m not saying is a bad thing, but…      Oh, here we go.      No, no, it’s not what you think! It’s just… it adds to the pressure, doesn’t it?

…and honestly, the whole thing with the car park passes at the doctors is just ridiculous, isn’t it? They’re saying you need a pass now, even just to drop someone off. It’s like they  want  people to be late for appointments. Oh, don't even get me started on that! I drove Mum down last week, and nearly got a ticket. Honestly, the attendant was so officious. Said “No Pass, No Parking - even for five minutes!” Five minutes, Brenda! She's eighty-two. It’s a nightmare. They say it’s to stop people using it for the village, but it’s just making life hard for patients. Exactly! It's all seemingly logical when they come up with these rules, but no one thinks about the practicalities. Speaking of Mum, how is she doing with her chest? Still a bit wheezy? A little. The doctor says it’s just a bit of a bug, but she’s understandably anxious. Reminds me of your Dad, actually, always worrying about every little sniffle. Do you remember when he convinced himself he had… what was it? Lupus, wasn’t it? Just because he felt a bit tired! Oh, God, yes! He was reading one of those health magazines and self-diagnosed. He practically had himself buried before we managed to convince him it was just a lack of sleep and too much gardening. He was a character, wasn't he? It feels like ages ago now. It does. It’s funny the things you remember. Did I ever tell you about old Mr. Hemmings from sixth form? The history teacher who smelled permanently of mothballs and stale biscuits? Oh, Mr. Hemmings! Vaguely. Was he the one who used to drone on about the Tudors for the entire lesson? That's the one! He used to say we were a “disappointing cohort.” Honestly, I was more bothered about getting a date with David at the time than the nuances of Henry VIII's wives. Though, looking back… maybe he had a point about us being distracted! We were young! That’s what sixth form was for. Still, I did alright, got my degree. It's funny though, I never thought I'd end up doing what I do. Proofreading and marketing… quite a leap from English Literature, really. You’re good at it though, aren't you? Always had an eye for detail.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of daftness on Twitter these days is astonishing. I used to find it useful for gauging public opinion on comms campaigns, you know? Real-time feedback. Now it's just… shouting into the void, mostly. Did you see that thread about the new oat milk latte? Three hundred replies, ninety percent of them just aggressively stating a preference for dairy. Aye, I did catch a glimpse. It’s a cesspit, isn’t it? Though, I’ve actually found it surprisingly useful for student engagement. Not for  serious  academic discourse, mind you. But I’ve started running a sort of “Ask Me Anything” session once a month, just dropping a link on the university’s Twitter feed. Really? That's clever. I wouldn't have thought students would bother. I always imagined them all on TikTok or Instagram, glued to those. You’d be surprised. There’s a contingent who appreciate the opportunity to pick my brain anonymously. Gets them to engage with the department in a way they might not otherwise. I get questions about everything, from course selections to career advice. Even occasional queries about the best pubs in town! The important questions! See, that’s the benefit of social media, isn’t it? It bypasses all the formal channels and lets you connect directly. Though, it also bypasses all filters, which is where the daftness comes in. We had a wee incident at work last week. Someone on the marketing team scheduled a tweet celebrating… National Sausage Roll Day. National Sausage Roll Day? Is that… real? Apparently. And it was fine, until someone in the comments pointed out we were simultaneously running a health awareness campaign about reducing processed meat intake. The PR team nearly had a collective heart attack. I had to draft a quick follow-up acknowledging the irony. Oh, that's a classic. The disconnect between departments. It's always a risk. We have similar things happen with the student union’s social media. They'll announce a vegan bake sale five minutes after the sports team posts pictures of a massive BBQ. It’s the speed of it all, isn’t it? Everything's instant. No time for thought. I try to schedule things carefully, but even then, you can't predict what kind of storm you’re walking into. I spent a good hour last Tuesday crafting a response to a perfectly reasonable complaint about our website.

Honestly, I’m still recovering. That “quick” volunteering shift at the festival turned into a full-on mud wrestling competition with a rogue bouncy castle. And then Liam decided  that  was the perfect time to tell me about his girlfriend. Oh, Liam. Always impeccable timing, isn't he? Mud wrestling a bouncy castle sounds…intense. You alright though? Didn't see any injuries when you stumbled in earlier. Just a lot of slightly damp indignation. Mostly indignation. My wellies are still caked. And yes, the timing really was something. I was handing out water bottles, he grabs my arm and launches into this whole thing about Chloe and how ‘amazing’ she is. Like, mate, I’m covered in mud, leave me alone! Men. Honestly. You deserve better timing for a life update, even from Liam. What’s Chloe like? Do you know her? Vaguely. We had a module together in second year, History of Art. She mostly just…existed quietly. Seemed nice enough, very into Pre-Raphaelites. It’s just…I didn't expect  him  to be settling down, you know? We always just had a very…casual, chaotic friendship. I get it. Still feels weird though, doesn’t it? Anyway, enough about Liam’s love life. You need feeding. I’m attempting a chilli. It’s probably going to be lethal, but I’ve got rice. And beer. Lethal sounds perfect, actually. Anything to distract me from the image of Liam gazing lovingly into Chloe’s eyes. You’re a lifesaver. How was  your  weekend? Quiet, I assume, compared to my muddy escapades? Relatively. I did a double shift on Saturday, which was…a shift. Mrs. Peterson decided to re-enact her entire life story to me, complete with dramatic pauses and hand gestures. It’s endearing until you realise it’s been going on for three hours and you still haven't done your medication round. Oh, bless her. They do keep you on your toes, don't they? It must be exhausting. I get stressed enough coordinating spreadsheets and chasing people for reports, I can’t imagine dealing with real people’s actual problems all day. It is. But it’s also…rewarding? When you actually connect, when they start to feel a little less lost. It's worth the Mrs. Petersons of the world. Though sometimes I fantasise about running away and opening a cake shop. Fewer existential crises, more buttercream.

…and honestly, Mum, I don’t think Uncle Barry  needs  a detailed itinerary. It stresses him out. He just wants to know roughly when things are happening and where he’s sleeping. Remember last Christmas? The timetable nearly sent him into orbit. Oh, don’t remind me. The colour drained from his face when he saw that spreadsheet you’d prepared, dear. Spreadsheet! For Christmas Day! Honestly. He’s a simple man, Barry. Just wants a pint and a bit of peace. He's not  that  simple, John. He just… operates on a different wavelength. He likes to feel prepared, even if appearing bewildered is part of the act. And, honestly, a little structure wouldn’t kill him. He ended up wandering into the garden looking for the nativity scene at 10am last year! Right, because  that  was my fault? I was trying to be helpful! And speaking of helpful, have we finalised the meals? I’m happy to do the roast on Sunday, but I was thinking a lighter something for Saturday night… maybe a pasta bake? A pasta bake sounds lovely, love. Though perhaps not  too  adventurous. Barry's palate hasn’t really evolved since the 1970s. He still thinks cheese and tomato pasta is exotic. He does, doesn't he? He once described a pesto pasta as "green spaghetti". But a pasta bake is safe. And it means less for you, Sarah. You've been run ragged at school this term. It  has  been rather chaotic. Year 6 are… energetic, to say the least. But I don’t mind cooking. It’s relaxing, actually. What about the journey down? John, are you still happy to pick Barry up from the train station? Of course. Though, I must say, I’m enjoying the new car for these longer trips. Much smoother ride than the old banger. You wouldn't believe the suspension on that thing! Every pothole felt like hitting a brick wall. Oh, tell us again about the car, John! It sounds marvellous. Is it comfortable? That’s important. Barry's back isn’t what it used to be. Comfortable? It's like sinking into a cloud! Leather seats, heated, lumbar support… the works. It's a completely different league. And the satnav is brilliant. Though, I nearly drove into a field the other day trying to adjust it. Old habits die hard, I suppose. Still prefer a good map, really.

… honestly, Arthur, I’m starting to think Spanish is designed to specifically frustrate me. I’ve been at this Duolingo lark for six months now, and all I can reliably say is “The dog is eating an apple.” Which, let's face it, is hardly a vital phrase for a trip to Barcelona, is it? Barcelona, eh? Ambitious. Six months is nothing, love. Absolutely nothing. I tried Italian once, years ago. Got as far as ordering a coffee and asking where the toilet was. And  that  took me a solid three months of flashcards. Spanish is a tricky one, though. All those verb conjugations! It’s a minefield. A minefield! That’s a perfect description. It’s not just the verbs, it's the… the  gendered  nouns! Why does a table need a gender? Is it a particularly flamboyant table? It makes no sense! And the pronunciation, don't even get me started. I sound like I’m gargling gravel when I try to roll my 'r's. Gravel, you say? Oh, you’re a natural then. Seriously though, Duolingo… it’s alright for vocab, but it’s no good for actually  speaking . It’s all robotic and… detached. I always found a good teacher makes all the difference. Remember when we did that Italian class together, briefly? Before I gave up on the whole thing? Vaguely. I remember mainly being distracted by the handsome instructor. But yes, having someone correct your pronunciation in real-time  is  helpful. I've been thinking about maybe finding a local conversation group. Though the thought of admitting to a room full of people that I struggle with ‘ser’ and ‘estar’ fills me with dread. ‘Ser’ and ‘estar’… the bane of every Spanish learner’s existence! Honestly, it’s a concept that just doesn’t translate easily for us English speakers, does it? It's one of those things that gets under your skin and just… niggles. You know, you get a bit obsessed. It’s funny, isn’t it? Countries where they grow up with two languages seem to have an easier time with it all. Like where? Give me an example. It's something I was reading about actually. Well, Spain itself, actually. Catalonia. They’re learning Castillian  and  Catalan from the moment they’re born. And then most kids pick up at least a smattering of English at school now. It’s got to give them a head start.

Right, Dad, I think we're down to the really… interesting stuff now. Mostly bank statements and stuff from 2017. Why do people  keep  so much of this? It's a paper avalanche. Well, your mother always said, “You never know when you might need it.” A bit of a hoarder, she was. Though nothing like your Auntie Brenda. Remember her stamp collection? Took up a whole room. These bank statements… might be useful for tax, I suppose. Or proving we actually  had  money at some point. Fair point. Although I highly doubt HMRC are going to come knocking asking about a twenty quid overdraft from 2017. Speaking of things you might need, have you booked those flights to Malaga yet? You said you were looking at EasyJet. I was, I was. Found a couple that look alright, leaving on the 14th. Problem is, the website is being a right pain. Keeps asking me to verify my identity with… some sort of document scan. And my scanner’s playing up again. Honestly, these computers! They're supposed to make life easier. Oh, the joys of online security. Let me have a look. I'm fairly good with that sort of thing. What document is it asking for? Passport, driving license? I can probably get your scanner working too, it's usually just a driver issue or something. It's all ones and zeros, Dad, honestly. It’s the passport. And yes, it's probably the driver again. It's just… frustrating. I can barely operate the TV remote these days, let alone wrestle with a scanner and a website demanding my soul. Actually, speaking of frustrating, did you see that article about Kelly Brook? Apparently she’s launching a new… cooking range? Kelly Brook? Cooking? That’s… unexpected. I didn’t even know she  could  cook. I thought she just… existed beautifully on magazine covers. It’s all marketing, I suppose. Although, I'm currently attempting to make a risotto, and frankly, it’s not going brilliantly. It's either crunchy rice or a gluey mess. No in-between. Risotto's tricky. Your mother made a fantastic one, though. She’d spend ages stirring it, always said the secret was good stock and patience. You need that patience. Like when you're trying to decipher this banking jargon! . What even  is  a “standing order mandate”? Sounds positively medieval. It’s essentially permission to take money from your account regularly.

… honestly, I still can’t believe they charged me that much. Four pounds eighty for diesel! Four eighty! It’s daylight robbery, it is. Welcome to the M25, love. Petrol stations around here operate on a completely different economic model to Sunderland, apparently. They assume everyone’s an investment banker. It’s not just  here , though. Even back home it’s creeping up. Remember when we could get it for a pound forty? Those were the days. I swear, I’m gonna have to start cycling everywhere. Though knowing my luck, I’d probably get run over by a biker. You and every other cyclist in the South East. There are a  lot  of bikers around here. Speaking of which, did you see that bloke on the Hayabusa earlier? Absolutely flying it. Reckless, mind, but impressive. Oh, aye, I saw him. Nearly gave me a heart attack. They just whizz past, don’t they? No respect for anyone. I don’t understand the appeal, honestly. All that leather and noise. It just seems… dangerous. And cold. It's the freedom, I think. And the speed. My cousin Mark’s really into it. He says it’s the closest he gets to feeling truly alive. He’s got a Triumph Bonneville. Classic. Not one of those crotch-rockets like the one we just saw. A Triumph, eh? Still sounds a bit… exposed. I’d rather be in a nice, metal box, thank you very much. Heated seats are  essential  in this weather, as you well know. You were moaning about the cold just five minutes ago. That was before you started ranting about petrol prices. It’s perspective, isn’t it? Cold hands are a minor inconvenience compared to financial ruin at the pumps. But seriously, you need to adjust your expectations. Everything’s more expensive down south. It’s just…the way it is. Easy for you to say, Mr. Consultant Engineer, earning the big bucks. It’s all relative, isn’t it? I'm stuck analysing sentence structures all day, not designing skyscrapers. Though, to be fair, there  is  a certain satisfaction in identifying a misplaced modifier. Oh, here we go. Don’t undersell yourself. Corpus linguistics is seriously clever stuff. Plus, you're good at it. And it’s contributing to the greater academic good. That’s worth more than a shiny building, arguably. You’re just saying that.

Right, so you’re still keen on getting extra coaching then, Leo? Your dad and I were talking about it. It's just…it’s a commitment, isn’t it? And quite an expensive one. Yeah, definitely! Mr. Henderson said I’ve got potential, Mum. Actual potential! He said my serve is coming along really well but my backhand needs… work. A lot of work. Henderson’s a good coach. Very methodical. Knows his stuff. He coached Amelia Davies, didn’t he? She did pretty well at county level. She did. Although I think she lost interest as soon as A-levels loomed. Too much pressure, I reckon. Anyway, Leo, it's not just the money. It’s the time. You’ve got GCSEs next year. We don't want tennis to impact on those. I know, I know. But I can manage it! I promise. I’ll just have to be really organised. I can do extra revision on the bus, maybe? And the coaching is only twice a week, after school on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Buses aren't exactly conducive to focused revision, are they? Though you are surprisingly good at blocking out chaos. Remember that time we were at Euston and you were completely absorbed in that book about… what was it? Quantum physics? It was just an introduction, Dad. And it was loud, but I needed something to read! Oh, he always has his nose in a book. It's endearing, if a bit disconcerting when he’s walking into lampposts. Look, Leo, we’re not saying no straight away. It’s just…Dad remembers when  he  was trying to be the next Roger Federer. Let’s not dwell on that, shall we? My peak athletic achievement was probably winning the inter-house table tennis competition at university. It was fierce, I assure you. Though, honestly, my tennis “career” ended rather abruptly with a pulled hamstring at a family holiday. I was trying to impress your Auntie Susan. You and Auntie Susan! You're always trying to impress Auntie Susan. He was! He spent weeks recovering. It’s easy to get carried away with ambition, especially when someone like Henderson is encouraging you. He's a good salesman, that man. He’s realistic though. Told me straight my forehand was a disaster when I tried a lesson a few years back. Said I looked like I was trying to swat a fly with a cricket bat.

Right, this is proper good, Mum. Honestly, best Christmas dinner ever. Though…are those…are those napkins shaped like pants?      They are, aren't they? Auntie Brenda sent them. Said she thought they’d be a bit of fun. I told her they were… questionable, but she’d already sent ‘em. Least they're clean, eh?      Questionable is an understatement. They’re deeply unsettling. It’s like Christmas dinner’s being watched over by a… brief army.      Brenda. Always Brenda. She means well, bless her. Though, last year’s singing toilet roll holder  was  pushing it. Anyway, has anyone actually started thinking about Boxing Day sales? I need a new telly.      Oh, don't you start on that already! You’ve just had Christmas dinner! I'm still full. Remember when you were little, and you'd try to eat the entire turkey yourself, David?      I was a growing lad! Needed my protein. Besides, your turkey was always exceptional, Mum. Still is. Speaking of, how do you manage to get it so moist every year? Mine always ends up drier than the Sahara.      Secret family recipe. And a generous amount of butter. Don’t tell anyone. We always have Christmas dinner here, don’t we? It wouldn’t  be  Christmas if we weren’t all squashed around this table.      Yeah, it's sound. Though, I was telling Liam and Chloe - you know, me uni mates - about how we always have Monopoly afterwards, and they were dead confused. Apparently, their families don't inflict that kind of torture on each other. They call it ‘Family Game Night From Hell’ now.      Oh, they’re not wrong. Monopoly always ends in arguments and flipped boards. Remember when you accused Grandad of cheating and nearly stormed off?      I  maintain  he was hiding money! Anyway, speaking of away from here…did you hear back from Aunt Susan about her trip to Florida?      She did. She's having a wonderful time. Said the weather’s glorious, obviously. She was complaining about the airport though, said security was a nightmare. And she nearly missed her flight trying to find decent tea. Apparently, American tea is a national disgrace.      She's a woman of strong opinions, our Susan. She wouldn’t settle for anything less than a proper cuppa. Remember when we tried to get her to go to New York instead? She said she’d rather wrestle an alligator.

Honestly, this week has been  mental  at work. We’re launching this new sustainability initiative, and it’s all meetings and spreadsheets and trying to convince people that reusable coffee cups are actually a good thing. It's exhausting.      Oh, dear. Sounds familiar. Though my battles are with teenagers and exam boards, not spreadsheets. You wouldn't believe the lengths some go to, trying to argue for special consideration. It’s always ‘my dog ate my homework’ or something equally…creative. How’s the project going otherwise? Is it actually  making  a difference, or is it just box-ticking?      Box-ticking. That’s all a lot of these things are, isn’t it? I've seen enough initiatives come and go in my time in agriculture to know that. Though, to be fair, the younger generation  are  more aware. Good on your company for at least trying. Speaking of trying, how’s that new recipe you were experimenting with, love? The one with the butternut squash?      It was…an experience. Let’s put it that way. I tried to make a butternut squash and sage risotto, and it ended up tasting faintly of sadness and burnt garlic. I think I underestimated the sage. It was  overpowering . I ended up ordering a takeaway. Honestly, I'm better at project coordinating than risotto-ing.      Oh, bless you! Risotto is notoriously tricky. It’s all in the constant stirring, you know. You need to be completely devoted to the risotto. I made a lovely one last week with mushrooms. I’ll send you the recipe. It’s quite simple, really. Though, thinking about it, it  did  take a good hour of my evening…      An hour? Good grief! That’s a long time for a Tuesday night. I’m simple, give me a good roast any day. Speaking of which, are we still on for dinner with the Millers next Saturday? I need to give Margaret a call.      Oh, the Millers! Yes, absolutely. I'm looking forward to it. It’ll be nice to catch up. They haven’t been themselves lately, have they? I heard from Susan that their daughter’s going through a rough patch.      Yes, poor Emily. She’s moved back in with them now, apparently. It's always hard on parents to see their children struggling. They were so proud of her doing so well at university. Still, they’re a strong family.

Right, onions are softening nicely. Honestly, I think I’ve used half a bottle of olive oil already. It’s just… everything seems to need olive oil these days. And speaking of needing things, how did the appraisal go? You were looking a bit peaky this morning. Oh, God, don’t even ask. It was…an experience. All boxes ticked, apparently. “Meets expectations,” which is code for “you’re perfectly adequate, don’t expect a raise, and please continue doing exactly what you’re doing.” Honestly, I could have written the report myself. It’s just so…beige. Beige. That's a perfect description of modern working life, isn’t it? Still, 'meets expectations’ isn’t  bad . It’s not a slap in the face. Fancy a pizza tonight, then? Forget the elaborate stew I was planning. We both deserve easy. A pizza sounds amazing, actually. Though, I did see Marks and Spencer are doing those stone-baked ones now, with the really fancy toppings. Remember how awful their food used to be? It's a genuine turnaround. Oh, I saw those! The chorizo and roasted pepper one looked particularly good. Although, honestly, their food hall in general is just…dangerous. I went in for a loaf of bread and came out with a truffle oil and some ridiculously expensive shortbread. It’s a conspiracy, I tell you. A delicious conspiracy! Speaking of conspiracies… did you see that documentary about equine welfare last night? Absolutely heartbreaking. The way those horses are treated in some places… It makes me furious. I didn’t! I was engrossed in  Trapped  again. Honestly, that series is just brilliant. So claustrophobic and gripping. Completely different mood to the  Walking Dead  which we were watching previously - that was just pure gore. Though, I do enjoy a good zombie apocalypse every now and then.  Trapped  is excellent, isn’t it? All that Icelandic bleakness. Much more my speed. Zombies feel… childish. Though, speaking of bleak, did you manage to finish that crossword I left on the kitchen table? I was stuck on 14 across for ages. I did! “Ancient vessel.” It was ‘Amphora’. Took me ages too, honestly I felt slightly smug when I got it. You know, I found a bottle of wine in the cellar the other day, dated 2009. Fourteen years old! I’m slightly terrified to open it. It could be spectacular, or it could taste like vinegar.

Right, so are we all still on for pre-drinks at mine then? I’ve finally cleared a space on me floor – after a right good tidy, mind. It looked like a bomb’d hit it, honestly. Yeah, definitely! Sounds lush. I'm already thinking about what to wear, though. This is the worst part, innit? Standing in front of your wardrobe for an hour and still feeling like you've got nowt to wear. Tell me about it! I've been doing the same. I’m torn between a dress and jeans & a nice top. It depends how much I plan on… well, you know. Moving. In heels. Heels? Oh, God, no. I've learned my lesson. Last time I wore heels on a night out I nearly ended up face-planting into a bin. I'm sticking to boots, thank you very much. Practical  and  stylish. Boots are good. Sensible. I’m going for the sparkly top and black jeans combo. Comfort is key, especially if we’re planning on a proper dance. Though, speaking of which, has anyone sussed out where we're actually  going  yet? I was thinking The Warehouse? It's always rammed, but the tunes are decent. Or maybe Club X? It’s a bit more…fancy. Depends if we want to feel like proper grown-ups, or just act a fool. Warehouse is always a winner for acting a fool, let's be honest. Fancy is overrated. Plus, I’ve already mentally prepared myself to spill a drink on someone at The Warehouse. It’s tradition. Oh, you’re a menace, Sarah! But yeah, Warehouse sounds good. Less pressure to look sophisticated. I'm more of a ‘accidentally elbow someone in the face while attempting a questionable dance move’ kinda gal. I’m with you both. Warehouse it is. Though, someone remind me to take a swig of water before I get there. My throat's already dry just  thinking  about shouting over the music. Good shout, Amy. And maybe a snack? I’m always ravenous before a night out. It's a survival tactic, obviously. You need fuel for dancing. And…potentially navigating crowds. Fuel is crucial! I’ve got crisps. And biscuits. Plus, I’ve got that new pink prosecco, so we can have a proper bubbly start to the night. But be warned, it’s strong stuff. Pink prosecco?! You are speaking my language, Chloe!

You know, I was reading an article this morning – completely ridiculous, honestly – about soulmates. Apparently, there are seven different ‘types’ of soulmate. Seven! As if finding  one  person you connect with isn’t complicated enough. Seven? Good grief. Sounds like someone’s trying to monetise existential angst. Honestly, I’ve always thought the ‘soulmate’ thing was a bit…overblown. Lovely idea, of course. Romantic. But a bit limiting, don't you think? Expecting one person to tick  all  the boxes. Exactly! It puts so much pressure on it. This article was saying the ‘catalyst’ soulmate exists to shake you up, the ‘growth’ soulmate helps you evolve… It sounds exhausting. I’m quite happy with the idea that you can have deep connections with multiple people throughout your life, each serving a different purpose. That makes far more sense, doesn’t it? A series of significant connections. It also explains why, sometimes, you look back on relationships and think, “Well,  that  was useful at the time.” Not necessarily romantic fulfilment, but… a lesson learned, a perspective gained. Precisely! It’s about the journey, isn't it? Which, speaking of journeys, reminded me of that conversation we had with Old Man Hemmings at the village fete. He was going on about past lives. Utterly bonkers, but…part of me wondered. Hemmings? The one who claimed he was a Roman centurion? And that his prize-winning marrow was imbued with the spirit of Julius Caesar? That’s the one! He was  very  emphatic. It got me thinking, though - If you could visit any period in history, genuinely  live  in it for a month, where would you go? No interfering, just observing. Ooh, that's a good one. Hmm… Probably Florence during the Renaissance. The art, the sheer explosion of creativity… I’d love to wander the streets, watch Michelangelo at work, eavesdrop on the conversations in the coffee houses. Though, knowing my luck, I’d probably end up a stable boy. You’d definitely be complaining about the hay! I think I’d go to Victorian London, surprisingly. All that smog and social structure, it's just… fascinating to me. Though I'd need a very good nose peg and a particularly sturdy pair of boots. London in the smog? Brave. So, you’d be quite happy observing the societal inequalities then? You, the eternally empathetic one? It's history, darling. I’d observe,  learn  from it.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork is just  insane . New regulations came in last month, something about data protection – honestly, it’s like they actively  want  us to fail. How are people supposed to keep up? Ugh, tell me about it. It's the same in my department. Endless forms for everything. Feels like half my job is just proving I  did  something, rather than actually  doing  it. It's soul-crushing, innit? At least you get a bonus at the end of the quarter if you hit your targets, right? I just get… a pat on the back. Don't even start with the paperwork, Amelia. I’m wading through sickness forms at the moment. Old Mr. Davies has got the flu  again . Honestly, you'd think he'd learn to get the jab. It sets off a domino effect, you see, then everyone else starts calling in ‘sympathy sick’. Oh, that’s dreadful. People just taking the mickey, is it? It’s always the same few. You’d think they'd have the decency to stay home when they're genuinely ill, though. Speaking of genuinely ill, how’s your mum, Carol? Last I heard she wasn’t brilliant with her hip. She’s…managing. Physio is a nightmare, apparently. She keeps saying the young physio doesn't understand what it's like to be her age. All this talk of ‘core strength’ and ‘mindfulness’ – she just wants it to stop hurting! It’s that generation, I think. Anything new is automatically suspect. It's funny, isn't it, how we all think like that about  other  generations? Like, people always moan about millennials being glued to their phones, but my Nan is constantly on Facebook, sharing dodgy articles about… everything. It’s the way of the world, darling. My sister keeps trying to get me into TikTok. Honestly, I just don’t get it. All those snippets of… whatever. It feels utterly exhausting. Though, she says it’s a fantastic way to learn new languages. Oh yeah? That’s interesting. I've been trying to brush up on my French Duolingo, but I keep getting distracted. It's hard to find the time. Remember that trip to Normandy we were planning last year? That feels like a lifetime ago. We should definitely revisit that. Though, France… all that newspaper striking. Makes you wonder what’s going on over there.

Right, so Liam’s actually managed to flood his kitchen. Again. Honestly, you’d think after the last time he’d learn to, like,  watch  the tap. No way! Seriously? Is it the same dodgy tap as before? The one he swore he’d fix with, like, three different types of sealant? Oh, I heard about that from Chloe. Apparently, it’s not the tap this time. He was trying to defrost a chicken under the hot tap. A whole chicken.  What?!  You're kidding me. That’s… that’s a new level of chaotic even for Liam. I mean, I’ve left toast burning, sure, but a flooded kitchen because of a defrosting chicken? That’s dedication to disaster. Dedication is one word for it. I'm picturing the Housing Officer’s face when Liam explains that one. They’re already giving him side-eye for the noise complaints. Speaking of Housing, did you guys get the email about council tax? My jaw dropped. Apparently, full-time students are exempt, which is good, but we have to  apply  for it. With proof of enrolment. What a palaver. Aye, I saw that. It’s a right pain, innit? More paperwork, more stress. They make it sound like we're all trying to pull a fast one. I’ve already scanned my student card over, just in case. My mam would have my hide if I got a council tax bill! She'd be saying "You should be saving that money, lass!" My parents are the same. They’re always going on about budgeting. Honestly, trying to explain student life to them is impossible. They think we’re living the high life, going out every night. They'd be shocked to know how much I spend on instant noodles. Tell me about it. My dad keeps asking about ‘investment opportunities’. Investment opportunities?! I’m barely covering rent and textbooks! Though, I did get a decent haul from the charity shop today - a vintage jacket for a fiver. Ooh, a fiver? That’s a steal! Where was this charity shop treasure trove? I need to up my shopping game. Everything in town is ridiculously overpriced. Especially those pretentious little boutiques. It's on Elm Street, near the park. They’re always rotating stock. I found a really good record player there last month. Talking about shopping, anyone going into town tomorrow? I need to get some… emergency biscuit supplies.

Right, this seafood risotto sounds proper good, doesn’t it? Though, honestly, after that bus journey from Pula, I could probably eat anything. Honestly, the state of those buses…packed like sardines.      You always were a drama queen, lass. It wasn’t  that  bad. And it’s Istria, love, you’ll get buses. They’re not exactly known for their luxury transport round here. How was Pula itself, though? Did you get to see the amphitheatre?      It was alright. The amphitheatre was…impressive, I suppose. Very Roman. But the heat! And those hills! I nearly died walking up to it. Honestly, I need a holiday from my holiday.      Did you see any mopeds? There’s loads here. Really fast ones. I reckon I could get one, just zip around Bolton on it.      Absolutely not. Your mother would have a fit. Remember your cousin Liam and his moped? Ended up in A&E, he did. Not a pretty sight.      Don’t even mention it. Three broken bones, and he swore he was being careful. Honestly, Michael, don't even think about it. You’ll be fine on your bike. Though, speaking of A&E, things are  mad  busy at the hospital right now. We’re chronically understaffed. It’s the same story everywhere, I suppose, but it's getting worse. Had a particularly rough shift last week.      Oh, Mum, that sounds awful. Honestly, you work so hard. You deserve a proper break, not just a week in Croatia with us lot. What was it this time?      Just…everything. A complicated birth, a poorly baby in SCBU, and then Mrs. Peterson’s husband had a fall. It all just piled up. It’s just…the emotional toll, you know? Seeing people at their most vulnerable.      It’s a demanding profession, definitely. High stress. You're a saint, honestly. You always have been. Though, on a lighter note, have you seen how much cheaper everything is here compared to Bolton? Even the supermarkets! I was looking at olive oil earlier - it's a fraction of the price.      You're always thinking about the price of things, Dad. But yeah, you’re right. Even just the fruit and veg is amazing. So much fresher. I’m trying to eat healthier now I’m at Uni, don’t want to put on a stone.      Uni's good, yeah? Are you enjoying it? Still doing all the… graphic design stuff?

…Right then. Back to civilisation, eh? Though I did rather enjoy the quiet, didn’t I? Even with all the…school children. Oh, you did. You were a natural with them, Arthur. Honestly, keeping them entertained on that windy beach for an hour? A miracle. And the YHA staff were so grateful for your help. Much more grateful than some of the youngsters they get, I daresay. Speaking of grateful, I’m grateful for a proper cup of tea and a biscuit after that drive. Cornwall's lovely, but it's a  long  way. How were the little cherubs, Arthur? Didn’t realise you'd volunteered for school trip duty alongside the YHA. Well, Maureen signed me up for the YHA, bless ‘er. Said I needed to get out more. And then young Timmy at the school - his mum, you know, does the flowers at the church - asked if I could lend a hand with their Year Fives. So, one minute I'm showing teenagers how to make a packed lunch, the next I’m explaining to eight-year-olds why crabs scuttle sideways. Honestly! Look at this one. You're practically surrounded. They all look utterly captivated, though. It's a good picture. Reminds me a bit of you with the lighthouse, actually. All those questions! That lighthouse  was  a challenge. "How high is it?" "What happens if the lamp breaks?" "Does someone live  inside ?" Little blighters never stopped asking! But it’s a beautiful spot, isn't it? Lizard Point. Dramatic. We had a good walk along the coast path, did Maureen and I. Though my knees weren't best pleased afterwards. Did you manage to get any decent photos of it? I’m planning a trip down that way myself next spring, for a bit of landscape photography. I've been meaning to go for ages. Oh, he took loads, David. Filled his memory card. Most of them are of Maureen pointing at things, though. She's a keen spotter, is my Maureen. "Look, Arthur! A gannet!" "Arthur, have you seen that rock formation?" She keeps me right, she does. I'd walk straight into the sea without her. Speaking of things she keeps me right about…she's booked us another trip. Oh? Where to this time? Not back to Cornwall already? Worse, or better, depending on how you look at it. She’s entered us into… "Yorkshire in a Day".

Right, this is proper good, this is. Honestly, ANON, you’ve outdone yourself. Yorkshire puddings…miles better than anything you get down south. Nothin' against your cookin', mind you, Liam, but it’s just…different. It  is  good, ANON, yeah. Proper tasty. Though, I gotta say, I'm not sure what a Yorkshire pudding even  is  properly. We never really had ‘em much growing up. Just roasties and gravy, you know? It’s basically…a savoury popover, Liam. Made from batter, cooked in hot fat. It’s designed to soak up all the gravy. Honestly, it’s a national treasure. And Georgie’s right, they’re noticeably better up north. It’s the water, probably. Or the sheer determination to make something amazing out of limited resources. Aye, determination! That’s it exactly. We 'ad to make our own entertainment, our own good food… We didn’t 'ave fancy production controlling jobs like some folk, did we? No offence, Chloe. None taken, Georgie. It’s a bit stressful, honestly. We’re launching a new product line next month and everything feels like it’s on fire. They want everything yesterday, and the supply chain is…well, let's just say it’s proving optimistic. Sounds rough, that. I’m just glad I’m slingin’ bricks, really. Less thinking, more doin’. Although my back  is  killin’ me today. Old Mrs. Henderson wanted a new garden wall and she’s got a garden that’s basically on a slope. Nightmare. Ooh, sounds hard work. You need a good brew and a lie down, love. Any luck with that girl, by the way? The one you were chattin’ up at the pub last week? Ah, Maya. Yeah, it was goin’ alright, actually. Took her to the cinema, she seemed to 'ave a good time. But then…she found out I'm a labourer. Oh no. Seriously? Yeah. Turns out she's studying law at the Uni. Said her dad was…disappointed. Like I’m gonna corrupt her or somethin’. Honestly, it was a bit insulting. That’s awful, Liam. People are so snobby! What’s wrong with honest work? My dad was a miner, and he was the most decent man I ever knew. He didn't need a fancy degree to know what was right and wrong. It's appalling. And it's the 21st century! You’d think people would be past that sort of thing.

Honestly, I’m still running on Barcelona time. Woke up this morning expecting sunshine and tapas, not grey skies and… toast. It feels wrong. Tell me about it! You look wrecked, in the best way possible. Worth the sleep deprivation though, right? Barcelona was amazing. Seriously, the architecture… Gaudi was a  genius . Amazing doesn't even cover it. It was just… vibrant. Everything felt so alive. And the food! I think I ate my weight in patatas bravas. Did you manage to try the churros with chocolate? Oh my GOD. I did! Near the harbour, right? They were incredible. Not quite as good as those we had in Paris last year, but a very close second. Though Paris will always have a special place in my heart, you know? First proper holiday with Ben… Oh, don't even  mention  Ben. He's been texting me non-stop about how he "missed me terribly." It’s a bit much, honestly. Like, I was gone for three days, not three years. Oh dear. Stage five clinger alert? Maybe he’s secretly worried you found a hotter Spaniard? Please. Though, a few of them were definitely giving me the eye. No, it’s just… he does this. Overcompensates with the grand gestures and declarations. It’s exhausting. I need someone who’s just… chill. I get that. It’s nice to feel wanted, but it needs to be sustainable, doesn’t it? Speaking of needing things… I need to figure out what I’m doing this weekend. Anything planned? Nothing concrete. I was thinking a massive duvet day. Catch up on ‘Severance’ - have you started it yet? Everyone at work is raving about it. Apparently, it’s properly mind-bending. No, not yet! It’s on my list though. I’ve been stuck on ‘The Bear’. It’s stressing me  out  watching it, all that kitchen chaos, but it’s brilliant. Honestly, I feel like I need a lie down just thinking about it. Work was manic this weekend. Short-staffed, and old Mrs. Higgins was having a particularly rough patch. Oh no, poor Mrs. Higgins. You’re such a saint, dealing with all that. It sounds draining. That’s why I’m glad I just wrangle spreadsheets for a living. Relatively stress-free. Though my boss is starting to hint about a promotion, which comes with more responsibility… and more spreadsheets. A promotion sounds good, though, doesn’t it?

…and honestly, the paperwork alone was enough to send me round the bend. Seventeen years I gave to that school, seventeen! You wouldn’t believe the hoops you have to jump through these days just to teach a child to read. Seventeen years is a  long  time. Dedicated. I wouldn’t last a week, I think. Too much…structure. I need to be my own boss, constantly reinventing things. Keeps the grey matter ticking over, you know? Reinventing things. That sounds exhausting in a different way. Though, I suppose marking two hundred sets of Year 6 SATs papers  is  a special kind of torture. What is it you  do  exactly? You mentioned something about being an entrepreneur, but… it still sounds a bit vague. It is a bit all over the place, admittedly. I started with a tech startup, developing an app for… well, essentially optimising delivery routes for small businesses. Did alright with that, sold it a couple of years ago. Now I’m focused on a boutique hotel concept. Trying to find decent locations, sorting out investment… the usual chaos. A hotel! That’s… quite a leap from delivery route optimisation. Though, I suppose both involve logistics in a way. Dorset’s full of small hotels, but nothing particularly…boutique. Mostly just B&Bs catering to ramblers. Exactly! I'm looking for something a bit different. Somewhere with character, a bit of luxury. I’ve even been scouting locations in Greece, but North Cyprus keeps pulling me back. It’s got a vibe, hasn't it? Relaxed, authentic… and the food is incredible. It really is. I’m only here for a week with my sister, a bit of a last-minute escape, really. Needed to get away from the drizzle and the endless school reports. She’s off gallivanting around the ruins, I’m more of a coffee-and-people-watching type. You a regular here, then? Not exactly. This is my third trip this year. I'm trying to get a feel for the area, suss out potential properties. I've spent most of my time driving around the Karpass peninsula, actually. Stunning coastline. But I find these little seaside restaurants are the best place to overhear local gossip – and get an honest opinion on things. Oh, absolutely! The local gossip network is unparalleled. Keeps you grounded. Although, sometimes I think it’s more rumour than fact. Still, it’s preferable to endless school board meetings.

… honestly, I just don’t  get  Liam. He left a half-eaten pot noodle on the coffee table again. A  half-eaten  one! It's like he thinks the cleaning fairies come round every night. Aye, classic Liam. He’s a good lad, but… domestic skills aren't exactly his strong suit, are they? Remember when he tried to do a wash and ended up turning all me white shirts pink? Oh god, don't remind me! I was still finding rogue pink fibres on stuff months later! It’s not just the mess, though. It’s the principle of the thing. We agreed, didn't we? Everyone pulls their weight. I'm studying for my finals, I’m already stressed to the eyeballs, and I’m constantly tidying up after him. I know, love, I know. It's frustrating. Though, to be fair, Sarah's no angel neither. She leaves her books  everywhere . It’s like a paper trail through the living room. You practically need a map to navigate to the telly. Oh, Sarah's different. She’s just… overwhelmed, I think. She's working two jobs to pay for her masters. It’s understandable she’s a bit chaotic. Liam just…doesn’t  see  the mess. He genuinely doesn’t register it, I swear. I pointed it out yesterday, the pot noodle, and he went “Oh, was that still there?” Like he'd completely forgotten! Right, the selective memory thing. Yeah, he does that. Remember when he ‘lost’ his keys for three days and they were on his head? Don't even! That was brilliant, but seriously annoying at the same time. It’s just…I’m starting to feel like a nag. And I hate nagging. I don't want to be ‘the house mum.’ You're not being a nag, you’re being reasonable. And someone needs to say something. Perhaps we should all just sit down and have a proper chat? A bit of a house meeting? I’m free tomorrow evening, after work. That’s a good idea. Actually, a  really  good idea. But I reckon Liam will just nod and agree and then go back to his old ways. He’s brilliant at agreeing with things and then completely failing to act on them. We can lay down some ground rules then. Like, ‘Pot noodles must be disposed of  immediately  after consumption.’ And maybe a chore chart?

Right, that’s  that  done with. Honestly, the queues at Sainsbury’s today were somethin’ else. Felt like everyone in Norwich had the same idea. Oh dear, you look flustered, Arthur. Let me see… Did you manage to get the digestive biscuits? I was really craving a cuppa with a digestive. Digestive biscuits? Of course, I got the digestive biscuits, Margaret! Wouldn’t dream of forgettin’ those. They were right at the front, actually, which was a small mercy. Though they've put the price up again, haven't they? Everything's goin' up! They always do, don’t they? It's the way of the world. Good. Now, did you get the tomatoes for my salad? The ones that aren’t too hard. I hate a hard tomato. Tomatoes… tomatoes… Ah, here we are. Look, I tried my best. They all felt a bit… firm, to be honest. But these seemed the least offensive. You can always leave ‘em a day or two on the windowsill to soften. Hmm. You’re right. They  are  a bit on the pale side. Still, beggars can’t be choosers, as they say. It’s just nice to have a proper salad again. I’m sick of sandwiches. Sandwiches are alright! I ‘ad a nice cheese and pickle on wholemeal. Simple pleasures, eh? Though the young lad at the deli counter tried to charge me extra for the pickle. Extra! For pickle! I told ‘im, I said, “Son, I’ve been buyin’ pickle longer than you’ve been alive!” Oh, Arthur, you and your battles with the supermarket staff. You're a fearsome negotiator. Did he back down? Eventually! After a bit o' back and forth. Said it was a new policy. New policy! It's all about squeezin' every last penny out of us, that’s what it is. Reminds me of old Man Hemmings down the road, always tryin’ to short-change folks at the village shop… Now, now, don't start on old Man Hemmings. That was fifty years ago, Arthur. He’s long gone. Let’s focus on the present. So, everything else alright? Milk, bread, the newspaper… Milk and bread are fine. Newspaper’s depressing as always. Wars and worries. Makes you glad you’re settled in with a cup of tea and a biscuit, doesn’t it? Though young Timothy called earlier, said his car’s packed in again.

Now then, lad, are you sure you’ve packed enough for your trip to London with school? It’s a long way to go and you don't want to be borrowing socks from your mates, do you? Your Gran and Grandad are proper worriers, you know. Yeah, Mum, I’ve got everything. Checked the list three times. Jacket, trainers, phone charger… the essentials. It's just a couple of nights. Don’t fuss. Essentials, he says! In our day, 'essentials' meant a sturdy pair of boots and a packed lunch. No fancy phone chargers needed! Mind you, we weren’t traipsing off to London, were we? Just the seaside at Withernsea. And  that  was an adventure. Aye, Withernsea. Used to get a right good sunburn down there. And the arcades! Spent a fortune on those fruit machines, I did. Never won a thing, mind. You always said that, Dad. But I seem to remember you bringing home a giant teddy bear once… a very wonky-eyed giant teddy bear. Ah, Bess, you’ve got a good memory, you have. Right, wonky-eyed he were, but little Sarah – that’s your cousin – loved him to bits. Gran, did you and Grandad ever go to London? Oh, once. Years and years ago. For the Queen’s Silver Jubilee. It was lovely, but terribly crowded. All those people! And the pigeons… monstrous things, they were. Nearly landed on your Grandad’s head. He wasn’t best pleased. Best pleased? I nearly had a heart attack! Thing was the size of a small dog. Thought it was going to steal my sandwiches. You and your sandwiches, Dad. Always thinking with your stomach. Now, about this trip, I’ve called the B&B and confirmed your room, Leo. They said they’ll keep your luggage safe before check-in. Brilliant, thanks Mum. You're the best. Do they have wifi? That’s the  real  essential. Wifi! What did we do before wifi, eh? We talked to each other. Imagine that! It's a different world now, Mum. Leo needs it for a school project, apparently. Although I suspect a bit of gaming will be involved too. Gaming, eh? What sort of games does this young’un play? Are they all shooting and explosions? Not really, Grandad. I’m into strategy games mostly. Building stuff, managing resources… it's actually quite complicated. Complicated, you say? Sounds a bit like trying to balance the household budget then!

Right, so I’m officially regretting that extra portion of chips last night. My trousers are feeling… snug. You lot all look remarkably unaffected, though. Chips are  always  worth it, mate. You just gotta resign yourself to the consequences. I’ve been hitting the gym a bit harder lately, seems to be buffering the damage, at least. Did you see that new fitness tracker everyone's banging on about? The ‘Halo Band’ or something? Oh god, don't even  start  on the fitness trackers. My cousin, Leo, got one.
