Edinburgh’s good, but feels a bit…close, doesn’t it? I was lookin’ at Thailand. Absolute madness, I know. Just escapin’ the Christmas madness. You two always go all-in, don't you? Fairy lights, the works... Well, someone’s gotta keep the tradition alive! Mum would have a fit if we didn’t. Last year she nearly cried when the fairy lights didn't twinkle properly. Said it wasn't Christmas without a perfectly illuminated grotto. She’s incorrigible! Still, Christmas at home is nice. Even with the over-the-top decorations. I’m more worried about what I’m gonna do with all my free time at uni. Everyone says it’s just constant work. That's what they tell ya. You’ll have parties, though. Loads of ‘em. Just watch your wallet. And don't believe everything people tell you, alright? Everyone's putting on a show, especially at uni. He's right, actually. It’s a bit of a performance. I miss the simplicity of Whitehaven sometimes, y’know?

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork for that ethics application nearly did me in. Three revisions! Three! You’d think after a Masters they’d trust me to know what ‘informed consent’  means  by now. Anyway, how are  you  holding up? Still drowning in alumni small talk? Drowning is putting it mildly. It's mostly people trying to work out what I  actually  do. “So, you…administer the research?” is the common refrain, delivered with a politely confused expression. It’s like they expect me to be filing things. Which, okay, sometimes I  do  file things, but it’s not all I do! How’s the actual research going, though? Anything exciting bubbling under the surface, apart from ethical nightmares? It's alright. We're finally getting some interesting data back from the dialect levelling study. Apparently, the young 'uns in Norfolk are adopting features from the London accent way faster than we predicted. It's… depressing, honestly. Like watching a bit of linguistic heritage just  fade . But fascinating, of course. This is why I do it, I suppose. Though I’m starting to dream in IPA symbols. Oh, that  is  interesting! And depressing, you’re right. It’s weird to think how quickly things change. I’ve been thinking about a holiday, actually, and it got me wondering… Have you ever been anywhere really… linguistically different? Like, not just France or Spain, but somewhere that really throws your ears for a loop? Ooh, good question. I did a summer volunteering thing in Romania after uni – didn’t do any specific linguistic work, sadly, just building stuff with Habitat for Humanity – but the Romanian was  wild . So different from anything I’d encountered before. The verb conjugations alone… My brain genuinely hurt trying to follow a basic conversation. It’s made me proper appreciate the relatively straightforward structure of English, for once. What about you? Any exotic linguistic adventures? Not quite as adventurous as Romania! I went to Iceland a couple of years ago. It’s just… ancient. Like, truly ancient. It’s barely changed in centuries, which is amazing. But trying to pronounce anything felt like trying to disassemble a bomb. And the place names! Unpronounceable. My mum kept asking me to say “Kirkjufell” and I just gave up. She was convinced I was making it up. Oh, I can imagine! Icelandic is a beast. It feels like it’s deliberately designed to foil English speakers.

…and honestly, the reading list for ‘Postcolonial Literature’ is  criminal . It's like Professor Davies actively  wants  us to fail. Five novels, three critical theory texts, and a bunch of articles… all due in two weeks. It's reet daft, innit? Aye, sounds about right for Davies. He's a proper academic, that one. Thinks suffering builds character, probably. Are you actually getting through it, or just… staring at the pages hoping something will osmosis into your brain? Mostly the staring, if I’m being honest. I got about fifty pages into Said’s  Orientalism  and I just… lost the will to live. It’s all very important and insightful, I'm sure, but it's draining the life outta me. You look far too relaxed for someone who’s supposed to be writing his thesis. Relaxed is a strong word. Strategically pausing. I had a particularly brutal session with the data this morning. Thankfully, managed to get a decent chunk done before my back started screaming. Which reminds me… I booked us a couples massage for Saturday. You deserve it after all this university stress. Ooh, you are a star! Seriously, that’s brilliant. My shoulders are permanently hunched from hunching over books. Proper knots in ‘em. A massage sounds like absolute heaven. Is it that new place near the market, ‘Serenity Now’? I heard good things. Aye, that’s the one. Apparently, they do hot stone massage. You’ll be a puddle by the end of it. I was thinking we could go for a proper dinner afterwards too. Celebrate surviving another week. Now  that’s  a plan. Though surviving a week of Davies’ lectures is a celebration in itself. Yesterday he spent twenty minutes dissecting a single semicolon. A  semicolon , for crying out loud! Oh, he is a special breed, isn’t he? Remember when he went on that tangent about the socio-political implications of punctuation in Victorian novels? It went on for a full hour. Don’t even remind me. I was sketching little caricatures of him with a ridiculously oversized quill pen. It's just… it's not engaging, you know? Like, I  want  to learn, I  am  interested in the subject, but he makes it so… dry. It's all theory and no actual, you know, talking about the stories themselves. I get that. It’s the same with some of my supervisors. They get so lost in the methodology they forget the actual point of the research.

…and honestly, the kids were  brilliant  with the pastry. A bit messy, naturally, but they really got stuck in. Leo even tried to make a little flag on top of his pie. It looked… abstract. Abstract is a polite word, love. More like a crumbled disaster. Still, effort counts for everything, doesn't it? This is a cracking pie, by the way. You’ve outdone yourself, Sarah. It  is  good, Sarah. Really. Though I maintain apple and blackberry is still the superior combination. You know I do. Oh, here we go again, Margaret! Cherry is a classic for a reason. It’s brighter, more summery. It feels… optimistic. Optimistic pie. I like that. We could all do with a bit of optimistic pie these days. Have you seen the news about Calais? Absolutely dreadful. Those poor people. It’s heartbreaking, isn’t it? And the politicians just bicker. Honestly, you'd think they could find some common ground to help, but no. It’s all about point-scoring. I was explaining it to my Year 6s today, in a very carefully worded way, obviously. It’s so difficult to talk to children about things like that. I tried to avoid it with my class, to be honest. They’re only Year 3. But little Ethan asked about ‘the people trying to get into England’ after seeing something on his mum’s phone. It’s creeping into their awareness, even at that age. I just talked about helping people who are having a hard time, generally. Sounds sensible. It’s a complicated issue, isn’t it? And all the talk of sending people to Rwanda… it feels so… inhuman. I remember when we had those boatloads arriving back in the nineties. Different scale, perhaps, but the underlying desperation was the same. It’s just… shifting the problem elsewhere and pretending it doesn't exist. It doesn't solve anything. Anyway, let's not ruin a lovely lunch talking about all that. How’s your sister, Margaret? Did she manage to get the results back from her scan? She did. Thankfully, it’s nothing serious. A bit of arthritis flaring up, which is what she suspected. She’s relieved, naturally. We were all on tenterhooks. She’s talking about coming to stay for a few days next month. That's good news. She’ll enjoy a bit of peace and quiet here. This house is always a bit of a haven, isn't it?

…and honestly, the tiling is just  awful . Absolutely dreadful. I mean, I knew Derek wasn’t a master craftsman, but I didn’t realise ‘enthusiastic amateur’ was his highest qualification. It's all slightly wonky, you see. Just…off. Derek, eh? Always a gamble, taking on a friend’s favour. I warned you about him, didn't I? Said he was better with a pint in hand than a trowel. You did, you did. I thought, “Oh, he’s a good bloke, how bad can it be?” Famous last words, John. Famous last words. It’s the bathroom, of course, the one room where shoddy workmanship is instantly, brutally obvious. Aye, the bathroom. The proving ground of any DIY attempt. My wife, Margaret, she insisted on doing the painting in ours last year. Thought she could save a bit of money. Ended up looking like a toddler had attacked it with a brush. Oh dear. My wife, Amelia, she’s completely hands-off when it comes to these things. She says she’s ‘artistically challenged’ and refuses to risk a domestic incident. She just wants it  done , and done properly. Which is proving… expensive. I’m practically funding the entire plumbing and tiling industry single-handedly. Tell me about it. We’re thinking of tackling the kitchen next. It's been on the cards for five years now, but every time I start looking at quotes, I feel a cold sweat come on. These kitchen fitters… they speak a different language, don’t they? ‘Soft close mechanisms’, ‘induction hobs’, ‘quartz worktops’… it’s all just jargon to justify an enormous bill. Precisely! And they all claim to be “fully insured and CRB checked,” yet when something goes wrong, they vanish faster than smoke. I had a plumber once, a chap called Kevin, vanished mid-job with my deposit. Left me with a half-installed sink and a rather large hole in the wall. Kevin, eh? Sounds charming. We had a similar experience with an electrician. Said he was an expert in rewiring old houses. Turned out his expertise extended only to taking your money! Still, I suppose it gives you something to complain about over coffee with colleagues. That’s certainly true. Honestly, John, finding a reliable tradesperson is harder than getting published these days. Speaking of which, did you see Professor Davies’ latest article in  The Journal ? Dreadful stuff. Completely missed the nuance of the post-structuralist argument.

Jaysus, that was a good curry, wasn’t it? Bit milder than I usually make, mind you. Didn’t want to blow young Leo’s head off. It  is  good, Mr. O’Connell. Though, I reckon a bit more chilli wouldn’t hurt. My mum makes hers properly spicy. Oh, don’t start him off, Liam. He’ll be demanding ghost peppers next. Honestly, you'd think he was raised on fire. And Leo, darling, no playing with your food. More! More!  Shiny!  No shiny for you, lad. That’s not for eating. Honestly, the things he tries to ingest… remember that time he tried to eat a screw? Don’t remind me. I nearly had a heart attack. It’s like he thinks metal is a delicacy. Speaking of delicacies, Liam, you were telling me about this…horrible history science book you're reading for school? It’s called ‘Horrible Science’ actually, and it’s brilliant! This one’s about the human body. Did you know your stomach acid can dissolve metal? That’s why he tries to eat it, probably! He thinks his stomach’s a super-power! Well, that’s a clever bit of justification for a toddler’s bad habits. Stomach acid doesn’t dissolve  everything , mind. And don't be giving him ideas. It’s rather alarming what they put in those books, isn’t it? Though, it’s clearly working. He’s absorbing  something . It also says you can feel pain because of tiny little bits in your nerves. Like…little signals. But what if you didn’t have signals? Could you still, like,  know  you were hurt? Now you're getting into some proper philosophical territory, son. That’s a question that's been bothering thinkers for centuries. It’s a bit beyond curry and bedtime, I reckon. Speaking of bedtime, what about Leo’s birthday next week? Have you any ideas, Liam? I was thinking the park, maybe? They're having that event with the bouncy castle and face painting. The park sounds grand. It’s a good shout. Though I was also thinking maybe a small gathering down at the pub, just family. A quiet pint, a bit of cake… A pub? Can  I  come? Absolutely not. You’re eleven, darling. That’s a conversation for another time. We’ll stick to the bouncy castle. Alright, alright. Park it is. Though, I'm still thinking I need to find a safe place to stick the birthday money.

…and she were absolutely  furious . Proper red in the face, she was. Said young Timmy ‘ad deliberately smeared pumpkin guts all over Mrs. Higgins’ prize-winning begonias. Honestly, the cheek of it! Though, I say, a bit of pumpkin never ‘urt anyone. Reminds me of Halloweens when I were a lad. Not like this modern carry-on, mind. Just a turnip lantern and a bit of mischief. Oh, Arthur, you and your stories! Mrs. Higgins  loved  those begonias. She entered them in the village show every year. But Timmy’s a good lad, just… energetic. Is Lily excited about Halloween this year? She didn’t say much last time I saw her. Yeah, kinda. It’s not as big a deal when you get older, is it? Everyone just expects you to be “too cool” for trick-or-treating. I might go with some friends, but mostly I’m just hoping for good sweets. It is a bit of a changing landscape, isn’t it? When I was teaching primary, it was always a frenzy of costumes and sugar-fueled mayhem. Now, the older ones are more interested in the spooky parties, the jump scares… it’s all become a bit commercialized, I think. How’s school going, Lily? Anything exciting happening? It's okay. History's boring. Mr. Davies just  reads  at us. I wish he'd make it more… interesting. We're doing the Tudors right now, and it’s all dates and kings. It’s not like seeing it, you know? Tudors, eh? Now there's a time! All that bother with ‘Enry the Eighth and his wives. Proper scandalous, that were. Costessey weren’t much different back then, I reckon. Just smaller. Fewer tractors, more horses. You should talk to your History teacher, dear. Maybe suggest some field trips? Or even just suggest he tell more stories. That’s what always captivated  me  in school - the storytelling. That’s excellent advice, Margaret. Lily, don’t be afraid to speak up. Teachers want to make the subject engaging, but they sometimes need a bit of prompting. And you’re right about seeing it. I try to incorporate more visuals, more immersive activities in my lessons. It makes all the difference. Have you been to any of the historical sites around Norwich? We went to the castle once, ages ago. It was alright. But I’d rather go horse-riding.

Honestly, this traffic is  mental . I thought leaving at 8am would avoid the worst of it, but look at this queue! It's barely moved in the last twenty minutes. Are we ever going to get to the steam fair? Dorset Steam Fair. Always a gamble, this. Remember when we came ten years ago? Same thing, miles and miles of cars. Though, I reckon it’s worse now, innit? More people about. Seems everyone’s got a car these days. It’s the school holidays, Dad. Bound to be busier. And everyone wants a bit of nostalgia, don’t they? Besides, it’s a lovely day for it. Just a shame about the standstill. Still, better than being stuck inside. Speaking of which, have you heard anything more about Gran’s housing situation? Not really. Mum’s been dealing with most of it. She said the council are being…difficult. Something about ‘suitable alternatives’ being limited. It’s just awful, really. She’s been at that flat for forty years, and they want her to move out because they’re ‘redeveloping’ the area. Redeveloping! That’s a fancy word for putting up expensive flats that no one local can afford. It’s the same everywhere, innit? London’s become a joke. Can’t even recognise the place anymore. All glass and steel, and nobody with a friendly face. They used to build council houses, proper homes for people, you know? They should. Gran deserves somewhere comfortable and near her doctors. She doesn’t  need  a fancy redevelopment. She needs somewhere safe and accessible. And I’m worried about the waiting list. Mum said it’s years long for anything decent. Mum mentioned something about sheltered housing, but Gran’s fiercely independent. She doesn’t want to be ‘put away’ as she calls it. She’s convinced they'll just forget about her in one of those places. Understandable, that. My sister, bless her, ended up in one. Nice enough place, but she hated it. Said it felt like a hospital. And the food! She said it were all mush. Still, it did take the pressure off her son, I suppose. He was workin' all hours just to keep her afloat. Exactly. That's what Mum's struggling with. She works full-time, and trying to sort Gran’s housing  and  her appointments is exhausting. Actually, talking of appointments… does anyone know if they have disabled parking at the steam fair?

…and honestly, the slugs were  brutal  last year. Absolutely decimated the hostas. I'm thinking this year, a proper barrier. Copper tape, maybe? Though I heard it needs replacing every season. It's just… exhausting, isn't it? Trying to outsmart nature. Oh, slugs are the bane of my existence! I tried the beer traps, but honestly, they just seemed to  enjoy  the little pub I'd set up for them. Copper tape is a good shout, but yeah, the cost does add up. Have you considered nematodes? Apparently, they’re pretty effective and a more long-term solution. Nematodes? No, haven't looked into those. Are they… complicated? I'm fairly new to all this serious gardening, you see. My nan always had a garden, and I helped a bit, but it was mostly deadheading roses and picking runner beans. This allotment thing feels…proper. Not at all! They’re microscopic worms that eat the slugs. You mix them with water and pour them on. It sounds a bit sci-fi, but it works. You can get them online, pretty easily. Speaking of proper, you’re right to feel like this is a step up from a few pots on a balcony. It’s a commitment. Which reminds me - how’s the plot looking? Have you cleared it yet? Mostly! There was a shocking amount of bindweed, though. Seriously, it was like it was  trying  to strangle everything. Took me a whole weekend just to get the bulk of it out. I’ve got a rotovator on loan from old Mr. Henderson next door. Going to give it a good going over next week, weather permitting. You’ve already started, haven’t you? I saw pictures on Facebook - looked amazing! I have, yeah. I'm a bit further along, I suppose. Being organized is kind of my job, so it spilled over. I’ve got the raised beds built, and I’m starting seeds indoors. Thinking of a ‘three sisters’ planting this year – maize, beans, and squash. Apparently, it’s really good for the soil. Have you planned what you're going to grow at all? Ooh, 'Three Sisters'! That sounds…very posh. I'm aiming for practical, I think. Loads of tomatoes, definitely. And courgettes – everyone always has too many courgettes, but I love them. Possibly some lettuce and spinach, if I can keep the pests off. I'd like to try growing potatoes, but I’m a bit intimidated.

Right, so I’m officially stressing. Like, proper stressing. Not just ‘oh, uni’s looming’ stressing, but actual ‘I’ve realised I have absolutely no clue what I’m doing with my life’ stressing. Sounds about right for late August, doesn’t it? You're not alone, love. Everyone’s having a quarter-life crisis before they even  have  a life, practically. What’s brought on this particular wave of existential dread? Is it Doncaster finally getting to you? Just kidding!… mostly. No, Doncaster's alright actually. It’s… well, it’s Maisie. She hasn’t replied to any of my texts since Saturday. And Saturday was just…fine. We went to that new vintage shop, had chips by the canal, the usual. Nothing weird happened. Now she’s just gone radio silent. Maisie? Oh, no. That  is  weird. She’s usually glued to her phone. Is it possible she’s just really busy with family stuff? Going away for the weekend, something like that? I thought that, but I checked her Instagram. She posted a story yesterday – just a picture of her cat, but still! A cat picture implies she’s  capable  of using a phone. It feels… deliberate, y’know? Like she’s avoiding me. Hmm. That does sound a bit dodgy. You two been alright lately? No little arguments or anything? Sometimes things fester, and people just need space to process, but they’re rubbish at communicating it. Not really. We had that thing last month about Leo – she thought I was spending too much time with him, which was silly. He’s just… friendly! But we talked it out, or I thought we had. Maybe she’s still hung up on that? It's just... she was so excited about coming to Leeds with me. We planned everything! The halls, the societies, even which supermarket does the best pasta. Oh, the supermarket planning is serious business. Right, okay. Look, don’t jump to conclusions. She might be having a horrible time with something completely unrelated. But… just in case, maybe try ringing her? A phone call can sometimes get a response when texts fail. I’ve thought about it, but I’m scared of sounding needy. Or worse, annoying. What if it  is  nothing and I’ve made it a massive drama? I'm rubbish at confrontation. You’re not annoying, you’re a caring friend! And honestly, sometimes a little “slightly worried, checkin’ in” vibe is exactly what people need.

Right, right, right… nearly got 'im. Come on, you daft bugger! Oh, and seriously, Beth, you wouldn’t  believe  the queues down at the library today. Absolute chaos. Needed a textbook for History, ended up waiting forty minutes just to get to the desk. Forty minutes? Blimey. That’s rough, lad. I just used the online resources, saved myself a trip. History, eh? Still struggling with the Tudors then? Honestly, it’s all just kings and queens nicking each other's wives, isn't it? Honestly, you two. It’s like listening to my nan and grandad bicker. Liam, you’re getting absolutely decimated. And Beth, online resources  are  a lifesaver, you're a smart cookie. Speaking of decimating, have you guys seen the new trailer for 'Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty'? Looks insane. Insane is an understatement, mate. The ray tracing… the story… it’s gonna be a proper graphical showcase. Though, honestly, I'm still working through the base game. It took ages to finally get a decent rig to run it properly. Remember when I was bragging about my graphics card last year? Turns out it was completely mid. Ugh! Got sniped! Right, that's it. I'm blaming the lag. And you, Raj, distracting me with talk of cyberpunks! Honestly. And yeah, I remember your graphics card debacle, Danny. You were proper red-faced about that one. Serves you right, Danny. All that boasting! But seriously, ‘Phantom Liberty’ looks tempting. Though my student loan account is currently weeping softly in the corner. Been needing new trainers for weeks, but games always win, don't they? Always. Trainers are a luxury. Digital immersion is a  necessity . Honestly, I’m thinking of getting one of those curved monitors. Complete sensory overload. It'll be like actually  being  in Night City. You know, I was talking to my cousin back in Manila, and he’s never even  heard  of Cyberpunk. Can you imagine? No way! He's been living under a rock. Manila's a massive gaming hub, isn't it? Loads of internet cafes and stuff. My mate’s auntie went there on holiday last year, said it was buzzing. Do they get all the newest releases out there straight away, though? Probably not right away, eh? Importing games must be a nightmare. Speaking of nightmares, I’m going to try this again. Less chat, more headshots. Right.

…Honestly, Doreen and I, back in ’78, look at us! Hair like… well, like a couple of startled scarecrows. Though she always said hers was deliberate. “Voluminous, Patricia,  voluminous !” she’d say. Remember Doreen? You met her a couple of times. Vaguely, yeah. The one with the…bright clothes? And a really booming laugh? I think I remember her dragging you onto the dance floor at Auntie Maggie’s 80th. Dragging is a polite word for it, love. Manhandled is more like it. But that was Doreen. Full of life. Not like some of the…well, the quieter ones we knew. Speaking of which, have you heard from Sarah lately? Haven't seen her name pop up on Facebook in ages. I messaged her last week, actually. She’s, um… she’s been a bit off-grid. Said she’s been really into old films. Proper, classic cinema. Like,  Casablanca  and stuff. Apparently, she’s joined a film society. A film society? Good Lord. Sarah? The girl who used to claim anything before the 90s was “boring and black and white”? That's a turn-up for the books. What brought that on, d’you reckon? She said she was feeling a bit… overstimulated with everything being  now, now, now . Social media, news cycles, work… She wanted something slower paced, more thoughtful. She saw  Casablanca  at a screening and it just…clicked, apparently. Hmm. Sounds sensible. Though I can’t say I’ve ever understood the appeal of those old films myself. Give me a good thriller any day. Something with a twist. Have you seen that new one,  The Silent Witness ? The one everyone’s talking about? Oh, yeah! I saw it last weekend with Ben. It was pretty good, kept you guessing. Though the ending was a bit… convenient, wasn’t it? Like they just needed to wrap things up quickly. Convenient! That’s putting it mildly. It felt like they’d written themselves into a corner and just threw in a random suspect. I tell you what, they don't make 'em like Hitchcock.  Psycho . Now  that’s  a thriller. You don’t get twists like that anymore. True. Though, thinking about it, Sarah was saying some of the older films had incredibly complex narratives, even if the special effects were… well, lacking. She was telling me about  Citizen Kane  – apparently, the camera work was revolutionary for its time.

…and honestly, the whole interview process was just  bizarre . They kept asking me about my ‘methodology’ for, and I quote, “eliciting naturalistic language data.” Like, I just… chat to people! Is that not methodology enough?      Oh, academia. Always needing to make things sound fancier than they are. “Naturalistic language data.” Sounds like you’re studying squirrels in a wood, not people’s everyday conversations. How’d you answer?      I tried to be diplomatic. Said something about a ‘flexible, ecologically valid approach’… which basically means I don’t force anyone to say anything they don’t want to. They didn't seem that impressed. Did you ever have anything like that when you were editing? Things being overly complicated for the sake of it?      All. The. Time. Especially with freelance clients. You’d get these briefs that were just… layers of unnecessary jargon. And then they’d be disappointed when you  clarified  things! Like, no, I can’t magically implement ‘synergistic content streams’, just tell me what you want the article to say! Anyway, enough work moaning. Tell me about this spa visit you were going on with Mum. Was it good?      Oh, it was  heaven . Honestly, exactly what I needed after that interview stress. Mum’s obsessed with those hot stone massages, apparently it realigns your chakras or something. I just went for a facial and slept for most of it. Bliss. Though, Mum insisted on making conversation with the therapist about…  The Undateables .      Oh, no! Mum and her  The Undateables  obsession! She’s completely invested, isn't she? She’s always analysing their dating strategies.      It’s a weekly thing. She’ll call me afterwards, dissecting every awkward moment. “She really should have mentioned her collection of porcelain dolls sooner, don’t you think?” Honestly. The poor therapist looked terrified.      Anyone fancy a biscuit? Digestive or chocolate? Heard you two chatting away. Sounds… intense.      Chocolate for me, please! And thank you. Intense is Mum's default setting when it comes to reality TV, especially that show. It’s a family tradition, really.      Thanks, love. It  is  intense. It’s just… sometimes I think she wants to be a relationship guru! She’s got very strong opinions. Speaking of strong opinions, have you seen that new magazine – ‘Modern Wellbeing’? It’s full of these articles about ‘self-care’ which mostly just involve spending a fortune on crystals and scented candles.      Oh, I flicked through it at the newsagent.

…and honestly, the manual was written by someone who clearly  hasn’t  ever actually  used  a washing machine. “Ensure optimal fabric care by selecting the ‘Delicates – Lunar Cycle’ setting.” Lunar Cycle?! What even  is  a Lunar Cycle wash? Is it supposed to mimic the moon’s gravitational pull on your knickers? You and technology, eh? It probably just means a really gentle spin. Though 'Lunar Cycle' does sound a bit… esoteric, doesn’t it? Is it still doing that weird thumping noise? I thought you said you’d had a look. I  did  have a look! I poked around, I tightened a few things, I even consulted a YouTube tutorial featuring a bloke with a questionable beard and a lot of tools. It worked for about two washes, then it started sounding like a herd of elephants tap-dancing inside it again. I swear, that machine is actively mocking me. Right. Okay. Elephants tap-dancing. That’s…concerning. Look, I’ll have a proper go at it tomorrow. I had a slightly less disastrous experience fixing my Nan’s dishwasher last month, maybe some of that knowledge is transferable. What are we having for tea, by the way? Smells good. It’s a hopeful attempt at a lentil shepherd’s pie. My mum’s recipe. Apparently, it’s “proper comfort food.” I’m not convinced lentils can  be  comforting, but we'll see. It needs tasting, obviously. Your mum makes a cracking shepherd’s pie, lentil or otherwise. She’s a wizard in the kitchen. Speaking of family, have you managed to get hold of your sister? I know you were trying to call her about the holiday. Aye, left her a message. She's probably swamped with work. She’s convinced she has to single-handedly save the NHS right now. Bless her, she’s always been dramatic. Wants to know if we can all go to the Lake District again. Remember last time? The torrential rain, the sheep blocking the road… Vaguely… mostly I remember the pub with the roaring fire and the phenomenal sticky toffee pudding. And you nearly falling in a bog. I did  not  nearly fall in a bog! I slipped! There's a difference! And the pudding was good, I’ll grant you, but the whole trip felt like a scene out of a particularly bleak British film. Have you seen anything good lately? I’m needing a cinematic escape from the impending washing machine doom.

…and honestly, the estate agent was  insisting  that house prices here are “going to boom.” Boom! In Hunsonby? I nearly choked on my tea. It's lovely, don’t get me wrong, but it’s not exactly Knightsbridge. Boom, is it? They say that everywhere, love. It's their job to say that. They get commission, don't they? Remember when we were looking near Basingstoke? “Investment opportunity,” they said. Ends up the whole area flooded two winters later. Basingstoke…God, that was a nightmare. All those identikit houses. And the traffic. Utterly soul-destroying. No wonder you were glad to get back up north, Moira. Though, Hunsonby  is …rural. Rural is good, Arthur! Rural is peace and quiet. After thirty years of marking trigonometry papers, I’m valuing peace and quiet above all else. Besides, it’s affordable. Relatively. That’s the key, isn’t it? We wouldn’t have got half this garden down south for what we paid. True. It’s just… the disparity is insane. My sister keeps moaning she can’t afford a shoe box in Guildford, and we’ve got a three-bedroom cottage with a garden big enough to lose a small child in. And it's not like wages are proportionally better down south, is it? Exactly! And it’s not just the wages. It's everything. The cost of a pint of milk, a loaf of bread… It's all inflated. And for what? To be closer to the “opportunity”? Most of that opportunity is just shuffling paper in a glass tower. That’s what I always said. All that hustle and bustle, and for what? Stress, mostly. Remember Mrs. Henderson? From the maths department? Drove herself into the ground trying to climb the ladder, ended up miserable and having to take early retirement anyway. Speaking of things driving people to early retirement…did you both see that documentary about the Volkswagen emissions scandal again? It was on Channel 4 last night. Honestly, the sheer  scale  of the deception is astonishing. Oh, that. Yes. Utterly disgraceful. Deliberately cheating on emissions tests... putting out more pollutants than they admitted. It makes you wonder what else companies are getting away with. And the impact on the environment! It’s horrific. And the way they tried to justify it, too. “Unforeseen technical issues.” Give us a break! It was a calculated decision to save money, plain and simple.

…No, honestly, Arthur, you didn’t  need  to tell young Timmy about the state of our finances. Honestly! The boy’s barely ten, what’s he going to do with that information? Worry himself sick? Well, I didn't  tell  him, precisely. He asked, didn't he? About the holiday, about whether we could go to Skegness again this year. I just… explained things were a bit tight. A bit. It weren’t like I laid out all the pension statements, Harold. You explained “a bit tight” to a ten-year-old and he came to  me  nearly in tears, saying Grandpa Arthur said they might not be able to afford a summer holiday  ever  again! Honestly, Arthur, you have a knack for upsetting people. It’s a gift, I tell you, a gift! Though I wish it weren't. I just... I get frustrated. We worked hard, you know? I spent years designing bridges, making sure they didn't fall down. And for what? This? Scrabbling around, worrying about every penny. Now, now, Harold. Don’t start on that again. Bridges is a worthy job. And you were good at it. It’s just… things changed. Pensions aren’t what they used to be, and… well, we didn't exactly plan for living this long, did we? That’s a bit harsh, Arthur. And you know that's not true. You both always said you wanted to see the grandchildren grow up. I did, yes. But I envisioned a slightly… more comfortable retirement. Not one where we have to consider selling the house just to cover repairs. Have you seen those new developments going up near the old airfield? They're putting up rabbit hutches for a fortune! They are a bit dear, aren't they? Small gardens, all crammed in. No room to swing a cat, let alone grow a vegetable patch. And they’re building them on the best farmland! It's scandalous. Remember Old Man Hemmings' fields? Glorious wheat he grew… now it’s all concrete. Exactly! It’s all about profit, isn’t it? Nobody cares about a bit of green space anymore. And the price of everything keeps going up. Have you seen the electricity bill this month? Makes you want to just stay in bed all day. Don't even mention it. I've been trying to get to grips with that new smart meter thing, and it’s driving me round the bend.

Honestly, this Biology essay is killing me. “Explain the evolutionary advantages of altruism.” Like, seriously? It just feels…pointless. Why would anyone  choose  to disadvantage themselves for someone else? It goes against everything. Tell me about it. Mine’s on genetic drift. Sounds cool, right? It’s literally just…random chance. How am I supposed to write two thousand words on  randomness ? I’ve spent the last hour staring at a picture of peppered moths. You guys are lucky. I’ve got Mr. Davies for History and he’s set us a project on the historical roots of modern feminism. It’s… a lot. And half the class are just making jokes about it. Oh,  those  guys. Still stuck in the Stone Age, are they? Honestly, some people just can’t handle anything that questions the status quo. But feminism is fascinating, actually. It's not just about hating men, you know? No, obviously. It's about equality. Though, trying to explain that to Ben and Tom… it's like talking to a brick wall. They were going on about how girls are too emotional to be leaders. Ugh. Classic. I swear, they think biology  explains  sexism. Like, “Oh, testosterone makes men dominant, therefore it’s natural.” They use ‘science’ to justify being rubbish people. Exactly! It’s frustrating. I was reading this article about how evolutionary psychology has been used to excuse discriminatory behaviour and it was…mind-blowing. How easily things can be twisted. It's weaponized pseudo-science, that’s what it is. They cherry-pick stuff to fit their pre-existing biases. Remember that video that went viral last week, the one with the guy explaining why men are inherently better at STEM? Oh god,  that  one. The comments section was a disaster. Just endless arguments and…well, you know. It got taken down pretty quickly though, thankfully. But it's still out there somewhere. The internet never forgets. It’s terrifying how quickly stuff like that spreads. It's like, one person says something completely bonkers, and suddenly everyone’s parroting it. Speaking of viral videos, did you see that dog trying to catch snowflakes? It's pure gold. No! Send me the link! We  need  a distraction from all this heavy stuff. It feels like every conversation turns into a debate about something world-changingly important. It’s because we’re actually thinking about this stuff, aren’t we?

Honestly, this recovery is taking  ages . I thought by now I’d be back to full pelt. Still aching, still tired… Dr. Sharma keeps saying it’s normal post-op, but “normal” is exhausting! Oh, love, you are looking a bit peaky still. Are you taking all your tablets, religiously? Don't skip any, even when you feel a tiny bit better. My Maureen never listens, and then she's back to square one with her arthritis. Aye, tablets are important. Though I swear they give you one problem to fix another! Remember when they put old Arthur on that water pill? He was glued to the loo for a week! Arthur and his bladder! That was a sight. No, you listen to the doctor, love. They know what they're doing. Though I always did say they over-prescribe these days. It's the infection risk, isn't it? That's what worries me. They keep checking for signs, and I’m just constantly thinking about it. My friend, Penelope, had a terrible post-op infection, ended up back in hospital for a week. Oh, don't even  mention  infections. Gives me the shivers. You need to build your strength up, that's what you need. Have you thought about acupuncture? Old Mrs. Higgins swears by it. Said it helped her after her hip replacement. Acupuncture? Hmm. I’m a bit… squeamish with needles. Nonsense! It doesn’t hurt. It's just a little prick. And it works wonders. I had it for my back, years ago, when I was helping your grandfather with the garden. Bent double for a week I was. Your grandfather was a strong man, though. Just a bit stubborn. Like you, actually. Always trying to do things yourself. Guilty as charged. Speaking of stubborn, has anyone heard from Daniel? He was supposed to come today, but no sign. He promised to help me with the car before its MOT. New tyres are needed, apparently. A small fortune! He called me yesterday, said he was stuck in London. Something about a big rugby match and a friend needing a lift. Typical Daniel! Always prioritising a game over his family. He gets that from his father, bless him. Always with the rugby. Never understood the appeal, myself. Give me a good game of bowls any day. Bowls is for old ladies, Mildred! Rugby’s a proper sport!

…and so, the ships would be absolutely packed, Elsie. Imagine trying to fit as many people as possible into, well, not even a proper room, but a hold of a ship. No space to sit, barely space to breathe. And they were chained together. Chained? Like… like a dog on a lead? A bit like that, love, but much, much worse. Imagine not being able to move your arms or legs properly, having to go to the toilet where you are, and being stuck like that for  weeks . Sometimes months. That’s awful! Why? Why would people DO that? That’s a really good question, Leo. It’s a very difficult thing to understand. People did it because they wanted to make money. They forced people from Africa to go to America and work on farms, growing things like cotton and tobacco. They didn’t pay them, they treated them terribly, and they thought they could just…take advantage of them. It’s called slavery. But that’s not fair! My teacher says sharing is caring. You are absolutely right, Elsie. It’s  completely  unfair. And that’s why it was so wrong. They didn’t see those people as… people. They saw them as things to be used. It took a long, long time and a lot of brave people fighting for it to be made illegal. Did they fight with swords? Like pirates? Sometimes they did fight, Leo. But it wasn’t always with swords. Sometimes they fought with words, writing letters, making speeches, and trying to convince people that slavery was wrong. Some people even helped slaves escape to freedom on a secret route called the Underground Railroad. Underground? Like a train? But under the ground? Sort of! It wasn’t a  real  railroad with trains, it was a network of secret routes and safe houses. People who believed slavery was wrong would hide slaves in their homes and help them travel north to places where slavery was illegal. It was very dangerous, but they were incredibly brave. Was it like in the war? People fighting for what’s right? In some ways, yes. Wars are often about fighting for what people believe in, although sometimes they are about other things too. Wars are incredibly sad, though. So many people get hurt or even die. Like in the Second World War, your Great-Grandpa George fought in that.

Honestly, I’m still reeling from that  Great British Bake Off  final. Matty deserved to win, didn’t he? Absolute artistry, that fella. Though Dan was a close second, bless him. You and your baking shows, Carol. It’s a bit… intense, isn’t it? All that precision. Give me a good detective drama any day. Have you started the new  Shetland  yet? Douglas Henshall’s departure left a bit of a hole, mind you.  Shetland  is good, Dad! Though I'm currently obsessed with that true crime documentary on Netflix about the con artist. It’s absolutely bonkers. The audacity of some people! Con artists, eh? There’s one living just around the corner from us, I reckon. Old Mrs. Higgins. Always asking for help with her garden, then conveniently ‘forgets’ to pay the lad who does it. Ah, Gladys Higgins. Now there’s a character. Used to come into the pub all the time, complaining about everything and everyone. Said my gravy was too thin once.  Too thin!  After forty years of making gravy! Oh, Arthur, you and your gravy! Still going on about that, are you? Anyway, speaking of neighbours, did you hear about the Millers' cat, Whiskers? Apparently, he’s gone missing. Poor things are distraught. No way! That fluffy ginger thing? He was always sunbathing on their car. It's awful when pets go missing. I saw a post on the local Facebook group. Everyone’s sharing it. It is worrying. That main road near them is so busy. Hopefully, he's just found a cosy shed somewhere. Remember when Buster ran off for three days? We were beside ourselves. Buster just wanted a bit of peace and quiet away from all the chaos, if I remember rightly. He was a smart dog, that one. He knew when things were getting a bit too lively with the grandkids. He did. Good old Buster. We haven’t had a dog since, have we? Too much responsibility at our age. Though a little Jack Russell running around might be nice... Arthur! Don’t even  think  about it. You barely manage to look after yourself, let alone a dog! Honestly, though, it's been quiet since Buster. Maybe too quiet. Grandma, you’re so dramatic! But I get it. It's nice to have a furry friend. I've been thinking about booking a holiday, actually. Somewhere with a beach.

Right, operation ‘Unload the Dishwasher’ is a go. Leo, darling, could you tackle the glasses? And Maisie, plates are all yours. Though, honestly, someone – and I’m looking at  you , Leo – seems to think leaving jam smeared on everything is a valid art form. But it  is  art, Mummy! It's abstract! Like Jackson Pollock! Oh, very clever. Jackson Pollock didn’t use raspberry jam, I suspect. Though, come to think of it, maybe he would have. Careful with that glass, love. I got a plate! A big one! Can I put the forks on it too? No, sweetheart, forks go in the cutlery basket. Remember? We talked about this. It's all about organisation. Like...like George Stephenson organising the railways. George who-now? Was he a wizard? Did he know Harry Potter? No, he wasn’t a wizard, although what he did was pretty magical in its own way! George Stephenson was a brilliant engineer. He built some of the very first steam locomotives - the ‘Rocket’ was his most famous one. He basically invented modern railways. A rocket? Like one that goes to space? Not quite. It was called the Rocket because it was super-fast for its time. Before Stephenson, getting around was really slow. Imagine travelling from Comberton to Norwich – where you were born, Maisie – taking days! Days?! That’s ages! I couldn't even  finish  reading ‘Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban’ in days! Exactly. Stephenson’s railways meant people and goods could travel much quicker, helping towns and cities grow. It changed everything. He had to figure out how to lay the tracks, build the engines, even make sure the trains didn't crash! It was a huge undertaking. Did he have helpers? Oh, absolutely. Lots of helpers! He needed engineers, builders, miners to get the coal for the engines… It was a massive team effort. He wasn’t doing it all on his own. Actually, it's a bit like unloading the dishwasher –  we  are a team effort, aren’t we? I'm a very good helper. Especially with abstract art. You are a  very  enthusiastic helper. Perhaps we stick to plates and cutlery for now. Did you know, George Stephenson started his life as a coal miner? He didn't have much education, but he was incredibly clever and determined to improve things. It just shows you, doesn't it? Does that mean I don't need to do my homework if I’m going to be an engineer?

Right, so I’m officially declaring this curry a success. Smells banging, innit? Though Liv, you were right, I  did  put too much chilli in last time. Nearly blew poor old Mark’s head off. Nearly? He was practically seeing stars! Honestly, Leo, you treat spice like it’s a personal challenge. And yeah, this smells amazing. Much better balanced. Are you still obsessing over Words With Friends, by the way? I saw you glued to your phone all afternoon. Obsessing is a strong word. Strategizing. There's a difference. Brenda – you remember Brenda from uni? – she’s absolutely dominating. She's got like, a vocabulary of obscure Scrabble words. It’s infuriating. Brenda, eh? The one who used to carry a dictionary in her handbag? Figures. Still running the supper club, then? I was thinking of advertising one at the café, but I’m a bit worried about all the… legal stuff. Food hygiene, licenses, all that jazz. Legal stuff is a nightmare, mate. Believe me. Tried to get a food van going back in Melbourne, nearly lost me shirt. You need a solicitor, no two ways about it. And insurance, buckets of it. Seriously? Just for a little supper club? That sounds mental. I thought it was just, like, inviting people over for a nice meal. Apparently not. Apparently, if you’re taking money, you’re a business. And businesses need to jump through hoops. I was hoping to just do a ‘bring your own booze’ thing and keep it relatively low-key. Oh, you could look into pop-up regulations. They’re usually a bit more relaxed. I found a really good website – PopUp Britain, I think it was - when I was thinking about doing a weekend bakery stall. Didn't end up happening, too much stress alongside the shop, but the info was solid. Pop-up’s alright, but they still wanna know your food safety plan. And where you're getting your ingredients. Gotta be documented, you know? Speaking of ingredients, this curry smells incredible. What’s the secret? Mum’s recipe. Strictly guarded. Though I may have added a splash of mango chutney. Don’t tell her. Good man. So, how's the job hunt going, Leo? Still applying for those graduate schemes? It’s a slog, to be honest. Loads of rejection emails. Apparently, “a strong academic record” doesn’t compensate for “lack of relevant experience.”

…and honestly, the sheer volume of detentions Mr. Harrison handed out today was ridiculous. Ten! For talking. Talking, I tell you! It's enough to make you question the profession sometimes, isn't it? Anyway, enough shop stewarding, how  was  your weekend, Anya? Did you manage to get to that pottery class you were talking about? Oh, hello, Sarah! Yes, it was… chaotic, but good. The pottery class was lovely, actually. Very therapeutic. Though, I think my “vase” looks more like a slightly wonky ashtray. Still, it’s  my  wonky ashtray! And yes, Mr. Harrison. He’s…enthusiastic about discipline. My brother used to have him for Geography. Said he expected absolute silence. Enthusiastic is putting it mildly. He's a stickler, alright. A wonky ashtray sounds charming, though! Much more useful, frankly. I tried to get into watercolour painting last year, but just ended up with muddy brown messes. I think I lack the patience. What about little Leo? How’s he doing? Is he still obsessed with dinosaurs? He is  completely  consumed. It’s all “T-Rex this” and “Velociraptor that.” It’s quite impressive, actually, how much he knows. He even corrected my pronunciation of Pterodactyl the other day! I had to Google it. He’s starting to get interested in building things now too, Lego mostly. It’s…loud. Oh, Lego. The bane of every parent’s existence. Tiny plastic landmines everywhere! My Thomas is 13 now, thankfully past the Lego stage. Though, he’s currently obsessed with coding. Staring at a screen all day. It’s a different kind of mess, I suppose. Did you manage to get anything nice to eat this weekend? I attempted a roast, and it was… a learning experience. Yorkshire puddings deflated, potatoes were rock solid. Oh dear! Roasts are tricky. I made borscht. My grandmother's recipe. It takes  all  day, but it's worth it. Leo loves it… eventually. He’s a bit suspicious of beetroot. I brought some in today, actually, if you’d like to try? It's in the fridge in the staff room. Just a small portion. Oh, Anya, you’re a star! That sounds absolutely lovely, actually. I haven’t had proper borscht in ages. Thank you. I'm definitely going to sneak some later. It’s so nice to have someone who actually  cooks  around here. Most of us live on instant noodles and biscuits, I suspect.

Right, is this music alright, or should I put summat else on? It’s a bit of a banger, innit? Remember when everyone was obsessed with this band at school?      It’s… energetic. Bit loud for this time of day, maybe? And yes, vaguely. You and your friends were always blasting  something  when I’d pick you up. Felt like a tiny rave in the backseat. Honestly, I think I’m still recovering.      Aye, that’s ‘cos you weren’t brought up on proper music, love. Give us a bit of the Stone Roses, now  that’s  a tune. Though, to be fair, anything’s better than what they play in that new shopping centre. It's all… beeps and boops.      Dad! Don't be ancient. And Mum, it’s not  that  loud! It’s just...enthusiastic. So, are we sticking to the list, or are you both gonna go rogue in Mothercare again? Last time we were in there, Dad nearly bought a full-sized rocking horse.      He said it was an investment! He was imagining grandchildren galloping around the garden. And I just wanted that sheepskin rug. It was beautiful. This time, we  need  the travel system. The survey on the house came back, didn’t it? And it’s… extensive.      Extensive is an understatement. Damp proofing, re-wiring, garden needs a complete overhaul… reckons the back wall’s moving. It's gonna be a right job lot. That’s why we need a proper, sturdy buggy. One that can handle any terrain, you know? Even cobbled streets. Don’t want the little one bouncing around like a ping pong ball.      Cobbled streets in Preston? Bit dramatic, aren't you? Honestly, moving house is such a stress. Remember when we moved from Gran’s? I spent the whole time convinced I’d left my favourite blanket behind. The fluffy blue one with the sheep on…      Oh, I remember that blanket. You clung to it for  years . You took it to college with you!      Well, it was comforting! And college was scary! All those new people… and everyone seemed to already have their ‘thing’. I just felt a bit lost. Actually, talking of things…did you see those weighted blankets in that shop we went to earlier? Said they were good for anxiety.      Aye, saw ‘em. Overpriced, if you ask me. A good hot water bottle does the same job.

Honestly, this raid was  brutal . Like, genuinely brutal. We wiped, like, ten times on the final boss. Ten! And it was always the same thing – Gareth just kept running into the fire. Gareth. Sounds about right. He was always a bit… impulsive, even when he was little. Remember when he tried to build a rocket out of garden gnomes and fireworks? How could I forget? Dad nearly had a heart attack. Though, to be fair, the gnome-rocket  did  look pretty impressive for about three seconds. But yeah, Gareth's in-game habits aren’t much different. Running headfirst into danger. It's endearing, in a frustrating way. Endearing?! It cost us hours! And my sleep schedule. I've got that psychology paper due next week, and I’m already behind. Professor Davies is terrifying. She looks right  through  you. Psychology, is it? Fascinating stuff. All that getting inside people’s heads. Is it anything like trying to figure out your father? Mum! It’s… complicated. We’re looking at cognitive biases at the moment, which is hilarious because you see them  everywhere . Like, Gareth thinking he can take on a fire dragon solo. Classic confirmation bias. He just keeps going, believing he’ll succeed eventually. See? Psychology  is  useful! Though I reckon a bit of common sense would help Gareth more. Speaking of which, are you two sorted for Christmas? We thinking the usual at Auntie Brenda’s? I think so. Unless anyone’s suddenly developed a craving for Christmas in Barbados? I did see some ridiculously cheap flights the other day. Just thinking aloud, obviously. Barbados sounds… amazing. But Auntie Brenda’s is tradition. And I need to be back for uni stuff. Plus, I suspect Barbados wouldn’t have adequate Wi-Fi for raiding. Priorities. Always thinking of the game. You're just like your brother. Though, I suspect your priorities were different when you were little. Remember when you insisted on wearing your fairy wings to the supermarket  every  time? Please don't remind me. Photographs exist. Horrifying photographs. So, Barbados is off the table. What about work, Liam? How’s the… freelance coding going? It's alright. Steady. Got a small project with a company in London, updating their website. Mostly just staring at lines of code for hours, trying to make things not break. It's a good way to pay rent, I suppose. Pays better than running around in virtual fantasy worlds.

…and honestly, the sheer amount of iron you need in Minecraft is  ridiculous . It’s like, you spend half your life mining iron just to make slightly better tools than wood. Honestly, diamonds are where it's at, but even getting to diamonds… the effort! But iron’s good for swords! You can beat zombies with an iron sword, Mummy. A wooden sword just… bounces off. Yeah! And you need iron for armour! Otherwise the creepers explode you. That’s very true, you both have a point. Iron  is  essential for survival. It's just… monotonous. Speaking of essential materials, did you know that copper is becoming really important in real life now? For, like, electrics and all sorts of things. It's a really good conductor. Copper? Like the pennies? Well, yes, like pennies. Although they don't make pennies  entirely  of copper anymore, it’s still a significant part. It's a much older metal than iron, you know. People were working with copper thousands of years before they figured out iron. Older than iron? Whoa. So, cavemen used copper? Some of them did! And gold too. Though gold is quite soft, isn’t it? Not very good for making swords, is it? More for… showing off. Like, Queen Elizabeth’s crown is probably mostly gold. Shiny! I want a crown. Can we make one out of gold in Minecraft? You can, but it wouldn’t be very practical. It wouldn't protect you from creepers. Now, what about fabrics? Cotton is really important, isn’t it? But have you ever wondered how they  make  cotton? From fluffy stuff? Like clouds? Well, sort of! It grows on plants, in big fluffy balls. And then they spin it into thread, and then weave the thread into cloth. It’s amazing. Silk is also really cool. It comes from silkworms. Silkworms eat leaves? I saw a caterpillar eat a leaf in the garden! Maybe it will make silk! It could, if it was a  silkworm  caterpillar! They build little cocoons around themselves, and people unravel the silk from the cocoon. It’s quite a process. It’s why silk used to be so expensive. Mummy, remember the story you made up about the Glowstone Guardians? Oh! The Glowstone Guardians! Yes! I’d almost forgotten about them. They lived in a cave made of amethyst and guarded all the diamonds! Exactly! And they were made of… what were they made of, do you remember?

…and honestly, the lecturer just kept going on about post-structuralism like it was the key to unlocking the universe. I swear, half the class were asleep. It's just  words , innit? Fancy words to make simple ideas sound complicated. Tell me about it. Mine was doing the same with Baudrillard. Simulation and hyperreality? Right, like I need to worry about that when I’m trying to figure out how to afford next week’s shop. Are you still practicing with the guitar, by the way? Haven’t heard you play in ages. I am, yeah. On and off. Been trying to learn that new Arctic Monkeys track. “There’d Better Be a Mirrorball”. It’s a nightmare, the chord changes are proper fiddly. It sounds alright when I get bits of it, but stringing it all together… forget about it. You still bashing away at yours? Nah, not so much lately. Life's just been… a lot. Plus, my flatmate’s been having proper loud parties every other night. Can't hear myself  think , let alone play. I keep meaning to have a word, but he’s a bit… intimidating, you know? Bit of a lad. Oh aye, I know the type. All bravado and no brain. Just tell ‘im. It’s your flat too. Though, knowing the lads around here… it's getting a bit worrying, isn’t it? Saw something on Facebook yesterday… What, about that… incident down by the park? Yeah, saw that too. Absolutely disgusting. Makes your blood run cold, doesn't it? What is  wrong  with people? It’s terrifying. It makes you feel sick to your stomach. And then you start looking at everyone differently, wondering… You know? I’ve been thinking about my little cousin, Lily. She’s only eight. Makes me want to keep her under lock and key. It does, doesn’t it? It's awful. You can't switch that feeling off. It just… sticks with you. It’s why I struggle with meeting new people, to be honest. Especially online. It’s just too easy for… well, you know. I get that completely. My mum’s always going on about being careful who I talk to. Says the world’s full of weirdos. Always has been, I suppose, but it feels… more prevalent now, with everything being online. It feels like you can't trust anyone. And the way they hide behind fake profiles and pretend to be something they’re not… it's creepy.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of reading for the EPQ is criminal. Like, seriously, Mrs. Davies just throws articles at you and expects you to synthesize them into…well, whatever she decides it needs to be synthesized  into . It's on the ethics of AI, which is interesting enough, but the workload… Tell me about it. Mine’s on the history of grime music which  sounds  fun, right? Loads of tunes. But then you get into copyright law and the socio-economic factors… it's less about the bangers and more about policy documents. Still, it’s better than actual lessons, innit? Anything beats double physics. You two are moaning! I’m doing mine on the impact of fast fashion, and all I’ve done is feel overwhelmingly guilty for the last three weeks. Every time I look at my wardrobe, I just see environmental destruction. Plus, sourcing data is a nightmare. Everyone’s trying to greenwash, so facts are… blurry. Woah, harsh. That  does  sound depressing. Hey, speaking of things that are depressing… did you see that article about the food bank use rising again? Locally even. It’s mad, isn’t it? Right here in Slough. Yeah, it’s awful. It’s… it’s easy to get caught up in our own little bubble, worrying about EPQs and university applications, and forget that people are properly struggling. Makes you think, doesn't it? Especially with everything going on in the world. Definitely. It makes all this hand-wringing about WHICH university seems a bit… trivial. I mean, I want to go to a good uni, obviously, but sometimes I wonder if I should be doing something more directly helpful. Like, volunteering or something. I’ve been thinking about that too. Remember old Mr. Henderson, the history teacher? He used to bang on about finding your ‘ikigai’ – your reason for being. Said university isn’t necessarily it for everyone. Mr. Henderson was proper intense. Remember when he tried to juggle oranges in class to explain the balance of power in Europe? It didn’t end well. Oh my god, yes! He nearly took out Mrs. Patel with an orange! That was legendary. Anyway, back to more serious things… have you guys sorted your Montenegro trip yet? Are we still on for July? Pretty much. Flights are booked, and I’ve found a decent little Airbnb in Kotor. Apparently, the views are insane.

…and honestly, the state of this kitchen is a  disgrace . I swear, someone used my washing up liquid to clean the floor last week. The  floor ! It smelled like lavender and desperation. Tell me about it. I came down this morning and there was a mountain of dishes that could house a small family. Honestly, I’m starting to think living in halls was cleaner. And cheaper. Cheaper is the key word, isn’t it? This accommodation is daylight robbery. I’m pretty sure my parents are actively questioning their life choices funding this. I mean, I love Lancaster, but fifteen hundred a month? For a room barely bigger than my old bedroom in Bolton? Fifteen hundred?! Seriously? I’m paying twelve-fifty and I still think it’s ridiculous. My mum keeps sending me passive-aggressive texts about “being sensible with my money” and “remembering the value of a pound”. Like I’m splashing out on yachts or something. Oh, mums. Mine's the same. Constantly asking if I’m ‘eating properly’ and then subtly implying I should be working three jobs alongside my degree to ‘contribute’. Like Falmouth isn’t far enough away already? She still treats me like I’m sixteen. Mine's not bad, actually. She’s more worried about me having enough fun. Which is…slightly terrifying. She keeps suggesting I join every society going, then asks me to send photos of every event. It’s intense. She lives for the ‘university experience’ through me, you know? Mine’s just…practical. Very focused on career prospects. Every conversation ends with “So, what internships are you looking at?” or “Have you thought about postgraduate study?”. It's exhausting. It's like university isn’t about  enjoying  things, it's just a stepping stone. Sounds rough. My dad just wants me to pass. That's it. Lowest expectations ever. He keeps going on about how proud he'd be if I just managed to not fail everything. Charming. That's…different. Bit brutal, innit? Though, I suppose it's nice to have low pressure? It's definitely a mood. Speaking of pressure... did you hear about Chloe from the history course failing her dissertation? Apparently, she had a complete meltdown last week. No way! Chloe's brilliant. What happened? Apparently, she spent the entire semester researching a really obscure topic, only to find out halfway through that there were literally no primary sources available.

…and honestly, the kids were  wild  at the Christmas market last weekend. Leo tried to barter a crayon drawing for a gingerbread man. A crayon drawing, can you believe it? He insisted it was a ‘very good drawing of a dinosaur’. Oh, Leo. He's a chip off the old block, that one, always negotiating. Reminds me of your father, actually. He once tried to trade Old Man Hemmings a box of slightly used fishing lures for a prize-winning marrow at the village fête. Oh, Dad! I’d forgotten that! Hemmings was furious. He practically chased Dad around the green. And Mum just stood there, mortified. It's good to know that gene is strong in this family. Though, perhaps not ideal for a TEFL teacher trying to maintain order in a classroom. Speaking of work, how are things going with the new intake? Still grappling with the subjunctive? Don’t even  start  me on the subjunctive. It's a nightmare! They just don't  get  it. I try explaining it with songs, with stories, with diagrams… nothing seems to stick. I’m starting to feel like a broken record. At least Mrs. Petrov, the Russian lady, is making good progress. She’s a real star. That’s lovely to hear. It's those small victories, isn’t it? Makes all the frustrations worthwhile. I've been doing a lot of online training lately – a bit soul-destroying, really. Endless PowerPoint presentations and people talking  at  you, not  with  you. It’s a far cry from the face-to-face workshops I used to run. Oh, yes? What kind of training? Still doing the project management stuff? Mostly. Though I did a brief stint last month helping a company revamp their customer service. Turns out they were losing clients hand over fist because their automated phone system was an absolute labyrinth. Apparently, people were giving up before even speaking to a human. Goodness! You’d think in this day and age they’d have figured that out. It's funny, isn’t it? How simple things can make such a big difference. Reminds me of Auntie Brenda. Brenda? Oh, go on. Tell me a Brenda story. They always brighten my day. Well, she called last week, completely flustered. Apparently, she tried to video call young Thomas in Australia for Christmas, but kept showing him her ceiling. For a good ten minutes, all Thomas got was a view of her cornices and a very blurry reflection of her head!

…and honestly, the traffic was mental getting here. Did you see they’ve put another set of speed cameras up on the A20? Seriously, it’s like they’re just farming money now. They’re everywhere. I’m half expecting to lose my license before I even  get  to Brighton. Farming money, you say? Sounds about right. They always do that when a new housing estate goes up. Crayford’s gone completely mental with the building, you wouldn’t recognise it. Used to be fields, now it’s just brick and…well, more brick. Did you get held up near the roundabout by the new Lidl? That’s chaos every day. No, thankfully avoided that. Though I did see the foundations for  another  one going in just past Brands Hatch. Brighton's looking increasingly appealing, just to escape the endless construction. How’s work been? Still battling the complaints? Oh, don’t even get me started. You wouldn’t believe the things people complain about now. One woman called because her delivery was five minutes late! Five minutes! I swear, some people have no perspective. And then old Mrs. Higgins was on about the colour of the packaging… Honestly, I think I’m developing a twitch. I had a bout of the flu last month, knocked me for six, couldn't even look at a computer screen. Ugh, sounds dreadful. Glad you're better now. Teaching's…teaching. Still mostly pronunciation drills and trying to explain the difference between ‘shall’ and ‘will’. It’s exhausting. But I think I’m finally getting the hang of online classes, which is something. It feels weird having not seen you in two years. Feels like a lifetime. Two years, eh? Doesn't seem possible. Time flies when you’re getting old, I suppose. So, Brighton proper? Any flat viewings lined up yet? You always did talk about moving down there. Remember that trip to Tanzania? You said you’d always wanted to live by the sea after that. I do! That was amazing, wasn’t it? The sunsets over the Indian Ocean… Anyway, yeah, got a couple of viewings next week. Fingers crossed. It’s expensive, though. And I’m starting to think I’ve put on a stone since I left Bedford. All the stress-eating. A stone? Don’t be daft. You're looking fine. Though I've probably put two on myself.

…and honestly, the student who argued that Derrida  supported  consumerism? I nearly choked on my tea. It was a masterclass in misreading, honestly. How was  your  day, love? Less philosophical warfare, I hope? Thankfully, yes. Though equally frustrating, in a different way. The university PR department decided my latest research on Victorian social reform needs “jazzing up” for the press release. Apparently, ‘nuance’ and ‘complex historical context’ don’t sell newspapers. They want me to focus on the  scandals . Oh,  don’t . They are the absolute worst. It’s always sensationalism over substance, isn’t it? Did they suggest a headline like, “Victorian Philanthropists: Secret Lives of the Upper Class!” or something equally dreadful? You are frighteningly accurate. It was… close. “Hidden Truths Behind Victorian Charity” was the final offering. I’ve told them I’ll review it, which is code for “I’ll tone it down so much it’s barely recognisable.” Anyway, enough work drama. I managed to grab those sourdough rolls you like from the market. And, possibly more importantly, I found a replacement for that ridiculous flamingo lamp your aunt gave us. Oh, thank goodness. I’ve been secretly plotting its disposal for months. It clashed with  everything . Sourdough sounds divine, though. I had a truly chaotic lunch break trying to navigate the city centre shops. I completely forgot we were out of coffee. The city centre on a Tuesday? Brave. Were the Christmas decorations still up? It felt stubbornly festive last time I ventured in there. Sadly, yes. And it was  packed . Honestly, felt like Black Friday all over again just for discounted bath bombs. I eventually managed to grab the coffee, but then got cornered by a woman trying to sell me aromatherapy oils. She insisted lavender would ‘unlock my creative potential’. Oh, those people. They’re relentless. Did you succumb? Unlock your inner artist with the power of scent? Tempted, honestly. I  am  marking essays until midnight… but no. I escaped with my sanity, and the coffee. Speaking of escaping, I was thinking we could try that new jazz club on Friday? The one Leo from the music department recommended? Ooh, yes! The Blue Note, wasn’t it? Leo has excellent taste. I'm definitely up for that. It's been ages since we've had a proper night out. Do you think we should book? It sounded quite popular. Good idea. I’ll check online now.

Right, onions are softening nicely. Though honestly, this whole beanbag project is distracting me from proper culinary focus. Are you  absolutely  sure we need a knitted beanbag, Alistair? It feels…ambitious. Ambitious, yes. Utterly necessary? Also yes. Think of the aesthetic, darling. The textured wool, the calming colour…it’ll pull the living room together. Far more than a commercially-made one ever could. Besides, you  said  you were bored. I said I was bored with transcribing legal depositions, not that I needed to take on a project that will consume my life for the next six months! Honestly, the amount of yarn…it’s taken over the spare room. And don’t even get me started on the tension. It’s all over the place. You’re a perfectionist, that’s your problem. A bit of wonky tension just adds character. Like a lovely, slightly uneven hand-painted mug. Anyway, how's the… spherical progress? Slow. Very slow. It looks less like a beanbag and more like a rapidly expanding, vaguely circular… something. I think I need to reassess the pattern. And possibly invest in some wrist supports. Speaking of expanding, have you seen the state of the bathroom? The bathroom? What about it? The shower curtain! It’s… distressing. That little sailboat motif was charming three years ago, but now it just looks pathetic. And the whole room needs a refresh. It’s looking a bit… beige. Beige is a perfectly respectable colour. Practical, even. Practical and soul-crushing. I was browsing online earlier and found this gorgeous teal paint. And some lovely seashell-themed accessories. Nothing too kitsch, mind you. Just a hint of coastal chic. Coastal chic in Edinburgh? Bit of a departure from our usual aesthetic, isn’t it? We’re more…sturdy Scottish practicality. Oh, don’t be such a traditionalist! A bit of colour wouldn’t hurt. And frankly, that shower curtain is actively depressing me. It’s a symbol of stagnant domesticity! I need change, Alistair. Colour! Texture! Possibly a small, tastefully placed nautical rope detail. Stagnant domesticity? Dramatic, much? Look, I'm happy to consider a new shower curtain. A sensible, non-sailboat one. But teal walls… we need to discuss that over supper. What are we having, anyway? It smells divine. It’s a slow-cooked lamb and rosemary stew. I was thinking root vegetables, and maybe some crusty bread for dipping.

Lovely brew, this. Not like the stuff they give you in the hospital, eh, Margaret? Tasted like dishwater, that did. And weak as anything. You say that every time, Arthur. And every time, I tell you, it  was  a hospital, not The Ritz. They’re not exactly known for their Earl Grey, are they? Still, glad you’re back ‘ome. It wasn’t the same with just me and young David rattling around. Morning, you two. Arthur, looking perkier already, I see. Margaret, still at it with the needles, eh? Another grandchild getting a new jumper? Oh, hello, Peter. It is for little Leo, actually. His mother says he’s growing like a weed. And you? Bills, I presume, judging by that pile. Mostly. Though there’s a rather official-looking envelope here, addressed to Arthur. Looks like something from the council. Don't tell me they're after you for leaving your bin out again? They are a right nuisance, them council folk. Always on at you about something. Bin day’s Tuesday, I know that! They just like to make a fuss. What does it say, Peter? My eyes ain’t what they used to be. Hmm… it’s about the proposed new development on the old airfield. They’re planning to build houses, quite a lot of them actually. A whole new estate, right on our doorstep. Oh, dear. More traffic. That road’s bad enough as it is. And what about young Farmer Giles? He’ll be furious if they take his fields. Furious? He’ll be absolutely livid! That airfield’s been empty for donkey’s years. Always thought they’d put a garden centre there, maybe. Something useful. Not more houses. We don't  need  more houses. Apparently, there’s a housing shortage. And this is deemed a ‘sustainable’ location. They’re promising improved infrastructure, better schools… the usual spiel. 'Sustainable'. They always say that. It'll mean more pressure on the doctor’s surgery, more kids in the schools already bursting at the seams, and less green space. Remember when we could walk to the woods from here, Arthur? Aye, I do. Used to take little Susan there, pick blackberries. Lovely days. They're building on all the good land, they are. Just concrete and bricks everywhere. It's a shame, that is. A proper shame. They’re holding a public consultation next week, at the village hall.

Honestly, this article about the cost of Christmas is  terrifying . They’re saying the average family is going to spend nearly £800 just on the big day. Eight hundred quid! It's madness. Well, they always  say  that, don't they, love? It’s designed to get people panicking and spending more. Though, even I’ve noticed the price of everything creeping up. The sprouts alone this year… scandalous. Yeah, everything’s a rip-off. I was looking at flights to Barcelona for a weekend in January – trying to find something to cheer myself up after the festive chaos – and they’re astronomical. It's cheaper to fly to New York sometimes! Barcelona sounds lovely, though. A bit of sunshine would do us all good, wouldn't it? I'm already dreading the post-Christmas slump. All that leftover turkey... ugh. Still, I’m trying to save up for that course next year, so a budget Christmas is definitely on the cards for me. You're a good girl, Brenda. Always thinking ahead. I’m trying to be sensible, but the kids... they've already started dropping hints about what they want. Little monsters. Daniel wants a new gaming console, apparently. Like the one he already has isn’t enough! Boys and their gadgets. It’s a universal language. Speaking of things they want, did you manage to get those garden gnomes Maureen was after? She’s been going on about them for weeks. Oh, no! Completely forgot. She mentioned a specific one, didn't she? The one with the fishing rod? I'll have to pop into town tomorrow. Are you going anywhere, Richard? Just a quick trip to see old man Hemmings. He’s not been well, apparently. Apparently, his hip's playing up again. He gets so lonely. Used to be a right character, Hemmings. Played a mean game of darts back in the day. Aw, that’s nice of you. It's easy to forget about the older generation, especially when we're all rushing around. Though, honestly, sometimes I feel like  I'm  the oldest generation when I’m explaining TikTok to my mum. It’s a whole different world to her. Oh, bless her! My nan thinks the internet is a series of tubes. Honestly! It’s funny, but you can see how easily people get left behind. Do you think I should start looking at accommodation for my placements in Brighton?

…and honestly, the driving here is something else, isn’t it? I thought Dorset roads were winding, but this is a whole different level of…character building. Did you have much trouble adjusting, Arthur? You’ve been here a good while now, haven't you? Adjusting is a… generous word, Margaret. Let’s just say it was an  experience . I’ve been here nearly five years now. Five years of near misses, unexpected goats in the road, and drivers who appear to believe indicator stalks are purely decorative. You get used to it, eventually. Or you develop a very loud horn hand. I favour the latter. A loud horn hand! That sounds… prudent. I’m still clinging to the politeness ingrained in me, waving apologetically even when  they  cut me off. Perhaps I need to adopt a more assertive approach. Though I doubt even the loudest honk would phase some of them. Politeness won’t get you very far, I’m afraid. They see it as weakness, you see. It’s a bit like… well, like trying to reason with a particularly stubborn donkey. Pointless. Have you been exploring much beyond Paphos? A little. We visited Kyrenia last week. Absolutely beautiful, the castle… and the harbour. But getting there was, as you predicted, an adventure. Endless roundabouts! Honestly, I felt like I was going in circles. And the speed… oh, the speed! Kyrenia’s lovely. Though it’s become rather touristy, hasn’t it? Full of Brits, mostly. And yes, the roundabouts are a menace. They treat them as more of a suggestion than a rule, really. Have you tried the local  halloumi ? Properly grilled, with a squeeze of lemon? Oh, yes!
