It wasn't easy. Spent a summer just listening to people in cafes, trying to mimic the rhythm. The pickle reminded me of the little stalls, bursting with life and…  character . You never really talk about the war much, do you? Or Vienna, for that matter. It’s all Italy and art after that. There are reasons for that, love. Some memories… they're best left gently covered. Vienna was… complicated. And Germany, well, let’s just say I had a strong desire to  distance  myself. Italy was sunshine and colour and a clean slate. Though, the Italian I picked up was rather dreadful, I suspect. Never quite mastered the subjunctive. Unlike you, with your Classics background. That’s a bit harsh. My Italian is… rusty. University took over, remember? All that Homer and Virgil. Useful for impressing people at parties, less so for ordering coffee in Rome. Which, ironically, I’ve never actually done. Never been to Rome? After all that studying? Scandalous! You must go. You absolutely  must . It’s filled with echoes of the past, just like your books. And the food… oh, the food! Better than any pickle, I assure you. Speaking of which, how's your dissertation coming along? Still wrestling with those ancient Greek metaphors? It’s…progressing. Slowly. The computer decided to have a meltdown yesterday. Lost about three hours of work. I swear, technology is designed to torment students. I spent the afternoon trying to recover files and nearly threw the thing out the window. Oh dear. Those machines! I still can't get my head around them.

Honestly, Dad, you're gripping the steering wheel like you’re trying to strangle it! It's just a bit of traffic, it’s not the M25 at rush hour. Relax, we’ll get to Dorset eventually. Easy for  you  to say, love. You're not the one driving. And it  is  like the M25, just…prettier scenery to distract from the chaos. People just don’t know how to use a roundabout anymore. Absolute menace, some of them. He’s got a point, actually. Saw someone nearly cause an accident in Basildon last week, just barged right in. Though Basildon’s just…a bit of a write-off, isn’t it? Never liked it there. Basildon isn’t  that  bad, Mum. It’s…evolving. Though I wouldn't want to live there. Speaking of places, remember when Aunt Carol tried to convince us to move to Slough? Said it was ‘up and coming’. Slough! Up and coming to what? A bigger puddle? No thank you. That woman’s got no sense. All concrete and…well, nothing nice. She always had odd ideas. Remember her obsession with Mantiques? Oh, don’t even mention the Mantiques. The living room was crammed! She tried to get your father interested, didn't she, dear? He absolutely hated it. Hated it! Said they were dust collectors and looked like someone had raided a shipwreck. And then she wanted me to help her sell them all on eBay! I don’t  do  eBay. Too much fiddling about. Honestly, these phones…always needing updates, passwords… It’s not that hard, Dad. I can show you again when we get there. You used to be good with computers, didn’t you? You built a PC back in the nineties… That was different! That was proper building. None of this pre-fabricated nonsense. That Windows 8 was the downfall, mind. Absolute disaster. Couldn’t find anything! It was a bit complicated, wasn't it? I stuck with Windows 7 for as long as I could. Anyway, how’s that dissertation coming along, darling? Still chasing those academic ghosts? It’s…progressing. I'm currently wrestling with post-structuralist theory and it's winning. It's surprisingly draining. I've spent the last two weeks just reading Foucault. Fou-what now? Sounds a bit French to me. Is that what they’re teaching you at university these days? No practical skills involved, I’ll bet.

Lovely brew this, Patricia. Just lovely. Reminds me of me mum’s, though she always did put a dash o’ brandy in hers, the cheeky woman. Not that  I’d  ever advocate such a thing at… well, this time o’ day. Brandy at ten in the mornin’, Arthur? You'd have been singin’ sea shanties in the garden! Though, to be fair, you don’t need much encouragement for that these days. How’s your knee feelin' after that little potter in the shed yesterday? Oh, it's complainin’, it is. Not as bad as it was, mind. A bit of a twinge when I bend, but nothing a good sit-down and a hot water bottle can’t sort. Been tryin’ to get that robin house finished. Little beggar’s been lookin’ at me with such hopeful eyes, sittin’ on the fence. Deserves a proper 'ome, he does. You’re a soft touch, you are. That robin's probably got half a dozen nests already. Still, it’s good to keep you occupied. All this quiet… sometimes I worry you’ll go stir-crazy. Remember when you took up whittlin’? That didn’t last long. Nearly took me eye out with a wood shaving! Now, that’s a bit harsh, Patricia! It slipped! And it was a particularly sharp shaving, I’ll have you know. Besides, whittlin’ is an art form! I was attempting a majestic eagle, you understand. It just… resembled a slightly disgruntled potato. A disgruntled potato, indeed. You always did have a vivid imagination, Arthur. Though sometimes I think you imagine things to fill the time. You were convinced Mrs. Higgins next door was trainin’ squirrels to steal her own birdseed last week. Well, weren't you listenin'? She  was  out there with a handful of peanuts, whisperin' to 'em! It’s plain as day, Patricia! And they were lookin’ at 'er funny, all shifty-eyed. Squirrels are no fools, you know. They’re clever little blighters. You’re incorrigible. Still, it’s… nice. Keeps things interestin’. It's quiet now, though, isn't it? With the children grown and flown. Feels like just yesterday little Emily was climbin’ on your knee, demandin’ a story about pirates. Aye. It does. They grow up too quick, don’t they? Seems like only yesterday I was teachin' young Thomas how to ride his bicycle, and he kept fallin’ off, bless him.

Mmm, this is lovely, this pasta bake. Proper comforting on a night like this. Honestly, it's been chucking it down all day. Makes you just want to hibernate, doesn’t it? It does, aye. Glad I managed to get the groceries before it  really  came down. Thought I was going to be swimming back from Tesco. And yeah, it's a good job, this. Better than braving the elements for a takeaway. How was your day? Anything exciting happen at the office? Not exciting, exactly. More… frustratingly bureaucratic. Spent three hours trying to get sign-off on a revised methodology for the user testing. Honestly, you'd think they'd trust me a bit more after the last project. It's just paperwork, paperwork, paperwork. Makes me long for the days of actually, you know,  doing  the research. Speaking of doing things… how's the PhD going? Still wrestling with that intractable data set? Don't even  mention  it. It's like it's actively trying to mislead me. I've run the regressions five different ways now, and I'm still getting anomalies. I think I might need to re-evaluate my entire approach. It's just… draining. Needed this pasta, honestly. And a proper good chat. Did you manage to catch up with Sarah and Liam at all this week? Briefly. Sarah messaged about that gig on Friday. The one at the Corn Exchange? Some indie band I’ve never heard of. She was asking if we were up for it. I said maybe, depending on how this sign-off saga pans out. It sounds a bit loud for me, to be honest. I’m getting too old for mosh pits, aren’t I? You’re hardly ancient! Though, to be fair, I feel my bones aching just thinking about a mosh pit these days. I’d be more up for a quiet pub night, actually. Or…you know…perhaps moving onto a board game after this? Remember how competitive we get with Scrabble? Oh, you  know  you cheat at Scrabble. You always try to sneak in words no one’s ever heard of. And it’s not just Scrabble. It's Monopoly, it's Cluedo... you weaponize board games! But yes, a quiet night sounds good too. This weather demands it. Have you been out in the garden at all this week? I was thinking about trying to get the roses pruned before the worst of the winter hits.

…and honestly, the sheer  audacity  of asking me to train someone to do my job while simultaneously implying my position is ‘under review’ is just… beyond. Like, pick a lane, right? Are you preparing me for redundancy or are you genuinely investing in the team? It's proper Geordie levels of passive-aggressive, if I'm being honest. Wow. That  is  rough. Sounds like classic corporate speak for "we're edging you out." Did you push back at all? You’re usually pretty good at calling that sort of thing out. Aye, I did. Tactfully, of course. I said something along the lines of “It's fantastic to build capacity within the team, but I’d appreciate clarity on long-term strategic goals to ensure effective knowledge transfer.” Basically, ‘What’s going on, then?’ in management-speak. She just… smiled. A very unsettling smile. Ugh, the smile. The worst. It's like they think ambiguous responses absolve them of responsibility. This is why I cling to the ivory tower of academia. Annoying supervisors, yes, but at least the battles are usually about footnotes and methodology, not your livelihood. You’re lucky. Though I remember you moaning about Professor Davies’ obsession with the semiotics of garden gnomes for months. Okay, fair point. That was… intense. But it wasn't the same as feeling like you might be out of a job. How secure  do  you feel, actually? Thinking about it, the research sector is pretty precarious anyway, even with a 'proper' job. Not very, to be blunt. It’s that feeling of being disposable, isn't it? Like, I spent three years doing a Masters, another four on a PhD, landed a relatively decent job...and it could all be gone because of budget cuts or restructuring. It's just… disheartening. And seeing how much students are paying now for university fees just adds to it. My little cousin just started at Leeds and the debt she’s racking up… it’s obscene. It is. It's genuinely criminal, the amount they charge. I feel guilty sometimes, thinking about how relatively debt-free I was when I did mine. Granted, I lived on instant noodles and worked every summer, but it felt…doable. It doesn't feel doable for young people now. Honestly, it feels like a deliberate attempt to limit social mobility. Exactly! And then they wonder why everyone's stressed and anxious.

Right, so this is… okay, it’s a bit cheesy, but the drawings are amazing, aren’t they? Look at the little badger’s face! It just  needs  a story behind it, though. Something a bit more… real. It  is  lovely, darling. Very colourful. But you’re right, it’s a bit… saccharine. All sunshine and rainbows. Life isn’t always like that, is it? Especially not family life. Ooh, what have we got here? A new addition to the library? Real life, you say? Aye, you’re spot on there. Try telling a child life is all sunshine and rainbows when their da’s moved back to London and they only see him every other weekend. Exactly! That’s… that’s kinda what I was thinking. Not specifically  that , Gran, but… complicated families. My mate, Leo, his mum and step-dad just split up. So now he's got two Christmases, but he’s really upset about not seeing his little brother as much. It's awful for them, isn't it? Poor Leo. And it's not just the split, it's the readjustment. The constant feeling of being pulled in two directions. I remember… well, you know. It’s hard on the kids. I was thinking maybe a story about a little fox cub who has a really big, complicated family tree. Like, proper sprawling, with step-siblings and half-brothers and aunts who live on different sides of the wood. A fox cub, eh? Good choice. Clever creatures, foxes. Adaptable. And a big family tree… now  that  I can get behind. My own family tree looks like a bramble patch. Honestly, trying to explain it all at family gatherings is exhausting. Especially the bits involving Uncle Hamish and… well, never mind. You always leave out the juicy bits, Mum. Remember when you started explaining about Great-Grandfather Angus and the sheep…? Shepherds and sheep are a sensitive topic! The point is, families come in all shapes and sizes. That’s what matters. And a fox cub is a good starting point. What's the problem the cub's facing? Well, he’s feeling a bit lost, like he doesn’t really fit in anywhere. He likes hanging out with his mum's side, but his dad’s new family feels very different. They have loads of rules, and they’re all really sporty, and he’s… not.

Right, honestly, this essay is killin’ me. ‘The socio-political ramifications of Thatcherism on Northern industrial towns’ – honestly, who  chooses  this stuff? I feel like I’m back in history class, but with more…despair. Oh god, sounds grim. I’m wading through case studies on sustainable urban development. It's not  bad , exactly, just…beige. Like really, really beige. Fancy a cuppa? I just made a fresh pot. Ooh, yes please. Strong, with a biscuit if you’ve got any of those ginger ones? That’d be a lifesaver. Thanks, love. You always know how to fix things. And beige? That's a special kind of depressing, innit? At least Thatcher was…vibrant, in a horrifying sort of way. Vibrant is…one word for it. Here you go. And yes, ginger biscuits secured. Right, vent away about Thatcher. It might distract me from thinking about concrete and green spaces. Though, thinking about it, Thatcher  did  concrete over a lot of green spaces… Oh, don't even get me started! My grandad used to work down at the pit. Lost everything when it closed. He never really forgave her. Anyway... I’m just feeling properly scruffy today, too. Procrastination levels are off the charts. I haven’t shaved me legs in…well, I don’t even want to  think  about it. Don’t feel bad! I’ve been rocking the au naturel look for a good week now. Winter is coming, no one’s going to notice a bit of fuzz. Besides, it’s 2024, who cares? Easy for you to say, you've always been more…relaxed about all that. I feel like a right yeti sometimes. My mum used to always go on about it, ‘a lady always keeps herself tidy’. It’s ingrained, I swear. Oh, mothers. Mine was obsessed with ensuring my eyebrows were perfectly shaped. It was a whole  operation  every Saturday morning. I rebelled by just…not doing it. Eventually, she gave up. It's just societal pressure, you know? It's not like hairy legs are going to suddenly render you incapable of critical thinking. True, true. But it's that feeling of…not living up to some unspoken standard. Plus, boyfriend’s mum's coming for tea next week.  That's  when the razor gets deployed. You know how mums are. They subtly assess everything. Ugh, the mother-in-law assessment. A classic.

…No, seriously, try saying ‘Wor’lass’ properly. Not like that! It's not 'War-lass', it’s more… ‘Wur-lass’. Like, the ‘u’ is almost swallowed. It means ‘woman’, but it's specifically North East, like, Sunderland. You’d never hear it down in Birmingham, would ya? Wur-lass. Right. Sounds…challenging. And potentially aggressive. I'm sticking with 'woman', thanks. Honestly, the way you lot mangle the vowels up north is fascinating. It’s a completely different language sometimes. Though, I suppose we’ve got our own peculiarities. You ever try to decipher a full Brummie dialect? It's a nightmare. Aggressive? Nay, it’s affectionate! Though, maybe it depends on who's saying it. And you’re one to talk about mangled vowels! "Babby" for baby? Honestly. Anyway, this is distracting me from the point. It’s a linguistic marvel, is what it is. Speaking of marvels, this pint’s going down a treat. Need another? Babbies deserve nicknames. It’s a nurturing thing! And yes, another would be lovely. This research of yours must be exhausting. All that… alphabet analysis and cultural nuance. It sounds intense. Reminds me slightly of that paper I was reading on the semiotics of football chants. Which, inevitably, led down a rabbit hole of racist abuse. Oh, don't even get me  started  on football chants. It’s dreadful, isn’t it? The sheer volume of it. I did a small section on it for my undergrad dissertation, actually. The coded language, the historical context… it’s all so deeply ingrained. It's not just harmless banter, is it? It’s a symptom of something much bigger. And yeah, this research  is  knackering. It's less alphabet analysis and more trying to convince people that linguistic diversity is something to celebrate, not… well, something to mock. Exactly. It's so easy to dismiss it as 'just lads having a laugh', but it normalises really damaging attitudes. It’s the same sort of casual dismissal you see with drug use, to be honest. Like, "Oh, a bit of a weekend spliff won't hurt anyone." It's a slippery slope, isn't it? Oh, God, don't go there. I had a… confrontation with an old school friend last month. He's got properly into the party scene, you know? Loads of ketamine, all that. Tried to get me to try it, said it would "open my mind".

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork for the Heritage Lottery Fund these days is just… exhausting. They want  everything  justified, down to the colour of the lime wash. It's not enough to say it’s historically accurate, you need three independent analyses proving the pigment was sourced locally in 1782! Oh, don’t I know it. It's gotten worse, hasn't it? They're trying to be more rigorous, I suppose, but it feels like they're actively discouraging smaller projects. Though, you’ve always been good at navigating that particular bureaucratic maze, Penelope. You’ve a knack for phrasing things  just  so. Years of practice, Doreen, years of practice! Though this one… St. Jude’s is a tough nut to crack. The roof needs completely re-thatching, which is expensive enough, but the structural issues with the north wall are significant. It's not just a case of replacing a few tiles. They’re worried about subsidence, and the preliminary surveys are suggesting…well, potential Roman foundations. Roman? In St. Jude’s, Little Puddleton? Heavens. That  does  complicate things. Has anyone checked the local archaeological records? There’s a surprising amount of Roman activity along the Thames corridor, and Little Puddleton isn't far off. Of course. The local history society is beside themselves with excitement. But excitement doesn’t pay for underpinning a wall, does it? They keep talking about a possible  villa , but I need concrete evidence for the HLF. A hopeful rumour isn't going to cut it. I was hoping your experience with the Manor House in Winslow might be useful. You dealt with similar foundation issues, didn’t you? Winslow was…challenging. We discovered a medieval well shaft considerably closer to the main structure than anyone anticipated. Similar problem – potential undermining and a need for incredibly careful excavation. What I learned from that, and it’s a lesson I’ve carried with me, is don't underestimate the power of a detailed phasing plan. The HLF loves to see a project broken down into manageable stages, with clear deliverables and contingency plans for unexpected finds. A phasing plan… yes, I’ve started one, but I feel it’s a bit… weak. I’ve gone for a three-stage approach - initial stabilisation of the wall, archaeological investigation, then the actual re-thatching. But it feels a little simplistic. Simplistic is good, to start with.

Right, so you’re telling me this professor actually  said  that Geordie was just ‘lazy English’? Honestly, the cheek of it! I mean, it's a distinct language variety with a fascinating history, not some…slurred attempt at Received Pronunciation. Yeah, I know, it was ridiculous. He was presenting on dialect levelling and somehow pivoted to dismissing regional accents as ‘impediments to clear communication’. Said something about it being a ‘strain on the listener’. I nearly walked out. I just… really, really wanted to tell him about the complex vowel shifts and the Norse influences in something like Sunderland speech. Oh, you should have! You absolutely should have. The Norse influence is  huge  up there, isn’t it? You can hear it in the vocabulary especially. Like ‘bairn’ for child, that's straight out of Old Norse. He probably thinks it's just a cute little quirk. He clearly hasn't done his homework. It’s infuriating when people treat linguistic diversity like a problem. Exactly! It’s not a problem, it’s a strength. And it’s not about laziness, it's about a completely different system evolving over centuries. It’s the same argument people use against code-switching, isn’t it? They see it as sloppy, when it’s actually a really sophisticated way of negotiating social situations and expressing identity. Spot on. It's all connected. Speaking of sophisticated, how's the PhD going? Still wrestling with the semantic priming stuff? Slowly but surely. I’ve finally gotten a decent dataset, which is a relief. It turns out getting 50 participants to consistently rate the relatedness of word pairs is surprisingly difficult. Everyone’s got an opinion about what ‘related’ means. It's made me realise how subjective language really is, even at a foundational level. Oh, I can imagine. Qualitative research is easy compared to trying to quantify something so… fluid. My current project is less about the intricacies of  how  people speak and more about  where  they’re speaking about things online. Sentiment analysis of social media data related to local council decisions. A bit less… poetic. Sounds useful though. And probably keeps you sane. Less existential dread than questioning the very nature of meaning. We’re definitely needing a holiday soon, aren’t we? I feel like I’m rapidly approaching burnout. Absolutely. I was thinking… Italy? We talked about Tuscany ages ago. Imagine, rolling hills, pasta, and no one batting an eyelid at enthusiastic hand gestures.

…and honestly, the amount of food they  waste  at school is criminal. Honestly, criminal. I saw a whole plate of perfectly good chips go straight in the bin yesterday. It makes you wonder where all our dinner money actually goes. Mummy, can you make me chips like Granny does? Hers are  way  better. They’re fluffy inside. Oh, darling, nobody makes chips like Granny. Nobody. We’ll have to have a Granny-chip making lesson soon. But school dinners…they’re supposed to be nutritious, aren’t they? Not just a mountain of beige. Beige is a good colour! Clowns are beige. And red! That's true, some clowns  are  beige. Or at least have beige bits. Where did that come from, Leo? We were talking about school dinners. Clowns eat chips too. In the circus! They juggle them! I don’t like clowns. They’re scary. Oh, sweetheart, some clowns are a bit silly, aren't they? Not all scary. Though I understand why you’d think so. Anyway, back to dinners. Did you two eat much today? Amelia? I had the chicken nuggets. And a tiny bit of broccoli. A tiny bit? We talked about trying at least three florets. But they’re…green! And bumpy! I know, they aren't the most exciting thing in the world. But they’re good for you, eh? Leo, what about you? I ate everything! Except the gravy. Gravy is…slimy. Okay, fair enough. Gravy  can  be a bit slimy. You did well to eat everything else. Right, so, about the tennis tournament next week. Their coach said they need £10 for the entry fee. I’ve got it covered, but I just wanted to make sure… Tennis? Are you coming to watch, Mummy? Of course, I am! I wouldn’t miss it. Will you be nervous? Maybe. If someone really good is playing against me. I want to be in the circus when I grow up. And have a lion! But a friendly lion. A friendly lion! That’s a good plan. You’d have to practice being very brave. Being in the circus sounds exciting. It's much more exciting than school dinners, that's for sure. Can we have Granny's roast chicken this weekend? Please, Mummy? We absolutely can. We’ll need to go shopping tomorrow. And maybe we can convince Granny to share her chip-making secrets. Can the lion have chips?

…and honestly, the sheer  audacity  of that ending! I mean, to kill off the protagonist  after  everything he’d been through? It felt completely unearned. Did you two think it worked? Oh, I thought it was rather clever, actually. A bit bleak, perhaps, but life  is  bleak sometimes, isn't it? All this Hollywood insistence on happy endings… it’s rarely truthful. Reminded me of something Graham Greene would write. I’m with Helen, Dad. It felt like a cheap shock tactic. All build-up and then…nothing. It didn’t serve the story, it just felt like the director wanted to be edgy. Though, I suppose that reflects the times, doesn’t it? Everything’s all about grabbing attention, regardless of substance. Exactly! It's the same problem I see cropping up in the debate at Cambridge last week, the one about teaching history. Everyone’s so focused on making it “relevant” – which usually means sensationalising it, focusing on the scandals and the controversies – that they forget the importance of context and nuance. Ah, yes, I read about that. All this fuss about “decolonising the curriculum.” Seems to me history  is  about colonisation, both the good and the bad. You can’t just airbrush it out. My history teacher at school, Mr. Penrose, was a firm believer in teaching the facts, as they were. No embellishment. It’s more complex than simply "teaching the facts", Dad. It's about  whose  facts are being prioritised, and the narratives that are being reinforced. A lot of the curriculum still feels very… Anglo-centric. And it’s not about erasure, it’s about broadening perspectives. And that’s where I agree with the calls for change. But I’m worried about the pendulum swinging too far. I had a student the other day who genuinely believed that everything pre-1900 was irrelevant because it wasn’t “inclusive” enough. It’s a fundamental misunderstanding of how history functions! That new national curriculum is…well, it’s a patchwork. Trying to please everyone and ending up pleasing no one. Seems to be the way with politicians these days. All fluff and no substance. Reminds me of that chap, Major, back in the nineties. Just…vanished into the background. Though, to be fair, things were quieter then. Less shouting. You’re right about the shouting, Dad. It's relentless now. And it seeps into everything, including education.

…Lovely bit o’ sun we’re gettin’ now, innit? Makes all the difference. Though, mind you, it doesn’t half highlight the dust on that dresser. Doreen, you haven't been givin’ it a proper goin’ over, ‘ave you? Oh, don’t start on the dresser, Arthur! I did it just last week. It’s the light, that’s all. Shows everything up. Besides, I’m concentratin’ on this cardigan for little Thomas. He’s growin’ like a weed, that boy. Reminds me of your grandfather, actually. Always climbin’ things. Your grandfather, Reginald, was a bit of a scamp, wasn't he, Arthur? I remember your mother telling tales of him scaling the apple tree in the orchard, much to the gardener’s displeasure. Always getting into mischief. Speaking of mischief, I was reading an article about the early days of policing. Apparently, the Metropolitan Police, back in 1829, were met with quite a bit of resistance. People weren't used to a uniformed presence, thought they were interfering. Imagine that now! Interferin’? They’re  always  interferin’! Though, I reckon back then, they ‘ad less to interfere with. No fancy computers and all that. Just a whistle and a strong pair of legs, eh? My father used to tell me about the village Bobby – knew everyone, solved everything with a bit o’ common sense. It's all so different. My grandmother used to talk about the Zeppelin raids during the First World War. Harrow was quite vulnerable, she said. They’d all pile down into the cellars, terrified. Imagine livin’ with that constant fear. A different kind of war entirely. Although, even then, the anxieties were… pervasive. My own grandfather fought in the trenches. He rarely spoke of it, but I remember him waking up screaming sometimes. It left its mark, you know? Those experiences…they echo down the generations. It makes you think about what’s happening now, doesn’t it? All this conflict… It does. I was examining some historical curriculum materials today - trying to assess how accurately we represent the complexities of the Second World War in schools. It’s easy to fall into simplistic narratives of good versus evil, but the reality was so much more nuanced. People struggling with impossible choices… Nuance, is it? Blimey. My grandmother, bless ‘er, she were born in Costessey, just down the road from where I grew up. Said her grandfather, old Silas, he was a bit of a poacher.

Honestly, Dad, it feels… weird. Really weird. Driving this route for the last time with Mum moving. It's like a chapter’s actually closing, isn’t it? Not just a visit ending. It is, lad. It is. Fifty-eight years in that house. Fifty-eight years of Christmases, birthdays, arguments… everything. Northamptonshire will be nice, smaller, easier for your Mum, but… it won’t be  home . Not straight away, anyway. You alright? You’ve been quiet. Just thinking, mostly. Thinking about Gran. She adored that garden. Remember how she used to win prizes for her roses? And all the time she spent correcting  my  English grammar, even when I was at university! "Incorrect subjunctive, Thomas!" she'd say, like I was still eight years old. Oh, your Gran. A force of nature, that woman. Strict as anything, but with a heart of gold. She was proud of you, you know, being a teacher and all. Though she probably still thought you should've gone into banking. More secure, she'd say. “A proper job for a clever boy.” Secure. Right. Like customer service is  insecure ? No offence, Dad. None taken. I’ve seen redundancies, lad. Plenty of them. It’s the way of things these days. Still, a mortgage is a mortgage, and everything’s going up. Speaking of, have you had any luck looking at places? You were saying something about needing a bigger flat, weren’t you? Sort of. It’s a nightmare. Everything’s either a shoebox or requires a second mortgage. I saw one in Brick Lane, looked amazing, but even with a deposit, the monthly payments were… astronomical. Makes me wonder if I should just stay put, even though it’s a bit cramped. Don’t rush into anything. It's a big commitment. Remember when I bought the house in Crayford? Thought it was perfect. Lovely little garden, good location. Didn’t realise the old fella next door collected gnomes. Hundreds of them. Drove me mad. Gnomes? Seriously? That’s… a story. A true story! And the damp. Oh, the damp. Spent years battling damp. That's why when we finally sold up, we vowed to rent for a bit. Less hassle. Your Mum’s been saying the same about the house. Too much to manage now. She's a bit worried about leaving all her friends, mind you. I know. We had a long chat last night.

…and honestly, the thought of trying to get her to choose between the salmon and the chicken now just feels…fraught. Last week she asked me three times what she had for breakfast, and it was a full English! Right? It’s… upsetting, isn’t it? Poor Nan. Maybe stick with chicken then? It's generally a safe bet, and easier to eat if she's a bit off her food. We don’t want her getting overwhelmed. Are we definitely doing the roast potatoes? They’re her favourite. Definitely roast potatoes. That's non-negotiable. I’ve already ordered the Maris Pipers. And sprouts, obviously, though I suspect she won’t touch them. She used to  love  sprouts. It’s just… everything feels different now. Speaking of which, have you thought about the table plan at all? I was thinking you on one side of her, I on the other. And maybe Uncle Peter opposite, he’s good at gently steering conversation. Sounds good. Opposite Nan is a good shout for Uncle Peter. He’ll keep her engaged. Should we put young Leo next to me? He adores her, even if she sometimes doesn’t quite remember who he is. It breaks my heart, but he’s so patient. Yes, Leo next to you is perfect. He’ll practically climb onto the table to show her his drawings. Honestly, it's the little ones who seem to cope with it best. They just accept things as they are, you know? Right, food mostly sorted. I picked up those lovely lavender candles from the market yesterday. They’re the ones she always comments on. Oh, good thinking! Lavender’s her scent. Are you doing one of your elaborate centrepieces, then? Last year’s was… a statement. A statement is putting it mildly! It nearly took out Auntie Mabel. No, no centrepieces this year. Just the candles. Less to navigate, less to worry about. I've been…distracted. I spent the afternoon trying to rearrange the kitchen cupboards. Utterly pointless, honestly. I just kept finding things and thinking, “Oh, she put this here…” It’s all a bit silly, isn't it? Not silly at all. It’s grief, I think. For what’s being lost. Remember how she used to insist on  exactly  where the tea bags went? It was a whole thing. Oh God, yes! And the biscuit tin had to be refilled every evening, no matter what.

…and honestly, the pain is just  ridiculous . Like, I knew it’d be bad, but this is a different level of bad. It feels like someone’s trying to dig out my brain with a spoon. Oh, no! Still awful then? I thought you said it was starting to ease up yesterday? Aye, well, yesterday was a momentary lapse into hope, I reckon. It’s back with a vengeance. And the holes… honestly, the holes are massive. They gave me this mouthwash, but it just feels like swishing around disinfectant in a cavern. Oh,  god . That sounds grim. Are you keeping up with the painkillers? You didn’t mention taking any last night. I am, I am! Just…they don't seem to be doing much. Mum keeps phoning, offering tips. “Warm salt water!” “Potato poultice!” Honestly, she's gone full folk remedy on me. It’s a bit much. Classic Mum. My Mum was exactly the same when I had my tonsils out. She tried to convince me that honey and lemon would cure everything. See! It's a universal motherly instinct to believe in nonsense when their kids are poorly. Speaking of parents…have you told yours about the house move yet? Yeah, I did. It…didn't go brilliantly. Dad’s already started listing all the reasons why it’s a terrible idea, predictably. Something about “leaving a good catchment area” and “losing all our equity.” Honestly, it’s like talking to a brick wall. Ugh, dads. Mine’s being relatively quiet, which is suspicious. Usually, he’s got an opinion on  everything . I’m putting money on him secretly thinking it’s a bad idea and building up to a lecture. Exactly! The silent treatment is always worse. So, are you dreading going back to uni then? After this whole…wisdom tooth fiasco? A bit. I'm gonna have to explain to Professor Davies why my essay's late, sounding like I've been gargling gravel. And then there's actually  being  there. I’ve gotten used to being at home, you know? Being fussed over, even if it's Mum offering potato poultices. I get that. It's weird, isn't it? Spending so long back in childhood, then having to re-adjust. I'm actually looking forward to getting back, though. Need to escape Cambridge and the parental units for a bit. Plus, I've already mentally planned out my entire term-time wardrobe.

…and honestly, the lactose-free Victoria sponge was a disaster. It just…didn’t  rise . It was like a sad, flat pancake pretending to be a cake. I think I need to find a different recipe. Maybe one with applesauce instead of butter? Was it for my birthday cake, Mummy? The one you promised with pink icing? No, sweetheart, that one’s still on track! This was just a practice run. A very  failed  practice run. Don’t worry, yours will be lovely. Right, Leo, what do you think we should do for our acts of kindness this week? Mrs. Peterson was saying her cat's been a bit lonely… Can we make her a card? With sparkly bits? Cats like sparkly bits, right? They  might  do! A card is a brilliant idea, Leo. We could draw a really lovely picture of Whiskers. And maybe we could bake Mrs. Peterson some – lactose-free – cookies? If I can actually get the recipe right this time. I can help decorate! We can put sprinkles on! Lots and lots of sprinkles! Absolutely, plenty of sprinkles. It’s important to remember acts of kindness don't have to be big things, do they? It’s the little things that often mean the most. Like… helping Dad with the washing up without being asked.  Groans . That's a big thing! Okay, fair point. Maybe we’ll start with the card and cookies then! Speaking of things happening, did you two know Chinese New Year is nearly here? Is that when we get red envelopes? Grandma sends us red envelopes! That’s right! Grandma always sends lovely red envelopes with a little bit of money inside. We could make some for each other? Though… we’re a little short on actual money at the moment. We could use the chess pieces! The pawns are like one pence, and the knights are like five pence! That's… remarkably clever, Leo. Using the chess pieces as money! Although, I suspect Dad might object to me paying the bills with a rook. I want the Queen! She's the most money! She's worth… a pound! A pound it is, then. We can make little ‘money’ pouches with red paper. We'll need to think of what kind things we can  buy  with our chess piece money too. Maybe an extra story at bedtime? Or choosing what’s on the dinner menu?

…and then Mr. Henderson just  completely  braked! Like, slammed on the brakes. It wasn’t even his fault, honestly, a seagull just flew right in front of his van. But it was so close, Mum! I thought we were going to end up  in  the van! Oh, darling, that sounds awful! Are you alright? No injuries? I was so worried when I got the call from the school. Just a shaken up Tilly is all I needed to hear, and my blood pressure shot up! I’m fine, honestly. Just a bit bruised on my arm where I hit the dashboard. And a massive headache that's  finally  starting to ease. They checked me out at the school, said I didn’t need to go to the hospital. Honestly, the worst part was Mrs. Davies going on and on about health and safety. Mrs. Davies. Of course. She’d find a regulation violation in paradise. Still, it’s good you’re okay. It just reminded me… remember when I had that little scrape on my knee falling off my bike when I was about your age? Vaguely. Was that the one you said made you feel like Alice falling down the rabbit hole? That’s the one! Everything just seemed… distorted, you know? Like the world tilted. And I remember the gravel was  huge . It felt like boulders! It's funny the things you remember. It left a proper scar, actually, you can still see it if you look closely. Yours won’t scar, will it? Just a bruise, I hope. I don’t think so. It doesn’t feel that deep. Anyway, it’s nothing compared to what happened to Leo. He proper twisted his ankle getting out of the bus. He’s got it in a cast. Oh, poor Leo! He's always been a bit clumsy. Speaking of clumsy…have you finished choosing music for the school play? I thought you were going to suggest something a bit more… upbeat than sea shanties. I did! But Miss Price said they needed something “period appropriate” for  Alice . Honestly. Sea shanties and Wonderland don’t exactly go hand-in-hand, do they? I'm trying to subtly slip in some Florence + The Machine. It fits the vibe, y’know? A bit whimsical and slightly unsettling. Florence is excellent. Very good taste. You’ve always had an eye for… aesthetic. Are you still working on your costume?

…and honestly, Harold, the sheer  audacity  of it all! They were arguing about visual impact! Visual impact! As if a gigantic metal tower poking into the sky is somehow less offensive than, I don’t know, a slightly wonky hedgerow. I spent the evening with the Chipping Norton lot, after our little chat yesterday, and they’re completely floundering. They’ve got passion, bless them, but no strategy. It’s always the way, Margaret. Passion is wonderful, gets people motivated, but it won't win you a Planning Appeal. You need facts, figures, really solid objections based on… well, actual planning law. Not just “it’s ugly.” Though, I entirely agree, they  are  often frightfully ugly. Ramsgate used to be lovely before they started slapping up those awful blocks of flats. Progress, Harold. Progress. Though I must say, I’m starting to think ‘progress’ has become a rather convenient excuse for developers to do exactly as they please, regardless of local concerns. I had a chap from a firm – wouldn’t tell me  which  firm, naturally – at the golf club last week, practically bragging about how they “navigate” the planning system. "Navigating" meaning greasing a few palms and finding loopholes, I expect. Exactly! And the local council… oh, don’t even get me started. Old Mr. Peterson on the Development Control Committee, I swear he’s been promised a consultancy role with the energy company if he votes through these applications. It wouldn't surprise me in the least. They claim independence, but it's all connected, isn't it? The money talks. It always does. And the subsidies! The amount of public money thrown at these renewable energy schemes, it’s staggering. While research into  actually  clever solutions – things like better energy storage, for instance – gets a pittance. We're putting all our eggs in one basket, relying on intermittent power sources, and pretending it’s all sorted. Storage  is  the key, Harold, you're right. That’s where the real innovation needs to happen. Hydrogen, maybe? Or even revisiting pumped hydro… it’s not glamorous, but it works. But no, it's all about the quick win, the headline-grabbing wind farm that can be thrown up in six months. It's about optics, not efficacy. They’re so short-sighted! I was reading an article about tidal energy, properly harnessing the power of the sea. Now  that  is a sustainable source.

Right, so you’ve had three lessons now, haven’t you, love? How are they going? Still battling with roundabouts, or have you conquered those demonic circles of doom? Dad, don’t exaggerate! They’re… challenging. It’s just coordinating everything. Mirror, signal, manoeuvre, and trying to remember which exit  is  the right one. My instructor, Ben, is very patient. He keeps saying I’m a natural worrier which isn’t exactly helpful. Ben sounds a sensible lad. And you  are  a worrier, darling. Always have been. Remember when you were little and convinced the garden gnome was going to steal your biscuits? Mum! That was one time! And he  looked  shifty. Shifty gnomes aside, the main thing is you’re getting on with it. Though, you'll need to think about insurance. It’s a minefield, that is. Especially for new drivers. We need to get some quotes, see what options are available. It’ll be expensive, mind you. I know, I’ve had a quick look. It’s terrifying. Black box technology seems the only remotely affordable option. Apparently, they track how you drive… feels a bit Big Brother-ish, doesn’t it? It’s for the best, love. Keeps you sensible. Your father nearly drove into a hedge once, thinking he could “beat the lights.” Luckily, it was a very soft hedge. That was forty years ago, Margaret! And it wasn’t a  soft  hedge, it was a hawthorn. And I was young and reckless! Things are different now. Safer cars, better roads… well, some roads. Still plenty of lunatics about. Anyway, insurance first. Then, we need to think about when you’ll be able to practice with me. That’s the plan. Ben said I need as much practice as possible. Are you… willing? I know you’re not the most  relaxed  passenger. I’m not a bad passenger! I just… have opinions. Constructive opinions. We’ll start on quiet lanes. No motorways, no town centres. Woburn Abbey, perhaps? Nice, wide roads, hardly any traffic. Brings back memories. Oh, Woburn. You used to take your sister there every summer. She always complained about the deer blocking the road. She complained about  everything , that one. Remember the holiday to Cornwall? Said the sand was too gritty. You two are terrible. So, Woburn it is then, potential driving practice and a trip down memory lane? Speaking of holidays, have you both booked anything for the summer?

Honestly, Dad, the parking around here is absolutely mental. I nearly got a ticket trying to pop into the shops this morning. Honestly, it's worse than Brighton, and  that's  saying something. Brighton, eh? Still thinking about moving down there then, are you? Good luck finding a parking space down there, girl! It's a nightmare, all those students and tourists. Though, I suppose it’s lively. Remember when we went to Brighton pier, decades ago? You were tiny, demanding a stick of rock. Nearly lost you in the crowd, I did. Oh, Dad! You tell that story every time. Yes, I’m still considering Brighton. It feels… freer, somehow. Less… suffocating. Plus, the sea air. It's just a lot to organise, isn't it? Finding a flat, the logistics of all my stuff… Logistics. Fancy word. It's just moving boxes, love. And your mother would have a fit if you left all your books behind. She’s already asking about you settling in and if you will visit enough. She's been on Facebook all morning, showing photos of your childhood to her friends, apparently. Oh, lord. Not the baby photos again. She’s obsessed with Facebook. And the notifications! Honestly, it's constant. I told her to turn them off. She said she’d “miss knowing what everyone’s having for lunch.” Honestly! People are strange these days, glued to those little screens. I wouldn’t know, of course. Never could get the hang of it. Reminds me of when colour television came out. Everyone said it was the future. Gave me a headache, to be honest. Speaking of headaches, I attempted to make that lentil soup recipe you gave me. It… didn't go well. It tasted like sadness and slightly burnt lentils. Oh dear. You need a good stock, see? That’s the secret. And a pinch of paprika. Your mother always made a killer lentil soup. Fed all the neighbourhood kids during the war, she did. Made do with what she had, she always said. Things were different then, you know. Everything in short supply. People helping each other. I know, I know. You've told me the stories. It's just… sometimes it feels so distant. Like a different world. Makes you think about things like food banks, doesn't it? That people are struggling like that  now , when we live in a supposed age of plenty.

…and honestly, the sheer  audacity  of Mr. Henderson to mark down my essay for ‘lack of original thought’ when I literally quoted a relatively obscure sonnet! It felt personal, you know? Like he just…doesn’t  like  me. Henderson sounds delightful. A real bastion of academic freedom, that one. Though, honestly, half the lecturers at Cardiff are just waiting for an excuse to fail someone. It builds their reputations, apparently. Exactly! It's a power trip. It’s not about the Shakespeare, it’s about  him . Speaking of Shakespeare, though, I’m starting to think everyone overestimates him. It’s good, obviously, but the hype… it’s a bit much, isn’t it? Blasphemy! You, a graduate student of English Literature, uttering such scandalous thoughts in public! You'll be burned at the stake! Though, I get what you mean. People treat him like he invented language, rather than just… really good at using it. It’s all a bit performative, isn't it? Like everyone's trying to sound incredibly clever  about  Shakespeare, rather than actually understanding him. Precisely! It's all layers of interpretation  about  the interpretation. It's exhausting. You know what  isn’t  exhausting? Trying to teach my uncle Barry to play golf. That's a truly Sisyphean task. Oh, God, Barry. The man who thinks wearing tweed automatically improves his swing? The very same! He genuinely believes his attire is directly proportional to his score. It’s hilarious and simultaneously infuriating. He keeps saying, “It’s about looking the part, lad!” as he slices another one into the rough. He's convinced he’s about to ‘win’ at golf any day now. The sheer delusion! The eternal optimism of the amateur. It’s endearing, in a ‘this man is actively harming my enjoyment of a perfectly good Sunday afternoon’ sort of way. My dad’s the same with bridge. Absolutely convinced he’s one card away from grand slam every single hand. It’s a family trait, I think. That unwavering belief in imminent victory, despite all evidence to the contrary. You know, I was thinking about surnames the other day. Yours is fairly common, right? Smith? Extremely. Honestly, it's a blessing and a curse. It's easy to remember, but trying to book anything online is a nightmare. "There are fifteen David Smiths already registered on this website." It's a constant battle. What about you?

…and honestly, the bride wanted  teal  chair covers. Teal! Like, who even  does  teal chair covers for a wedding? It clashed with everything. I spent a good hour on the phone trying to explain to her that dusty rose would be far more flattering to the venue. She was having none of it, mind. Absolutely none. Teal, eh? Sounds… ambitious. My day was a bit more straightforward – mostly shifting bricks. Though old man Hemmings nearly took my head off with a wheelbarrow. Said I was ‘dawdling’. Dawdling! On a building site. The cheek of it. Oh, Hemmings. He’s a menace. I swear he enjoys the power trip. Speaking of stressful days, I had a production deadline looming and, of course, three different suppliers let me down. It was a miracle the line didn’t halt completely. Honestly, sometimes I think I need a holiday just to recover from  work . Tell me about it! Events are supposed to be glamorous, aren’t they? All smiles and champagne. Reality is chasing down florists and praying the sound system doesn’t pack in. It's exhausting. What are your weekend plans, then? Need to de-stress after all this. Not much planned, to be honest. Might head down the pub with a few of the lads. Watch the football. Keep it simple. Trying to save a bit of money, you know? Rent's gone up again, and it's feeling it. I’m still stuck living with me mum, which… isn’t ideal at 25, is it? No, not especially. I’m thinking of looking for a flat share. This house is lovely, but it's a bit  big  for one person, and the bills are eye-watering. Plus, my flatmate moved out and I'm starting to talk to the plants. It’s a slippery slope. Ooh, a flat share sounds good. Cambridge is pricey though, isn’t it? I'm lucky enough to still be at home with me folks. It's not the be-all and end-all, but it means I can actually put a bit of money away. It's just... Doncaster feels a million miles away when you're trying to build a life here. Reckon it is. Everything's expensive down south. Even a pint. Though, saying that, I’m trying to cut down. Doctor said my cholesterol’s a bit high. Apparently, a diet of bacon sandwiches and pints doesn’t qualify as 'healthy living'.

…and honestly, the picture quality on this blasted Skype is awful, isn’t it? I can barely make out your face, Derek. Looks like I’m talking to a blurry potato. Nah, you’re alright, Arthur. Just a bit pixelated. Mine looks alright to me. Though, you  are  looking a bit ruddy. Been out in that garden of yours, have ya? Probably soaking up what little sun we get. Speaking of sun, did you manage to catch any of that eclipse yesterday? Just a sliver, sadly. Clouds kept rolling in. I did have the special glasses, mind you. Got ‘em off that internet, proper safe ones. Nearly went blind once looking at a sunspot through a camera lens when I was a lad – don’t recommend it. Anyway, what about you, Sheila? Did you see much? A little bit, yes. Enough to appreciate it. Though, it did get me thinking, didn’t it? About space, and how tiny we are. All these fancy theories about black holes and the beginnings of everything… it’s mind-boggling. I was watching a documentary last night about the cosmos, absolutely fascinating. Reminds me of that painting programme we used to watch, "The Joy of Painting" with Bob Ross. Peaceful, that was. Not like all this…political correctness these days. Peaceful is right. Though, that Bob Ross was a bit… repetitive, wasn’t he? “Happy little trees” and all that. Still, can’t fault his skill. And Sheila’s right about the space stuff. Makes you feel small. I read something the other day about how everything started with a singularity, a point smaller than an atom. Can you imagine? Singularities…aye. That’s what I was reading about too. Complicated stuff, beyond my old engineer’s brain, if I'm honest. Though, building bridges and dams felt pretty cosmic at the time! Speaking of building, I've been weeding the herb garden. Trying to get it looking respectable. Been meaning to try growing some basil again, got a recipe for pesto… Wonderful! Fresh pesto is lovely. I’ve been trying to get my tomatoes going but they are so slow this year. I think I need to give them a good feed. Are you still battling with that bamboo, Arthur? It's a menace, isn't it? The bamboo is a constant war, Sheila. A constant, green, spreading war! I’m having to dig it up every other week.

…and honestly, the traffic on the A19 was mental. Absolutely mental. I swear, every single person decided to take a holiday  today . Did it take you ages to get over from Harpenden? Ages is an understatement. Honestly, I was starting to question my life choices. Google Maps said three hours, it took nearly four and a half. And the M1… don’t even get me started. It was just… solid. You're lucky you only had the A19 to contend with. Still, Sunderland eh? Not a place I’ve spent much time. Aye, well, it’s not exactly on the tourist trail, is it? People tend to fly  over  us to get to Scotland. But it's home. And you wouldn’t believe the restaurants that have opened up recently. Remember when the only decent thing was a chippy and maybe a pub grub place? Vaguely. I think we went to that, uh… The Mariner’s something-or-other, years ago? It was…filling. But not exactly Michelin star material. Is it  actually  getting better food-wise? Honestly, yeah. There's this Lebanese place, Zaytoun, it’s brilliant. And a proper Italian, not just pizza and pasta. Then there’s this new tapas bar… it's surprising. Though, half the time I still end up back at my mam's for a Sunday dinner. You can’t beat it. My mum's Sunday roasts are legendary, but she’d kill me if I said that out loud. She's very modest. We were talking about houses last week, actually. She's thinking of downsizing now Dad’s… well. Anyway, she was looking at places near St Albans Cathedral. Have you ever been? St Albans? Just passing through, once. It’s proper lovely though, isn’t it? Old, proper old. We've got Durham Cathedral, obviously. It's a bit… bigger. And sits on a hill. More imposing, maybe? Though I’m massively biased. I’ve seen pictures of Durham. It  is  spectacular. Very… Northern. Ours is more… gentle. A bit like the entire county of Hertfordshire, to be honest. Not exactly dramatic landscapes. Though there's some nice countryside if you look for it. Gentle is a good word for it. Everything’s so… neat down south. Up here, things are a bit more… rugged. And the buses are always late. Always. You can set your watch by how late they are.

Aye, listen to that one. Lovely bit o’ song. Think it’s a robin, isn’t it? Though they all sound so similar these days, don’t they? I used to be right good at identifyin’ ‘em, back when I spent more time ramblin’ t' moors. It  is  nice. You’re right, though, they all meld into a chorus after a while. I think you are spot on with the Robin. Though I had a blackbird visit my bird feeder this morning – a right cheeky one, he was, staring right into the kitchen window. It got me thinking… I really need to get a new bird feeder. The plastic one’s cracked all to heck. Ooh, that’s a good plan. You get a proper metal one, one wi’ a cage around it. Keeps those pesky squirrels out. Though, mind you, I saw Old Mrs. Higgins tryin’ to climb up the oak tree yesterday to get to the feeder. Nearly gave me a heart attack! Oh, bless her. She’s a character, isn't she? Still spry for her age, though. Speaking of things givin’ me a heart attack... I swore I’d smashed my alarm clock to smithereens this morning. Nearly didn't wake up. It was set for half past six, and I only registered it at quarter to seven. Dreadful start to the day. Half past six?! Good heavens, woman! What on earth for? You’re retired, aren’t ya? I haven't seen an alarm clock in years. I just wake up when I’m good and ready, usually when the sun’s peekin’ through the curtains. Though I did have a terrible nosebleed last week, woke me right up  with  a start, that did. Well, I like to keep a routine. And I had that dentist appointment. Which, by the way, was… an experience. He’s got hands like a blacksmith. Honestly, I thought he was tryin’ to excavate a new cave system in my mouth! Dentists. Don’t even mention ‘em. I had a filling fall out last month. Absolute agony. Reminded me o’ me Dad, actually. He had terrible trouble with his teeth. Though his was… well, it turned out to be something else entirely. Throat cancer, y’know. Terrible business. Oh dear, I didn’t realise. That  is  awful. It’s a dreadful thing, isn’t it? So easily missed too. It makes you think, doesn't it?

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of perfectly curated lives on Instagram is exhausting. Little Bethany from school was showing me her mother’s holiday photos – Maldives, private villa, daily spa treatments. It’s just…not real, is it? Makes you feel a bit rubbish about a wet Tuesday in Cambridge, frankly. Oh, don’t even get me started on Instagram. I’ve started actively unfollowing people if they’re just relentlessly ‘on’. It’s performative happiness. Though, ironically, I  do  use it to promote the support group I run for single parents. It's a really useful tool for reaching people, but the rest of it… a minefield. How are things with you, actually? Last time we spoke you were… still going through IVF, weren’t you? That was the plan. We did another round, and… it didn't take. Honestly, Sarah, it was the final straw. It's not the physical side, though that's grim enough. It's the emotional toll, the constant hope and then… nothing. Mark and I just… drifted apart during it all. We're officially separated now. Oh, Amelia, I’m so sorry. That’s awful. I had no idea. You always seemed so… solid. Mark’s a lovely man. He is. And it wasn’t a dramatic falling out, thankfully. More of a slow, sad realization that we both wanted different things, and the IVF just exposed that. He wants the whole ‘family’ picture, two kids, a dog, the suburban dream. And I… I think I’m okay with the idea of forging a different path. And, well, I'm actually considering going for it alone. Going for it alone? As in… solo parenthood? Possibly. I’ve been doing a lot of thinking. And researching. And frankly, the idea is terrifying, but also… liberating. I've always wanted a child, and I don’t want to spend my forties waiting for ‘Mr. Right 2.0’ to come along. I'm looking into donor insemination. Wow. That’s… brave. It is a huge undertaking, though. It’s not easy, as you know from my work. But you're a brilliant teacher – patient, strong, incredibly resourceful. You'd be a fantastic mum, regardless. Thanks, that means a lot. What about you? Still battling fires as a social worker? It always sounded so draining. It is. It really is. But it's also incredibly rewarding. Although, I'm starting to feel a bit… burnt out, if I’m honest.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of marking I had last week was  criminal . Sixteen year olds, you know? They think a comma is some sort of optional extra. It’s like pulling teeth getting them to understand basic sentence structure. Sixteen year olds haven’t changed a bit, love. Had a classroom full of ‘em for thirty years. Always been the same. Think they know everything already. Though, I suppose back then it was more about split infinitives and less about… what are they obsessed with now? TikTok grammar? Worse! It’s abbreviations. Everything’s ‘lol’ and ‘idk’ bleeding into their essays. And don’t even  mention  full stops. It’s a lost cause, I tell you. It's disheartening when you've spent years studying linguistics, you know, the beautiful nuance of language, and they’re just… reducing it to emojis. Ah, well. You’re a language teacher, aren’t you? You’re fighting a losing battle then, aren’t you? Still, good on you for trying. I retired from teaching history, thankfully. Less concerned with the subtleties of the English language, more concerned with dates and battles. Though getting them to remember the causes of the English Civil War was a similar struggle, I admit. It’s the principle of it! And it's not just the grammar. It’s the apathy. They just don’t  care . It's a bit worrying for the future, isn't it? Speaking of the future, how's young Thomas doing? Last I heard he was thinking about university? He got in! Aston, to study engineering. Absolutely thrilled. A bit nervous about moving away, mind you. He’s always been a bit of a homebody. Your niece, Emily, she’s doing well too, isn’t she? I saw her down at the park with her little one the other day. She is! Absolutely thriving. Little Leo is a whirlwind, though. Keeps her on her toes. She says she wouldn’t swap it for the world, of course, but I suspect she needs a full week of uninterrupted sleep! It's a massive change for her, she was always so career-focused. It is, isn’t it? Completely turns your world upside down. Though, mind you, things are a bit dicey in this neighbourhood for young families. Heard about that break-in on Willow Road last week? Shocking. Oh, I did hear something! Awful.

…and honestly, lass, this brew's not a patch on what me mam makes. It's all about the water, y'know? Cambridge water just doesn’t  have  the right… mineral content, or somethin'. It's a scientific fact, probably. Oh, don't start with the water, Alfie. You say that about every cup of tea south of the Humber. It's perfectly decent. Besides, ANON’s made a lovely spread. These scones are really good. Did you try the clotted cream? They are rather good scones, yes. Though I’m still mourning the lack of a proper German  Käsekuchen . Everything's a bit…beige here, food-wise. No offense, of course. Beige? That’s a bit harsh, isn’t it, Ben? It’s classic British afternoon tea. It  should  be beige. Though I agree, a bit of variety is always welcome. Anyone seen that new Wes Anderson film yet? I thought it was visually stunning, but the plot felt a bit…thin. Wes Anderson? Is that the fella who does all them quirky, symmetrical films? I tried watchin' one once,  The Grand Budapest Hotel , think it was. Fell asleep fifteen minutes in. Too much fussin', not enough… punch. Give me a good action film any day. Or a gritty Northern drama. Alfie, you fall asleep during  everything . Remember that documentary about puffins we watched last month? You were out cold before they even showed the mating dance! And I liked  The Grand Budapest Hotel . It was whimsical. It’s not all about explosions, you know. Speaking of whimsical, has anyone heard that new band, "The Lunar Echoes"? They’re doing a gig in London next week. It's a bit indie-pop, but with some really interesting electronic elements. My sister's obsessed, she keeps sending me links. The Lunar Echoes… vaguely rings a bell. Are they the ones who did that remix of the old Joy Division track? I thought that was quite clever. I’ve been listening to a lot of classical lately, trying to cultivate some… sophistication, I suppose. It’s good for the brain, apparently. Keeps the cognitive decline at bay. Cognitive decline? You're only just turnin' thirty, lad! What are you on about? I'm more worried about me knees givin' out from walkin’ round Cambridge. All these cobblestones… a nightmare. And speaking of sophisticated, I tried listenin’ to opera once. Sounded like someone was bein’ murdered.

…and honestly, the weights room at the new PureGym is just  packed . Like, shoulder-to-shoulder at peak times. It's ridiculous. I went yesterday after work, thinking I could get a good session in, and ended up spending half an hour just waiting for a bench press.      Oh, no way! I’ve been meaning to check that one out. I thought it being bigger would mean more space. My current gym’s okay, but it's getting a little…samey. I need new motivation.      Samey is exactly the word! I nearly cancelled my membership last month because I was just doing the same circuit every single time. Then I remembered I’d already paid for the year. The joys of direct debit, eh?      Tell me about it. I just signed up for a climbing gym. Completely different challenge. Though my arms are screaming at me already. It’s a good scream though, you know? A productive scream.      Climbing, that's cool! Always wanted to try that. A bit beyond my coordination levels, I reckon. I’m firmly rooted in weights. Speaking of things needing coordination, anyone fancy a weekend away? I was looking at a cycling trip in the Peak District. They’ve got some decent routes.      Ooh, the Peak District sounds lovely. Though… the weather forecast is looking pretty grim for the next week, isn't it? It's been non-stop rain here in Cambridge. Feels like November, not June.      Absolutely miserable. I swear my flat’s developing damp just from looking at the sky. Cycling in that? No thanks. I’m holding out for a proper heatwave before I commit to outdoor adventures. I’m thinking maybe Portugal? Been ages since I’ve had proper sunshine.      Portugal sounds ambitious, Maya. You’re thinking big! I wouldn’t mind a little break somewhere… maybe Cornwall? It's easier and the coastal paths are pretty stunning. Plus, less chance of getting absolutely baked in the sun.      Cornwall's a good shout, Noah. Maybe a bit closer to home. I'm just desperate to get out of Cambridge for a bit. It's feeling very small at the moment. And speaking of needing an escape, anyone hear about Mrs. Henderson’s kids’ camp? Apparently, it's fully booked already.      Oh, the one at Grantchester Meadows? Yes! My mum was asking about that for her grandkids. Said they started taking bookings in March.

Honestly, this is painful to watch. Newcastle are playing like they’ve never seen a football before. And it's only half-time! Come on, now, Geordie lass. Don’t be so dramatic. It's a bit scrappy, yeah, but they’ve had their chances. And it  is  just half-time. Plenty of time to pull it back. Though, I’ll admit, that defending was… optimistic. Optimistic? It was shambolic! Honestly, I don't know what Eddie Howe is telling them in the changing room. They’re letting them run rings around them. I thought this season was supposed to be different. Remember all the hype? Top four finish? Champions League? Hype is hype. It's always overblown. Though, I did get sucked into it a bit myself. It's just, you know, football. It’s unpredictable. Still, a good game, regardless. Better than doomscrolling on Twitter, anyway. Speaking of which, did you see anything about that new Wes Anderson film? Oh,  Asteroid City ? Yeah, trailers look brilliant. Very…Wes Anderson. All symmetry and muted colours. Proper quirky. Trying to convince my mam to go with me. She thinks anything that isn't a period drama with Colin Firth is ‘rubbish’. Your mam is a woman of strong opinions! She’d probably say the same about this game, if she was watching. "Too much running about, not enough manners." Though, she did enjoy  Paddington … That’s a loophole.  Paddington  is universally loved. And it  does  have a certain British decorum. Anyway, back to footballing disasters. Look at that – another giveaway! Honestly, I’m starting to think I should just switch over to something else. Maybe watch that documentary about David Hockney you mentioned? Good shout. Though, stick it out a little longer. It might get more interesting. And plus, we've got those eggs we need to decorate for Easter tomorrow. I was thinking we could try and do those really intricate Ukrainian egg designs. Ooh, ambitious! I remember seeing those online. They’re beautiful, but they look incredibly fiddly. Do we even have the right tools? I think all we’ve got is some felt tips and a few stray glitter pens left over from Christmas. We can improvise! It’s the spirit of Easter, isn’t it? Plus, I did order a proper pysanky kit. Should be here sometime this week. It's a bit late, I know, but I thought it would be a nice thing to try.

Ah, now look at young Leo there. Must’ve been… eight, maybe nine? At that funfair down in Midleton. He was obsessed with those whirly-gig rides, weren’t he? Nearly threw up every time, God love him, but he'd queue right back up for another go. Wow, he  does  look green! And is that… Uncle David trying to win him a giant teddy? He  never  wins anything at funfairs. No, he doesn’t. He's got the worst luck, your father. He’d lose money on a sure thing. But he always pretends he’s a master strategist. Remember that time he tried to knock down those milk bottles at the Bray carnival? Spent a fortune. Oh, Bray! I took your mother there every year. Lovely spot. Used to be proper seaside glamour there, back in the day. Not like these modern funfairs, all flashing lights and sticky floors. Glamour’s a strong word, Moira! It was always a bit… chaotic. Though, to be fair, Leo loved the chaos. He’s a bit like his grandfather in that way, always needs a bit of excitement. Speaking of excitement, did you see anything of the London Marathon on the telly, Margaret? I caught bits and pieces, while trying to stop little Thomas dismantling the sofa. It looked brutal. All those people, pushing themselves... Mrs. Henderson at school ran it! She’s amazing. She finished in, like, four hours and something. Four hours? That's a proper achievement, so it is. I tried to run a marathon myself, years ago. Made it about ten miles before my knees started screaming. I’m more of a pint-and-a-chat man these days. Running! Give me a good walk any day. I used to walk miles with the children when they were little. Building up their little legs. Reminds me, I must ask Leo if he's still doing the cross-country at school. He is, and he’s actually quite good. He's got a bit of a competitive streak, just like you, Mother. Remember when you wouldn’t let anyone win at Scrabble? A bit of healthy competition never hurt anyone! It builds character. Though, perhaps I was…  enthusiastic  occasionally. Now, tell me about this Iceland trip you were talking about, Colm. Is it definitely on? It is. Booked the flights last week. We’re going in October, hoping to catch the Northern Lights.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of emails I had to wade through this week was ridiculous. It’s like everyone suddenly decided Monday was the perfect day to launch every project they’ve been putting off for months. Did you manage to escape the deluge, Carol? Escape is a strong word, Penelope. More… navigate. There was a payroll issue, naturally. Old Mr. Henderson's NI number was entered incorrectly  again . Honestly, you’d think after thirty years he’d remember it! But it wasn't  too  bad. Though Mum was on the phone, predictably, wanting to know if I’d remembered to put the bins out. Oh, mothers. They're a constant, aren't they? Mine still rings to ask if I'm wearing enough layers, even in August. Speaking of constant, this apple crumble is heavenly. You’ve outdone yourself, again. It’s just my nan’s recipe. Simple, really. Apples, butter, a dash of cinnamon… and a whole lot of love, I suppose. Mum used to make it too, though she always insisted on adding raisins. Ruined it, if you ask me. Raisins are perfectly lovely, dear. Though I do agree, a good Bramley apple needs little embellishment. You know, your grandmother, Penelope, she was a champion crumble maker. Used to win prizes at the village fete, she did. Really, Gran? I didn’t know that! You’ve always been a woman of hidden talents. It's funny the things you find out, isn't it? It’s a small world. I was talking to a client just yesterday – a Mr. Davies – and it turns out his sister went to school with my brother in Boston! Oh, it  is  a small world! I ran into Mrs. Peterson from down the road at the supermarket last week. Haven’t seen her since… well, since my wedding, I think! She was asking after your father, Penelope. Said he still talks about that cricket match they played against the village team back in ‘78. Oh, Dad and his cricket stories. Endless. He’s still convinced he was robbed of a century. Remember when we used to play cricket in the garden, Carol? Using Mum’s laundry baskets as stumps? How could I forget? And you were  always  cheating, trying to move the stumps when nobody was looking! I was the umpire, naturally. Strict but fair. Then we moved onto ‘shops’ didn't we?

…Honestly, Doreen, this coronation chicken is a bit dry, innit? Not like your mum used to make. She always had a lovely dollop of mango chutney in hers. Gave it a bit of…zing, you know? Oh, Harold, you always say that. You say  everything  isn’t quite like my mum’s. It's a legacy, I suppose. And honestly, you’ve had three sandwiches already! Don’t need an excuse to complain. I used a new recipe, tried to be a bit healthier with the mayonnaise. Healthier? At our age, Doreen? What's the point of being 'healthy' when you're practically antique furniture? A bit of proper mayo never hurt anyone. Though, come to think of it, Old Man Hemmings did have a bad turn after the village fete…but that was probably the pickled onions. Always blaming something else, aren’t you? It was probably just his heart, Harold. Poor man. Still, you’re avoiding the point. I thought we could talk about… well, about Arthur. Arthur? What about him? Still sending those postcards from Australia? Showing off, the young rascal. Says he’s found some sort of…opportunity, didn't he? Something to do with sheep. Not exactly. He called, actually. Quite a long call. He wants to…well, he wants us to consider moving. Moving?! Where to? Australia? Are you mad? I haven’t even mastered the remote control as it is, let alone a different continent! And what about the garden? My tomatoes are just coming along nicely! No, no, not Australia. He’s bought a little cottage in Cornwall. Says it’s much closer. He wants us to come and live near him. He’s worried about us, Harold. Getting on a bit, him saying. Needing help… Worried, is he? After all the trouble he caused when he was a lad! Sneaking out, failing his exams… now  he’s  the responsible one, wanting to put us in a home for the elderly disguised as a Cornish cottage. It isn’t a home for the elderly, Harold! It’s a perfectly nice cottage. And he’s not trying to get rid of us, he's trying to look after us. He remembers how lonely we were after your sister passed. He's thinking ahead. Lonely? We’re not lonely! We have each other, don’t we? And Mrs. Higgins pops round for a chat. And the telly.

…and honestly, little Timmy actually  ate  a glittery pom-pom. A whole one. I thought I was going to have to call his mum, thinking he’d choked, but no, just crunching away happily. Apparently, they taste like…nothing. Which is even more worrying, innit? Oh,  no ! That’s awful, and hilarious. Kids are just… absorbent. Like little, chaotic sponges. I had one try to trade me a half-eaten biscuit for a stapler yesterday. A  stapler , Elsie! What does a six-year-old even  do  with a stapler? Oh my god, that is peak primary school. Honestly, the things you hear. Reminds me of my little cousin, Leo. Tried to convince my aunt he’d trained the cat to do algebra. Apparently, Patches was ‘very good at x and y’. Patches doing algebra! That's brilliant. Right, okay, shifting gears. Has anyone actually, you know,  started  thinking about Christmas presents? I’m already panicking. My Nan keeps hinting she wants a “fancy foot warmer.” A fancy foot warmer! What even  is  a fancy foot warmer?! Oh, don’t even get me started on the present stress. My brother and his girlfriend are doing “experiences only” this year. Which sounds lovely, ‘til you realise you have to, like, buy them a pottery class or something. And then pray they actually enjoy it. Experiences are a nightmare. Last year, I got my Dad a hot air balloon ride. He’s terrified of heights. He sent me a very polite, very passive-aggressive text saying, “That was… adventurous.” I think he meant terrifying. Oh dear god. See, I'm terrible at adventurous gifts. I'd rather just get people socks. Good quality socks though, obviously. Like, cashmere socks. Is that too much? No, cashmere socks are  always  a win. Practical and posh. Speaking of practical, my car is making this awful clunking noise again. I swear, it’s like a disgruntled robot suffering from indigestion. Oh no! Not again! Is it the same thing as last time? The exhaust? You’re going to end up spending your entire Christmas bonus on car repairs. Probably! It is, actually. The mechanic said something about needing a whole new system, and I just nodded along pretending to understand what he was saying. I'm pretty sure he saw right through me. Men. Mechanics especially. They just speak a different language. My uncle, bless him, he thinks he's a car expert.

…and honestly, the state of the garden is a disgrace. Absolute disgrace. Old Man Hemmings next door  says  he’s going to tidy it, but he's been sayin’ that for six months now. It's a jungle out there, a proper jungle. You wouldn't believe the bindweed.      Oh, don’t start on Old Man Hemmings, Klaus. You know he’s got arthritis something awful. He  tries . It’s just…slow going. And frankly, a bit of wilderness is nice. Keeps the foxes happy.      It's a bit rough around here, isn't it? I mean, compared to where I used to work, near Smithdown Road. Everything was so…polished. Though, you pay for that polish, don’t you? This area feels…real.      Real messy. Like Ron Weasley’s bedroom.      Aye, a bit like that, lad. Real messy. But it has character. Though, I do worry about the increased…activity, you know? Down by the docks. Saw a group of lads hanging about the other night, looking a bit shifty.      Oh, don’t worry yourself, Klaus. It’s always been like that. Just kids being kids, mostly. Though, I did hear Mrs. Davies talking about some trouble with a motorbike being stolen.      It’s worrying, though, isn't it? With everything going on in the world… ISIS and all. Makes you think twice about letting your kids walk home from school alone.      Exactly! It used to be you worried about the odd scuffle, maybe a broken window. Now… it feels different. It’s all so…globalised, even here in L8. I was reading an article about radicalisation online, targeting vulnerable young people. Dreadful stuff.      Is ISIS like Voldemort? Really bad and wants to take over everything?      In a way, love. But real. Not magic. Much, much worse than magic.      A very apt comparison, actually, young man. Voldemort was a demagogue, preying on fear. ISIS does the same, only with… considerably more destructive means. Speaking of destructive, how’s your mum doing, Marie? I haven’t seen her at the shops lately.      Oh, she’s been poorly, Klaus. A bad chest. The doctor thinks it might be bronchitis. She’s mostly laid up, which isn't like her. She's usually volunteering at the school, helping with the reading group. I’m trying to cover everything, but it’s a struggle with the house and everything.      I'm sorry to hear that.

Honestly, Nepal feels…daunting. I’ve done quite a bit of travelling, you know, mostly Europe when the children were little, a bit of North Africa, but nothing like  Nepal . It’s the altitude that bothers me, I think. Remember that trip to the Dolomites, Margaret? Even  that  left me breathless, and that wasn’t nearly as high. Oh, the Dolomites! Lovely, weren’t they?
