Though I mostly remember the price of the wine! But Nepal… well, it will be different. I went to Thailand a few years back, and the heat and humidity were shocking, really. But you acclimatise, don’t you? And the scenery… I’ve seen pictures, it’s breathtaking. Are you worried about the food? I’m always a bit cautious with street food, even now. Speaking of food, has anyone been to the Village Shop lately? They’ve started doing those posh sausages – the ones with apple and something, I can’t remember. They’re frightfully expensive, but apparently, they’re lovely. Of course, I still prefer a good Cumberland, but… one has to try new things. Though frankly, I find their coffee dreadful. Oh, the Village Shop! They’ve upped their prices something awful. I tried to get some decent coffee there last week and nearly had a heart attack. I get mine from the Farm Shop now. It’s a bit of a drive, but it’s worth it. And yes, new sausages are a bit much. My Arthur’s a whizz with a sausage, you know. Makes a proper batch every other week. It reminds me of wartime, actually, making do and mending, knowing exactly what went  into  your food. Wartime food... My mother-in-law, bless her, had the most incredible story. She was born in Siberia, you see, and when the war started, escaped  across  Russia, all the way to Africa! Can you imagine? No proper food for months, travelling on carts, sleeping rough… She always said she appreciated a good roast beef after that, and wasn’t fussy about what sort of vegetable accompanied it. Goodness me, that's a story! I’ve been dealing with a different sort of hardship lately - the new free school meals system. Honestly, it’s a nightmare. Trying to cater for all the allergies and intolerances... We've got three gluten-free children in Year 3 alone! It's not just gluten, either - nuts, eggs, dairy… Lunchboxes are basically minefields.

Right, so then the speaker, this bloke, he’s going on about ‘synergy’ for a full ten minutes. Synergy! Like we’re all suddenly gonna magically work better just by  saying  the word. Honestly, I nearly choked on my tea. You wouldn’t believe the state of some of these motivational speakers, would ya? Oh, I  totally  would believe it. My aunt Brenda went on one of those team-building retreats. Came back talking about ‘blue sky thinking’ and ‘moving the goalposts’ non-stop for weeks. Drove my mum mad. Was this for the food & beverage conference? Aye, that’s the one. It’s always the same with these things, isn’t it? Loads of money spent, fancy venue, and then some charlatan waffling on about buzzwords. At least the catering was decent, I’ll give ‘em that. Though apparently, old Mr. Henderson complained his vol-au-vents were ‘too flaky’. Honestly. Vol-au-vents and complaints…sounds like a typical Tuesday for someone organising events, doesn’t it, Amy? Want a biscuit? Ginger nut? Cheers, Chloe! And you’ve hit the nail on the head. It's always  something . I'm starting to think people just go to these things to find things to moan about. Being flaky is their full-time job. So, how  is  the new job going overall? Besides the flaky vol-au-vent clientele. You’ve been at it a couple of months now, haven't you? Is it… chaotic? I’m imagining a lot of last-minute panics. Chaotic is an understatement. It's a whirlwind. It’s not the actual events that are the issue, it’s the build-up. Emails multiply like rabbits, people changing their minds, dietary requirements appearing five minutes before the deadline… It’s a miracle anything actually  happens . But… it's good, innit? Keeps me on my toes. Though I miss just… sitting down and  thinking  sometimes, you know? I get that. My job’s fairly steady, thankfully. Mostly data entry and booking meetings. Not exactly stimulating, but it has its moments. Plus, the office gossip is  excellent . How’s Cambridge treating you, anyway, Liv? You’ve been here almost a year now, haven't you? It's good! Really good. It took a while to adjust coming from London – everything feels so… peaceful. And slow. But in a nice way, mostly. The work's demanding at the plant, lots of pressure to keep production streamlined, but the team’s brilliant.

…and honestly, the sheer  audacity  of them, David. Saying it’s ‘underutilised’. Old Man Hemmings practically  lives  there. And Mrs. Patel does her computer classes. It's more than just books, you know? It's a community hub. Mmmhmm. Borough council are just… short-sighted. Always are. They see a patch of land, think ‘luxury flats’, and ignore everything else. It’s infuriating. Though, to be fair, Plumstead library isn’t exactly bustling on a Tuesday afternoon, is it? That’s because everyone’s at work! Or doing the school run! They’ve deliberately chosen times to go and observe when it  will  be quiet. It’s manipulation, that’s what it is. We need to fight this. I was thinking… a petition. A proper one, online and paper, and we get everyone to sign. A petition? Good idea. I can help with that. I'm fairly tech-savvy, I could set up the online one, no problem. Though getting paper signatures… that’ll be a slog. Remember the one for the bus route change? Hours we spent standing outside Tesco. I do. Frostbite and disgruntled commuters. But it worked, didn’t it? They rerouted it. We have to be visible, David. Relentless. I’ve already started drafting some wording. Something about the vital role of libraries in fostering literacy and community… a bit worthy, perhaps, but it needs to be impactful. Sounds good. Less ‘worthy’ and more ‘what will happen to our kids if they take away their access to free resources’ is always a good angle. People react to that. Right, my shift. Back to the coal face, unfortunately. Another four hours of spreadsheets and passive-aggressive emails. Oh, don't remind me about work. My ears are still ringing from transcribing that legal deposition yesterday. Honestly, the amount of jargon! I felt my brain cells actively  dying . It was all about ‘due diligence’ and ‘contractual obligations’. Dreadful. Tell me about it. My boss is obsessed with ‘synergies’ and ‘optimising workflows’. It's corporate speak gone mad. Honestly, I think he just likes the sound of his own voice. Speaking of brain-frying things… have you been doing any of those Lumosity things? Brain training apps? Briefly. I downloaded one. Found it… incredibly frustrating. I couldn't remember the ridiculous mnemonics they gave me. ‘My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles’ for the planets, anyone? It just added another layer of remembering.

…and honestly, Doreen, you wouldn’t  believe  the cheek of ‘em. Two of ‘em this morning, right on the doorstep. Jehovah’s Witnesses again. Honestly, I said, “Look, I’ve told you lot before, I'm not interested. I've got my own beliefs, thank you very much.” They just keep coming back. Persistent, they are. Positively relentless. Aye, they do that, don’t they, Arthur? Been gettin’ ‘em myself, regular as clockwork. Young lad this time, looked barely out of school. I just shut the door, mind. No point in arguin’. Waste of breath, that is. You get nowhere. Oh, they were round last week. I gave the young lady a biscuit though. Seemed a nice girl. Doesn't mean I'm convertin’, mind! Just…polite. Though I do wonder if they think a biscuit will sway us. A biscuit! Doreen, you’re too kind! It encourages 'em, it does. It’s like feedin’ a pigeon. They’ll be back tomorrow, expectin’ a digestive. Speaking of which, this ploughman’s is lovely, thank you, Doreen. Finest you’ve made yet, I reckon. Though a bit more pickle wouldn’t go amiss, eh? Always moanin’ about the pickle, Arthur. You'd put pickle on yer toast if you could get away with it. Did you hear young Timmy Barker's finally gettin' married? To that girl from Dereham, the one with the red hair? Oh, yes! Lovely couple. Though I do worry about him. She’s a bit…strong-willed, isn’t she? He’s always been a bit of a pushover, poor Timmy. Reminds me a bit of when Harold and I first got together. I wore the trousers, always have done, really. Harold didn’t seem to mind, though. You two were always a good team. Marriage. A tricky business, ain't it? Used to be you could rely on a good village wedding, a proper knees-up. Now they all go off to the Maldives or somewhere. No sense of community. Don’t start on the Maldives, Arthur. You know what I think of all that flashiness. Remember old Mr. Peterson? Swore blind he wouldn’t pay taxes anymore, said it was all goin’ to waste on fancy foreign holidays. Ah, Peterson. A character alright. Always complainin' about the council. And his garden! Never tidy. A real eyesore, it was. You could hardly get down the lane for all his clutter.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of logs Old Man Hemmings delivered is ridiculous. It's piled up nearly to the shed roof! I feel like we're preparing for an ice age, not just winter. Are you  sure  we needed quite so many? He’s a generous soul, love. And a good price, remember? We did get a discount. Besides, with this log burner you insisted on… well, it’s a hungry beast, isn’t it? Much better than that gas fire, though. No arguing about that, I hope? Oh, a log burner is  essential . Reminds me of the school common room. Always a cheery glow. Though, we had a proper groundsman dealing with the wood back then, not a harassed administrator and a transcriber trying to organise it all. Harassed is the word, Margaret. Absolutely harassed. Though, I must say, the burner does look rather splendid in here. Makes the room. Reminds me of our old school library, actually. All dark wood and warmth. Still, too many logs  are  a fire hazard, you know. Tidiness is next to godliness. Tidiness is impossible with two cats shedding everywhere! And don’t even get me started on the state of the sofa. I’ve been meaning to get it re-upholstered for ages. Found a lovely man down at the antique shop in Rye, he does amazing work. Rye? You went to Rye again? Honestly, you’ll bankrupt us with all those antique shop trips! Remember that little porcelain shepherdess? Still haven’t forgiven you for that one. Oh, don’t be stingy, Alistair. A little indulgence is good for the soul. Besides, a good antique is an investment, or so they say. Speaking of investments… how's the budget looking, dear? You were fretting about it last week. The budget is… looming. It’s all those little bits and pieces adding up. And the potential cost of the sofa. And, well, your trip back from Tokyo last month wasn’t exactly cheap, Mum. Although it was lovely to have you. Tokyo! Amazing city. Though, I find the travelling rather exhausting these days. Everything feels so… frenetic. Give me a quiet Scottish loch any day. Reminds me of my childhood summers. It’s funny, isn't it? You've lived in England for decades, Dad, but you still identify as Scottish. Naturally! It’s in the blood. Though, I do admit, the mashed potato here is superior to anything I had in Japan.

…and honestly, the whole thing’s a fiddle, isn’t it? This council tax. Went up again this year. For what? They haven’t fixed a pothole on my road in fifteen years. Fifteen years, Arthur! Fifteen years? You’re a lucky one then, Derek. They haven't even  looked  at the road outside my place since Maggie Thatcher was in power. Seriously. It’s like driving over the moon. And the amount they want now… back in my day, it was a reasonable sum. A fella could afford it on his pension without needing to eat biscuits for dinner every night. Biscuits are a perfectly good dinner, Arthur. Particularly Hobnobs. But you’ve got a point. It’s daylight robbery. And then they wonder why people don’t recycle properly. If they spent less on fancy schemes and more on actually  collecting  the bins when they’re supposed to… Oh, don’t even get me started on recycling! I had Mrs. Higgins next door practically lecturing me last week because I put a yogurt pot in the wrong bin. A yogurt pot! Honestly, it’s like we’re all supposed to be experts in plastics and polymers. It’s the principle of the thing, Margaret. They make it so complicated, people just give up. Like that new Sat Nav I got. Supposed to be the latest model, voice activation and everything. Utter rubbish. Keeps trying to take me through fields! I ended up near Attleborough last Tuesday, ended up on a farm track. Nearly lost a tyre. A farm track, eh? Serves you right for trusting those things, Derek. I’ve always said a good old-fashioned map is best. You know where you are with a map. My brother, he got completely lost in Scotland a few years back, relying on one of those Sat Navs. Ended up miles from anywhere, had to call the Mountain Rescue. Goodness me! Scotland sounds lovely, though. A bit remote, maybe, but lovely. I always wanted to go. Though, frankly, driving anywhere these days fills me with dread. The traffic! And the young drivers. No manners. They're all glued to their phones. Speaking of remote, did you see that programme on TV the other night? About that bloke who lives on that island off the Hebrides? No electricity, no running water, catches his own fish… Aye, I saw that. Mad as a brush, that fella.

That was a grand bit of roasted chicken, Mary. Honestly, a grand bit. Though, I’m still thinkin’ about that laptop. Young Leo’s been beside himself since it went belly up. It  is  belly up, Dad. Properly broken. I tried everything you told me, Ctrl+Alt+Delete, restarting… nothing. It just… black screens. Honestly, Liam, you’d think it was the end of the world the way he’s carrying on. It’s just a computer. Though, I can see why he's upset, he needs it for schoolwork. Did you check the warranty again? Aye, I did. And that’s the kicker, isn’t it? Expired last month. By a week! A  week , Mary. Talk about bad luck. Seems they’re happy to sell ya the thing, but not so happy to stand over it when it kicks the bucket. It's just the principle of the thing. 'Poof!' Like magic! Gone black! He was playing that new racing game, the really realistic one. I reckon he probably pushed it too hard. Realistically, it was probably a graphics card issue. I had a look inside, and it  looks  like it, anyhow. I might be able to salvage it, order a replacement card online. It’s fiddly, but I’ve done worse. Fiddly is an understatement, Liam. You’ll be covered in dust and tiny screws for a week. Leo, stop poking your brother, darling. And do you have any idea how much those cards cost? Not a fortune, thankfully. About eighty quid or so, but if I can get it working, it's cheaper than a new laptop, that's for sure. Speaking of costs, has anyone sorted out the transport for the rugby tomorrow? I promised young Finn I’d take him and Mikey. I can go with them, Dad. I don’t mind. Unless you want to watch the match  with  us, then it might get a bit… loud. Appreciate that, son. Loud's grand with you! I think I will, though. I'll need someone to keep an eye on Finn and Mikey; they're like two little whirlwinds when they get excited. Now, is anyone else raging for more sauce with their fajitas? This stuff is good, even if it  is  a bit sweet. Oh, I am. It’s actually quite good with the chicken, isn’t it? A little too much sugar, but… we’ll allow it.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of glitter that ended up in the fairy garden was concerning. It’s everywhere. I’m still finding it in my hair. It  needed  glitter, Mummy! Fairies  love  glitter. Like, even more than pizza. No way! Pizza is the best! Even better than finding dinosaur bones! A very strong claim, Leo. A very strong claim indeed. Though, you did get rather excited about that little fossil we found in the garden. Right, pizza. Who wants another slice? I ordered a large, hopefully that was enough. Me! But can I have one with only pepperoni? And can I build a little house for the pepperoni on my slice? I want a mushroom one! And can we talk about Nessie again? Is she real? One pepperoni house coming right up, Elsie. And Leo, we  have  talked about Nessie ad nauseam. We’ve looked at pictures, watched documentaries... she’s a legend. A  very  famous legend, but probably not real. But what if she  is  real? What if she’s really good at hiding? Maybe she’s wearing camouflage? That’s…a good point. Very clever thinking, Leo. Maybe she is. But that begs the question, why would a giant, prehistoric monster need camouflage? To trick people! So they don't take her picture and put her on the telly! She likes being secret. That’s a clever fairy garden mind at work, Elsie. Speaking of secrets… you two have been awfully quiet all afternoon. Any secret plans brewing? We were trying to do handstands! But I keep falling over. Elsie’s getting better, though. I can almost hold it for five seconds now! It’s really hard. You have to…wiggle your toes, apparently. Mr. Harrison told us. Mr. Harrison gives excellent advice. Toes are key. It’s all about core strength, you know. Though maybe wait until  after  the pizza before attempting acrobatics. Right, Elsie, are you enjoying yours? It’s good! But… I wanted to wear my sparkly party dress to eat pizza. Your sparkly party dress? Elsie, darling, that’s a bit…much for a Tuesday night pizza. I think she should wear it! It would be really shiny! Like Nessie’s scales! Well, now you’re trying to gang up on me. Fine,  if  you promise not to spill pizza sauce on it. But if you do, you're washing it! Yay! Sparkly pizza party!

Honestly, this is  miles  better than that little place we had lunch yesterday. That pasta… it tasted like it’d been sitting under a heat lamp since Tuesday. This Peka though… proper lovely.      Aye, you were right to be dubious, love. Tourist traps, they are. This is what you get when you get a little off the beaten track. Old Man Miro’s been doing this Peka for forty years, I reckon. You can taste the experience.      It’s good. Really good. But I’m trying to get a signal to upload this photo to Insta. The light’s perfect. It shows off the colours of Rovinj really well.      Rovinj  is  photogenic. Reminds me a bit of a smaller, slightly more… chaotic, Venice. Though I’m still partial to Pula. All that Roman history. It’s impressive. You know, I was working with a firm that did some consultancy for the local council there a few years back. They were trying to revitalize the amphitheatre.      Pula was alright, a bit too busy for me. I preferred Motovun. So peaceful, wandering around the walls. But honestly, the drive up was terrifying. Those single-track roads! I thought we were going to end up in a ditch.      You and your driving! You’ve never driven in Bolton traffic, have you? Those roads are nothing. Remember Mrs. Higgins trying to parallel park her Rover? That was a sight to behold.      What’s a Rover? Is it like, a really old car? Like something from Grandad’s shed?      More or less. They stopped making them ages ago. And yeah, Bolton traffic is… a unique experience. Especially around the market.      Speaking of unique experiences, I was reading an article on the plane about vertical farming. Apparently, they’re developing these systems that can produce food in completely controlled environments. Imagine, no more worrying about weather affecting crops. Steve Jobs would have loved that kind of innovation.      Vertical farming? Sounds a bit… sterile, doesn't it? I like the thought of things growing naturally, in the sun. That’s what this food here tastes like - sunshine and fresh air. Though, I did recently read about lab-grown meat. Now  that  I found disturbing.      Oh, don’t get me started on lab-grown meat. It feels… wrong. I mean, I’m not exactly a vegan, but there’s something about the idea of something grown in a petri dish.

Right proper lunch that was, Doreen. Though I still say you put too much pepper in the coleslaw. Gives me a tickle, it does. And you know I ain’t got the strongest stomach these days. Oh, don't be daft, Arthur. A little pepper never hurt anyone. It  needs  a bit of something, doesn’t it? Besides, you had two helpings. You didn't complain then! And Harold, are you listening to us, or just staring at the telly again? Mmm? Just… catching the news. Dreadful business, this debt collection agency thing. Apparently, they’re getting rather aggressive. Read an article about it in  The Telegraph  this morning. Seems a lot of people were mis-sold PPI years ago and are now facing the consequences. Aggressive is an understatement. My sister-in-law, Brenda, is absolutely beside herself. They're threatening court action, even though she’s already paid out a substantial amount. It's a scandal, honestly. These companies… vultures, that's what they are. PPI… sounds like one of them fancy new illnesses. Always somethin’ new, innit? I’ve never understood all that financial business anyway. Always left that to your mother, Doreen. She was the sensible one with the money. Now, are we still on for Marjorie’s party next Saturday? She’s been on about it for weeks. Of course, we are, Arthur. I've already got a new outfit. Though I swear, finding something decent these days is harder than it used to be. Everything’s too…flashy. And Harold, you  are  ignoring us! Are you even listening about Marjorie’s party? Sorry, Doreen. Just thinking about Brenda. She's rather fragile, you know. I’m going to have a word with our solicitor, see if there's anything he can do. It’s utterly stressful for her. Party sounds good though. A distraction, certainly. Good idea, Harold. And Arthur, yes, we’re all going to Marjorie’s. I promised to help with the singing. She's trying to get a little choir going for the hymns. Apparently, they haven’t had a proper sing in St. Alban’s Abbey for months. Singing, eh? Now there’s a thought. I used to sing in the church choir back in Costessey. Proper bass, I was. Though my voice ain't what it was, not by a long chalk. Still, a good chorus always lifts the spirits.

Honestly, that was a  long  day. Another string of benefit fraud cases. You’d think people would just… be honest. It's so draining, hearing all the stories. Though, Mr. Henderson’s attempt to claim for a non-existent chihuahua was… something else. Oh, aye. You get all sorts, don’t ye? I’ve seen a man try to claim he couldn’t attend jury duty because his goldfish was having an existential crisis. A  goldfish , mind you! This job keeps ye grounded, that’s for sure. Though it’s a bit depressing sometimes, seeing folk in trouble. Exactly! And the sheer volume… I sometimes wonder if the system is actually helping, or just… processing. I mean, is a £200 fine going to change someone's circumstances, or just push them further down? It makes you question things, doesn’t it? Especially when you're trying to teach ethics and responsible citizenship to teenagers all day. It does, lass. It really does. My own grandson, wee Jamie, he's at uni now, studying… well, something with computers, I canna remember the name of it. He was saying the other day how broken everything is. The climate, the economy, politics... He’s got a point, of course. Though he thinks everything can be fixed with an app. Bless him. That’s the generation, isn’t it? Optimistic despite everything. My sister’s daughter is the same. She’s convinced solar panels on every roof are the answer to everything. Which, to be fair, isn't a terrible idea. It’s just… the logistics, the cost. It’s all so complicated. Getting anywhere these days feels expensive, doesn't it? The trains are a joke. Don’t even  start  me on the trains! I had to come all the way from Birmingham New Street today. Delayed, packed like sardines, and cost me a fortune. Back in my day, you could get a return to London for a fiver. A  fiver ! Now it’s… highway robbery. I miss the days of a decent bus service, myself. Reliable, affordable… I know. It makes travelling seem like a luxury, rather than something accessible. I’d love to go back to Italy, you know? I spent a year teaching English near Florence after university. The food, the people, the sunshine… But the thought of the flights and the cost of living there now… it feels out of reach.

…and honestly, the best part of the day wasn’t  getting  the good grade back on that essay, it was seeing your faces when I told you. That was brilliant. Truly brilliant. Mummy, you got a  really  good grade! Like, a superstar grade! Better than mine in spelling? I got eight right! Eight is  excellent , darling! Absolutely fantastic. But my grade was… well, it meant the headteacher emailed me personally. It's not about the grade itself, you see. It’s about knowing you two were so pleased for me. That's what makes me happy. If we had loads and loads of money, would that make you happy too? Like, a mountain of money? A REALLY big mountain? Bigger than Mr. Henderson’s garden shed? Oh, goodness. A mountain bigger than Mr. Henderson’s shed? That’s a very big mountain. Well, money can  help  with happiness, I suppose. It could buy us a new swing set for the garden, or maybe a trip to the seaside. We could buy ALL the ice cream! Every flavour! And sprinkles! And a robot! A robot that does my homework! A robot homework-doer… tempting, I admit. But you know, even with all the ice cream and robot helpers in the world, it wouldn’t automatically make us happy, would it? Why not? Because happiness isn’t  in  things, sweetie. It’s… well, it's more about how we  feel  inside. It’s about spending time together, laughing, and helping each other. Like when we built the fort in the living room? Even though it took ages and Mummy said it was a bit messy? Exactly! Remember how much fun we had? That wasn’t about anything we bought. It was about  doing  something together. It was about teamwork and imagination. That's the stuff that truly makes me happy. If we had loads of money, we wouldn’t have time to build forts. We'd be too busy… spending it! You’re a very clever girl. You might be right. It's easy to get caught up in wanting more and more things, isn't it? But sometimes, the simple things are the best. Do you know what rhymes with ‘happy’? … flappy? Like a bird? That’s a good one! Flappy is a good rhyme. But I was thinking of ‘crappy’. As in, a bad day. Because even on a crappy day, we can still find little things to be happy about.

Honestly, Mr. Davies is  obsessed  with China. Like, every lesson somehow circles back to their economic growth. It's Geography, not 'China Studies 101'! He was going on about Shenzhen again today, calling it the next Silicon Valley. Tell me about it! He practically drooled when talking about their high-speed rail. I get it, it’s impressive, but it’s not  relevant  to the causes of desertification, is it? Which is what the actual lesson was supposed to be about. It feels like he’s prepping us all to be international business people or something. Exactly! And then he started talking about investment. “Think about the opportunities, lads!” he said. Opportunities for  who , Mr. Davies? I’m trying to figure out if I even want to go to uni, let alone invest in some tech startup in Guangdong province. He even mentioned patents. Said loads of people are making fortunes applying for patents in China because the system is… easier? I don’t even understand what a patent  is  properly, never mind how to exploit one in a different country. Apparently, it’s like, you invent something, and you get legal protection so no one else can copy it for a set amount of time? My cousin Mark’s been looking into it. He’s got this idea for a self-watering plant pot. Properly nerdy, but he reckons it could be big. A self-watering plant pot? Seriously? That's… niche. But I suppose if it’s innovative enough… He’s the engineering one, isn't he? Always tinkering with stuff. I'm more of a ‘what’s the point?’ kind of guy. I keep thinking about careers. Everyone’s asking what we want to do. It's terrifying. Tell me about it. My mum’s convinced I should be a doctor. Says it's 'stable'. Stable sounds… boring. I was actually thinking something to do with game design. But then Mr. Davies started going on about AI and how all creative jobs will be automated within ten years. Wonderful. See! That’s what I mean! It's like, whatever you choose, it's automatically going to be useless in the future. I’ve been looking at finance, maybe. It's… money. Everyone needs money. And apparently, understanding how China’s economy works is a massive advantage in investment banking. Mr. Davies would be pleased. Ugh, don’t tell me you're considering investment banking.

… honestly, I think that run was a bit ambitious for a first one back. My legs are  screaming . You were a machine, gliding down like it was nothing. Oh, come on, don't exaggerate! You were fine! Just a little rusty, that’s all. It’s been three years, isn't it? Since Austria? I’m just naturally gifted, clearly. Naturally gifted at making me feel inadequate, more like. Remember that time in Austria when you ended up in that…snowdrift? Gifted then, were you? Okay, low blow. That was a rogue drift! And I  did  get myself out, eventually. Besides, you face-planted shortly after. We’re even. Anyway, are you going to eat those fries or just stare at them mournfully? They're lovely, proper chips, not those skinny things we get back home. I'm trying to build up the strength to move my legs again, thank you very much. And yes, these are excellent. This place is surprisingly good. I was expecting… Bulgarian hotel food. Not this. Me too! I read some awful reviews online, but it's been a pleasant surprise. Right, so, skiing tomorrow. Gentle slopes only for you, I think. Perhaps we could stick with the nursery slopes for a bit? Just to ease you back in. The nursery slopes? Seriously? I’m not  that  bad. Just… cautious. How are the kids enjoying it? Have they managed to stay upright? They're loving it! Leo's showing off already, thinks he's an Olympic athlete. Honestly, the instructor looks terrified. Maisie’s a bit more sensible, taking it slowly. They both had hot chocolate and are currently plotting a snowball fight against Dad. He’s blissfully unaware. Oh, that’s brilliant. He’ll be a wreck. He hates snow down his neck. Did you manage to speak to Mum and Dad this morning? They were trying to video call but the signal was terrible. I did, briefly. Mum was going on about the weather back home – apparently it’s freezing and grey. She said to tell you she’s worried about you hurting yourself. You know what she’s like. Of course. Mum always worries. It's her full-time job. Tell her I’m being sensible. Which, clearly, I am. Mostly. Have you heard from Sarah and Mark? Are they still planning on joining us on Friday? Yes, they are! They’re driving up, apparently.

…Right, just a little off the side here, dear. Honestly, you didn’t say a  word  about wanting it this short last time! Are you sure? It's… becoming quite aerodynamic. Just trust me, Elsie. It’ll suit me. Less to worry about when I’m bending down fiddling with those racket strings. Speaking of which, back to the plan. Cable ties. Seriously, you think it’ll hold? It feels…a bit Heath Robinson, doesn’t it? Heath Robinson! Oh, you are a one. It's ingenious, Arthur, that’s what it is. And perfectly practical. We’re not expecting to launch rockets, just reinforce a string bed. We’ve gone through three rackets this month with those pesky breaks, and new strings are costing a fortune. Cable ties are pennies. We need to calculate the cost per racket saved. That's our marketing angle - 'Save Money, Save Your Game!’ Good point, good point. Though 'Save Your Game!' sounds a bit… dramatic for badminton, don't you think? And what about dimensions? We need to get the right size cable ties. Too big and they’re floppy, too small and… well, they won’t tie. And the weight! Will it noticeably affect the racket's balance? We’ll need to experiment. Get a mixed bag of sizes. And the weight will be negligible. Honestly, Arthur, you're overthinking it. It's a simple fix. Remember old Mr. Henderson at the village hall? He used to use sticky tape on everything.  Everything . This is an improvement on sticky tape, surely. Henderson and his tape… a legend. But this is different. We’re talking about potentially starting a small business here. It’s not just about fixing  our  rackets. We could offer a racket repair service! We could even… call it ‘Fleet Racket Repairs!’ ‘Fleet’? What on earth gave you ‘Fleet’? That sounds like a…a cleaning company! Well, it implies a collection, a number… a  fleet  of rackets being expertly repaired! It’s catchy! It’s… It’s dreadful! No. Absolutely not. How about something simple? ‘String Solutions’? ‘Racket Rescue’? Honestly, Arthur. 'Fleet'… Honestly. Now, hold still, I'm trying to get a straight line here. Oh dear. What? What is it? Oh, Arthur! I… I think I’ve… I’ve nicked your ear. And…  oh dear . It looks like I’ve taken a stripe out of your hair! A bright white stripe!

Now, that one… that one’s a bit…much, innit? All those colours clashin’ about like a flock o’ startled pigeons. Your mother picked that one out, didn't she, love? Always ‘ad a fondness for the… bold. Bold is one word for it, Arthur. “Overpowering” is another. Yes, I did. It reminded me of a sunset we saw in Spain, years ago. Though, I admit, looking at it now… it’s a bit much for the hallway. Perhaps a smaller room? It’s interesting, though, isn’t it? How colour affects us. It's a really good example of Abstract Expressionism – the artist isn’t trying to  represent  something, they’re trying to express an emotion. Rothko did similar things, but, arguably, with more subtlety. Exactly. It’s about the feeling it evokes, rather than a literal depiction. The clashing colours, as you put it Arthur, are likely intentional. They’re meant to be unsettling, perhaps representing inner turmoil or… a chaotic energy. Turmoil? Chaotic energy? Sounds like a Tuesday at the bingo hall, that does. No, honestly, I prefer a nice landscape. Somethin’ you can recognize. Trees, fields… maybe a cow or two. Now  that's  art. Somethin’ peaceful. Oh, Arthur, you and your landscapes! Don't you get tired of looking at green fields? It's lovely, of course, but it doesn’t  make  you think, does it? This, at least, makes you react. Even if that reaction is "good heavens, what a mess!" It’s about developing a visual language, I think. When you look at something abstract, initially it can seem meaningless, but the more you look, the more you start to notice the composition, the brushstrokes… the artist's intent, even if it's not immediately obvious. We teach it to the students – starting with simple exercises, like just looking at a colour for five minutes and writing down everything it makes you  feel . It's a good exercise. It breaks down the preconceptions of what art ‘should’ be. It’s easy to get hung up on realism, on wanting to see things accurately portrayed. But that's just one form of art. Think about music – you don’t need lyrics to feel something powerful from a piece of music, do you? Music I understand. A good old sing-along. But pictures… well, I went to that modern art gallery in London with you two, didn't I?

…and honestly, Chloe just  had  to tell everyone about her promotion on Instagram before her boss even officially announced it. Like, who does that? It’s just… desperate. Oh, Chloe. Predictable. She lives for external validation, doesn’t she? Remember when she cried because her TikTok didn't get enough likes? It was a picture of her cat! Don't even  go  there. The cat was cute, but the drama! It was a full-blown crisis. Anyway, rant over. Work was… work. Mr. Henderson tried to explain the Gantt chart to me  again  like I'm five. I swear he thinks because I'm the youngest on the team, I’m automatically inept. Ugh, the condescension is real. You’ve got a first-class degree, you’re perfectly capable. He's probably just worried about looking like he doesn't understand it himself. Old people problems. How was the ward today? Anything exciting, apart from the usual chaos? Exciting is… not the word I’d use for someone having a full-blown panic attack at 8 am. It was mostly trying to de-escalate things. Honestly, sometimes I wish I’d just stayed in academia. Less emotionally draining, definitely. But then you wouldn’t be  you . You'd be stuck writing endless essays on obscure Victorian poets. Plus, you're brilliant at the whole project coordination thing. You bring order to chaos, which, let's be honest, is a skill we both need in our lives. Speaking of chaos, look at this kitchen. Oh god. It’s a disaster zone, isn’t it? We said we’d do this tonight. We  always  say we’ll do it tonight. And then we end up talking about Chloe’s Instagram and Mr. Henderson’s condescension. Procrastination is a powerful force. It really is. It’s like, the sheer  effort  of moving things from A to B… it’s exhausting. And then it just gets messy again by tomorrow. It’s a Sisyphean task. You're getting very philosophical about dirty dishes. I blame the English language. Why do we have so many words for the same thing? It’s utterly baffling. Honestly, it wastes brain space, which could be used for, say, cleaning. You’re right! It's true! Like 'clean,' 'tidy,' 'immaculate,' 'spotless'… they all basically mean the same thing, just with varying degrees of poshness! It’s a conspiracy to keep us distracted.

Honestly, another day, another fire to put out for Mr. Henderson. He genuinely doesn’t seem to grasp how a calendar works. Three meetings booked for the  same  time. Honestly, it’s like herding cats. Sounds about right. He always struck me as… creatively organised. Still, you handle it brilliantly, love. You’re the oil in that machine. Did you manage to get that report finalised for him? The one about the server upgrades? Almost. I’m just waiting on a final sign-off from accounts. Apparently, the projected costs have ‘shifted’. God knows what that means. It’ll probably involve me spending another hour chasing someone down a corridor. It's infuriating when people don’t just say what they mean. Politicians, basically. Though Henderson’s closer to a particularly flustered badger, isn't he? Speaking of infuriating habits… I had another one of those cravings today. Oh? Don't tell me… you nearly succumbed to the nicotine demon? Nearly. Driving back from that site visit to Reading, stuck in traffic… it just flared up. I haven’t had a proper cigarette in six months, and I’m still surprised how strong the urge can be. Though, thankfully, I had those ginger chews. Saved my life, probably. You still… indulging occasionally? Not cigarettes, thankfully. Gave those up properly years ago. But wine… well, let’s just say a stressful day at the office sometimes requires a very large glass of Sauvignon Blanc. Don’t judge. No judgement. We all have our things. It’s funny, isn’t it? We spend so much time striving for intelligence, higher education, but sometimes a bit of common sense is worth ten PhDs. Henderson's got plenty of the former, shockingly little of the latter. Absolutely. It’s all well and good being ‘clever’, but if you can’t apply it practically… it’s just wasted brainpower. I was reading an article the other day about how different cultures value those things differently. Like, some Asian cultures place a far higher emphasis on practical wisdom and experience than formal qualifications. Interesting. Makes sense. My sister went to India last year, volunteering with a women's empowerment charity. She was saying how… well, it’s complicated. She kept getting frustrated with what  seemed  like illogical decisions, but then she realised it was rooted in centuries of social norms, a completely different way of looking at things.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of mud was astonishing. I thought we’d be scrubbing you two for  hours . Honestly, Leo, you looked like a swamp monster! But it was  fun  mud, Mummy! Really squelchy. And I made a mud pie for Farmer Giles’ pig. He didn't eat it, though. He just snuffled it. It was a  very  good pie, with sticks and everything. I’m sure it was a masterpiece, darling. Though I suspect pigs have slightly different culinary tastes. Did you both manage to actually  touch  any of the animals, or were you too busy wallowing? I stroked a sheep! A really fluffy one. It smelled like… hay and sheep. Mine nibbled my jumper! A goat. A naughty goat. Miss Peterson would  not  have liked that. Oh, don't even mention Miss Peterson. How was school today, then? Any better than yesterday? I got a gold star! For colouring. I coloured a dinosaur. A T-Rex. A T-Rex! Excellent! Show me later. And Lila? I…I had to sit on the thinking step. Oh, Lila. What happened this time, love? Ethan kept copying my drawing of a unicorn. And then he said mine wasn’t sparkly enough. So I told him his unicorn looked like a horse with a pointy hat. Well, he  does  sound a bit rude, doesn’t he? But perhaps telling him his unicorn had a pointy hat wasn’t the nicest way to respond. The thinking step isn’t a punishment, sweetheart, it's a chance to calm down and think about how we can be kinder. Was it a  big  thinking step? Not enormous, no. Just a little one. Enough to give you a moment to breathe. Anyway, enough about school. This farm trip has given me an appetite. What do we fancy for tea? I was thinking maybe pasta with a tomato sauce? Can we have fish fingers too?  Please ? Fish fingers  and  pasta? That’s a rather ambitious meal, isn’t it? Perhaps fish fingers  with  pasta? And peas! Don't forget the peas. They're my favourite. Peas are  always  included, Leo. Never forget the peas. Right, pasta, fish fingers, and peas it is. While I'm getting that going, would you two like to pick a DVD? We could watch something cosy after tea. Can we watch the one with the singing animals? The really colourful one? No!

Right, milk first for me, always. Though Gran always said tea made  properly  is tea made after the milk’s gone in. She was a woman of strong opinions, our Gran. And even stronger knitting. Honestly, the Aran sweaters she churned out… you could moor a boat with those things. Moor a boat, ha! That’s a good image. My Nan was more into doilies. Endless, lacey doilies. Covered  everything . It's funny, isn't it, how these things stick with you? I was just thinking about the Olympics actually, watching the opening ceremony highlights. It’s giving me major Nan vibes, the pageantry, all the…  stuff . The Olympics  are  a bit much, aren’t they? All that patriotic fervour. Though I did get properly sucked into the swimming last time. Adam Peaty, remember him? Absolute unit. And he was from… Stoke, wasn't he? Not exactly Cambridge University material. Yeah, Stoke-on-Trent. Didn’t he have some issues with his mental health recently though? Saw something about him pulling out of some competitions. It's a bit sobering, seeing these athletes who seem invincible struggle with things. Makes you think about the pressure. It’s a world away from knitting, that’s for sure. Aye, it is. Though knitting can be surprisingly stressful, if you’re trying to get a cable knit right. It's a delicate balance between relaxing and deeply frustrating. Speaking of stressful, did you see what that Timothée Chalamet was wearing at the Golden Globes? Honestly, the backless suit? A bit… much. Oh,  that . I did see pictures. It was… a choice. Very avant-garde. I think he's trying to cement himself as some kind of style icon. I’m not convinced. It felt a little… desperate? Like he was  asking  for attention. He’s got the acting talent, he doesn’t need to rely on backless suits. Exactly! It’s the same with some modern art, isn’t it? Like, you look at a white canvas with a single black line on it and people are going on about “the existential angst of the modern age”. Give me a Turner seascape any day. Now  that’s  art. Something you can actually look at and enjoy without needing a philosophical degree. Turner is good. Although I've been getting into Rothko lately. The colour fields... they're surprisingly calming. It's less about 'looking  at  something' and more about experiencing it, I think.

…Honestly, Harold, that was a lovely scone. Proper clotted cream, not that watery stuff you get these days. Right, so, museums then? You were looking a bit peaky after that IMAX film yesterday. All that…  whoosh  and 3D. Gave you a headache, didn’t it? Headache’s gone now, thankfully. Though honestly, Maureen, ‘Avatar: The Way of Water’ was a bit much. Beautiful to  look  at, mind you, but three hours of blue people? My bum was numb before the halfway mark. And the price! Robbery, pure robbery. I still think the Natural History Museum is a better shout. Less… strenuous on the eyes, and free! Oh, the Natural History Museum  is  lovely. But we did that last time we were down. And you complained about the crowds then, remember? Said you couldn't see the dinosaurs for the school trips. I was thinking the V&A? They’ve got that new exhibit on 19th-century photography, and I know how you like a good bit of history. Photography, eh? Hmm. Is it all black and white and dusty looking portraits? No offence, love, but it doesn’t exactly set the pulse racing, does it? I’d rather see something… tangible. Like a proper Roman artefact. Maybe the British Museum? Though getting there on the Tube is always a nightmare. The British Museum is doable. We can get the Piccadilly line straight to Russell Square. It’s just... packed, isn't it? And last time, we spent half an hour just trying to get near the Rosetta Stone. Honestly, you'd think they were giving it away. The V&A is a bit more spread out, and they've got that lovely cafe. We could have a nice sit-down after looking at all the old crockery. Crockery? Maureen, really? You know my knees aren’t what they used to be and all that wandering around… I'm not built for museums anymore. It’s all standing and looking, isn’t it? I liked the Churchill War Rooms, that was alright. You could sit down in some of the rooms, and it was actually  interesting . Felt a bit more... relevant. Relevant? Harold, Victorian photography is relevant! It shows the social conditions of the time, the development of technology… It's not just "old crockery", as you put it. Honestly, you’re impossible. We're trying to do something cultured for once, not just wander around looking at wartime bunkers.

… honestly, the traffic getting back from the university today was mental. Absolutely mental. It took me nearly an hour just to get across the city. You wouldn’t believe it. Anyway, pint still good? Still excellent, actually. Tsingtao's growing on me, you know? Not quite a proper pint of bitter, obviously, but surprisingly refreshing. And yes, the traffic  is  legendary here. I took the metro, thankfully. Speaking of things that are legendary… Christmas is looming. Have you given any thought to what we're doing this year? Looms is the right word. It feels a bit… surreal being here for Christmas. Last year, we tried to do a proper British Christmas, but trying to find cranberries was a logistical nightmare! I’m all for simplifying this year. A nice dinner, some good company, and maybe a film. You hosting again? Your flat’s definitely more… spread out than mine. I was thinking so, yeah. I've got a slightly bigger oven, and frankly, the thought of attempting a roast in your kitchen fills me with dread. We  need  to get organised though. Last year’s cranberry saga was… traumatic. Remind me again, how did we end up using pomegranate seeds? Desperation, pure desperation! I found this little shop, apparently selling “Western ingredients” but it was mostly dried fruit and nuts no one wanted. Pomegranate was the closest colour. It… wasn't the same. Look, let's do a proper guest list. You, me, Sarah and Mark, definitely. What about old man Henderson from the History department? He always seems a bit lonely around the holidays. Henderson? Hmm. Good shout. He’s a bit of a curmudgeon, but he does tell some amazing stories about his time in Hong Kong. Okay, add him to the list. How about Li Wei? She’s been really helpful with my research, and it would be nice to include her. She hasn’t experienced a traditional Western Christmas before, I don’t think. Excellent idea! The more the merrier. Though, we'll have to give her the full briefing on crackers and those little paper hats. She'd probably think we’ve all lost it. Speaking of 'lost it', have you seen anything decent at the cinema lately? I need a distraction from marking essays. I was thinking a Christmas film might be appropriate. I saw ‘Home Alone’ re-released last week. Total nostalgia trip, honestly.

… honestly, the replies to that tweet were  brutal . Like, I was just offering a slightly nuanced take on Greggs’ new vegan sausage roll and suddenly I’m public enemy number one for anyone who enjoys a bit of pork. Oh god, Twitter. Don't even get me started. I spent twenty minutes this afternoon trying to explain to someone why a sourdough starter  needs  feeding. They were convinced I was deliberately sabotaging their baking attempt. People are wild. Tell me about it. I had a bloke in the café today who genuinely tried to argue that a flat white is just a latte with less milk. Less milk! I nearly lost it. Honestly, some people shouldn’t be allowed caffeine. Right? It’s genuinely baffling. It's like they think you personally offended their grandmother when you politely correct them. Anyway, worse than Twitter arguments, though, are the online reviews. Oh,  don't . I’m bracing myself for the weekend. Last week, someone gave my bakery one star because "the croissants weren’t flaky  enough ." Flaky enough! Like, I'm not a magician, Sharon! It’s a Tuesday! Haha, Sharon. Classic. I get that. I had a three-star review last month because someone said the music was “too upbeat for a rainy day.” Too upbeat! It was Amy Winehouse! What's wrong with Amy Winehouse? It’s just… the entitlement, innit? They feel like they’re owed a perfect experience, and if it’s not exactly what they envisioned, you’re getting a dressing down online. I saw a restaurant in Margate getting absolutely rinsed because their pot plants ‘didn’t match the aesthetic’. Margate! Oh, I was thinking about that actually. Remember we said about me maybe opening a little pastry cafe down there? Yeah! You were talking about a cute little place near the Old Town. What’s the latest? Well, I found a space. It’s tiny, but it's got  good  light. It’s above this vintage shop, really quirky. But… it needs a  lot  of work. Like, a major revamp. Oh nice! What kind of revamp are we talking? Painting? New flooring? Electricals? Because that last one gets pricey quick. All of the above. And the current owner has, shall we say, interesting taste. Lots of floral wallpaper. Think… your nan’s living room, but more intense. I was thinking a really clean, minimal look.

Honestly, this is lovely. Just what I needed after marking those exam papers all afternoon. Little monsters, most of them. Though, Leo, you were a shining star, weren’t you? Mmmhmm. Mrs. Davies said I did really well on the history bit. Though the essay… I ran out of time. Mummy, is this raspberry a bird’s egg? It’s small and round! Oh, darling, no. Raspberries grow on bushes. Bird’s eggs come from birds! Remember we saw the robin building a nest in the garden? Oh. But it  looks  like an egg. Can I have chocolate ice cream after dinner? Please? We’ll see, sweetheart. You need to eat some of your broccoli first. It’ll make you strong enough to go biking with Leo tomorrow. Biking? Are we going to Ashton Court? We could try the downhill track! Maybe, maybe. We’ll see how your exam results are looking overall. And if Leo remembers to pump up his tyres this time. Last time was a disaster. You’re terrible, you really are. Threatening a child with no downhill biking! Though, he  did  nearly wobble into Old Man Hemmings’ prize-winning roses… He nearly flattened them! It was a near miss. Anyway, talking of gardens, I finally managed to get the netting up around the raspberry canes. The birds were having a field day. They were practically stripping the bushes bare. We saw a blue tit trying to build a nest in the shed. It kept dropping bits of fluff and string. It was funny. Fluff! Like Winston the gerbil’s bedding? Winston needs fresh water. He keeps looking at me. Right, I’ll get Winston sorted after I’ve finished helping Oisin with his dinner. He’s decided spaghetti is now the enemy. Apparently, it's "too long." Children and their food. Honestly. It’s a constant battle. When I was growing up, you ate what was put in front of you and didn't complain. We had a lovely vegetable garden; Mum was obsessed with growing marrow. Huge marrows. Marrow? What do you even  do  with marrow? Oh, you can make soup, chutney, boat races out of the skins… all sorts of things. It was a very 1970s childhood. Everything was orange and brown, and slightly…sad. Sounds charming! Though, I do recall my gran always trying to force-feed me sprouts. I used to hide them in my napkin.

Honestly, Doreen, I’m completely knackered. This week at work has been… something else. Accounts haven’t balanced, Mr. Henderson is breathing down my neck about targets, and then young Tim in marketing decided to ‘innovate’ the reporting system. It’s chaos. I need a proper sit down and a good gossip, which is precisely why I'm so glad you could pop round. And Nan, you alright, dear? You’ve been quiet. Oh, love, work's always a bit of a pickle, innit? Though I don't reckon I've ever had a 'Tim in marketing' causing me trouble. Mostly it's just making sure Mrs. Higgins hasn’t left a trail of biscuit crumbs from the sofa to the kitchen. Speaking of which, I need to do a proper shop tomorrow. The cupboards are looking bare. Thinking I might try that new supermarket on Oundle Road – heard they do a good deal on washing powder. Just thinking, that’s all. Thinking about Elsie. Poor thing’s been feeling poorly again. Said her arthritis is playing her up something awful. I keep offering to pop round with a bit of shepherd’s pie – always cheers her up – but she keeps saying no. Stubborn as a mule, that one. Elsie’s always been a bit fiercely independent, hasn’t she? But honestly, Nan, you  have  to keep offering. She probably just says no to be polite, but secretly wants it. I can go round with you if you like? It wouldn't take long, and we could make a proper fuss. It would do  us  good too, getting out. That's a lovely idea, actually. Elsie does like a bit of company. Though I tell you what, she’s got a right eye for detail, that one. Last time I visited, she pointed out a tiny fluffball under her sofa that I'd completely missed! I’d be mortified if she judged my cleaning. Oh, Doreen! Elsie judges everyone and everything! It's part of her charm. Anyway, speaking of needing a bit of attention… my eyebrows are looking a right state. I think I need to book an appointment with Fatima. Honestly, they grow faster than weeds. Fatima’s a good girl. Always a cheerful word. You remember when I used to go to Mrs. Patterson for my perms? She’d practically torture me with those rollers! Now  that  was a painful experience.

Honestly, this is bliss. Just… quiet. Well,  relatively  quiet, with a tiny human demanding attention every few hours. How did you manage this, constantly, with Leo? Oh, you get used to the demands, Mum. It's exhausting, of course, but… it’s a nice kind of exhausting. And Leo was a champion sleeper eventually. Honestly, the first three months were the hardest. Are you finding weaning okay? You seemed a bit stressed about it yesterday. I am, a bit. It’s just… she makes the  faces . You know, the scrunchy, disgusted faces when I offer her something that isn't milk. Is that normal? I feel like I’m inflicting torture! Perfectly normal! It's a whole new sensation for them, the texture and the tastes. She's probably just overwhelmed. Start with really bland, single-ingredient purees. Sweet potato, carrot, that sort of thing. Don't push it if she’s really refusing. Just try again another time. Think of it as exposure therapy for tiny tastebuds. Exposure therapy! You make it sound so… clinical! But you’re right. I’m probably putting too much pressure on it. Still, it feels like everyone has different advice. Old wives tales coming out of the woodwork. Auntie Brenda was on about feeding her mashed-up biscuits at six months! Oh, Brenda. Always one for a shortcut. Ignore her. Stick to the advice from your health visitor and what feels right for  you  and the baby. That's all that matters. Speaking of people offering advice… did Sarah finally confirm if she’s free for dinner on Tuesday? Yes! She called this morning. She and Mark are both in, thankfully. She’s been absolutely frantic with house renovations, poor thing. Apparently, they found asbestos. Oh, no! That's awful. No wonder she's stressed. Hopefully, it hasn’t set them back too much. It’ll be good to catch up properly, though. It feels like ages. Has Dad RSVP’d yet? He said he  might  be able to make it. Typical. Something about a bridge club tournament. Honestly, sometimes I think that bridge club is his first love. Honestly, you're probably right! But at least he's considering it. We'll take what we can get. It would be nice for him to see the baby, and you know how much he loves Sarah's rhubarb crumble. He does indeed. A strategic crumble offering  might  be required.

Honestly, it’s just… flat. I keep waiting for a hill, a proper rise, and it just doesn’t  happen . It’s lovely, don’t get me wrong, the fields are gorgeous in this light, but after London, it's so…level. You say that like it’s a bad thing! You spent ten years dodging double-decker buses up hills in Hampstead, you should be rejoicing in the lack of incline. Your calves will thank you. My calves might, but my aesthetic sensibilities are suffering. It feels…incomplete. Like a painting missing a crucial shadow. Everything just stretches on and on. It’s beautiful, vast, but… lacking drama. Norwich was a bit more undulating, even. Norwich  has  those little hills coming into the city from the north, you’re right. But this is the Broads, love. It's a different kind of beauty. Think about the way the light reflects off the water, how the sky just seems to go on forever. That’s the drama here, it’s just…horizontal drama. Horizontal drama. I like that. But even looking at those villages… they just sit  in  the landscape, don't they? They don’t cling to hillsides like you get in, say, the Cotswolds. They feel…exposed. Vulnerable. Exposed, maybe. But there's a certain honesty about it, isn't there? They haven’t been trying to hide from anything. They've just… grown with the land, not  on  it. Think about the history, too. This whole area was underwater for centuries. These villages were built on these little islands, deliberately. They  had  to be plain, functional. That’s a good point. I hadn't really thought about the fenland aspect. It's easy to forget, looking at it now, so dry and golden. And you’re right about the honesty. It’s not trying to be picturesque. It just  is . Exactly. It's a working landscape. These fields aren’t here for show; someone’s livelihood depends on them. It’s different from those chocolate-box villages built for tourists. Although, I suppose  we  are tourists, in a way. Guilty as charged. Temporary tourists. Though I'm hoping to become a more permanent fixture eventually. Honestly, it's growing on me. It’s just…so different. I'm used to having a landmark, a hill to orientate myself by. Here, I swear I get disorientated after five minutes.

…and honestly, the sheer  audacity  of him, thinking he could just waltz in and redesign the entire database schema after six months? Like, I spent a year building that! A YEAR! Woah, hold on. That’s…intense. Is this about Liam at work again? The new data science guy? The very same. He’s got this “disruptive” energy, which is just code for ‘I haven’t bothered to actually  understand  what anyone else has done.’ He kept saying it wasn’t “scalable.” Scalable! It’s a database of biscuit recipes, Liam, not a global financial system! Biscuit recipes. Right. Still, that sounds frustrating. You’re the corpus admin, you  are  the database whisperer. He should be asking you for guidance, not trying to bulldoze over everything. Exactly! And the worst part is, old Mr. Henderson, bless ‘im, just keeps saying “Oh, fresh perspectives are good!” Fresh perspectives don’t involve deleting meticulously curated tags, Henderson! It's a nightmare. Anyway, enough about work making me want to fling myself into the Wear. Want to actually talk about something…fun? Did you see that new Wes Anderson film?  Asteroid City ? I did, actually. Last night. Visually stunning, as always, but… I don’t know. Felt a bit…empty, didn’t it? Like all style, no substance. See! I knew I wasn’t the only one. Everyone online is raving about it, like it's the second coming, but I just found it…cold. All that symmetrical perfection, it felt a bit sterile. Give me  Rushmore  any day. Definitely  Rushmore . Or  The Royal Tenenbaums . Those have  heart . This one felt like he was deliberately trying to be Wes Anderson, rather than just  being  Wes Anderson. It's hard to explain. You get it! It's like he's showing off how clever he is, instead of telling a story. Speaking of things being deliberately…difficult…have you seen the state of the roads lately? Honestly, it’s a cyclist’s paradise and a driver’s absolute hell. Oh, don't even get me started on the cyclists. It's not all of them, obviously, but some of them just have no spatial awareness. Flying through red lights, weaving in and out of traffic…it's terrifying. I know, right? I was nearly taken out on the A19 last week. This lad, no helmet, headphones in, just…pedaled right out. I braked so hard I nearly gave the poor woman in the car behind me whiplash.

Honestly, this is  exactly  what I needed. London feels… oppressive at times, even when it’s not raining. Everything is just  on . Here, you can actually hear yourself think. And smell things other than exhaust fumes. You say that every time we come back to Norfolk, don’t you? It’s the fresh air, darling. Glorious, unadulterated fresh air. Though, even I have to admit, the constant bleating of sheep is…distinctive. Look, bluebells! A whole carpet of them. They’re stunning, aren’t they? It reminds me of when I was little, Gran would take me foraging for wild garlic near Reepham. She knew every flower, every herb… it was like having a walking botanical encyclopedia. She’d always say bluebells were a sign spring had truly arrived. Your grandmother was a force of nature. Right, about forces of nature… I was reading an interesting paper yesterday, relating agricultural output to regional dialects. Bizarre, I know. Oh, do tell. Sounds delightfully niche. Is it another one of your post-structuralist arguments about language shaping reality? A little bit, admittedly. The argument was that areas historically reliant on cash crops – like sugar beet here in Norfolk – developed more concise and pragmatic language, focused on efficiency and transaction. Less flowery, less… descriptive, perhaps. That's… surprisingly insightful. I mean, you can see it, can’t you? The language of farming is very direct. “Yield,” “rotation,” “fertilizer.” No room for poetic flourishes when you’re dealing with margins. It's so different to, say, the layered vocabulary of someone immersed in Anglo-Saxon literature. Exactly! And the paper linked it to lower levels of linguistic diversity in those areas over time. Fewer loanwords used, a stronger adherence to core English structures. It’s all a bit bleak though, isn’t it? The idea that economic factors can erode language. It is. It feels…reductionist, somehow. Though I suppose it’s not entirely surprising. Economic pressures dictate so much. It makes me think about my research, actually. Trying to link medieval land ownership patterns to the distribution of certain surnames… you start to see the echoes of those economic forces everywhere. It's all connected, isn't it? Speaking of interconnectedness, did you see the football last night? Absolutely dreadful defending from Spurs. Don’t even  start  me. I was screaming at the television. Absolutely pathetic. I honestly don’t know how they keep attracting such expensive players and consistently underperform.

…and honestly, the parking situation ‘round there is a nightmare. Absolute nightmare. I was thinking maybe we could get the train if we go to that new Italian place near Monument? It's supposed to be really good. The train? Really? That’s… dedication. Especially after you spent all that time moaning about Northern Rail delays last week. And, like, Monument’s a trek from the restaurant, isn’t it? Aye, it is a bit of a walk, but it’s better than circling for half an hour trying to find a space that probably doesn't exist. Honestly, driving in Newcastle is stressing me out just  thinking  about it. Remember that time we went to see that exhibition? Nearly ended up in the Tyne! Dramatic, as always. I handled that perfectly, by the way. Textbook parallel parking, even under pressure. You were just… providing moral support. And a lot of shouting. I was concerned for your welfare! And the car’s! It’s a lovely car, your Mini, but it’s  your  lovely car. I'd rather not contribute to any bodywork repairs. So, train it is? Or we could just… not go? No, no, let’s go. I’m up for the Italian. We just need a plan. Maybe we could try and park at the MetroCentre and get the Metro in? It's a bit further out, but parking's usually easier. That’s… actually a good shout. Alright, MetroCentre it is. You navigate, though. You’re the mapping expert. I still can’t get my head around why they built the Angel of the North where they did. It’s just… fields. It’s a landmark! Iconic, even. Besides, it’s a good vantage point. You can see for miles. More importantly, have you seen any updates on the Wimbledon scores? Djokovic is looking pretty unstoppable. Honestly, tennis just isn’t my thing. All that grunting. It’s distracting. I'd rather watch the footie. How’s Sunderland doing, anyway? Don't tell me it’s still…  Sunderland.  Progress is being made. Slowly. They’ve got a new striker, apparently. A young lad. Might be one to watch. Though, let’s be realistic, promotion next season is still a long shot. A long shot is an understatement. They’ll be fighting relegation again, mark my words. Speaking of fighting… how’s the flat hunt going for your mate, Liam?

…and honestly, the whole thing with that actor, the one from  that  film, it’s just… exhausting, isn’t it? All the details coming out. It feels so intrusive, even if he  did  do what they say. Poor woman, either way. Do you follow any of it, Doreen? A little bit, love. Mostly what my daughter tells me. She’s got the telly on  all  day. It’s all very sad, innit? And a right mess. I prefer watching the birds, to be honest. Much more peaceful. Absolutely. Much more… grounding. I was watching a documentary about geese migrating the other day. Extraordinary, the distances they travel. Geese! Oh, we’ve got a whole gaggle of ‘em down by the park at the moment. Proper nuisance, they are. Leaving… well, you know. Everywhere. But beautiful to watch, when they take off all together. Old Mrs. Higgins gets terribly cross about them. Says they’re ruining her flowerbeds. Oh, bless Mrs. Higgins. She  does  take her gardening seriously. Where exactly are they congregating, down by the river? Further up, actually. Near the new estate, by the playing field. Loads of long grass. Perfect for nibbling, I suppose. And safe from the dogs. Though they still try their luck. I saw one little lad yesterday, letting his terrier chase them - his mum wasn’t pleased! Terriers. Always chasing  something . My Albert, God rest his soul, had a Jack Russell. Little terror. Spent his days after squirrels. Never caught one, mind you. Just enjoyed the pursuit. Hello, Margaret! Didn't realise you were awake. We were just talking about the geese down at the park. Geese, are we? Aye, I remember when there weren’t so many. Used to be just a few wild ones, coming over in the winter. Now they're everywhere. This used to be all fields, you know. Before they built all these houses. Proper countryside. It has changed, hasn’t it? I remember when you could walk for miles and not see a soul. Now it’s all traffic and building works. Though, I suppose, people need places to live. It’s a tricky balance, isn’t it? Progress versus preservation. Did you see that documentary about the Bewick's swans? They fly all the way from Siberia! Incredible stamina. They used to winter around here more frequently, apparently, but the numbers are dwindling. Siberia! Goodness me. All that way.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of marking I had last week was  criminal . Sixteen year olds writing essays on Victorian poetry – you’d think they’d managed to invent the stuff themselves, the way some of them just… make things up. Oh, tell me about it. I’m so glad I switched to primary. Little ones are far less prone to fabricating poetic devices, thankfully. Though the glitter… the glitter is a whole other battle. How was the interview, by the way? You said you had that thing at the grammar school? It was… an experience. Very ‘structured’. Lots of talk about ‘raising attainment’ and ‘data-driven learning’. They wanted me to demonstrate how I’d implement their new assessment framework. It felt less like a conversation about teaching and more like an audit. Ugh. Sounds awful. You’re far too good for all that. Honestly, they’d be lucky to have you. Did you feel you clicked with them? Not particularly. The Head of Department seemed lovely, genuinely, but the other two… very… polished. Like they were reciting a script. And they asked me about my ‘unique selling point’ as a teacher. What  is  a unique selling point when you just want to inspire a love of language? God, that’s dreadful. It’s like we're selling washing machines, isn't it? Not shaping young minds. Still, don’t write it off yet. Sometimes they take ages to get back to you. Speaking of shaping young minds, how's little Leo doing? Is he talking yet? He's babbling like mad, all ‘da-da’ and ‘ma-ma’ but nothing concrete, really. He’s started this thing where he throws his puree at the wall. Sweet potato is his weapon of choice. It’s… artistic, I suppose. Oh, brilliant! My niece, Maisie, went through a similar phase with peas. My sister swore the kitchen looked like a Jackson Pollock painting. It’s just exploring, isn’t it? They're tiny scientists. That’s what I keep telling myself. It’s just… exhausting. And the sleep deprivation is real. I haven’t had a full night’s sleep since… well, since before Leo arrived, obviously. Tell me about it. I remember when my brother and his wife first had Olivia. They looked like zombies. They tried to convince me it was ‘amazing’ and ‘life-changing’, and it is, of course, but don’t let anyone tell you it's all sunshine and roses.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of emails I had to clear this morning was  criminal . Like, who needs fifteen different updates on the same bloody bolt order? It's a bolt! Fifteen? Seriously? Sounds like someone's overcompensating for…something. Maybe a fear of bolts falling off? Probably. It’s just… exhausting. It feels like I spend more time  managing  the work than actually  doing  the work. Which is ironic, considering my job title. Production Controller. Controller of… chaos, more like. Tell me about it. My boss is obsessed with colour-coded spreadsheets. Colour-coded! Like the actual information changes depending on if it's in cerulean blue or periwinkle. It’s madness. Anyway, enough work gripes. We're supposed to be having a nice, relaxing evening. So, future plans? Still thinking about that Masters, then? That's the plan. Or, it  was  the plan. I'm starting to have… doubts. It feels a bit… pointless, suddenly. Another qualification, more debt, for what? To potentially end up controlling even  more  bolts? Pointless? No way! You’re brilliant at what you do, but you’ve always said you felt it wasn’t… fulfilling. The Masters in Environmental Management is genuinely something you’re passionate about. Remember all those documentaries you used to make me watch about sustainable farming? Yes, and then I'd fall asleep halfway through the one about compost! Look, I  am  passionate. It's just... daunting. Moving back to uni, the pressure, finding somewhere to live in Cambridge that isn’t a glorified cupboard… and the career prospects afterwards. What if I finish and there aren’t any jobs? Jobs will be there. The whole ‘green’ sector is booming, isn't it? And you’re good at networking, you always have been. Honestly, you could sell ice to Eskimos. Plus, we could flatshare again! Remember how much fun we had in second year? Though, admittedly, the kitchen situation was… questionable. Questionable is an understatement. It was a biohazard zone. But yeah, that was a good year. Still. It’s just… a big shift. You seem so… settled. You've got your admin job, your beautiful garden, your cat who clearly runs the house. Winston  absolutely  runs the house. Don't underestimate his power. But settled doesn’t mean complacent. I'm thinking about doing a part-time online course in graphic design. Just for me, you know? Something creative.

Right, honestly, I'm fuming. Absolutely  fuming . He had the cheek to ‘like’ her photo on Insta, like, a week after we supposedly ‘broke up’. A  week , Rach! Oh, Liam? Seriously? Still at it then? I thought you said he was, like, super remorseful and all that? All apologies and promises to be better? Remorseful for about five minutes, apparently. Long enough to get what he wanted, then straight back to…well, whatever it is he thinks he’s doing. It wasn’t even a good photo, mind. Just her pulling a silly face with a filter on. Like he’s trying to show me something. Ugh, the passive aggression is  exhausting . Men, honestly. They’re all the same, aren't they? You deserve better, Em. Proper better. You’re too good for him fiddling about. You two sound like you’re reliving high school drama. Still obsessing over Instagram likes? Honestly. Is this why you dragged me all the way to Nice? I could be enjoying the view, not hearing about boys. Easy for you to say, Chloe! You’ve been happily coupled up with Ben for, what, three years now? You’ve forgotten what it’s like to have your heart trampled on by a dodgy lad. And it's not  just  the like, it's the principle of it! She’s got a point, Chloe. It's just… everything. It makes you question everything he ever said. Was any of it real? And it's made worse because it’s  her . Sarah. The one I explicitly said I didn’t like, remember? Okay, okay, I’m sorry. I just… I always thought you two were both a bit strong for Liam, to be frank. He always seemed a bit… underwhelming. And honestly, Sarah’s a bit of a headcase. What do you even see in each other? That’s what  I  keep asking myself! It’s like I was blinded by… I don't know, the idea of having  a  boyfriend? Everyone else seemed to have one. And he was… available. Stupid, I know. She's right, Em. You were rushing it. Remember when you said you just wanted to prove you could 'keep' one? That was a red flag right there. Don't remind me! I was being ridiculous. I just felt… pressured. Everyone was talking about their relationships and I felt like I was falling behind.

…Honestly, this shepherd’s pie is  exactly  what I needed after that day. Honestly, a nightmare with Mrs. Henderson and her insistence on using Comic Sans in a professional brochure. Comic Sans! The audacity. Mmm, it  is  good, Mum. Is there any extra gravy? You’ll get a second helping if you finish your veg, young man. And Sarah, honestly, people and their font choices… it’s a battle. I had a contractor trying to convince me lime green was a good colour for the new warehouse signage. Lime green! See! It’s a societal breakdown, I tell you. A complete lack of aesthetic sensibility. Though lime green  is  a bit much. Anyway, how was the hockey match, Leo? You were looking a bit glum when you came in. We lost. Again. Brutal. Old Mr. Davies, the ref, was definitely favouring the Falcons. Every penalty went their way. Was it a close game though? Did you almost score? I heard you had a good run. I  did  have a good run, yeah. Got past their defence, but their goalie was… well, let’s just say he was in the zone. Blocked everything. It was 3-1 in the end. Frustrating. Oh, that’s a shame. Still, you can’t win them all. It’s the taking part that counts, isn’t it? Though I suspect that’s a phrase uttered by people who have never actually  tried  to win anything competitively. Very true. Listen, about that weekend away… I was thinking, if we book now, we might get a good deal on a cottage in the Lake District. It's not too far, and we could do some walking. The Lake District? Cool! Can we take the dog? Possibly. We need to find a dog-friendly cottage. That might limit our options slightly, but it’s doable. I’m happy with the Lakes. It's beautiful there. We haven't had a proper family break in ages. Sounds alright. As long as there’s phone signal. Need to be able to update my FIFA team. Prioritising virtual football over actual scenery? Typical. But, fair enough. I’ll have a look at cottages with decent broadband. Speaking of which, did you manage to get hold of Mark today, Sarah? He was meant to send me those operational cost breakdowns. He messaged me earlier. Said he was stuck in meetings all day, apparently some crisis with the Johnson account.

… honestly, I still can’t believe your Aunt Brenda tried to set you up with  Derek . Derek! The one who collects garden gnomes? Don't remind me. It was mortifying. She cornered me at Christmas, all bright-eyed and bushy-tailed, saying, “Oh, he’s  such  a good provider, and you girls need stability!” Stability? As if my life is some crumbling Victorian mansion needing underpinning. She's just… Brenda. Perpetually matchmaking. I swear she thinks everyone's life will be instantly improved by being paired with someone she approves of. Remember when she tried to convince me Martin from the village was ‘a good catch’ because he owned a tractor? Oh god, yes! The tractor. You handled that brilliantly, by the way. Just subtly shifting the conversation to the rising price of fertiliser. Derailed her perfectly. I tried a similar tactic with Derek and his gnomes – mentioned a potential promotion at work, hoping to imply I was too busy for… gnome-related pursuits. It didn’t land. It rarely does with Brenda. She’s a force of nature. Still, you’re doing amazingly well without a gnome-loving partner. You’ve got your photography, you’re travelling… this trip is incredible. Look at these trees! Honestly, they’re otherworldly. They are, aren’t they? I’ve taken about a thousand photos already. My phone is screaming at me for storage space. It's good to be away, though. A proper break. Everything felt so… grey back home. Work was just endless spreadsheets and passive-aggressive emails. Temping, right? Still? Yep. Still temping. It pays the bills, but my soul is slowly eroding. I applied for that marketing assistant role at the museum, but haven’t heard back. Probably went to someone with ‘more relevant experience’, which is code for ‘younger and willing to work for peanuts’. Don’t be so down on yourself! You  have  relevant experience. You did that fabulous campaign for the local arts festival, remember? And your degree is brilliant. It’s just… London is a shark tank. Tell me about it. Mum keeps asking when I’m going to settle down and get a ‘proper job’. As if both aren’t achievable simultaneously. She doesn’t understand the modern world.
