But it's not the same, is it? Used to be, you  knew  ‘em. Knew where they’d been brought up, went to school, what pubs they frequented. Now they live in gated communities and fly in and out. Exactly. That sense of community. It's been… diluted. It's a rather sad commentary on broader societal shifts, I think. A microcosm of what’s happened with globalization and the free market. Speaking of which, how’s the trade been lately? Still getting plenty of students needing lifts to the University? Aye, keeps me goin'. Though, since Brexit, it's definitely slowed down. Fewer Erasmus students, less international conferences…a noticeable difference. Folks are put off, I reckon. Too much hassle and red tape. The government promised us all sorts, didn’t they? “Take back control” and all that. Seems to me, it’s just swapped one set of rules for another, more complicated set. That’s a remarkably astute observation, actually. I often try to explain to my students the levels of complexity involved in international relations, and Brexit is such a… potent, and frankly depressing, example. It's simple slogans masking deeply complicated realities. And the irony, of course, is Liverpool voted overwhelmingly to remain.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of data in the BNC is just… overwhelming. I've been trying to isolate regional variations in the use of ‘right’ as a discourse marker, and it's like wading through treacle. Every other sentence has 'right' in it! It’s fascinating, of course, but my eyes are square. Oh, bless you. Sounds massively tedious. I feel your pain with big data, though. Just trying to keep on top of submissions for the magazine is a spreadsheet nightmare. Though, at least mine isn’t historical linguistics. Have you had any luck with the geographical tagging? Is southern English ‘right’ demonstrably different from, say, Yorkshire ‘right’? That's the frustrating part! It  seems  like there are subtle differences in intonation, but trying to quantify that from transcripts… impossible. I keep thinking I need audio recordings, but that’s a whole other funding application. Speaking of hopeless tasks, I tried updating my LinkedIn profile yesterday. It’s just… so performative, isn't it? All 'synergy' and 'leveraging best practices'. Ugh. LinkedIn. Oh, don't even  start  me. Such a strange little world. All boasting and carefully curated self-presentation. I avoid it like the plague. Is it necessary for your line of work, though? Increasingly, unfortunately. Apparently, it's where all the research funding bodies now scout for potential collaborators. It feels so… American. Everything’s ‘growth hacking’ and ‘disrupting’. It is a bit much, isn't it? I've got mine, because… well, everyone does. It's like having a digital business card. I mostly just ignore the 'inspirational quotes' people share. Speaking of avoiding things, I'm currently avoiding booking flights. I’m meant to be going to see Mum in Wales next month, but the thought of flying is actively making me queasy. Oh, no! You always get so anxious. Remember that time going to Spain? You practically had a panic attack at Heathrow. Have you tried any of those calming apps? Tried them. Deep breathing. Visualisation. Nothing seems to work. I just… hate the feeling of being completely out of control. Being hurtled through the air in a metal tube. It's ridiculous, I know. I long for the days when you could take a ferry everywhere! I completely understand. It's a very primal fear. Though, there are some places worth facing it for. I was thinking about the Maldives recently… purely for research purposes, obviously. .

Right, so I'm thinking red wine reduction for the lamb. Bit fancy, yeah? Though knowing my luck, it’ll just taste like burnt sugar. Don’t be so dramatic, Leo. You make a perfectly decent lamb. And honestly, after the week I’ve had, ‘decent’ is all I’m asking for. How's the dissertation going, by the way? Still wrestling with post-structuralism? Wrestling is a good word for it. It’s less wrestling and more being repeatedly flattened by it, to be honest. I think I’m finally making some headway though. Found a new angle on Baudrillard… might actually be onto something. Though it needs, like, a thousand more footnotes. Speaking of needing things… did you manage to confirm with Marco he's still free for Christmas? I did. He’s bringing his infamous potato salad. Prepare yourself. Apparently, he’s been perfecting the recipe for  years . Honestly, I think he treats it like a national treasure. Classic Marco. Seriously though, is he alright? He sounded a bit… flat on the phone last week. He said work's been a nightmare. New boss, apparently a real micro-manager. Honestly, the publishing world sounds brutal. Which reminds me, how are those interns doing at your uni library? Any likely candidates for a placement with me next summer? I’m starting to think about applications already. Oh, they’re a mixed bag. One's obsessed with TikTok and keeps trying to catalogue memes. Another’s brilliant, incredibly efficient, but also... slightly terrifyingly organized. The one I’d recommend, Priya, is doing a history degree - impeccable research skills. I’ll send you her CV. Helloooo! Am I interrupting a culinary masterpiece? Smells amazing in here, even with the… onion-induced tears, Leo? Zara! No, not at all. We were just plotting Christmas and bemoaning the state of modern publishing. Leo’s attempting a red wine reduction. Oh lovely. Christmas plans! I need to hear everything. My mum’s already started subtly hinting about wanting a new kitchen for Christmas. A  new kitchen ! As if. Your mum’s ambitious. My mum just wants a nice scented candle and a quiet evening. Relatively speaking. So, Christmas at yours this year then, Zara? We  might  be able to swing it. Depends on how the renovation goes. Remember that damp patch in the downstairs loo? It turned out to be...a lot more than a damp patch.

Honestly, this risotto is being  difficult . I swear, Birmingham water just doesn’t behave the same way as Hitchin water. It needs… something. More stock, maybe? Hitchin water having special risotto-making properties, is it? You’re telling me your childhood village is the key to perfect creamy rice? Don't be ridiculous! It’s just… I used to make this  all  the time at home, and it was effortless. This feels like I’m wrestling with it. Maybe it’s the altitude? Is Birmingham significantly higher than Herts? I think you're grasping at straws, love. It's probably just you being overly critical. It smells amazing, actually. Though speaking of difficult… I tried that new Pilates class yesterday. Oh. My. Goodness. The one near the canal? I’ve been meaning to look into that. Is it any good? I'm trying to get back into  something  after… well, you know. The flu. Still recovering, really. Good is an understatement. It’s brutal! The instructor, Beatrice, looks like she’s carved from granite and has zero sympathy. I genuinely thought my core would give up halfway through. Honestly, I felt like a floppy fish. A floppy fish! That's a wonderful image. See? That's the benefit of finally admitting defeat and doing something gentle. I attempted a HIIT class last year and nearly pulled a hamstring. I stuck to gentle yoga for a while after that. Gentle yoga sounds considerably more appealing at this moment. Though, to be fair, the studio  is  lovely. Right on the canal, big windows, lots of light. Afterwards, we all went for a green juice – which tasted precisely as virtuous as it sounds. So, how was teaching today? Any particularly colourful linguistic mishaps? Oh, you know. The usual. Year 9 trying to use ‘literally’ in every other sentence. I’m starting to suspect they're doing it deliberately just to wind me up. And then young Thomas decided he was going to describe his weekend using only Shakespearean English. It was… ambitious. Oh, Thomas! He’s a character. Still, at least it’s engaging. Beats marking endless essays on ‘To Kill a Mockingbird,’ doesn't it? I’m interviewing a chef tomorrow for a piece on Birmingham’s burgeoning foodie scene. Ooh, interesting! Are you going to try any of his food as part of the interview? Because if so, I volunteer as tribute.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of essays I’ve marked this week is criminal. It's like they  deliberately  misunderstand the prompt just to see what I’ll write in the feedback. Honestly, Ben, it’s exhausting. Tell me about it. My inbox is a graveyard of semi-coherent arguments. Though, yours is philosophy, right? At least they’re  trying  to grapple with big ideas, even if they mostly end up sounding like undergraduates attempting performance art. Mine are marketing students. It's all buzzwords and very little substance. That does sound… bleak. Performance art sounds generous, actually. Some of them just re-state the lecture notes as if that counts as analysis. It feels incredibly demoralising, doesn’t it? Like you’re shouting into the void. Massively. It makes you question the whole point, doesn’t it? Though I had a good one today, actually. Properly engaged with Foucault. Made me remember why I signed up for this in the first place. Small victories. Oh, good! You  need  those. I haven't had one of those in… well, a week, at least. Speaking of needing things… I really need a foot spa. My toes are suffering. Your toes? What’s happened to your toes? Beyond the usual academic-induced stress, obviously. Honestly? I've been neglecting them. The humidity here is dreadful for nail health, and I keep forgetting to clip them properly. They’re reaching alarming lengths. I'm starting to feel like a mythical creature. A mythical creature with exceptionally long toe nails. I’ll have to picture that. You should get one of those little electric foot files. They’re surprisingly effective. And rather satisfying. I’ve been thinking about it. Maybe a self-care Sunday is in order. But first, I need to battle this essay mountain. Actually, that reminds me, did you hear back from Sarah about the weekend? She was meant to let us know if she could make it to that dumpling place we talked about. She texted this morning. She’s got a family thing. Apparently, her Aunt Mildred's prize-winning begonias are having a crisis. Aunt Mildred and her begonias. Of course. She’s... dedicated. Is that the right word? Dedicated is… polite. Obsessed is probably more accurate. But good on her, I suppose. Though it's a shame about the dumplings. It would've been nice to catch up properly.

…and honestly, the whole thing just felt  pointless . Three hours of CGI dragons and brooding heroes. It’s like they forgot to write actual dialogue. Did you see the latest ‘House of the Dragon’ prequel? It’s marginally better, but still… Dragons, eh? Not really my thing, actually. I saw a bit of the first ‘Game of Thrones’ series when everyone was talking about it, but it all felt a bit…much. Too much gratuitous violence. Though, I will admit, the political intrigue was pretty clever. What about you, still teaching French and Spanish? Still battling teenagers with their verb conjugations? Still battling! Though, this year’s Year 11s are surprisingly decent. They actually  want  to learn. It’s a pleasant change. And yes, still French and Spanish. Though the head is hinting at needing someone to cover Italian next year. Which would be…challenging. I took a year of it at uni, but that was ages ago. Italian, eh? You always did pick up languages easily. I struggled with French at school. Absolutely murdered the pronunciation. Mrs. Davies used to wince every time I opened my mouth. Remember her? Little, terrifying woman. Oh god, Mrs. Davies! She had a stare that could curdle milk. She was strict, though, you can’t deny she got results. Speaking of terrifying, have you seen what’s happening with that Russell Brand situation? Honestly, it’s just…awful. Dreadful. Absolutely dreadful. I saw some of the allegations online. I always thought he was a bit of a showman, a bit…performative. But that’s beyond performative, isn’t it? It makes you question everything you thought you knew. You read some of these things online, and you start wondering what else is going on under the surface. It does, doesn’t it? It feeds into all those…well, all those conspiracy theories. Like, it’s easy to fall down a rabbit hole. My brother's  completely  convinced the government is controlling the weather. Honestly, I just roll my eyes. Your brother? Still on that? He was obsessed with crop circles back in the 90s! I think he just enjoys having something to believe in that’s outside the mainstream. Though, I have to admit, sometimes you do wonder… about things. Not weather control, necessarily, but…the power structures, the way things are really run. I get that. It’s healthy to be a bit skeptical.

Dad, honestly, are you  sure  this is the right way? We’ve been on the M5 for ages. It all looks…grey. Just grey roads and grey fields. It’s depressing! Alright, alright, no need for the drama, Elsie. I’ve got the satnav on, haven’t I? And it's telling me we're on track for Bodmin Moor. We’re getting closer to Jamaica Inn, you know. Remember you wanted to see that? Daphne du Maurier, all atmospheric and spooky. Yeah, but even spooky needs  something  to look at. It’s like someone drained all the colour out of England. Except for those wind turbines. They’re… aggressively white. Why are they always white? Practicality, love. Easier to spot for aircraft, I reckon. And they reflect the sunlight. Though I suppose white  is  a bit clinical, isn’t it? Makes you think of the Wizard of Oz, doesn't it? Suddenly everything bursting into colour. Ooh, good point! Dorothy landing in Oz. Though I prefer Sherlock Holmes, actually. Everything in those stories feels very…precise. Black and white, logical. Although Conan Doyle did describe London pretty vividly, didn’t he? All foggy and smoggy. He did indeed. Though if he were writing now, he’d probably be baffled by texts. Can you imagine Holmes trying to work out a cryptic emoji? "The culprit, Watson, clearly signalled their intent with a grinning face…but what did it  mean ?!" That would be brilliant! It's so different from how people used to communicate. Like, telegrams! Grandma used to talk about sending telegrams. So formal. Formal and expensive! Before that, it was all about the telegraph, Morse code. Dot dash, dot dot… I remember trying to learn it as a lad. Never got the hang of it. Then you’ve got Braille, a whole different system for reading. Amazing, really, how clever people are. It is. It makes you think about languages, doesn’t it? All these different ways of expressing things. Do you think Lewis Carroll ever thought about that when he was writing  Alice in Wonderland ? He practically invented his own language in that book. He probably did. A proper eccentric, that one. Always messing with logic and language. Speaking of stories, you packed your fairy tale collection, right? For the evenings in the caravan? Yes! And my new poetry book. I wanted to try and write some poems inspired by the scenery.

Aye, honestly, the price of a loaf of bread these days is scandalous. Back home, you could get a proper sliced white for… well, not much more than a quid, even last year. Down here it’s nearly two fifty! Is it just Somerset being pricey, or is it everywhere like that now? Somerset’s always been a bit of a… well, a different kettle of fish, lass. Always had a premium on things. But no, it’s gone up everywhere. Everything’s gone up. Though, mind you, a quid for a loaf? When  I  were a lad, a loaf was tuppence ha’penny. And a cinema ticket? Sixpence! Sixpence to see a proper film. Not these… superhero explosions they have now. Sixpence! Grandad, you're winding us up. That's... unimaginable. Though, I do agree cinema prices are getting ridiculous. I was looking at going to see that new sci-fi, and it’s fifteen quid a ticket! I could practically rent a whole flat for a week for that. Speaking of which, rent in London is just… obscene. I'm lucky I’m still living with my parents while I save up. Tell me about it! I had a flat in Sunderland for a while, and even  that  was pushing it. Though, it wasn't Wincanton prices, that's for sure. What was it like growing up around here, Grandad? Different to Manchester, I bet? Oh, vastly different. Manchester was all hustle and bustle, industry. During the war, everything was geared towards the factories. My dad worked at Ferranti, making radar equipment. Scary times, dodging the bombs. Though, we were lucky. Timperley didn't get hit too bad. This area, Somerset, was mostly farmland, quiet. Everyone knew everyone. Still remember old Mr. Higgins and his apple orchard… World War Two must have been incredible to live through. I mean, reading about it in history books is one thing, but actually remembering… Did you ever think about joining up, Grandad? I tried, lad. I really did. But they said I was needed more at BT. Essential service, you see. Maintaining the communications. Not glamorous, but important. Spent the whole war glued to a telephone exchange. Kept me safe, that did. Though, I always felt a bit guilty that I wasn't doing more. Well, you  were  doing something important! Keeping everyone connected is massive. I'm glad you were safe. My grandma, she was a land girl.

Right, Mum, let’s try and actually  make  a list for clearing out the attic. It feels like we’ve been saying we’ll do it for about six months now. And honestly, the thought of all that stuff… it's a bit overwhelming. Oh, don't I know it. Your father held onto  everything . Said it might be useful one day. Useful for what, I never did find out. Though, bless him, he did have a point about some of those old tools. You’ve still got his toolbox, haven’t you? It’s a good quality one. Yeah, definitely keeping the toolbox. The attic is less tools, more… Christmas decorations from 1987 and boxes labelled “Important Documents” that are just old school reports. It's a archaeological dig up there. And then there's the wedding stuff… Oh? Already thinking about the wedding then? Thought you were still enjoying being engaged. Enjoying it immensely! But realistically, sorting through this house is going to unlock a load of…things. Memories, stuff we need to deal with. And potentially things we could  use  for the wedding? Floral arrangements, maybe? Or old photo frames. I’m just trying to be practical. Always the pragmatist, you were. Even as a little boy, organizing your Lego. Floral arrangements from the attic, that's ambitious, dear. Though I do recall a lovely silk flower garland your Auntie Maureen made... probably disintegrated by now. Speaking of practicality, how are you feeling? Jet lag still hitting you hard after that flight back from Japan? It’s fading, thankfully. Still waking up at odd hours though. It’s weird, isn’t it? Your body remembers the time difference even when your brain tries to ignore it. I keep having dreams about vending machines and polite bowing. Sounds lovely, actually. You always did love travelling. Your grandfather, God rest his soul, had that same wanderlust. He’d tell me stories about sailing around the Mediterranean. Did I ever tell you about the weaver fish he caught off the coast of Crete? Apparently, it glowed in the dark. I think you have! Several times. It’s become a family legend, the glowing weaver fish. Though I suspect a little embellishment with each retelling. Mum, seriously though, about the house… are you still feeling okay about everything? Selling it and moving to the flat? I worry you're doing it too quickly.

“Honestly, look at that one. It’s like… a tiny, alien spaceship. Do you think I could grow orchids, d’ya reckon? Our windowsill gets decent light now we’ve finally cleared all yer books off it.” “Harsh. They weren’t  all  my books. And orchids? You? The woman who almost killed a cactus? It’s a bold move, love, a  very  bold move.” “Hey! The cactus was… a victim of circumstance. I went away for a week and forgot to ask Mrs. Higgins to water it. It’s not my fault it decided to expire dramatically. Orchids are different. They’re…fussy, but beautiful. Like a really complicated hairstyle.” “Speaking of complicated hairstyles, did you see Amelia’s new ‘do? She went full 80s perm. It’s… a choice. A very strong choice.” “Oh, I saw it on Instagram. It’s… commitment. Massive commitment. Good for her, though, isn’t it? Just doing what makes her happy. It’s a world away from my usual ‘chuck it up in a bun and hope for the best’ approach.” “Exactly. Though, honestly, that bun suits you. Practical. Like your approach to, well, everything. Unlike the NHS trying to be practical these days. Did you see that report about the waiting lists? It’s beyond a joke.” “I did. It’s terrifying, isn't it? My nan needs a hip replacement and they’re saying it could be eighteen months. Eighteen months! She’s in constant pain. It just feels…crumbling. All the good intentions, the brilliant staff, and it's just overwhelmed.” “It feels like they’re constantly putting plasters on things instead of actually fixing the core problems. Which, let’s face it, partially stems from years of underfunding and also… well, the A-Level reforms haven't helped. Fewer people studying STEM subjects, so fewer aspiring doctors and nurses.” "Aye, that’s a good point. I remember all that fuss when they changed the curriculum. It felt like they were prioritising 'employability' over actual knowledge. Which is ironic, considering we haven’t got enough properly trained people for vital jobs like healthcare.” “Precisely. And then you've got the petrol crisis thrown into the mix. Makes you wonder what’s next. It’s like a domino effect of bad decisions and unforeseen consequences. Are we heading for a full-blown Seventies throwback?” "Don’t even  say  that! I was a bairn in the Seventies, but my mam used to tell me stories about queues for petrol and power cuts.

…and honestly, the reading list for Medieval History is  insane . Like, three books a week minimum. And half of ‘em are about the Black Plague. Honestly, I'm starting to feel a bit… plague-y just  thinking  about it. Oh god, really? I thought Medieval History would be all knights and castles. Sounds… grim. My Victorian Literature course is bad enough - all repressed emotions and consumption. At least it’s not actively about death on a massive scale. Aye, well, at least you’re reading. I'm struggling to even  start  my dissertation proposal. It's on the representation of women in early Romantic poetry, and the more I read, the more I realise it's been done to death. Literally! Every woman’s either a tragic muse or a virtuous angel. It's so frustrating. Tell me about it! Mine’s on the socio-economic impact of deindustrialisation in the North East. Basically, Sunderland’s decline in poetry form. Joy. It's just a load of statistics masquerading as literary criticism. You’d think being at uni would be more… inspiring. Inspiring? Ha! I'm more inspired to find a part-time job so I can actually afford to, y’know,  live  while I'm supposed to be inspiring. This student loan doesn’t stretch to oat lattes and textbooks, does it? I reckon I could get something at the pub down the road - they're always looking for staff. It's the same in Leeds, everything’s so expensive. I'm trying to save for a trip to Italy next summer, but it feels utterly impossible. I’ve been looking at tutoring, maybe GCSE English. At least it uses something I’m actually good at. Tutoring’s not a bad shout. I was thinking of going back to the pub I worked at over the summer, but my mam’s going on about ‘career development’ and ‘relevant experience’. As if pouring pints doesn't teach you anything about people! Your mam sounds… ambitious. Mine's just happy I'm not living at home, to be honest. Though she does keep asking if I’ve met any “nice doctors” at uni. It's like, Mam, I'm studying Sociology, not medicine! Oh, bless ‘em. They just want us settled, don’t they? Speaking of settled, anyone else think this whole ‘single and thriving’ thing is massively overrated? It's hard work, innit?

…and honestly, the whole weekend just felt  exhausting . Like I was performing friendship, you know? Constantly trying to find things to talk about, nodding along to stories that didn’t really…land. It just didn’t feel natural anymore. Oh God, I  hate  that feeling. The performing bit. It’s like you’re both going through the motions, but the spark’s completely gone. Happened with Sarah, a couple of years ago. We’d been thick as thieves since uni, but then she got really into…well, let’s just say very intense lifestyle stuff, and I just couldn’t relate. Tried for a while, but it just became draining. Exactly! Draining is the perfect word. It’s not that she’d  done  anything, with Chloe. She’s still perfectly lovely, just… different. We used to have so much in common, book clubs, terrible cinema choices, complaining about work. Now it’s all about pilates and organic gardening. Which is great for her, genuinely, but I feel like I’m speaking a different language. It’s the shift, isn't it? People evolve, and sometimes you just evolve  away  from each other. But then the awkward bit is… how do you actually let it fade? Just ghosting feels awful, and a big confrontation feels even worse. I practically engineered my decline with Sarah. Became ‘really busy’ a lot. ‘Really busy’ is the universal excuse! I’m mastering it, I think. But I feel guilty. She messaged yesterday asking if I wanted to go to that new art exhibition, and I just… stalled. Said I needed to check my schedule. I’ve got a perfectly free Saturday. Don’t feel guilty! Seriously. You’re not obligated to maintain a friendship just because you  have  in the past. It’s okay to admit that something isn’t working for you anymore. Maybe instead of outright cancelling, you could suggest something less…involved? Like, “Oh, the exhibition sounds great, but I'm feeling a bit overwhelmed this weekend, maybe we could just grab a coffee sometime next week?” It keeps the door slightly ajar without committing to a huge chunk of your time. That’s…actually really good advice. A coffee feels manageable. Less pressure. It's the big things, the weekends away, the long dinners, that feel so forced now. It’s like, I’m pretending to have a fantastic time when I'm internally cataloguing all the things I'd rather be doing.

Honestly, Gran, this quiche is  chef’s kiss . You’ve really outdone yourself. Better than anything they serve in the uni canteen, that’s for sure. Which is saying something, ‘cause the canteen’s…well, it exists. Oh, stop it, darling. It's just a simple recipe. Though, I did use that Gruyère you brought back from France last year. That makes all the difference, doesn't it? Reminds me of Vienna, actually. Their cheese… oh, the cheese! Not quite the same as English cheddar, but… different. It does. It elevates the whole thing. France was…intense. Good intense, though. The uni trip was mostly just wandering around lost and trying to remember GCSE French, but the food made up for it. How was your exhibition setup going? Did everything arrive in one piece? Mostly. Old Man Hemmings from next door “helped” unload the van and nearly dropped ‘The Blue Period’ – honestly, the drama! I had to wrestle it from him. It’s up now though, and looking rather lovely, if I do say so myself. Opening night is next Friday. You  must  come. Of course, I’ll be there! Wouldn’t miss it. I'm just buried in essays at the moment. Dissertation’s looming large, and it's currently resembling a particularly chaotic abstract painting itself. All over the place. Oh, those dissertations. I remember helping your mother with hers. History, wasn’t it? Something about the Suffragettes? She was rather passionate, your mother. Still is. Have you spoken to her recently? She was asking about you. Yeah, spoke to Mum yesterday. She’s fussing about Christmas already, trying to coordinate everyone. It’s… a lot. She's thinking of dragging us all to Cornwall again. Cornwall! Oh, that reminds me of your Aunt Clara. She always adored Cornwall. Spent summers there as a girl, apparently. Said the light was magical. She never really talked about her childhood much, did she? Always so…reserved. Not really. Mum said something happened when she was young, but Clara never wanted to discuss it. It always felt a bit…sad, you know? She was lovely, though. Proper eccentric, always with a bird feather in her hair. She was. A true original. She had that artist’s eye, even if she didn’t pursue it professionally. I always wished she had. Speaking of artists, did you read that review of the Hockney exhibition? In  The Guardian ?

Honestly, I still feel a bit sick from that pierogi feast last night. Should we have eaten  before  even thinking about a gym session? It was a terrible idea. My stomach was doing somersaults during those squats. You and your delicate constitution, Auntie Carol! It was delicious, though, wasn't it? And you  did  manage the squats. Maybe just… fewer next time? Besides, it’s a long drive to Białka. We need the fuel. Are you comfortable driving for another couple of hours? I’m starting to feel a little… road-hypnotized. Comfortable enough. This campervan handles beautifully, actually. It’s a world away from driving the old Mini back in Cambridge. Though, I do miss Cambridge sometimes. And yes, the pierogi were good, ridiculously so. It's just… the timing. It feels distinctly un-English to eat so heavily before exercise. We're taught to gently 'fuel' – a banana, a yogurt. Not a mountain of potato dumplings. Oh,  that’s  it? It's a cultural thing? I just figured you were a bit of a fussy eater. Seriously though, Poland has different ideas about everything. And you’re right, it’s nice to just… indulge. We deserve it after hauling ourselves around Europe in this metal box. Speaking of which, what time do you reckon we'll get there? Google Maps is being spectacularly unhelpful. Google Maps  is  useless sometimes. Let me see… judging by the speed and the distance… and factoring in a coffee stop, I’d say around 4pm? That gives us enough time for another gym session before dinner. Are you planning another body-pumping extravaganza? Maybe. I’m feeling pretty good today. It’s surprisingly liberating, getting stronger. It's almost… political, isn’t it? Taking up space, being physically capable. Especially as a woman. I've noticed a real difference in the gyms here versus back home. Fewer judgemental stares, less… lingering. That's a very interesting point, actually. I've always found gyms rather intimidating. All that… displaying. And the assumptions! Back home, if a woman lifts anything heavier than a cosmetic bag, you get raised eyebrows. It’s that ridiculous expectation of fragility. I suppose things are changing, slowly. But the sexism is still so deeply ingrained. Exactly! And it’s not just the weightlifting. It’s the whole culture. The amount of space men take up physically, the confidence with which they claim equipment… It's subtly exhausting to navigate.

…and honestly, that mug feels  right . Not like these mass-produced things. You can feel the hand in it, can’t you? Old Man Hemmings really knew what he was doing, even if his prices were a bit steep. Still, worth every penny for a proper brew. More milk, love? Aye, a splash, thank you, Barbara. Lovely mug it is. Not too heavy, not too thin. Reminds me o’ one Elsie Bottomley had. Elsie, you remember Elsie? Lived up on Thornton Road. She collected them, she did. Every shape and size. Filled her kitchen cupboards to bursting. Vaguely. Elsie…wasn't she the one who tripped over Mr. Grimshaw’s cat and broke her wrist? That was her! Poor Elsie. Mr. Grimshaw was furious, you can imagine. Said Tibbles hadn’t done anything wrong, just minding his own business. Typical Grimshaw, always taking the side of animals. Although, Tibbles  was  a handsome cat. Still, she ended up needing a cast right up to her elbow. Terrible accident, that. Oh dear. Speaking of accidents, I was nearly a goner yesterday while trying to change that bulb in the hallway. The ladder wobbled, and I swear I saw my life flash before my eyes. Thankfully, young Thomas was here and grabbed me. He’s a strong lad, thankfully. Oh, Barbara! You must be careful. You're not as young as you used to be, you know. Thomas is a good lad, though. Always willing to lend a hand. Did the power go off again when you were fiddling about with the electrics? Seems like it’s been happening more and more often. It did, actually! Just as I was about to screw the new one in. Went off with a little pop. Of course. Always at the most inconvenient moment. Luckily, it only lasted about ten minutes. I’m starting to think we need to get one of those generator things. A generator! Sounds like something out of a war film. Though, I suppose it’d be handy. Remember that time we had that storm in '63? We were without power for three days! Had to get candles from old Mrs. Higgins next door. She always had a stockpile of everything. I remember hearing about that one. We weren't living here then, still in Shipley. Honestly, it's been a lovely few days weather-wise, hasn't it? Perfect for the garden. I spent most of Saturday deadheading the roses.

Honestly, Mum, a week in Cornwall feels…a bit tame, doesn’t it? Everyone’s going to Cornwall this year. It's going to be rammed. Tame? Elsie, darling, it’s a lovely, relaxing break. We haven't  had  a relaxing break in ages. Remember last year with Uncle Barry and the camping trip? The midges nearly carried little Leo away! Cornwall has beautiful beaches, cream teas… And decent fish and chips. Don't underestimate the importance of a good chippy on holiday, you two. Though, to be fair, Hastings does alright on that front… not Yorkshire levels of good, mind. Yeah, okay, the fish and chips will be good. But what about doing something  different ? We always go to the seaside. What about Italy? Or even… Greece? I saw some amazing photos of Santorini in a magazine at school. Santorini is lovely, but Elsie, that's a  considerable  jump in budget. And besides, your father’s back isn’t brilliant on long flights these days. Cornwall is a drive, it's manageable. We can stop for lunch, stretch our legs… She’s got a point, love. Italy would be brilliant, but it’s a fair old trek. Remember that time we tried to drive to the Lake District and I ended up with a bad back for a month? Not repeating  that  particular experience. Although… maybe a bit of Tuscany? Short flights are available. Tuscany  would  be amazing! Vineyards, pasta, everything! But Dad wouldn't like all the hills, would he? He complains about walking up Telham Hill. Elsie! Don’t exaggerate. He manages perfectly well. And Tuscany is a lovely suggestion, but realistically, it’s pushing it. Let’s stick with Cornwall. We’ve booked a little cottage near St Ives. Apparently, it has a sea view. St Ives is alright. Gets a bit crowded, though. Still, can't complain about the art scene. Remember old Mr. Penrose? Wonderful fella. Used to play jazz down at the pub back in the day. Mr. Penrose? The painter? I think I've seen his work in a book. But honestly, do we  have  to invite Auntie Brenda and Uncle Geoff? They spend the whole time complaining about everything. Elsie, that's very unkind. They're family. And they've been looking forward to joining us. Aye, they’re a pair alright. Brenda’s obsessed with her prize-winning geraniums and Geoff just wants to talk about betting on the horses.

Honestly, Heath Ledger in that film was just…  chef’s kiss . Like, Patrick Verona is the blueprint. Don’t even try to tell me otherwise, Chloe. Oh, here we go. The Heath Ledger appreciation society is now in session, hosted by Elsie. Yes, yes, he was dreamy. But don’t pretend you weren’t also totally rooting for Kat to get with Joey. He was sweet! Sweet is… nice. But it’s not  Heath Ledger  sweet. It’s not brooding, poetic, challenges-you-to-be-better sweet. Joey was… vanilla. Plus, the paintball scene? Iconic. Okay, okay, you’ve made your point. Paintball  was  good. Speaking of challenges though, I’m absolutely dreading Mr. Davies’ history essay. “The impact of the Industrial Revolution on Cambridge.” Like, seriously? Cambridge  during  the Industrial Revolution? It's so niche! Ugh, tell me about it! I’ve barely started. I keep getting distracted thinking about… you guessed it… Heath Ledger. But also, trying to figure out if my grandma actually  lived  through any of that. She was born in, like, 1920. Oh, that’s a good angle! You could interview her. Proper primary source material. Mr. Davies would love that. Honestly, he's such a stickler for originality. Remember when Ben wrote about Roman gladiators and Davies marked him down because it wasn’t ‘locally relevant’? Oh god,  yes ! Ben was fuming for weeks. He was like, ‘Rome influenced everything! It's still relevant!’ And Davies just stared at him with that disapproving look. I’m aiming to avoid  that  level of disappointment. Me too. It's just… so much work. I was thinking, maybe after exams, we could finally go to London? Remember we were talking about it ages ago? See that exhibition at the V&A? The one on theatre costumes? Ooh, yes! The one with all the Shakespearean stuff? That would be amazing! But… money. My mum’s been hinting at needing a new washing machine. That’s usually code for ‘no fun allowed for the next six months.’ Right. The eternal washing machine saga. My parents are the same. Maybe we could look into those train deals? And pack our own sandwiches? Become masters of budget travel? Operation: Budget London is a go. We’d have to plan it properly, though. Research free museums, walk everywhere… possibly smuggle snacks. Smuggling snacks is  essential . And we need to hit up that little vintage shop in Covent Garden, the one with all the quirky jewellery.

Now, you say this… Facebook… it’s got pictures of everyone’s dinner on it? Honestly. What’s the point of  that ? Back in my day, if you had a nice bit of scampi, you  ate  it, you didn't photograph it for strangers. Oh, Arthur, you say that every time! It’s not just dinner, dear. It’s…keeping in touch. Seeing what the grandchildren are up to. Things like that. Though I must say, Brenda next door posts a  lot  of cat photos. It’s quite overwhelming. It's a bit of everything, really, Gran. A way to share snippets of life. I use it mostly for professional networking, actually. Keeping up with research in my field. But yes, there’s also the cat photos. And the dinner. And everything in between. It's become incredibly pervasive. You almost  need  it these days for events, groups... even just knowing what's going on locally. We've got a university research group on there, makes organising things much easier. Pervasive… that sounds a right nasty word. Sounds like a disease. Which reminds me, did young Emily ever get chicken pox? I’ve a feeling she was dodging it at school. Always a bit of a clever clogs, wasn't she? Used to wrap herself in bubble wrap when playing outside, just in case. Oh, that Emily! Yes, she did eventually. Got it dreadful, poor lamb. Little spots  everywhere . Though honestly, I suspect she enjoyed the attention. It was all “Look at me, Mummy!” and “Poor Emily!” It’s interesting, isn’t it, how anxieties manifest? Emily's bubble wrap… it sounds a little bit like some of the behaviours associated with Obsessive Compulsive Disorder. Not to diagnose, obviously, but there's a link between anxiety and repetitive behaviours. I actually lecture on the psychology of anxiety. That's a good point, actually. The need for control, the feeling of needing to perform certain actions to prevent something bad happening... it's a spectrum. And it's often rooted in something deeper. OCD? Sounds foreign. Like one of those continental things. We didn't 'ave illnesses with fancy names like that in my day. You were just a bit… peculiar. Old Man Hemmings down the lane used to count every blade of grass on his lawn. Everyone just said he was a bit odd. Never thought there was a  name  for it.

…and honestly, the traffic getting  to  Folkestone was a nightmare. Absolutely chock-a-block. Nearly didn’t make the ferry, we didn’t. Honestly, you wouldn’t believe it.      Folkestone, again? Every summer, Mum? Don’t you ever fancy going  somewhere  different? Like, Spain or something? Somewhere with actual sun?      Now, now, Chloe. Your mother likes her seaside traditions. Besides, it’s easy enough to get a day trip to France from Folkestone. And she's got her sister there, hasn't she?      I do! And Brenda makes the most incredible scones. It’s just… comfortable, you know? Familiar. Plus, I can practice my dreadful French. "Où est la gare?" is about my limit, sadly.      It's a start! I've been trying to learn German, actually. For a work project. It's…challenging. All those declensions. Sounds like someone clearing their throat constantly.      German, eh? My Grandad fought in Germany, you know. Said they were a stern lot. Didn’t say much else about it, though. He wasn't one for reminiscing. Kept himself to himself, he did.      Your Grandad, Arthur, was a good man. Remember him always pottering about in his garden, always a pint in hand? He had a Morris Minor, didn’t he? Bright blue. A proper little car.      Oh god, the Morris Minor! I remember being crammed in the back of that thing on family outings. It smelled of pipe tobacco and damp dog. No air con, obviously.      Oh, you always were a fussy one, Chloe! It was character-building! And Arthur loved that car. Polished it every Sunday. He swore it was more reliable than anything modern. He’d say, “These new cars, all computers and nonsense!”      He wasn’t wrong, you know. Simpler times, in a lot of ways. Though I wouldn't trade the central heating for all the Morris Minors in Kent. Remember the winters we used to have? Frozen pipes, layering up…      Dad, you make it sound like the Dark Ages. I wasn't even a twinkle in your eye back then.      No, no, it wasn’t  that  bad. Just…different. We made do. Used to have to thaw the door lock with a watering can of warm water.      My old man used to do that too! He had an Austin A40 Farina. Now  that  was a car. Proper style. Though it leaked like a sieve.      Farina! That's a blast from the past.

…and honestly, the sound at that festival was atrocious. Like, genuinely awful. You could barely hear Liam sing over the bass. It completely ruined “Supersonic” –  ruined  it, I tell you. Blimey, that's rough. Which festival was this again? Glasto? No, Boardmasters. Down here, actually. Thought I’d catch them playing a bit closer to home. Should have known better. Still, seeing them live, even a slightly muffled version, is better than nothing. Did you manage to catch anyone good recently? You were saying you were working every other weekend. Yeah, work’s been a bit manic since the summer season kicked off. Haven't had much chance to go to gigs, sadly. Though I did manage to sneak out to see IDLES at the Exeter Phoenix a few weeks back. Properly mental, as always. Proper energy. IDLES! Nice one. I’ve only seen them once, back in Notts at Rock City. They just… hit you, don’t they? No messing about. Speaking of hitting things, how's the drumming going? Still bashing away in your dad’s shed? Still is, yeah. Though Dad keeps threatening to build a proper soundproof room if I don’t quieten down. Found a new local band, actually. Trying to gig around Devon. They're a bit rough around the edges, but the drummer’s solid, and they’re doing some interesting stuff. Sort of post-punk revival but with a bit more… funk, I guess? Sounds good. Is it a full band? Any recordings online? I’m always looking for new things to listen to. I’ve been stuck on this new Fontaines D.C. album for weeks now. Yeah, full band. They're called ‘Static Bloom’. They’ve got a couple of tracks up on Bandcamp, I’ll send you the link. Honestly, though, they’re better live. You get a real feel for their energy. How’s the uni life treating you? Still buried in books? Buried, but… almost free! Dissertation's finally submitted. Feeling the relief, to be honest. It was on the socio-political impact of Britpop, oddly enough. Got quite obsessed with Blur and Oasis again while researching. No way! That's actually really cool. I’ve always wondered about that whole period. All the hype, the media… feels like it was a different world. So, what now? Internship lined up? That's the scary part. Trying to find something.

…Honestly, this is just what I needed. A bit of peace and quiet. Though ‘quiet’ is a generous word, isn’t it? This place is buzzing. It’s alright. More atmosphere, like. Better than being stuck in, listening to Dad’s radio. He was on about some cricket thing for hours this morning. Oh, don’t start on your father and his cricket. It’s his therapy, you know. Keeps him sane. Anyway, have you given any more thought to Durham for the summer holiday? I was looking at campsites… Durham’s…fine. Bit boring, though, innit? All old buildings and stuff. Can’t we go somewhere with, like, a beach? Or a theme park? A beach in Durham? Now  that  would be a sight. We discussed this, lad. Your Auntie Maureen’s birthday is the weekend after we were thinking of going. She’d be absolutely gutted if we weren’t there for her domino drive. The domino drive. Seriously? That’s what you call a holiday? Old ladies and clicking dominoes? It’s tradition! And it’s good to see her. Besides, they have a cracking buffet. Look, I need to pick up a few things from the shops after this. Milk, bread, those fancy biscuits you like…anything else you want me to add to the list? Actually, yeah. New headphones. These ones are packed. And… can I get that new football top? Everyone at school’s got one. Headphone’s alright. The football top…we’ll see. It’s awfully expensive. Right, let’s get back to Durham. I found a campsite near Crook Hall. Apparently, it’s haunted. Haunted? Seriously? Like…ghosts? That’s what the website says. Apparently, a monk wanders the grounds. Though I suspect it’s just a marketing ploy. I saw old Mrs. Higgins from next door in the drive-through earlier. She was shouting at the poor lad in the booth because her coffee wasn't sweet enough. Honestly, the drama. She’s a character, that one. Did you see that bloke in the red car earlier? He was trying to parallel park for about ten minutes. Kept bumping into the kerb. Oh, I did! It was painful to watch. You know, I keep meaning to check out that new cafe that opened up near the station. "Brew & Bite," I think it's called. They have a loyalty card, apparently. Buy ten coffees, get one free.

…and honestly, the sound quality on that recording is  awful . I spent ages getting different people to say “The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog” – all different accents, you know, for my phonetics class – and it just sounds like they’re talking through a tin can. Sounds about right for a university budget. Remember that dodgy microphone in the language lab? Sounded like it was recorded in a cardboard box. Good to see you again, by the way. It's been… what, three years? Since graduation? Sussex suits you. Bit…posh, isn’t it? Compared to Brum. Too posh for your liking, then? Nah, it’s alright. Bit of a nightmare getting the post redirected, though. Royal Mail clearly thinks Bedford is where I still live. And yeah, ages. Feels longer. How’s work? Still crunching numbers and finding glitches? Still doing the assurance thing. Pays the bills. Actually, pays a lot of bills. Got a decent pay rise this year. Starting to think about… you know…proper grown-up stuff. Oh? Like what kind of “proper grown-up stuff”? Don't tell me you’re joining a golf club. Worse. Sarah’s pregnant. Blimey! No way! Sarah? That’s… huge news! Congratulations, man! When did you find out? Is she alright? Found out a couple of months ago. She's good, a bit queasy sometimes, but mostly good. It's terrifying, to be honest. Suddenly I'm thinking about nappies and… mortgages. Proper terrifying. And the cost of everything these days! I can imagine! It's mental, isn’t it? Everything’s gone up. Even a pint of milk feels like a luxury. We were talking about budgets in class today, ironically. Students have  no  concept. Speaking of which, how are you managing financially? Thinking about joint accounts and all that jazz? That's the next battle. Sarah wants everything joint, naturally. I'm…hesitant. I've worked hard for what I've got. Feels weird sharing it all. But I suppose that’s part of the package, isn’t it? She’s already started looking at prams. Online, thankfully. We don't actually  need  to go into a shop yet. Sensible. Have you thought about names? Actually, don't answer that. That’s a conversation I'm deliberately avoiding with my sister and her partner. It’s a minefield. Remember Dave from Uni? He went to South Korea to teach English after we graduated.

…and honestly, the guilt is awful, isn’t it? Even knowing it was what she  wanted . Saying ‘yes’ to assisted dying felt…like giving up on her, even though she was the one desperately fighting for control  through  it. It does, doesn’t it? That’s a whole other layer of grief, isn't it? The ‘should I have…’, ‘could I have…’ It’s exhausting just thinking about it. My Auntie Brenda, different situation entirely – breast cancer, spread everywhere – she clung on. Refused to even  talk  about palliative care properly. It was brutal watching her…and for Uncle George, even more so. He was determined to keep her going, even when she was clearly in pain. It’s that wanting to fix things, isn’t it? We're so programmed to  do  something, to find a solution. And when there isn’t one…it’s just devastating. With Mum, she was so pragmatic. She’d always said, "I've lived a good life, I don't want to become a shell." She’d researched everything, had the legal stuff sorted months in advance. It still feels…unnatural. Absolutely. And people have  opinions , don’t they? So many opinions. I had a colleague, bless her, meant well, say, “Oh, you must be so relieved it’s over,” and I just…froze. It’s not  relief . It's…emptiness. A profound, aching emptiness. How are the kids coping? Little Ethan was so close to your Mum. Ethan’s…lost. Absolutely lost. He keeps asking when she’s coming back for tea. We’re trying to explain, gently, but he doesn’t really understand ‘peacefully’ or ‘no more pain’. Leo, being older, he gets it a bit more, but he’s withdrawn. He's stopped going to football practice, which is  so  unlike him. He says it just doesn’t feel…right…without her cheering him on. Oh, my heart aches for them. It’s good they have each other, though. Siblings help navigate this stuff. Have you thought about some bereavement counselling for them? There are some excellent child psychologists around here. I can dig out a few numbers if you like. That's really kind of you, thank you. We’ve talked about it. Leo’s leaning towards it, I think. Ethan…he’s just clinging to me. I'm trying to be strong for both of them, but honestly, I feel like I’m barely holding it together myself.

Honestly, this chicken is lovely, isn't it? Though I suspect your father spent more time supervising me than actually  doing  the cooking.      It’s good, Mum. Though I think I preferred lasagne last week. Did you see Alex’s serve in tennis practice today? It was  massive . Completely whizzed past Mr. Henderson.      Ah, the joys of teenage metabolism and burgeoning athleticism. Good for Alex. You’re keeping up with your practice, though, aren’t you, Leo? It’s good discipline.      Yeah, I am. It’s alright. Bit cold today though. We were doing volleys and my hands were freezing. It's better when it's warmer. Mr. Henderson is pushing us hard for the county trials.      That’s brilliant, Leo! County trials are a big deal. Are you still thinking about taking that coaching badge, Alex? It could be a good earner, and you’re certainly good enough to teach others.      I dunno, Mum. It's loads of time, and I’m worried about messing up my own game focusing on everyone else’s. Plus, football season’s starting soon. I’ve made the squad again.      That’s excellent news about the football, Alex. Balancing both will be tough, though. Remember what happened with your GCSEs last year? Too much on your plate.      Exactly. It’s all about having a plan. Speaking of plans... Did you have a chance to look at those apprenticeship schemes I sent you, Leo? The engineering one at JCB looked particularly good.      I glanced at them. It looks… boring. All about precision and measurements. I’d rather just go to uni. Everyone’s applying to uni.      Everyone doesn’t  have  to go to university, darling. And there’s absolutely nothing wrong with a skilled trade. Think about the money you could earn and the job security. University debt is crippling these days.      She has a point, Leo. A good apprenticeship can be a fantastic launchpad. I actually considered one myself, before I ended up doing my Masters. It’s a viable path, not a failure to launch, as some people think.      So, you didn’t always want to be an Operations Manager, Dad?      No, not exactly. I had grand plans to be a landscape architect! Then I realised how much maths was involved… and swiftly revised my ambitions.      He’s very good with spreadsheets, though. It's a very different skillset! Have you been following the news at all?

Honestly, this is  lovely . Proper countryside whizzing by. Much better than staring at a laptop screen, eh? Though, thinking about the dissertation… that’s looming, isn’t it? Lancaster's supposed to have a good library, at least. Looming is an understatement. It’s basically breathing down my neck at this point. Lancaster  does  have a good library, apparently. And the campus looks amazing in the photos. Are you still mostly focusing on the dialectal variations in prepositions, or have you shifted gears? Still on prepositions. It’s… a rabbit hole, honestly. The more you look, the more you find. I’m currently wrestling with the use of 'at' and 'in' when discussing smaller villages around Aylesbury. Proper local variations, you wouldn’t believe. It's fascinating, but writing about it is, well, a slog. You? How’s the data coming along for your project? It’s… complicated. I was hoping to have a solid chunk written before this trip, but Dad’s redundancy threw everything off. Just dealing with  that  has been exhausting. All the forms, the meetings… it’s just draining. He’s taking it surprisingly well, though. Oh, no, that’s awful! I’m so sorry to hear that, Em. That’s a huge stressor for everyone. Especially now. Is he looking at anything already? It’s rubbish that companies are still doing that, isn’t it? Especially after everything the last few years. He’s applying for similar roles, obviously. But he’s also… considering retraining. Something completely different, actually. He was always a bit of a whiz with computers as a kid, apparently. Thinking about coding. Crazy, right? A fifty-year-old learning to code! Not crazy at all! Good on him! It’s never too late. And honestly, it sounds like a smart move. More job security in that field, too, probably. Speaking of different things… are you tempted to nip down to the coast while we're up there? I’ve heard Morecambe Bay is beautiful. That sounds good, actually. A bit of sea air would do us both good. Though, I remember Mum telling me a story about a cockle disaster there, years ago? Something about people illegally harvesting and… well, it wasn't pretty. Oh, blimey, I think I remember hearing something about that on the news. Awful. But hopefully things are a bit more regulated now. And we won't be trying to  harvest  any cockles!

…and then Liam  actually  tried to argue with the barman that his pint was too full. Too full! Like, mate, you're getting extra beer, what’s the problem? It’s a win, innit? Proper Liam, that. He’ll find a complaint in paradise, our Liam. Still, you gotta admire the commitment to getting his money’s worth. Did he get away with it? Eventually. After about ten minutes of pointing and muttering about ‘consumer rights’. The barman just topped it up again, probably to shut him up. Honestly, it’s exhausting being around him sometimes. How's your coursework going though? You looked a bit stressed earlier? It’s…ongoing. That History essay on the industrial revolution is killing me. I keep getting bogged down in the detail. It's just dates and names and factories. Where’s the  story  in it all? You're on English Lit, yeah? You lot get to read proper books. We do, but it's not all flowery language and romance, you know. I’m dissecting  Wuthering Heights  at the moment. It’s bleak. Proper Yorkshire bleak, actually. All windswept moors and brooding men. Makes you appreciate central heating, honestly. Haha, fair enough. Still sounds better than ‘the impact of steam power on textile production’. Speaking of Yorkshire, have you heard anything new from The Reytons? I saw they posted something on Instagram about a new single. Ooh, no! I haven't checked. Let me have a look… Oh aye! “Another Weekend,” right? It’s decent. Not as good as ‘Hull is Dead’ obviously, but still, solid Reytons. You going to the gig in Sheffield next month? I’m trying to! Tickets sold out ages ago, but I'm on the waiting list. Fingers crossed. It’d be brilliant. Remember when we saw them at Leadmill last year? Absolute chaos. Don't I just! Old man nearly lost his dentures in the pit. Absolute scenes. It’s the best, though, isn’t it? Proper local bands. It feels… real, you know? Not like all that manufactured pop rubbish. Totally. It's just…  us . And it's nice that they sing about places we know. Like, they actually sing about Conisbrough! No one sings about Conisbrough. They’re giving Conisbrough the cultural recognition it deserves. Speaking of recognising things, have you spoken to Sarah lately? I haven’t seen her since she started that new job in Leeds.

Right, okay. Another city falls to the relentless march of disease. Honestly, Rhys, your relentless focus on eradicating Black in Cairo is  killing  us! We need to contain, not cure, at this stage!      Now, now, Carys. Cairo’s a hotspot, innit? Gotta nip it in the bud. Besides, I had a perfectly good plan! Three research stations, two cards… it was coming together. You're the one constantly jetting off to Atlanta when we’ve got outbreaks in Essen and St. Petersburg!      Sounds like the usual Pandemic chaos. Anyone want more tea? This one’s got a little ginger in – helps with the existential dread of global disease outbreaks, apparently.      I think Rhys is right about Cairo. It’s strategic. Although… the yellow cubes are multiplying like rabbits.      Strategic is one thing, Rhys, but you’re forgetting Carys has the Medic! She’s the one who should be bouncing around, mopping up your messes.      Thank you, Megan! Finally, some support. And I  am  mopping up messes! It’s just... I feel like every time I get a handle on something, three more outbreaks occur. This is less strategic gameplay and more controlled panic.      Ah, Pandemic. Brings back memories. Played it endlessly with my grandchildren when they were little. Little blighters were always beating me, clever things. It's all about resource management, you see. And a bit of luck, of course.      Luck has  nothing  to do with it, Dai! It’s pure skill. Okay, maybe a little luck. Look, Carys, if you hadn't used your dispatcher card to send me to Bangkok instead of Cairo…      Bangkok was  dying , Rhys! Three cubes already! Cairo had two! Basic triage! It's like you haven't learnt anything from my medical training.      Anyone else think it's hilarious watching Carys and Rhys argue over fictional disease control? It’s like watching the UN Security Council.      It  is  quite entertaining.      Don’t encourage him, Ben. He'll just get more stubborn. Rhys, darling, maybe just consider Carys's perspective for a moment?      Fine, fine. But if this whole thing goes south, I'm blaming the Bangkok detour. So, where are the yellow cubes popping up now?      South America is looking grim. Bogota and Lima are both at three, and I think I just saw a fourth drop in Sao Paulo.      Oh dear. South America is always tricky. You need a quick response there.

…and honestly, the whole thing was just  bonkers . Did you see Mr. Tumble trying to fly? Honestly, a grown man with a spotty bag thinking he could take off! It was the CBeebies pantomime, wasn't it? Absolutely ridiculous, but they both loved it. It was REALLY good! The sparkly bits were the BEST! And when the dinosaur roared?  Roar!  I liked the pirate! He had a really big sword and he said “Ahoy Matey!” a LOT. He did, didn’t he? A  lot . Honestly, I think they were more excited about the bits they recognised from their shows than the actual story. Though, it was a good story. Speaking of which…Have you two given any more thought to what you want to do for your birthdays this summer? They’re so close together, we need a plan. I want a unicorn party! With a HUGE cake! And all my friends! I want a LEGO party! A really, REALLY big LEGO castle! And a bouncy castle! Right, a unicorn  and  a LEGO castle. That sounds…ambitious. Perhaps we can combine them? A mythical LEGO castle? We could get those LEGO unicorn sets. Is that a thing? No! Unicorns are REAL! They live in sparkly forests! Yeah! And they fight dragons with LEGO swords! Of course, they do. Silly me. Right, a sparkly forest and dragon-fighting LEGO swords it is. We’ll have to see what garden space allows, honestly. And maybe limit the friend list a bit, otherwise, it’ll be like hosting a small festival. Remember last year? Absolute chaos. Last year was fun! I lost my favourite dinosaur in the garden! You did, and we found him eventually, tucked under the rose bushes. Right, so, birthdays… then Mother’s Day is looming. I’m not expecting much, just a slightly less chaotic breakfast in bed would be nice. I can make you a card! A sparkly one! And I can draw a picture of you with a crown! Because you're the queen! Oh, you are both the sweetest. That sounds wonderful. Actually, talking of sparkly things and drawings… have you seen that new show on CBeebies, ‘The Colour Monster’? It’s really quite clever. It talks about feelings and how to name them. I watched that! The yellow monster was happy! And the blue monster was sad! He looked like he needed a hug. Exactly! It’s a really good way to get them talking about how they’re feeling.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork involved with even  thinking  about moving back to Germany is just…exhausting. I spent three hours on the phone yesterday just untangling residency rules. Three hours! For a  potential  move! Three hours? Good grief, David. You'd think after living there as a kid, it would be simpler. Though, knowing bureaucracy, I suppose not. Still, are you seriously considering it? After all this talk about how much you like it here? Aye, it does seem a bit of a U-turn. You were practically singing London’s praises last week, especially after that open-air theatre performance. Remember how you raved about it? I  did  enjoy the theatre, I won’t lie. And I do like it here, genuinely. But my mum's health isn't brilliant, is it? And my sister’s struggling to manage everything on her own. Someone needs to be closer, and…well, I’m the logical choice. Less rooted here, career-wise. That makes sense. Family first, and all that. Still, it's a big shift. What about work? Have you looked at engineering positions over there? Plenty. That’s not the issue, surprisingly. There’s a decent company in Stuttgart, said to be really innovative, but the salary...it’s significantly lower than what I earn now. And the cost of living, while different, isn’t  that  much cheaper. It's a compromise, isn’t it? A big one. It always is. It’s the emotional price tag that's the hardest to calculate, I think. You’ll miss us, won’t you? Don’t pretend you won’t. Of course I will! Who else is going to tolerate my terrible attempts at cooking German food? Speaking of which, anyone fancy trying my Sauerbraten next week? It’s…an acquired taste. Oh, god. I remember last time. It tasted faintly of Christmas and regret. No thank you, darling. I'll stick to your reliably bland shepherd’s pie. Hey! It’s a national dish! And it’s not bland. It’s…rustic. Rustic is a polite word for it. Seriously though, David, have you considered all the implications for your, you know…dating life? Oh, don't even  start  with the internet dating horror stories again, Chloe. Remember last month? The 'spiritual healer' who wanted to cleanse my aura? And the one who insisted she could communicate with dolphins? Honestly, it's like they're actively trying to find the most eccentric people possible.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of Lego my brother had was astounding. It wasn't just one set, it was… a Lego city. Covering the entire spare room. Mum and Dad were constantly stepping on the little bricks. I distinctly remember Dad yelling, “Another one! It’s a Lego landmine in here!” Good times, though, really. Did either of you have a Lego obsession? Oh, my goodness, yes! Not quite to the scale of your brother, Sarah, but I definitely had a phase. Though mine was more focused on building houses. Very detailed houses, meticulously planned. I used to design extensions and everything. I wanted to be an architect, you know. Briefly. Then I realised how much maths was involved and… well, HR felt a bit safer. What about you, Chloe? You always seemed a bit more… artsy? Me? Lego wasn't really my thing. I was all about Sylvanian Families. Little woodland creatures living in tiny houses. I had the whole village, complete with a bakery and a school. I’d spend hours making up stories for them. It sounds ridiculous now, but it was seriously important to me. My mum still has the original house somewhere, I think. She refuses to throw it away. It’s a bit of a shrine to my childhood, apparently. Sylvanian Families! Oh, I remember those! They were so cute. My cousin had a huge collection. It's funny how those early interests shape us, isn’t it? You designing houses, Chloe, likely sparked something. And you, Chloe, the storyteller… accounting isn't  completely  devoid of narrative, is it? You're telling the story of the company's finances! A slightly less fluffy version, admittedly. You’re trying to make me feel better about spreadsheets, Sarah? It’s not working, but I appreciate the effort. Though you're right, there  is  a story there, I suppose. A very dry story. My mum always said my attention to detail came from those Lego houses. Everything had to be  just so . It's probably why I'm so pedantic about paperwork! It's mad how much our upbringing influences us. I’ve started noticing differences in how we all speak, too. It's subtle, but it’s there. Sarah, you've got that slightly broader vowel sound... very Lincolnshire. It's lovely. Oh, you can hear that? I hadn’t realised. Growing up in Boston, Lincolnshire, you don't exactly think about your accent being  distinctive .

…and then the seagull  actually  tried to steal Dad’s sandwich right off his plate! It was audacious, honestly. He barely even flinched, just glared at it. No way! Dad and birds have a complicated relationship, don’t they? Remember the incident with the pigeon in Venice? He was convinced it was a government spy. Aye, well, he's always been a bit…sensitive to wildlife. Though, to be fair, that seagull  did  look well cheeky. We were sat outside that little café in Whitby, weren’t we, love? Lovely crab sandwiches, they were. Beautiful crab sandwiches. And the weather was surprisingly decent for Whitby. We got lucky. Usually, it's blowing a gale up there. Didn't feel like November at all. So, Whitby was the highlight then? You made it to the Abbey, right? I was picturing you two wandering around looking all gothic. We did! Of course, we did. Though ‘wandering’ is a strong word. More like a gentle stroll with frequent stops for me to catch my breath on benches. Those steps up to the Abbey are a killer! But the views… oh, the views were breathtaking. I’ve got loads of pictures on my phone, I’ll show you later. Mum took about a hundred of the sea. It’s mostly just grey waves, to be honest. She’s a woman of simple pleasures, your mother. A good view and a cup of tea. That’s all she needs. I spent most of the time trying to find a decent pub. Found a lovely little one tucked away, The Ship Inn. Good local ale. Sounds perfect, Dad. Did you guys do anything besides historical sites and pubs? Anything… adventurous? Adventurous? At our age, dear? Getting out of bed  is  an adventure these days. No, we didn’t go bungee jumping or anything daft. We did go on a boat trip though, round the coast. Saw some seals bobbing about. Seals! Excellent. Mum loves seals. Did she try to adopt one? She nearly tried to adopt a stray kitten last week. Almost. She was giving it a name and everything. Thankfully, the owner turned up before things went too far. The seals were safer from her affections. Although, she  did  try to feed one a biscuit. I had to wrestle it out of her hand. Oh, Mum! You’re incorrigible. So, how did you get on with the driving, Dad?

Right, I officially need more coffee. This week has been…something else. The simulations keep throwing up anomalies. It’s like the universe  wants  this bridge to fall down. Oh, don’t say that! You’ll jinx it. Anomalies, huh? What kind? Structural integrity stuff? Yeah, precisely. Wind shear calculations are consistently showing stress points we didn’t anticipate. We’ve checked and re-checked the initial data, the modelling software…everything. It’s really frustrating. Feels like I’m missing something obvious. Sounds stressful. Though, honestly, ‘stressful’ feels like the default setting these days. Did you see that article about the comedian, Leo Maxwell? Apparently he’s completely cancelled himself over that tweet. Oh,  him ? The one about…well, I won’t repeat it, but it was incredibly insensitive. Good riddance, I say. You can’t just say things like that and expect no consequences. Honestly, I try to avoid all that celebrity nonsense. It’s all performative outrage anyway. Give me a good engineering problem to chew on any day. Less drama. Easier said than done, isn’t it? Sometimes the news feels like one giant drama. Speaking of drama… how’s Sarah? Still giving you the silent treatment over the… incident with the cheese? Please, don’t. It was  one  slice of her fancy brie! And I offered to replace it. She’s being completely unreasonable. It’s been three days. Three days of pointed sighs and passive-aggressive dishwashing. Oh, dear. You are in the doghouse. You know she’s a bit particular about her cheese. Maybe take her out? Somewhere nice? I thought about it. But she said she needs ‘space to process her emotions’. What even  is  that? Is there a formula for quantifying emotional processing? I bet there is, actually. Probably involving complex algorithms. You are incorrigible. Look, just acknowledge you were wrong, offer a genuinely nice gesture—flowers, a foot massage, something—and apologise. Women are surprisingly forgiving if you actually  try . Honestly, Sarah just appreciates thoughtfulness. Don't overthink it. Remember when she was upset about her aunt's birthday and you built that little photo frame with all the family pictures? She was over the moon. Alright, alright. Point taken. I’ll grovel. Flowers  and  a foot massage, then. Is that enough? Maybe I should design a bespoke cheese storage unit as well? You're going overboard. Just the flowers and massage will do.

…and honestly, the satnav just decided I was going to drive  through  Mrs. Higgins’ garden. Like, actively routing me through her prize-winning roses. I had to override it three times! It’s possessed, I tell you. Possessed? Sounds like you need a software update, then. Though, to be fair, Google Maps tried to send me down a footpath last week. A  very  muddy footpath. Footpath? You’re lucky it didn’t try and take you across the River Nene! Mine’s alright, mostly. Though it once told me a roundabout was a left turn. A roundabout! Roundabouts are a menace anyway. Should be banned, the lot of 'em. Confuse the life out of everyone. You youngsters and your fancy gadgets though…back in my day, we had a map. And a good sense of direction, usually. A map! Reg, you make it sound like we’re living in the Stone Age. Though I do admit, sometimes a paper map feels… less stressful. Especially when you’re trying to navigate your mum’s directions. Oh god, your mum. Speaking of which, how’s she doing with the decorating? Last I heard it was still…beige. Beige apocalypse is putting it mildly. She’s decided she wants “feature walls”. Which, in her world, means slightly darker beige. I’m trying to subtly suggest a colour, but she's a fortress of neutral tones. She keeps showing me pictures of rooms that look like hospitals. Feature walls…sounds stressful. I’m just happy if I can get the paint on straight. Honestly, I’m thinking of just leaving the walls bare. Easier life. You'd be surprised what a bit of proper wallpaper can do. Got a friend, used to be a docker, right? He papered his whole house with nautical charts. Said it reminded him of his travels. A bit much, if you ask me, but each to their own. Nautical charts… that's…a statement. Hey Reg, how are things with the Warrant Officer life? Still shipping off to far-flung places? Not so much shipping these days, more… organising the shipping. Bureaucracy, mostly. Though they’re talking about a potential secondment to Saudi Arabia next year. Saudi Arabia? Wow. That’s…hot. Literally. And culturally…a big change from Liverpool. That’s putting it mild. My wife isn’t thrilled, to say the least. Says she wants to stay put and finally get the garden sorted.

… honestly, I think it’s the pollen. Absolutely blooming everywhere, isn’t it? My sinuses have been a disaster all week. Feels like someone’s stuffed cotton wool up them. Oh, you poor thing! Stockholm  is  gorgeous this time of year, but the birch pollen is notorious. I’ve been managing with antihistamines, but even I’m feeling a bit…fuzzy-headed. You should really get some, Dave. Don't suffer in silence. It’s quite a spectacle, though, isn’t it? Look at those Rhododendrons! The sheer variety…Honestly, I was reading an article about the work the head gardener here does; apparently, they have a whole team dedicated just to deadheading. Can you imagine? Deadheading? Sounds…intense. I struggle to keep a basil plant alive, let alone orchestrate a rhododendron army. Though, you’re right, it  is  beautiful. Makes you appreciate the effort. And no, antihistamines are on the list, just haven't got around to it. I tried steaming, thinking it might help clear things, but mostly just felt like a slightly damp, congested man. Steaming? Bless you! You sound exactly like my Dad trying a 'natural remedy'. He once tried oil of clove for a toothache… it was a disaster. Antihistamines are the way to go, seriously. I can pick some up for you, if you like? There’s a pharmacy just near Gamla Stan. Speaking of remedies, I was telling a client about the benefits of forest bathing –  shinrin-yoku  – the other day. Apparently, the phytoncides released by the trees boost your immune system. We’re basically getting a dose of free medicine just by being here! Though, admittedly, a dose of pollen comes with it. Forest bathing, eh? Sounds wonderfully pretentious and slightly terrifying. I'm picturing myself lying naked amongst the pines. Perhaps I’ll stick to the antihistamines, thanks. Though, I do try and get out for a walk most days. Keeps the brain from turning to mush, even if the nose is blocked. How's work, Sarah? Still battling PR disasters? Oh, please don’t even ask! I’ve been mediating between a very outspoken chef and a rather sensitive food blogger all week. It's exhausting. Honestly, sometimes I feel like a professional apologist. Still, pays the bills. This teaching gig on the side helps, actually. Keeps me grounded. It's the 'always on' culture, isn't it? Everyone expecting instant responses, hot takes… It’s relentless.

Honestly, Dad, you wouldn’t  believe  what Brenda said at Uni today. She reckons my accent is getting… softer. Softer! Like I’m losing my Kentishness.      Kentishness, is it? Sounds a bit precious, don't it, love? You’ve been away at university for three years now. Accents shift. It's natural. Mine’s probably gone all… woolly since I retired. Nobody to talk to proper anymore, just the telly.      It  is  funny how accents change, though. I’ve noticed my own adapting a bit, working in care. You pick up bits and pieces from everyone, don’t you? Especially the phrasing. Old Mrs. Higgins keeps saying “right proper” about everything. It’s rubbed off, I swear.      Sounds exhausting. All that talkin’.      It's not  just  the accent, it's the  sound  of my voice, apparently. Brenda said I sound… less like I grew up in Gillingham. She's studying linguistics, so she’s all technical about it. “Vowel elongation” and “glottal stops decreasing.” Honestly.      Linguistics, eh? Sounds like a load of old codswallop to me. You sound perfectly alright, love. A bit posh maybe, now you're all educated. Remember that little scamp you were, always yellin’ across the garden? That was a proper Kent accent.      Speaking of yelling, how  is  Sarah? I haven’t spoken to her in ages. Is she still… struggling with Mark?      Don't. Please. It’s a mess, alright? He's… well, he’s been at it again. Drinking. She kicked him out again last week. It’s just awful for little Leo.      Leo's alright. Tough kid. He just wants to play Minecraft all day. Says his dad promised him a new server, but…you know.      That’s a right shame. Poor Sarah. That no-good Mark. Always was a bit of a drifter. She needs to be strong, look after herself. And that child. Custody is a nightmare, though. I’ve seen it with friends. Complicated.      It is. And she's trying to work, trying to manage everything on her own. It’s not fair on her, or Leo. Does she have any support? Has she spoken to a solicitor?      She’s got a bit of legal aid, but it’s slow. And Mum's trying to help, of course, but… Mum and Mark have never gotten on, so it’s complicated. It always is. Remember when  you  and Mum used to argue about Dad and everything?

…and honestly, the whole thing was a disaster. A beautiful, flaming disaster. I was attempting a Baked Alaska for Aunt Mildred’s birthday, you know, really going all out. And I hadn’t quite grasped the…speed… required for the meringue. It browned before the ice cream even  thought  about freezing. Sounds… messy. Like, really messy. Was it still edible? Edible? Leo, darling, it was a sticky, sugary, slightly burnt lump. Aunt Mildred was very polite, of course. Said it had “character”. Honestly, I think she secretly hated it. It reminded me of that time your father tried to grate cheese directly into boiling pasta water. Dad?! No way! Didn’t that just…melt into nothing? Precisely! A stringy, milky mess. He insisted it would “infuse the flavour”. It infused disappointment, mostly. Though, thinking about it, it  was  a very early experiment in fusion cuisine. Haha! Speaking of messy, are we still on for sorting the Halloween decorations tomorrow? Mum said she bought, like, a  ton  of spider webs. Absolutely! Though I’m putting my foot down about the life-sized ghoul she found online. It’s…unsettling. And I'm worried it might genuinely frighten little Timmy next door.
