… honestly, the level of basic grammar some of my online students have is appalling. I mean,  appalling . You’d think after twelve years of schooling, they’d at least grasp subject-verb agreement. It's mostly Asian students, though, so perhaps the teaching styles are just… different. Tell me about it! Though mine are mostly Italian, and it's less grammar and more just… a complete inability to construct a coherent sentence. They all want to sound like Shakespeare, instantly, and get frustrated when I tell them to master the present perfect  first . It's exhausting. Still, at least it’s a job, right? I’m still chipping away at this student loan though. It feels… monumental. A job. A very, very part-time job. And yes, the loans are terrifying. You've got it so much worse than my generation did, honestly. We had grants, even. Now it's just debt, debt, debt. And then you look at my pension prospects… well, let’s not even go there. It’s just another worry. Did you see that article about the government pushing back the retirement age  again ? Ugh, don't even start me. It’s infuriating. They expect us to work until we drop, and for what? A pittance? I’ve started seriously considering going back abroad for a bit. Maybe South America. Decent money, low cost of living, sunshine… sounds better than grey Bury, doesn’t it? Sounds idyllic. Though the thought of navigating a new bureaucracy fills me with dread. Remember Mrs. Higgins trying to get her car MOT-ed in Spain? Absolute chaos. She ended up just driving it until it completely fell apart. Oh God, yes! The Higgins family and their vehicular adventures. That’s a story for the ages. Seriously though, the idea of teaching in Colombia or Argentina is really appealing. I was scrolling through Netflix last night and there was this documentary about teaching English in Patagonia… it looked incredible. Patagonia  is  incredible. Though bracing. Very bracing. You'd need a good coat. I've been binge-watching "The Crown" again. It’s utterly ridiculous, of course, but so addictive. Although, the recent seasons… the whole thing with Diana feels… exploitative, somehow. I agree. It flirts with being respectful, then just dives straight into sensationalism. It’s tricky, isn’t it? That line between legitimate storytelling and just… cashing in. And it brings up all sorts of questions about privacy and consent.

…and honestly, the lecturer just kept going on about Bayesian statistics. Like, alright, it's important, but after an hour and a half, you just glaze over, yeah? It’s brutal prepping for these A-Levels. Tell me about it! Physics is trying to actively kill my brain cells. At least Maths, when it gets tricky, feels… satisfyingly tricky, you know? Not just relentlessly abstract. Speaking of which, have you properly thought about Human Sciences at Oxford? You seemed a bit on the fence last week. I am still on the fence. It  sounds  amazing – the whole interdisciplinary thing, being able to dip into everything. But is it…useful? Like, what do you  do  with a Human Sciences degree? Everyone says Maths is a guaranteed ticket somewhere. Useful is overrated, mate. Do what you enjoy! Besides, loads of people end up not working in what they studied. And Human Sciences isn’t exactly worthless. Think consultancy, policy, research… it’s broad. Way broader than pure Maths, honestly. You’d be good at it, you always were the one arguing about why people did things in History. Yeah, but arguing about Henry VIII isn’t quite the same as… applying sociological theory to global issues, is it? Anyway, you’re right about Maths being a ‘ticket’. Dad’s practically built my future around it. He keeps talking about investment banking. Ugh, your dad. He’s a bit keen, isn’t he? Look, you need to do what  you  want. Speaking of things we need to do… I’m thinking we should hit up that new sports bar in here, "The Dugout," after this? They’ve got decent wings and a good selection of beers. Need to properly celebrate surviving another mock exam. Beers? Are you sure? It’s still pretty early, even for a Saturday. And my mum would absolutely kill me if she found out. Relax, it’ll be one or two. Just to take the edge off. Besides, I’m pretty sure Westfield security is more worried about shoplifters than two sixth-formers having a cheeky half. We deserve it. We’ve been grinding. Hmm. Okay, alright. One half, maximum. But if your dad calls asking where I am, I’m blaming you. So, if not investment banking, what are  you  thinking, realistically? Honestly? I'm still leaning towards something Maths-heavy, probably Warwick. Their course structure is pretty good.

…and that, my dear, is why your National Insurance contributions aren’t just vanishing into thin air. It’s a fund, see? A pot for when you need it - your state pension, unemployment benefit, all that sort of thing. Though goodness knows if it’ll  be  there when you actually need it, the way things are going. Right, so it’s… almost like a collective savings account for the country? A bit like a really, really big ISA? That’s a decent analogy, actually. A very decent analogy. Though it’s more complicated than an ISA, of course. And less control over it, naturally. The government decides how it’s invested, and frankly, they haven't always got the best track record, have they? Remember Black Wednesday? Vaguely. Mum mentioned it once, something about currency… Anyway, so NI contributions pay for future benefits. What about income tax, then? That feels like just… disappearing. Disappearing? No, no, not disappearing. Though it certainly  feels  like it, doesn’t it? Income tax funds everything else. The NHS, schools, roads, the police, defence… all of it. It’s a monstrous sum of money they collect each year, you wouldn’t believe. And most folks have no idea where it all goes. Well, that’s what’s frustrating, isn’t it? I understand  that  it’s supposed to go to those things, but you hear so much about waste and mismanagement… and then they announce another tax hike. It makes you wonder. It does indeed. And this latest one… the increase to National Insurance again, supposedly to fund social care… it's a sticking plaster on a gaping wound, if you ask me. They’re not addressing the underlying problems, just throwing money at them. Why aren't they addressing the underlying problems? Is it just… political? Oh, entirely political, love. It always is. Look at the demographics. We’ve got an ageing population. More people living longer, needing more care. But fewer younger people paying into the system to support them. It's a mathematical problem, really, but nobody wants to talk about the difficult solutions. Like…? Well, raising the retirement age is one. Not popular, naturally. Means people have to work longer. But it keeps contributions coming in. Another is… well, encouraging more immigration. Which  also  isn't popular, for all sorts of reasons. And then there’s the question of means-testing everything.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of emails is just  insane . I swear, half my job is just wading through endless threads about spreadsheets and deadlines. It’s all ‘urgent’ apparently, even when it clearly isn’t. Oh, love, tell me about it. Sounds familiar. Though spreadsheets aren’t my biggest enemy, it's the invigilators. Trying to get them to understand the rules for late arrivals…it’s like herding cats. Honestly, teenagers are easier. That  does  sound stressful. At least spreadsheets are predictable. People aren’t. Did you manage to get Aunt Carol to stop sending you chain letters on WhatsApp? She sent me one about a lost dog needing rehoming, and the photo was clearly from a stock image website! Don't even  mention  Aunt Carol. I’ve had to mute her for a week. She’s convinced 5G is controlling our minds now, you know. I tried to explain it’s just radio waves, but apparently, I’m ‘blinded by the government’. It’s exhausting. How’s Mum coping with everything? She seemed a bit frazzled last time I spoke to her. She’s…managing. Dad’s been ‘helping’ with the garden, which basically means he’s re-arranged everything into a completely illogical system and then complained he can’t find the hose. It's a classic Dad move, really. She’s trying to be supportive, but I think even she’s reaching breaking point. He keeps wanting to build a koi pond. A  koi pond , Mum! In November! Oh, your father. He’s never changed. Always had grand ideas with zero practical application. Remember when he tried to build a self-watering system for the tomatoes out of plastic bottles and duct tape? It flooded the entire patio. Oh god, yes! And then blamed the bottles. Honestly, sometimes I think they actively try to wind each other up. How’s Mark? Still glued to his allotment? Absolutely. He's obsessed. He's entering some kind of giant vegetable competition next month. He’s particularly proud of his marrow. It’s frankly obscene. It could probably be used as a boat. He’s been talking about ‘nitrogen levels’ and ‘companion planting’ for weeks. That sounds…intense. Good for him, though. Keeps him busy. I’m thinking of joining that pottery class I told you about. I need a hobby that doesn’t involve staring at a screen.

Aye, that’s better. Proper brew. Not like that wishy-washy stuff they try to pass off down south, eh? Though I suppose young Mr. Harding down at the consultancy wouldn’t know a proper cuppa if it slapped him in the face. Dad, you say that about  everyone  south of Darlington. And Liam probably  does  know a good cuppa, he just has different priorities, like… structural integrity of buildings and whatnot. He’s a consultant engineer, remember? Not a tea connoisseur. Speaking of priorities, I brought the Malbec. Thought we could have a proper evening in. How’s the job hunting going, by the way? Any luck with those applications, Arthur? Waste of time, the lot of 'em. “Experience required.” Experience doing what, eh? Sitting here, polishing the telly remote? They want youngsters like you two, fresh out of university, with all the latest qualifications. Biomedical science ain't exactly in high demand these days, especially from someone who’s been…ah…between engagements for a bit. Don’t be so defeatist, Dad. You’ve got a brilliant mind. You practically built my science fair project in secondary school. Remember the exploding volcano? Aye, and nearly burnt the kitchen down! Your mother wasn’t best pleased. Still, a grand spectacle, it was. Did well, didn't it? First prize. It did. It was legendary. Listen, there are agencies that specialise in getting people back into work after a career break. I can send you a couple of links. Might be worth a shot, even just to talk to someone. I’ve had a look, lad. Most of 'em are just trying to sell you something. And frankly, I'm happy enough pottering about. Enjoying me retirement, as it were. Though a bit more spending money wouldn't go amiss, mind. Especially if we're having a Malbec night. We were thinking of having Sarah and Ben round next weekend, Dad. Fancy a games night? I finally got hold of that new Scrabble edition with the rotating board. It’s fiendishly difficult. Sarah and Ben? Good eggs, them. Always a bit of laugh. Scrabble eh? I’m warning you now, I’m a word wizard. Years of reading medical journals, you know. All those complicated Latin names...gives you an edge. Though I might need a refresher on the current slang. You’ll be dropping ‘yeet’ and ‘sus’ before you know it.

… honestly, the kids were  brutal  this week. Absolute chaos. I think it's the sugar, honestly. Parents let them loose with chocolate biscuits all weekend and then wonder why they’re bouncing off the walls on Monday. Tell me about it! I had a Year 9 class who decided that interpretive dance was the most appropriate response to a Shakespeare sonnet. Interpretive dance, Sarah! I mean, creative, yes, but… not what the syllabus intended. How was your TEFL lot? Any existential crises about the present perfect? Worse, honestly. A full-on mutiny over irregular verbs. Apparently, they’re ‘unfair’. Unfair! Like grammar operates on democratic principles. I tried to explain it was about historical linguistic shifts, but I just got blank stares. It's exhausting, trying to make it engaging when they just want to talk about TikTok. Did you hear about the conference next term? The one in Brighton? Oh, the 'Future of English' one? Yes! I signed up ages ago. Thinking of submitting a paper, actually. A bit ambitious, I know, but I've been doing some research on the impact of social media slang on formal writing and thought it might be relevant. What about you? Are you going? I’d  love  to go, but the school’s being… difficult. Apparently, ‘professional development’ needs to fit within a very narrow budgetary window. And, knowing our head, that window is currently slammed shut and bolted. It's infuriating. It’s always ‘we value our staff’ and then when you actually  want  to improve your skills, it’s suddenly a logistical nightmare. Ugh, the classic. It's always the same. They want us to be innovative and inspiring educators, but then balk at the cost of, you know,  actually  investing in us. I'm lucky, my school is usually pretty good with the conference budget. Though last year, they made us share hotel rooms. Can you believe it? Share?! No way! That's… degrading. Especially when you consider the travel involved. I spent most of last year’s conference trying to politely avoid my colleague who insisted on narrating every single session. Like,  literally  out loud, in a whisper, the entire time. “Oh, look, she's talking about phonetics… very interesting…” Oh, Lord. I had a similar experience with someone who kept asking completely irrelevant questions just to show how clever they were. It completely derailed the keynote speaker's talk on postcolonial literature.

Oh, this is lovely, isn’t it? Just gliding along. Though honestly, Polish roads… a bit more…characterful than Cambridge, wouldn't you say? I swear every five minutes it feels like we hit a pothole designed specifically for campervans. Characterful is one word for it. I think ‘agricultural’ is another fairly accurate description. But hey, at least the scenery is good. All those fields… Are you regretting coming yet, Eleanor? You were a bit hesitant about the whole campervan thing initially. Regretting? No, no. Not at all. It’s… refreshing. A bit rustic, perhaps, but a far cry from the beige monotony of my life back home. Though honestly, I haven't  done  anything remotely physical like driving this for… well, decades. My core is protesting mildly. Have you been keeping up with your running? You were training for that half-marathon, weren’t you? I was! But training’s taken a backseat since we started this trip. It’s hard to prioritise pounding the pavement when you’re trying not to pound the suspension of Brenda here . Though I did a quick circuit in that little park in Tarnow this morning. Felt good to move. You should join me tomorrow if we stop somewhere with a bit of green. Oh, goodness. Me? Running? That’s a prospect that fills me with… extreme disinterest. More of a gentle stroll, perhaps? I was reading an article the other day about the benefits of ‘forest bathing’. Apparently, it’s incredibly good for lowering cortisol levels. Much more my speed. Forest bathing! Sounds a bit… New Age, doesn’t it? Still, if it works. You know, sometimes I think people put way too much pressure on themselves to achieve this ‘perfect’ physique. Always comparing themselves on social media. It’s exhausting. Absolutely. It's all so… manufactured. I remember when I was younger, it was magazines. Now it’s Instagram. The pressure hasn't changed, just the platform. It’s all about curated perfection, not real life. Speaking of real life, how’s the teaching going? Still battling teenagers and grammatical errors? You know me too well. It’s good, actually. Challenging, of course. I’m teaching a class of Ukrainian refugees online, as well as my regular students. It's incredibly rewarding, but also… heartbreaking, hearing their stories. Makes you realise how lucky we are. It does. It’s funny, isn't it?

…and honestly, the sheer audacity of them. Sailing across the North Sea in those longboats. It wasn't just raiding, you know? It was  exploration . They reached North America centuries before Columbus. Completely forgotten for ages. It’s funny isn't it, how history gets rewritten, or just…lost? Like all that stuff about the pyramids. Everyone thinks Egypt, but there’s increasing evidence of similar structures being built all over the place, almost simultaneously. Makes you wonder about a shared knowledge, doesn’t it? Or a very…global catastrophe that prompted the same solutions in different places. Now  that ’s a thought. Though the tectonic activity around those periods…it’s intense. Imagine the disruption. Speaking of disruption, have you been reading anything about telomeres lately? Old Man Flanagan down the road was going on about them. Says he's taking some supplement, convinced it'll keep him going 'til he's 120. Flanagan. Bless him. Always chasing the fountain of youth. I skimmed an article, something about them shortening with age and being linked to cellular decay. It's all fascinating, but I'm more concerned with getting little Leo to actually  say  “Mama” before he turns three. Delayed speech is worrying me, you know? His cousin was a late talker, but… Ah, now don't be fretting too much. Kids develop at their own pace. It wouldn't hurt to get him checked, of course, but comparison is the thief of joy, as they say. Remember my cousin Seamus? Didn't say a word 'til he was four. Now he's a solicitor, arguing the toss all day long! Though, on the subject of longevity, it  is  strange how life expectancy keeps creeping up. What is it now, globally? Early seventies? Around 73, I think. But it’s hugely skewed, isn’t it? Depending on where you’re born. And the quality of life in those extra years. It's not just about  how long  you live, it’s about  how  you live. All this talk of immortality…it seems a bit pointless if you’re spending half of it in a care home. True enough. And the ethical implications! Imagine if we could genuinely extend life indefinitely. Overpopulation, resource depletion… Honestly, we're already having trouble managing things  now . Look at the energy crisis. Everyone talks about renewables, which is good, but they're not a magic bullet.

Right, so I was thinking, for Nana’s birthday, instead of a massive present, we could take her to that Italian place in Lytham? The one with the fairy lights? She  loves  fairy lights. Ooh, good shout, love. Bella Italia? That’s a nice idea. More memorable than, you know, another knitted tea cosy, bless her. Though she  does  appreciate a good tea cosy… Aye, Bella Italia’s decent. Though it's a bit pricey, isn’t it? We’re tryin’ to watch the pennies a bit at the moment, with… well, everything. And young Arthur's nearly outgrown that highchair, we’ll need a new one soon. A proper one, not just a booster. Grandpa! You're always talking about money! It's Nana's birthday! And we have those vouchers from Christmas, remember? The ones from that gift experience place? We could put them towards it. He has a point, darling. It  is  Nana, and saving for a new highchair is sensible, but… let’s not rain on the birthday parade. We can look at highchairs next month. I saw a really good one online, adjustable and everything. Though truthfully, it was a bit frighteningly expensive. Expensive is an understatement these days! Everything’s gone up. Honestly, I remember when you could get a decent Sunday dinner for a fiver. Fiver! Now… it’s robbery. Speaking of things going up, did you see the price of chicken feed? Ridiculous. Agnes and Beatrice are going to have to earn their keep laying extra eggs! Not the chickens again, Grandpa. Honestly, you talk about those birds more than you talk about me getting my A-Level results. Now, now, Arthur. She’s right. We need to focus on supporting Imogen, not obsessing over poultry. How are your revision sessions going, sweetheart? They’re… going. History is driving me mental. All those dates and treaties. It's like, who even remembers the Treaty of Rome? Although… it's kinda relevant now, isn't it? With everything that's happened with Brexit… Brexit. Don't get me started. A right mess, that was. Should've stayed in, if you ask me. More stable. Better for business. This whole thing’s made importing things a nightmare. Even getting decent coffee beans is a faff. Honestly, this coffee maker is on its last legs anyway. I swear it takes ten minutes to brew a single cup.

Honestly, Chloe, it's listing to the left again. I swear this tree has a mind of its own. And it’s barely December! We haven’t even got to the proper festive rush yet. Mum, it’s…characterful. And you  did  say I could decorate it this year. Strategic leaning is a design choice. Besides, you were the one insisting on the biggest tree B&Q had. Characterful is a polite word for ‘about to fall over and take out Mrs. Higgins’ prize-winning geraniums’. Speaking of which, did you see her putting up her lights? She's gone all out this year, inflatable snowmen  and  a reindeer. It's…a lot. Oh, Mrs. Higgins. She’s committed to Christmas. It's sweet, really. Though I did nearly drive into a snowman on the way home from work yesterday, someone had it on their lawn. Committed is one word. Competitive is another. Remember last year when she tried to one-up us with the singing reindeer? Poor Winston nearly had a heart attack. Winston  does  hate loud noises. He’s such a grumpy old man. He was giving me the stink eye this morning because I dared to trim his claws. Honestly, he acts like I’m performing open-heart surgery. He’s a cat, dear. Dramatic by nature. My hands are aching just  thinking  about trying to do  my  nails. I've been meaning to book an appointment, but work’s been manic. Old Mrs. Peterson took a tumble last night, thankfully nothing broken, but she needed observing all night. Oh no, poor Mrs. Peterson! You’re always picking up the pieces, Mum. It must be exhausting. How did your shift go otherwise? Long. It always is this time of year. Everyone seems to fall apart the minute the temperature drops below freezing. It's just… a lot of coughs and colds and minor injuries. But it's good to help, you know? It feels worthwhile. What about you? How’s the copywriting going? Any interesting briefs? It's alright. I'm working on a campaign for a German Christmas market – which is actually quite fascinating. I’ve been doing a lot of research into German traditions. Did you know that Advent wreaths originated in 16th-century Germany with Lutherans? It's not just about candles, apparently, there's a whole symbolism to it. Really? That's interesting. I just thought it looked nice.

Right. Officially moved in. Though ‘moved in’ currently feels a lot like ‘surrounded by cardboard’. You alright, love? You look…overwhelmed. Overwhelmed is a polite word, Ben. It’s…beige. Very,  very  beige. And echoey. Did you realise how echoey it would be? It feels like shouting into a canyon. It'll warm up once we get stuff in here! And beige is…neutral. A blank canvas! Besides, the light is fantastic, isn't it? Look at the way it comes in the window. And think of all the possibilities! We can paint, put up pictures… Possibilities that involve finding somewhere to  sit  first, perhaps? I’ve been standing for the last hour. Where's the sofa even? Ah, good point. It's still in the van. I was going to tackle the bedroom first, but you're right. Sofa takes priority. Whilst I wrestle that up the stairs, can you maybe…start looking at where things might go? And possibly locate the kettle? I desperately need tea. Kettle located! And I’ll do a sweep for anything resembling a comfortable chair. Urgent matters first. Speaking of urgent, have you sorted the internet? I’m already picturing a weekend of blissful nothingness hampered by buffering circles. That's…a slightly sore point. I tried calling them earlier, but it’s a forty-five minute wait. Apparently, everyone in Sussex decides to move simultaneously. I’ll give it another go later. We’ll survive on books and each other for a few hours, yeah? If ‘survive’ involves you attempting to assemble flat-pack furniture while I read, then yes. Definitely. And what about food? I'm starving. We didn't exactly pack a gourmet meal amongst the boxes. I grabbed some biscuits and some fruit. Not exactly a feast, but it’s something. There’s a really good farm shop just down the road, apparently. Apparently, they do amazing seasonal stuff. It's practically shouting "autumn vibes" right now with pumpkins and apples everywhere. We should go tomorrow. That sounds lovely. Though I suspect ‘amazing seasonal stuff’ is code for ‘expensive’. We need to find a proper supermarket too. And…what's the rubbish collection situation? Don't tell me it's complicated. It  is  complicated. Different bins for different things, collection days vary depending on your postcode…I downloaded an app, apparently it tells you everything. I haven't deciphered it yet. We’ll be fined within a week, I’m predicting.

…and honestly, the carbonara was  criminal . Like, offensively bland. You’d think Bills could manage carbonara, wouldn’t you? It’s not exactly rocket science. Oh no! Really? I always thought Bills was pretty safe. I’m going for the halloumi and harissa burger, actually. I saw a picture on Instagram and it looked… substantial. How are you finding it being back in Peterborough, anyway? Feels weird seeing you not surrounded by library books, doesn’t it? It does, honestly. It’s… quieter. And everyone’s talking about houses and mortgages and… things. Which is terrifying. The carbonara disappointment aside, this is nice. It’s good to just  talk  properly, you know? Not frantically typing replies on a group chat. And Peterborough is… Peterborough. It hasn’t changed much. Progress is… slow. Tell me about it! Everyone back home is already planning weddings and ‘settling down’. My mum keeps subtly asking about career progression and 'meeting nice young men'. It’s exhausting. This placement is brilliant, though, really stretching me. It's with a marketing firm in Leicester, so a bit of a commute, but worth it. What about this project co-ordinator role? How’s that going? Is it all spreadsheets and meetings? Spreadsheets and meetings is a shockingly accurate description, unfortunately. It’s…fine. It pays the bills. It’s mostly organising things for engineers, which mostly involves them emailing me panicking about deadlines. It's a gentle introduction to 'real life', I suppose. It definitely doesn’t feel like putting my degree to use, though. Remember that dissertation we were so proud of? Feels like a lifetime ago. Oh god, don't remind me! Mine’s gathering dust on a hard drive somewhere. I think Mum tried to frame the cover page once. It was awkward. But hey, at least we  did  them. Remember that all-nighter in the library, fuelled by instant coffee and sheer desperation? We were convinced we’d fail. Oh my goodness, yes! And then bumping into Professor Davies looking utterly horrified at our state. He just shook his head and walked away. We swore he thought we were living there. Actually, that reminds me… Have you spoken to Liam recently? I heard through the grapevine he's travelling Southeast Asia. No way! Liam’s actually doing it? I saw a fleeting post on Facebook, but thought it was a bit of a brag. He always talked about backpacking, but I didn't think he’d actually go for it.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of beige in this Cambridge pub is astonishing. It's like they actively tried to drain all joy from the decor. Not a patch on a proper Northern boozer, mind. You wouldn’t catch a pint of proper stout being served in a half-hearted glass like this back home. You and your Northern pride, eh? It’s not  that  bad, is it? It's…refined. A Cambridge kind of refined. Though, you’re right about the stout glass. Looks like something you’d get lemonade in. How’s the research going, anyway? Still wrestling with those datasets? Wrestling is putting it mildly. It’s the kind of datasets that look innocent enough, then reveal themselves to be riddled with inconsistencies. It's all about predicting consumer behaviour based on social media trends, which, let's be real, is mostly people shouting opinions into the void. I swear, half my job is data cleaning, the other half is trying to explain to people why cleaning data is  actually  important work. What about you? Is the PhD still trying to kill you slowly? Oh, it’s a persistent threat. I'm at the literature review stage now, which is basically just reading endless papers and feeling increasingly inadequate. It’s on the socio-economic impact of post-industrial decline, so… a lot of grim reading. It’s making me feel strangely nostalgic for Birmingham factories, which is a feeling I definitely didn't anticipate. Sounds… cheerful. It's amazing how academic work manages to suck all the joy out of everything. Still, at least you're not stuck interpreting the latest TikTok dance craze as a signal of macroeconomic shifts. Honestly, some of the theories my boss comes up with… Oh god. You’ve got to share some of those. Speaking of things you shouldn’t take seriously, did you see what Chloe was wearing on Instagram? That neon green jumpsuit. Honestly, it was a  choice . Oh,  please  don’t even get me started. It looked like something a highlighter pen threw up. It’s not even about it being “bad” fashion, it’s just… aggressively  loud . I’m more of a classic shapes, muted colours kind of girl. You know, sensible shoes that don’t scream 'Look at me!'. Although, thinking of Sunderland fashion… sometimes you see things that are loud for entirely different reasons. Different how?

Aye, Grandma, it's right mental what's goin' on wi' politics these days, innit? Mr. Sunak’s tryin' to sort out all this mess, but it feels like he's just puttin' a plaster on a broken leg, you know? Everything's just… expensive. Expensive? Lad,  expensive  is when a loaf of bread cost sixpence and your grandfather thought  that  was a scandal. You young’uns have no idea. Though, I’ll grant you, it’s not lookin’ rosy now, is it? Sunak… a clever lad, I suppose, but a bit… distant, aren't he? Never struck me as one who'd know the price of a pint of milk, let alone how to help those who can barely afford one. Exactly! And all this talk about the Labour lot comin' back into power... Grandad used to say Labour were all talk and no trousers. But things have changed, haven't they? Like, Keir Starmer seems… different. More sensible, maybe? Sensible is a funny word in politics, love. They all  seem  sensible when they’re after your vote. Your grandfather was a staunch Conservative, you know. Said Labour would bankrupt the country. He worked down at the railway, he did, and they were always havin’ trouble with strikes. He wasn't a fan of unions, put it that way. But even he admitted things weren’t always fair. The rich gettin’ richer and the poor… well, struggling. That hasn’t changed much, eh? Nah, it hasn't. And it's not just that, it’s all the stuff on the news. This war in Ukraine, and what’s happenin’ in the Middle East… it’s scary. Like, are we gonna be alright? Are they gonna start another world war? Oh, lad. Wars. I remember… I was just a girl during the Second World War. We had air raids, rationing… everything was different. It’s terrible what's happening now, truly terrible. But the world’s  always  had conflict, in one form or another. You have to try and not let it overwhelm you. And listen to both sides, not just what the telly tells you. The telly's got an agenda, you know. But how do you know what to believe, though? Everyone's shoutin' at each other on social media, and all the newspapers are biased. It's proper confusing. Old Mr. Henderson down the street keeps goin’ on about conspiracy theories, says it’s all a big plot… Mr. Henderson has always been a bit of a character.

Now, Leo, I’ve noticed you’ve been using your phone  during  dinner again. Honestly, it's not the done thing, is it? Back when I was your age, you wouldn’t  dream  of it. Your mother and I try to make these family meals a bit of a… a connection point, you know? But Dad, it's just a quick check. Ms. Davies set homework on Teams and… and everyone’s talking about the blood moon tonight. Gotta see the pics. Leo, your father’s right. It  is  nice to just… be present. Put the phone away, love. We can look at pictures of the moon  after  we’ve finished eating. It's a beautiful one tonight, apparently. I read about it online earlier - well, before dinner started. Oh, the blood moon! I remember when those used to stir up a proper fuss. Folk used to think it was a bad omen, you know. Wolves howling and all that. Nonsense, of course, but a good story nonetheless. Though, I must say, it  is  a stunning sight. Aye, Granny’s right. It’s beautiful. It's just… it feels disrespectful when you're glued to the screen. We haven't had a proper family dinner like this in ages, what with work and everything. Sorry, Dad. It's just…it's hard to switch off. Everything happens online now. I know it is, darling. It’s different for your generation. It wasn't like that when  I  was growing up. We ate dinner, and then we… talked. Or listened to the radio. Simple as that. Goodness me, yes. And argue we did! Your grandfather, rest his soul, and I could have a right ding-dong over the state of politics. All while polishing off a hearty plate of stew. Those were the days. Speaking of hearty plates…are you managing alright, love? You’ve barely touched your shepherd’s pie. Oh, it's lovely, really. Just…exhausted, I suppose. Little Thomas decided 6am was a perfectly reasonable time to start the day. It's wonderful having him, truly, but it's tiring. That's a smallie for you. Full of beans! Still, you’re doing a grand job, dear. I remember when your father was that age - a whirlwind! Can I be excused after I finish my pie? I promised Ben I’d help him with his science project tonight.

… honestly, Arthur, I still can’t quite believe the result back in ‘14. All that fuss, all that energy, and for what? They stayed put. Seems a bit deflating, doesn’t it? Though I suppose better deflating than… well, you know. Deflating is a good word for it, George. A right waste of everyone’s time, if you ask me. Though I always suspected they'd vote to stay. Too much to lose, financially speaking. Still, all that talk of independence. You’d have thought they’d have learned from the last time they tried it, centuries ago. Anyway, enough about Scotland. How did that interview go with the college? The one for the part-time lecturing? Oh, it was… alright. Perfectly alright. Which, I suspect, means I didn't get it. It was a younger crowd on the panel, very enthusiastic about ‘innovative pedagogy’ and ‘student-led learning’. I tried to explain that sometimes a good, solid lecture just  works , but they looked at me like I’d suggested bringing back the stocks. Ha! Sounds about right. They always want something new, don’t they? Doesn’t mean the old ways aren’t effective. You’ve been teaching for forty years, George. You know what works. Don't let a bunch of youngsters tell you otherwise. It's just… frustrating, Arthur. I liked the idea of keeping busy, of still being  useful . Retirement is… well, it's quiet. Too quiet, perhaps. And Margaret keeps hinting I need a hobby. A  hobby ! After a lifetime dedicated to shaping young minds, she thinks I need to take up birdwatching. Margaret’s a good woman, but she doesn’t understand the academic life. She thinks if it doesn’t involve spreadsheets and profit margins, it’s frivolous. Speaking of which, I had a bit of a row with Derek this morning. You remember Derek, from the shop? Vaguely. Bit of a grumbler, wasn't he? Grumbler is putting it mildly. He’s been complaining that I’m not pulling my weight since I handed over more responsibility to young Emily. Says I’m ‘taking the easy life’. Easy! I’ve been building that business for thirty years, George! Thirty years! And now I’m supposed to just… vanish? Honestly, the cheek of it. People don't like change, Arthur. Especially when it threatens their little routines. You've given Emily a chance, and that’s commendable.

Honestly, Dad, are you  sure  this is the quickest way? We’ve been going around this roundabout five times now. Feels like we're doing laps for fun. And my back’s killin’ me with all this art stuff in the boot.      Now, Aaron, your dad knows these roads like the back of his hand. He used to deliver papers all over this area. Besides, it’s a nice day for a drive, isn't it? Look at the clouds – proper fluffy.      I  am  taking the quickest route! Google Maps is a load of rubbish sometimes, you know. It sent me down a farm track last month trying to get to Bletchley. A  farm track ! And it's not just about knowing the roads, Ann. It's about avoiding the congestion on the A1. Trust me.      He’s got a point about Google Maps, actually. It tried to route me through a pedestrian zone last week when I was heading to my tuition. Honestly, the things it suggests…      Tuition? How's that going, Liam? Still explaining the difference between ‘there’, ‘their’ and ‘they’re’ to confused international students?      You know me too well, Aaron. It’s… rewarding. Though some of the pronunciation challenges are wild. One student kept calling a ‘ship’ a ‘sheep’. It took ten minutes to figure that one out.      Oh, bless 'em. Reminds me of old Mr. Henderson at the supermarket. He always called courgettes 'cucumber-things'. Lovely man, but a bit muddled. Speaking of supermarkets, I’m dreading the price of everything these days. Went for a loaf of bread yesterday and nearly had a heart attack.      Don’t even get me started on the supermarkets. They try and sneak up the prices on everything and call it ‘shrinkflation’. It’s daylight robbery! Remember when a chocolate biscuit cost… well, not this much?      Remember when petrol didn’t cost an arm and a leg? Seriously, by the time I've filled up the van for work, I've blown half my wages. Which is why I’m still living at home, by the way – not that anyone lets me forget.      Oh, Aaron, don't be like that. It's good to have you around. And it saves you on board game nights, doesn’t it? Who’s up for Monopoly when we get there? I've been practicing my ruthless property acquisition tactics.      You and your ruthless tactics, Ann!

Aye, grandad, honestly, you’d think after all these years driving ‘round Manchester you’d be used to roundabouts. You nearly gave us both heart attacks back there! Honestly, I thought you were going to go straight across that one. Now, lass, don’t you go fretting. I haven’t lost  all  my marbles yet. It's just…they keep changing ‘em, you know? Back in my day, a roundabout was a roundabout. Now they’ve got lanes, and markings, and all sorts of fandangles. Confuses an old man, it does. Besides, I was admiring that field. Lovely cows in it. They  were  rather impressive cows, actually. Looked like Jerseys, didn't they? Lovely creamy colour. I was running some quick calculations in my head about optimal grazing patterns based on herd size and land area... Oh, here we go. You and your calculations, Leo. Leave the cows alone! Grandad, you weren’t admiring the cows, you were trying to remember if you’d left the gas on when you were a lad. Be honest. Now, that's a bit harsh, isn't it? I  do  enjoy a good bit of livestock. Reminds me of my uncle’s farm near Altrincham. He had prize-winning sheep, he did. Southdowns, I think. Fluffy things. And a particularly grumpy bull. Nearly took my hat off once. Southdowns are excellent for lamb production, naturally. High quality fleece too, though the market's a bit volatile at the moment… Leo! Stop it. Grandad, did you ever actually  work  on a farm, or just visit your uncle? I'm trying to picture you mucking out a stable. It’s…difficult. Never mucked out a stable in my life! Far too good for that, I was. But I used to help with the haymaking. Backbreaking work, it was. Hot as blazes in the summer. Didn’t mind though, good honest work. And my auntie always made the best sandwiches. Egg and cress, every time. Egg and cress, lovely. Though I'm more of a ham and pickle kinda girl myself. You still driving us to Auntie Brenda’s, by the way? Because if you’re going to keep trying to take out roundabouts, I might just tell her we got a flat tire. Actually, I was thinking, on the way back, if we have time, we could possibly detour past the new wind farm near Dunstable. The blade design is quite innovative.

Honestly, this parsnip is roasted to perfection. Though I say so myself. I’ve been experimenting, you know, now I’ve… well, now I  have  the time to experiment. Retirement is a lot of cooking, apparently. It  is  lovely, Mary. You’ve really outdone yourself. Though knowing you, it probably involves some sort of complicated calculation to get the roasting time just right? You were always obsessing over angles and ratios even when making a cup of tea. There’s a bit of Pythagoras in everything, dear. You’d be surprised. And don't start on the tea! Angles are crucial for optimal steeping, naturally. How was your day, love? Anything interesting come across your desk? Lots of sporting events needing transcription, I imagine? Mmm, lamb’s good. Really good. Though I still maintain your roast potatoes are better, Mary. A slightly crispier exterior, perhaps? Just a thought. Oh,  now  you’re a food critic, are you, David? After years of accepting whatever I put in front of you? And the potatoes  are  perfectly crisp, thank you very much! Don’t start a potato war, you two. It’s too early in the week. David, did you manage that walk you were planning? The weather’s been surprisingly decent. Got about halfway up Skiddaw. Brilliant views. Though my knees are complaining. Getting old is… inconvenient. I keep meaning to join that walking group the village advertised. Good exercise, good company, and all that. You should absolutely go! It’s wonderful for you to get out. And it’ll get you away from endlessly re-watching documentaries about oil rigs. Though I admit, some of them are… strangely fascinating. Speaking of getting out, the choir practice was good. We're starting to work on a new piece for the village fete. It's a bit challenging, lots of harmonies. Old Mrs. Henderson nearly had a meltdown trying to get the altos in tune. Oh, that sounds delightful! You have such a lovely voice, dear. Remember young Thomas Miller, from my last class? The one who couldn’t tell his isosceles from his equilateral? He's auditioning for a stage school down in London. Apparently, he’s found his calling. Good on him. Never understood all that geometry business myself. Always preferred something a bit… practical. Though I suppose a good understanding of angles  was  useful in surveying… back in the day. It’s amazing how things turn out, isn’t it?

…and honestly, the main thing Mrs. Davies said about Leo was that he’s ‘a delightful distraction’. A  delightful distraction ! What does that even  mean ? Is that good? Bad? Somewhere in between? It means I talk too much, doesn’t it? Well, she did say he has brilliant ideas, massively creative, but… struggles to focus. Which, let's be honest, we already knew. And Elsie, you were a star apparently! Really engaged, asked good questions… I liked drawing pictures of the characters! Miss Peterson said my picture of the Queen of Hearts was  amazing . It  was  amazing, darling. Absolutely lovely. Though a bit… menacing, perhaps? Mine was Captain Hook! He's way cooler than Peter Pan. He is a classic villain, isn't he? Right, dinner. Who’s having broccoli? Don’t all answer at once. Leo, please don’t start reciting pirate shanties while I’m trying to get everyone to eat their greens. But Mum! Pirates need to eat greens to stay strong for sword fighting! That’s… a surprisingly good point. Okay, one piece of broccoli for sword-fighting fuel. Elsie, how was your day apart from the Queen of Hearts? We talked about World Book Day costumes. Amelia wants to be Hermione Granger again, but she was Hermione last year. A valid point! It’s good to mix it up. Have you thought about what you'd like to be? I want to be Pippi Longstocking! She’s so strong and she has a monkey! Pippi Longstocking is a bit weird. I’m going to be… a circus strongman! I've been practising my muscles. Very impressive. Right. Now, about after school tomorrow. I’ve got that staff meeting, so I won’t be able to pick you both up from after-school club. Would you be okay going to Grandma’s? Yeah! Grandma makes amazing cookies. And she lets me play with the kittens! Perfect. I’ll give her a ring. Oh, and speaking of…weird, you won’t believe what Jasper’s little boy asked me about today. What? Did he ask about dinosaurs? No! He asked me… He asked me what cooked human flesh smells like.  Ew!  That’s disgusting! I know, right?! I was completely taken aback. I just said, “That’s a very inappropriate question, and we don’t talk about things like that.” Honestly, where do these kids  come up  with these ideas?

…and honestly, young Mikey down at O’Connell’s Curtains is a menace. A  menace , I tell ya. Nearly took me eye out with a measuring tape yesterday. Said he was ‘learning the ropes’. Ropes! He was wielding sharp metal, Mary! Oh, don't start on the curtain shop again, Declan. He’s a kid. They're clumsy. Though, yes, I did hear Mrs. O’Malley complaining about a wonky hemline. It’s just a bit of weekend work, isn’t it? Keeps him out of trouble. Me wanna curtains! Shiny ones! Shiny ones, is it? Well, a grand idea, Oisin. Though I must say, I remember wee Jamie McTavish, a terror he was, 'learning the ropes' in his father’s butcher shop. Nearly lopped off a finger with a cleaver. Turns out, youthful enthusiasm lacking… precision. Precision! That’s what’s missing! It’s not just the clumsiness, Mary, it’s the complete lack of attention. Anyway, back to more pressing matters. Oisin's birthday. Have we settled on the bouncy castle? We've  looked  at bouncy castles. They’re extortionate! And frankly, terrifying. I'm leaning towards a simple party in the garden, a few friends, and that Paw Patrol cake he's been obsessing over. Paw Paw Paw Patrol! Cake! Big cake! A garden party sounds lovely. And Paw Patrol… is that the one with the dogs? They seem a sensible bunch. Though, not quite as strategic as a good game of rugby, now. Are you still going to the match next Saturday, Declan? Absolutely. Promised young Paddy I’d take him. He's turning into a proper little Munster supporter. Though trying to explain the offside rule to him is… a challenge. He keeps shouting “He ran with the ball!” like it's a personal insult. Honestly, you'd think it was a crime against humanity. Speaking of running with things… Oisin’s started making up words again. Yesterday he asked for ‘splooshie juice’. ‘Splooshie juice’? Now  that's  a good one. He gets that from somewhere. Is it me? Am I unknowingly introducing ‘splooshie juice’ into his vocabulary? Likely a combination of influences. Children are excellent linguistic innovators. It’s quite fascinating, actually. They bypass the need for conventional structures. It's pure creativity! Fascinating is one word for it. Dizzying is another. It makes understanding him… a lottery. I was on the phone to the council about that tax on the rental property, and he was yelling about needing ‘flowery biscuits’.

Right, so are we still on for Scrabble after this? I’ve been mentally cataloguing all the double and triple word squares, proper strategizing and all that. Honestly, it’s a bit sad how much I think about it. Strategizing? You? I thought you just threw down whatever letters looked prettiest. Though, I admit, last time you  did  manage to get 'quixotic’ on a triple word score. That was…impressive. Pretty letters  do  help, aye. Though I’m more about maximising point potential. Less about aesthetics, more about… brutal efficiency. I’m telling you, someone needs to learn the two-letter word list. It's a game-changer. Brutal efficiency, Liam? You’re a research assistant, not a mercenary! And I know the two-letter words! ‘Xi,’ ‘za,’ ‘jo’… alright, maybe not  all  of them. But I’m working on it. It's just, they feel…unsatisfying to play. Like cheating. Cheating? It's perfectly legitimate! It's all about exploiting the rules, Chloe. That’s what engineering teaches you, really. Finding the weaknesses in a system. Oh, here we go with the ‘everything is an engineering problem’ speech. Honestly, Ben, you see the world through the lens of stress tests and load bearing. It’s exhausting. He’s got a point, though. It's strategic. Like when I finally landed 'fez' on a double letter score last week, felt like a proper win. Though my Auntie Maureen claimed I was showing off. Said it wasn't polite to flaunt one’s vocabulary. Your Auntie Maureen thinks Monopoly is a blood sport. She’s not a reliable gauge of acceptable social behaviour. Speaking of which, how's the house hunt going? Still nowhere decent in Cambridge? Everything's a shoebox or costs a fortune. It’s… challenging. Apparently, ‘bijou’ is estate agent code for ‘you can touch both walls at once’. And the competition is insane. Apparently, I’m up against a software engineer who offered £50,000  over  asking price on a place yesterday. Fifty grand?! That's mental. Even for Cambridge. I thought Liverpool was expensive, but that's another level. Honestly, you'd need a lottery win to afford anything decent here. Honestly. It’s mad. Makes you wonder if leaving the North was a good idea, even for a job like yours. Though, you can't get a decent corpus linguistics position in Hertfordshire, can you? Precisely.

…and honestly, the lecture just  drifted . Like, Professor Davies was talking about post-structuralism and I swear his voice just… faded. Next thing I knew, Liam was nudging me and the slides had changed three times. I’m convinced I dreamt half of it. Proper napped in a lecture hall, can you believe it? Oh, you are awful! Only you, Sal. Davies is a monotone legend, though, isn’t he? He could read the phone book and put everyone to sleep. Still, a lecture nap? Bold move. Did you get caught? Nah, I played it cool. Just sort of blinked really slowly and nodded. Liam covered for me, said I was “deeply contemplating” the material. He’s a good lad, Liam. Speaking of which, did you see what he posted on Insta last night? That throwback pic from sixth form? Oh God, yeah! The one with the questionable hair and even more questionable fashion choices? I almost choked on my tea. We all looked… optimistic, let’s put it that way. Utterly and completely clueless. Optimistic is a kind word for ‘actively embarrassing’. Remember when I thought those enormous platform boots were a good idea? I genuinely thought I looked cool. They were… a statement. A very loud, very wobbly statement. And don't even get me started on the eyeliner. You used to draw it on like wings, remember? Giant wings. Don’t remind me! Mum still brings it up. Every Christmas, without fail, she'll say something like, “Oh, remember when you thought you were Amy Winehouse?” It’s torture, honestly. Speaking of your mum, there she is now. Wave! She’s got a pint of Guinness, naturally. She’s proper settled in this place, isn't she? The Poacher’s her second home. Hey Mum! Yeah, she loves it here. Feels safe, I think. She's always saying it's 'friendly'. She'll be wanting to know all our business in a minute. "So, any nice young men, Sal?" Predictable. “Are you eating properly? You look a bit thin.” She's relentless. Though, she  does  make a brilliant roast, you’ve gotta give her that. True. The roast is non-negotiable. Listen, I wanted to ask about that gig you were going on about last week? The one with… Static Bloom? Oh, it was brilliant! Absolutely brilliant. They were playing at The Cellar. Proper small venue, really intimate.

…and honestly, the sheer  audacity  of Mr. Henderson to suggest our extension would ‘detract from the character of the street’. As if his perfectly symmetrical, pebble-dashed monstrosity is some kind of architectural masterpiece! You’re still fuming about that, then? I thought you’d calmed down after the meeting. It’s just Henderson being Henderson. A man who genuinely believes magnolia is a bold colour choice. It's not  just  Henderson, Ben. It’s the whole committee. They seemed completely swayed by his objections. Did you see Mrs. Davies practically nodding along with everything he said? It felt… pre-determined. They are a notoriously difficult bunch. Especially when it comes to anything that isn't a bland, brick-veneer semi. Remember old Mrs. Peterson wanting to paint her front door turquoise? Absolute uproar. Exactly! And we’re not talking turquoise! We’re talking a sympathetic extension, designed by a qualified architect, that  improves  the flow of the house and adds barely any height. I spent weeks preparing that application, with all the supporting documentation… and for what? To be told it might not “fit in”? You did a fantastic job with the application, genuinely. It’s incredibly thorough. We just need to think strategically about how we proceed. Do we appeal? Or do we try and address their concerns and resubmit? I’m leaning towards resubmission, but with a few tweaks. Maybe dial back the size slightly, even though it’s already minimal. And definitely,  definitely  get a heritage statement commissioned. Highlight the historical context of the area, demonstrate that the design is respectful… all that jazz. That’s sensible. A heritage statement will add weight. Expensive, though, isn’t it? It is. But less expensive than a protracted legal battle, I suspect. And frankly, I’d rather not spend the next six months wrangling with the council. Speaking of expensive… have you had any luck with online valuations for the flat? A few. They're all over the place, as you'd expect. Rightmove suggests around £380,000, Zoopla’s a bit more optimistic at £400,000. But those are just algorithms. I spoke to Mark at Harrison & Cole – you know, the estate agent near Clapham Junction? – and he thinks realistically we’re looking at £375,000, maybe pushing £380,000 with a good marketing campaign. That's… lower than I’d hoped. We put so much work into modernising it.

…and honestly, the queue at Sainsbury’s was  insane . I swear, everyone decided to do their big shop at exactly 6pm on a Tuesday. It took me nearly an hour just to get the pasta and pesto! Oh, no way! Tuesday isn’t even peak Sainsbury’s, is it? I usually go then to avoid the weekend rush. You’re not kidding about queues though, are you? I popped in for milk this morning and it was surprisingly busy. People are clearly panic-buying something, I reckon. Panic-buying what, though? Everything seemed normal, just…lots of people. Honestly, I was contemplating abandoning the trolley and just ordering a takeaway. Speaking of which, have you seen Mrs. Henderson’s new boyfriend? He was loading a  mountain  of ready meals into his car yesterday. Oh, Kevin? No, but that doesn’t surprise me. She’s always been a bit of a convenience food queen. He seems…nice enough, I guess. A bit quiet. Did you hear she told everyone he’s a ‘property developer’? A property developer?! Apparently, he fixes leaky taps for a living. Old Man Hemmings told my mum. Mum's already made a judgement. It’s gold dust, honestly, the gossip around here. Anyway, enough about Mrs. Henderson’s questionable romance. How was your shift yesterday? Rough? Ugh, pretty intense. We had a new admission, a young lad, really struggling. It’s just… draining, you know? Even when you feel like you’re helping, it’s a long process. It's good to be back in the flat though. Proper chilled vibes. Did you manage to watch that film we talked about, 'Saltburn'? Ooh, yes! I watched it last night. Woah. That was… something. I’m still processing it, to be honest. A bit disturbing, wasn't it? And Emerald Fennell really does love a shocking scene. Disturbing is an understatement! I’ve heard mixed reviews. Some people thought it was brilliant satire, others thought it was just… gratuitous. I'm on the fence. I might give it a go this weekend. I need something to take my mind off things. Fancy a day out on Saturday? We could go to Brighton. Brighton! Yes! That sounds amazing. It feels like ages since we’ve done something properly fun. Fish and chips on the pier, questionable arcades… perfect. Have you heard from any of the old gang from school lately?

Right, seriously, look at that meerkat. Proper little gangster, isn’t he? Standing all upright, surveying his kingdom. Makes you think about… well, not much really, just how knackered I am. This flat’s a state. You say that  every  time we watch a nature documentary, Liam. It’s become your catchphrase. And it  is  a bit messy, yeah, but not a state. We lived in student digs, remember? This is positively Buckingham Palace compared to that. Buckingham Palace with a mountain of laundry and a suspicious smell coming from the kitchen. Speaking of, are you ordering takeaway again tonight? I’m trying to be good, you know? Operation: Lose the Lockdown Lard is still in effect. Oh, don't start. You had a massive portion of chips with your lunch. And besides, I saw an ad for that new Thai place on Lark Lane. They’ve got a student discount. Strategic investment in deliciousness, I'd call it. Student discount? Even though we’re both fully qualified professionals now? That’s… cheeky. These advertising companies, eh? They’re masters of manipulation. Remember that one about the washing powder, making everything seem all bright and airy? Absolute rubbish. Our clothes still end up grey. You’re such a cynic. It’s just marketing, babe. They’re just trying to sell things. It's a bit like NLP, really. Understanding how people  think  to influence them. I was reading an article about it for work today – fascinating stuff. Apparently, framing is everything. NLP? Sounds a bit…shifty, doesn’t it? Like something out of a film. Anyroad, I'm more bothered about the sheer volume of ads we get bombarded with now. Every five minutes on telly, another one. It's relentless. And they're all for things you don't need. Like… giant inflatable unicorns for the garden. Who even  buys  those? Probably the same people who spend all their money on online shopping. Speaking of which, I got a cracking deal on those running shoes I was telling you about. Forty percent off! It's practically a civic duty to save money, wouldn’t you agree? A civic duty? You've been spending too much time with those psychology books. Listen, I think I’m going to brave the car boot sale on Sunday. I need a new bookshelf. Mine's falling apart. Plus, you never know what treasures you can unearth.

Honestly, this weather is  doing  my head in. One minute it’s sunshine, the next it’s threatening a downpour. Makes planning anything impossible. And honestly, I need a weekend away. I’m starting to feel like a houseplant. Tell me about it! I spent half of Saturday washing the car, and then it poured. Pointless, utterly pointless. Though, a weekend away sounds excellent. Where are you thinking? We were vaguely talking about the Cotswolds a while back? Cotswolds are lovely, but rammed with tourists. You want peaceful? Head north. Peak District? Yorkshire Dales? Yorkshire’s got it all, really. Plus, the pubs are better. No offence, Amelia. None taken, Mark! I’m quite partial to a good Yorkshire pudding, I admit. It's just…getting Liam to agree is the issue. He’s obsessed with house-hunting at the moment. Every single spare minute is spent scrolling through Rightmove. Oh, the joys of property portals. That’s all Ben and I talk about too. We finally saw a place we both liked last week, but it needs  so  much work. Apparently, “character features” is estate agent code for “structurally unsound.” Oh, that’s brilliant, Chloe! You’ve hit the nail on the head. We looked at a ‘doer-upper’ last month and the floorboards were held together with hope and prayer. Honestly, the thought of the work… I’m sticking with renting for a bit longer, thank you very much. It's a crazy market, isn't it? Everything's overpriced. I’m starting to think we’ll be forever stuck in this little semi. Still, it's got a garden, so I can't complain  too  much. Speaking of which, anyone tried that new Italian place, ‘Bella Notte’, down the Hagley Road? I went a couple of weeks ago. Food was alright, nothing special. A bit pricey for what it was, I thought. The atmosphere was good though, very lively. I've been meaning to go. I'm always looking for decent pasta. Although, I've discovered this amazing app for recipe ideas - 'Kitchen Stories'. It's genuinely changed my cooking. Before, it was mostly beige. Now, colour! Ooh, I’ll have to download that! I’m forever in a rut. It's either pasta or a very sad salad. I’ve been trying to get back into writing, though. I started a short story last month, but I'm struggling with the ending.

…and honestly, the whole estate was mud. Just  mud . We moved into what is now quite a respectable area, didn’t we, but back then, it was all building sites and half-finished houses. I remember thinking, ‘Where have we come to?’ After Almondsbury, it felt… raw. Though, of course, it was affordable. You youngsters wouldn't believe how much a house cost back then. Affordable is an understatement, Margaret! I remember house hunting with Brenda – that was my wife, you lot know – and being absolutely gobsmacked at the prices. Even so, getting a mortgage was a trial. I’d just started at Northwood, and they wanted references from practically my primary school headmaster! Not the same as a permanent post, apparently. Ramsgate was…different. A seaside town, full of life. This felt very… inland. You think  you  had trouble with mortgages? Try explaining to a bank why you needed funds for a practice. They looked at me like I was asking to finance a moon landing. Being a dentist, you see, wasn’t quite the societal pillar it is now. Though, I did have a rather funny interview for the post at the General. Oh, go on, David. We’ve heard snippets over the years, but never the full story. I’m all ears. Well, the interview panel was rather…stuffy. Very formal. One particularly severe gentleman kept peering at my teeth! I mean,  at  my teeth! As if judging the quality of my dental work based on my own. I nearly burst out laughing. I stammered something about routine check-ups, and he just raised an eyebrow. I got the job, thankfully. But I swear, he was still evaluating my molars as I shook his hand. Oh, David, that's brilliant! You’ve always had a way of recounting a story. But finding accommodation after landing the job… that was a nightmare for everyone, wasn’t it? I recall you two searching for ages. Ages! Every house was either a damp Victorian terrace or a concrete box waiting to fall down. Eventually, we found a little semi in Kings Norton. Needed  everything  doing to it, but it was ours. And Brenda had fantastic ideas… some of them worked, some of them… well, let’s just say the wallpaper didn’t always stay on the wall. We had a similar experience. I was lecturing at the university, which gave me a bit more leverage, but even then, finding somewhere decent was hard.

…and honestly, the chipped glaze on that particular teapot is what  made  it. People always want perfection, don’t they? But it’s the little flaws that tell a story, I always say. Had a woman practically argue with me over it, wanting a discount because of the chip. Honestly! It was part o’ its charm. You sound exactly as I imagined an antique dealer would be, Marion. A champion of the imperfect. I always found that fascinating, the way you could see a life layered into an object. My work was… well, very different. Everything had to be  precise . Every sound, every articulation. No room for charming chips, shall we say? Precise, eh? You were a… a speech therapist, you said? That’s a proper skill, that is. I can barely get a straight answer out of young Thomas down the road, let alone untangle someone’s tongue! What was that like, dealing with folks, helping them find their voice? It was immensely rewarding, actually. Challenging, of course. So much depends on early childhood, doesn’t it? I spent years working with children who’d had difficult starts, and it was incredible witnessing their progress. Though, frustrating at times. It made you very aware of social disparities, you know? Some children simply didn't have the same opportunities for language development, and that followed them. I trained in London initially, then worked mostly around Bristol. You wouldn't believe the accents! Bristol, aye. A bit…rough around the edges, wouldn’t you say? Though, good for business, sometimes. Plenty of interesting pieces turn up in those parts. I spent most of my working life right here in Taunton, though. Had a little gallery on the High Street for… oh, nearly thirty years. Started it after university, really. My parents weren’t overly keen - wanted me to ‘settle down’ and marry a farmer, like a good Somerset girl should – but I had a knack for spotting a bargain, a good eye, and a bit o’ stubbornness. Sounds like a winning combination! My parents were… different. We moved to Australia when I was six, from just outside Manchester. My father was a botanist, chasing rare orchids, apparently. It was a bit of a shock to the system, leaving England. Everything was so… bright. And noisy. And full of insects! Australia! Crikey. Never been. Always fancied it, though. Seems a long way to go for orchids, don't it?

Right, so, are we thinking roast potatoes  and  dauphinoise? It feels…ambitious, even for Christmas dinner. And I still haven’t figured out the gravy situation. Is it a proper beef dripping thing, or a cheat’s red wine number? Calm down, Leo. Ambitious is good! It’s Christmas! And beef dripping, definitely. No cheating on the gravy. Though, I was thinking about making those little gingerbread men for dessert. You know, the ones with the ridiculously tiny icing buttons? Gingerbread men… yeah, good shout. Less pressure than a full-on Yule log. Although, Mum always did a cracking Yule log. Remember? It always looked like a proper forest scene. She'd spend days on it. Days! She did love her Christmas baking. Speaking of, I’m almost sold on doing a candy cane flavoured buttercream for the cupcakes this year. It’s a bit…much, isn’t it? But people seem to love that sort of thing. A bit much is  exactly  what Christmas demands! Go for it. Though, if you start putting edible glitter on everything, I’m staging an intervention. Last year’s glitter explosion took weeks to clean up. Honestly, you're such a grump. It was festive! Anyway, how's the tattoo healing? Still looking…vibrant? It’s fine! It’s a bit itchy, that's all. And yes, the colours are still popping. It’s a masterpiece. You’d appreciate it more if you actually  got  a tattoo. I appreciate art on skin, just not necessarily on  my  skin. I’m happy with baking as my creative outlet. Much less permanent.      Sorry I’m late! Train was a nightmare. Honestly, Birmingham to London at this time of year… total chaos. What smells so good? Are you two planning world domination through festive baking again? Just a standard Christmas dinner blueprint, Chloe. Leo’s having a minor existential crisis over the gravy. Gravy is serious business. Right, I’ve got the first round of decorations. Found a little vintage shop in Brum and scored loads of proper old-fashioned baubles. Not that plastic rubbish. Oh, brilliant! So, proper glass ones? The kind your nan used to have? Exactly! And I got this amazing garland made of dried oranges and cinnamon sticks. It smells incredible. Although, transporting it on the train… let’s just say a few cinnamon sticks didn't make it. Oh, that sounds lovely!

Right, Cambridge is officially in the rear-view. Honestly, felt like I was living in a postcard for the last three years. A  very  stressful postcard, mind you, but still…pretty. Stressful is an understatement, darling. You looked like you hadn't slept a full eight hours since, well, since you started that thesis. Though, it  is  done now, isn't it? Officially handed in? The weight off your shoulders must be immense. Officially handed in. Freedom. Glorious, glorious freedom. Though now the question is…what  do  I do with it? That’s the bit that’s actually stressing me out now, if you can believe it. Less academic pressure, more… existential dread. Oh, the classic post-thesis crisis. Perfectly normal. We all go through it. Remember your cousin, Leo? Spent a month convinced he was going to become a goat farmer. Don't remind me. Thankfully, that passed. Still, I feel a bit lost. London feels…loud. And expensive. Thinking about flats already gives me palpitations. Everything’s so tiny for the money. London  is  a beast when it comes to housing. It’s gotten worse, even since I was your age. Have you actually started seriously looking? Or are you just browsing Rightmove and despairing, like most graduates I know? A bit of both, to be honest. I’ve seen a few places in… well, mostly Zones 2 and 3. Nothing amazing. A cupboard with a window, basically. I was thinking maybe a flatshare to start with? Ease myself back into the real world, save some pennies. That’s sensible. And a good way to meet people. Though, if you're going to do a flatshare, be careful who you choose. Remember what happened to Amelia? Ended up living with a conspiracy theorist who believed pigeons were government drones. Right, noted. Avoiding pigeon-obsessed flatmates. Perhaps. Though, honestly, I’m starting to wonder if I should just…not rush into anything. Maybe a bit of travel? I’ve got a few mates thinking about backpacking through Southeast Asia. Travel is wonderful, darling, a fantastic experience. But have you thought about what that does for your actual long-term plans? The thesis was good, very good, your tutor said so. Have you considered applying for any graduate schemes? They close pretty quickly, you know. I  have  looked. A couple of things in publishing, which obviously makes sense, given the English degree.

…and honestly, the train was  packed . Coming from Aylesbury, I’m used to a bit of a commute, but this was another level. Everyone seemed to be heading for Alumni Day, though. Did you have any trouble getting here? Oh, it wasn't too bad, actually. Drove down from Lincoln. A surprisingly easy drive, all things considered. Though parking around Cambridge is always…an adventure. You’re from Buckinghamshire, right? I always think of rolling hills and red kites when I think of that area. That’s pretty accurate! It's lovely. I do miss the countryside when I’m stuck in the city for work, though. I’m a Language Research Coordinator, funnily enough, dealing with a lot of digital data these days, which feels a million miles from, well, actual languages sometimes. What about you? What brings you to the Faculty today? I'm the Research Administrator, so similar, just slightly more of the paperwork side of things. It's good to get out of the office and actually  see  people who benefit from the research. It's nice to be back in the Law Faculty, feels like ages since I graduated. Excuse me, hope I’m not intruding. Fascinating to hear you two discussing the practicalities of research. Always good to see younger faces engaged. I'm Professor Alistair Finch. Used to lecture here for…well, a long time. Not at all, Professor Finch! Lovely to meet you. I’m Chloe, and this is Emily. We were just comparing travel stories, really. A pleasure to meet you too, Professor. I'm Emily. Are you an alumnus yourself, then? Indeed. Several decades ago now. My field was, and still is, primarily historical linguistics, though I spent a good chunk of my career dabbling in archaeology. Excavated a rather significant village site in Shropshire, not far from where I grew up – Oswestry. A surprisingly rich history, that corner of England. Oh, really? That’s incredible! I did a module on archaeological linguistics during my Masters. We looked at how language change can be traced through material culture. It's fascinating. Were there any particular finds at your site that shed light on the language spoken there? Actually, yes. A number of runestones, mostly fragments, but with enough preserved to suggest a very early form of Old English, heavily influenced by Brythonic languages. It's a truly remarkable area. It got me thinking a lot about the migrations and interactions of different groups.

… honestly, the deadline's just looming, yeah? Dissertation’s a beast. And Professor Davies keeps changing his mind about what he  wants  it to be about. It's driving me round the bend. Another pint anyone? Sounds stressful, Leo. Though, you always say that, don't you? Every deadline is a looming beast. I’d say a beast is kneading dough for six hours straight, but each to their own. Another one for me actually, please, Sarah? This sourdough starter is demanding. Coming right up, Poppy. Leo, you’re a drama queen, plain and simple. But uni  is  hard. Just remember to breathe. I’m just grateful my biggest stress is whether the oat milk delivery will be on time. Honestly, the hipsters will riot if I run out. Oat milk riots… sounds about right for 2024. Tell me about it. I spent the whole day wrangling a location permit for a shoot. Bureaucracy just loves to eat your soul. It’s funny, isn’t it? We all did degrees, supposed to be building amazing careers, and we’re all battling… logistical nightmares. Logistical nightmares and existential dread! That’s a pretty accurate summary of post-grad life. Speaking of careers, I saw this TikTok the other day, some bloke claiming young people don't want jobs, we just want to be 'influencers'. Absolute rubbish. It’s not  wanting  to be an influencer, it’s feeling like nothing else is accessible. Ugh, those videos. They’re so… reductive. I worked my backside off to get my degree, then another two years perfecting my patisserie. It’s not glamorous. It’s hot, it’s early mornings, and my hands are permanently covered in flour. But it's  mine . And it pays the bills. Exactly! It's about having something to be proud of, something real. It’s all well and good being an 'influencer', showing off your life, but what happens when the algorithm changes, eh? I left sixth form, didn't go to uni, and built this cafe from the ground up. It’s hard graft, but I wouldn't trade it. I think there's a class element to it too. A lot of those narratives conveniently ignore the privilege of even  being able  to chase that influencer dream. Buying the equipment, having the time, the safety net… Access is everything. I'm lucky, my parents helped me get a foothold in the industry, got me internships.

Honestly, this week has been…a lot. The students are particularly draining at the moment. It's not even the work, it’s the  expectations . Everyone wants extensions, special consideration… it’s exhausting constantly navigating it all. Tell me about it. Mine are all convinced they’re on the cusp of groundbreaking discoveries, then can’t actually explain the basic principles. Did you hear back about that funding application, by the way? The one for the research into…what was it, Victorian female poets? No, not yet. I’m not holding my breath. It feels like everything is going to funding streams that are tied to…well, let’s just say more ‘impactful’ research. Apparently, analysing Christina Rossetti’s use of symbolism isn’t going to ‘boost the economy’. The eternal struggle. Everything’s got to be quantified, hasn’t it? It's utterly ridiculous. You’d think, working in higher education, we’d be valuing intellectual curiosity for its own sake. Speaking of things needing quantifying…did you see that article about the NHS waiting lists? Absolutely appalling. Don’t even  start  me on the NHS. My mum’s waiting for a hip replacement, and they’ve pushed it back again. She's in constant pain, and they just keep saying “prioritisation”. Prioritising what, exactly? Letting people suffer? And then you hear about all the private healthcare companies posting record profits. It’s sickening. It really is. I know old Mr. Henderson down the street finally went private for his cataract surgery. Said he couldn’t bear waiting any longer. It shouldn’t be like that. Everyone deserves decent healthcare, regardless of their postcode or their bank balance. It's supposed to be a fundamental right. Exactly! It's all linked, isn’t it? Years of underfunding, privatisation creeping in…and now we’re all paying the price. And the politicians just spout platitudes. Did you catch that disastrous interview with the Health Secretary on  Question Time ? He didn't have a single coherent answer. I switched it off after five minutes. Utterly hopeless. They're all Teflon-coated these days, aren't they? Nothing sticks. It makes you wonder if they actually believe anything anymore, or if it’s all just performance. Probably the latter. Though, on a completely different note, have you seen  The Tourist  on BBC One? Jamie Dornan is surprisingly good in it. Not exactly highbrow, but a decent bit of escapism after a day dealing with student plagiarism and NHS woes.

Honestly, this is lovely, ANON. You really  do  make the best shepherd’s pie. It reminds me so much of Mother’s, though she always used a bit more Worcester sauce, I think. Do you put Worcester sauce in yours, dear? It’s delicious, ANON. Seriously, best comfort food. And yes, a dash of Worcester sauce, Mrs. H. Though I think ANON’s secret ingredient is the sweet potato in the mash – adds a lovely sweetness. Sweet potato, eh? That’s a modern twist. In my day, it was all Maris Piper and butter, and that was that. No fancy additions. Although, I suppose even school dinners have improved since then. Slightly. Remember those grey, gelatinous things they called custard? Oh, don’t  start  on the school dinners, Arthur. I spent half my career trying to instill a love of literature in children fuelled by horrors like that. It’s a wonder they could concentrate! Though, speaking of things from the past… Did you see young Emily’s graduation photos online? Absolutely radiant. I did! She looked amazing. Such a proud moment for all of you. What’s she planning to do now? Still aiming for that research post in Bristol? That’s the plan. She’s got a couple of interviews lined up, which is encouraging. It’s a tough field, astrophysics, but she’s got the brains for it. Always did. Remember when she was little and used to ask the most outlandish questions about black holes? Drove me mad, trying to explain it all! She got that from her grandfather, you know. Your father, Arthur, was obsessed with science fiction as a boy. Used to spend hours building rockets out of cardboard boxes. Though his scientific explanations were…a little unorthodox, shall we say? Unorthodox is putting it mildly! He believed in little green men, that one did. Always said they communicated through the static on the wireless. But he was a good man, your father, Margaret. Had a twinkle in his eye. It’s funny, the things families pass down. I've been trying to get my nan to understand video calling for weeks. She just stares at the screen and asks where the television presenter is! She’s convinced I’m talking  to  someone in the TV, not  on  it. Oh, dear. They're not all tech-savvy, are they? I try to avoid it myself, if I’m honest.
