But I’m in for drinks, absolutely. Somewhere a bit…lively, yeah? I need to de-stress after dealing with transcription errors all day.      Lively sounds good. The Eagle and Child? It’s a bit touristy, but it’s always buzzing. And we can definitely do the paperclip thing, Chloe. I'm picturing a glorious, abstract Horace. Though maybe someone with actual artistic talent should lead that endeavour…      Eagle and Child sounds good. Though, just throwing it out there, there's that new tapas place, ‘Alma’, on Mill Road. Really good reviews. A bit more…adult, perhaps. And speaking of adulting, someone needs to remind me to book the room for the focus groups next week. Completely slipped my mind.      Alma sounds lovely, actually. A bit less…historic Cambridge. Always ending up explaining to US colleagues why everything’s so old. And focus groups, good shout, Sarah. I can add it to my list. Right, back to Horace. Are we all agreed on the timing? Five-thirty, then?      Five-thirty works for me. I'll start prepping the eulogy. Something suitably dramatic, I think. “Horace, a weaver of webs, a master of the microclimate…”      Oh god, no. Please don't actually give a eulogy. A quick ‘Cheers to Horace, may your eight legs rest in peace!’ will suffice. I'm still trying to convince myself it wasn’t a particularly large daddy longlegs.      I did see Dave trying to gently scoop him up in a mug. It was… endearing. He really didn’t want to squish him. Said his niece loves spiders.      Bless Dave.

Honestly, I’m  drowning  in homework. Mr. Harrison genuinely thinks we have no lives outside of double Biology. Did you get the practice questions on Mendelian genetics? They're brutal. Tell me about it! I spent, like, three hours on those last night. And I  still  feel like I barely scratched the surface. I kept getting tripped up on the dihybrid crosses. It just…doesn’t click, you know? It feels so removed from anything real. Like, when are we ever going to need to work out the probability of pea plant colours in real life? Exactly! And he expects us to understand Punnett squares like it’s breathing. Honestly, I think he forgets we’re fifteen, not postgraduate genetics researchers. Mrs. Davies in Chemistry is much better. She actually explains things, and makes it relevant. Remember that practical we did with the titration? That was actually cool. Oh yeah! When we were trying to neutralise the acid and it kept changing colour? That was good. Although, I nearly spilled it all over my new trainers. Mum would  have  killed me. Oh god, disaster averted, then! Speaking of mothers… mine is already asking about my mock results. "Have you started revising? What are your targets? Are you aiming for all 9s?" It's only October! I feel like I’m being pressured to have my entire future mapped out. Ugh, same. My mum keeps talking about university applications. University! I haven’t even decided what I’m having for dinner tonight, let alone what I want to study for the next three years! She was showing me prospectuses yesterday. It's terrifying. Did you hear about Chloe Baker? She’s already decided she wants to study Medicine at Oxford. No way! Chloe? Seriously? That’s… intense. She's always been super focused, but even that's a bit much. I’m still trying to figure out if I actually  like  History. It’s alright, but I'm not sure it’s ‘life-long passion’ material, you know? I get that. I’m leaning towards Art, but even then… it’s a bit scary thinking about making a career out of something creative. What if I’m not good enough? What if I end up working in a shop for the rest of my life? Don’t be silly. You’re brilliant at Art! Remember that portrait you did of your Grandad? It was amazing.

Honestly, Mum, this lasagne is  amazing . You’ve really outdone yourself. It’s better than Luigi’s, and that’s saying something. Oh, don’t be daft, love. Luigi’s is a proper establishment. But thank you, pet. I used a bit of extra nutmeg, that’s the secret. And a good dollop of ricotta, mind. Can’t skimp on the ricotta. It  is  good, really good. Though, after a day of spreadsheets, anything tastes pretty amazing, to be fair. This week has been… well, a week. Tell me about it. The new database system at work is a disaster. It's supposed to make things easier, but it's just created more work for everyone. I spent all morning inputting the same data twice because the systems wouldn't sync! Oh, the joys of ‘modernisation’, eh? They always promise you the world and deliver a headache. Still, at least you  have  a job, eh? Some folks are struggling just to get by these days. Old Mr. Henderson down the street lost his job at the factory last month. Dreadful. That’s awful. It’s just… frustrating. My project's behind schedule now because everyone’s tied up fixing glitches in the software. And old man Davies, the boss, keeps breathing down my neck. He just doesn’t understand the limitations of the tech. Davies, honestly. He still uses a flip phone, doesn’t he? It’s a miracle he’s even managed to navigate email. How’s that new assistant of yours settling in, then? The one you mentioned last week? Sarah? She’s brilliant. Really efficient, picks things up quickly. She actually suggested a workaround for one of the database issues, and it worked! Davies took all the credit, naturally. Men! Always taking the credit. Now, tell me about your Auntie Carol. I haven't heard from her in ages. Is she still gallivanting around Europe? Yes! She just sent a postcard from Italy last week. Rome, this time. Apparently, she’s taking a pasta-making course. Honestly, she’s living her best life. She keeps saying I need to be more spontaneous. Auntie Carol’s a legend. I wish I had her courage to just… up and go. I’m stuck in Peterborough, battling spreadsheets. Peterborough’s a nice enough place, love. But you do need a bit of adventure now and then. You two should go away for a weekend.

…and honestly, the whole thing was just a disaster. He insisted on making a ‘potion’ in the garden, using everything he could find. Apparently, it needed ‘essence of slug’ which, thankfully, he didn’t manage to acquire. But the state of the flowerbeds… Honestly, Brenda, it looked like a bomb had hit them. Oh, teenagers. They’re all the same, aren’t they? My Darren went through a phase of building elaborate forts in the living room. Used every cushion, blanket, chair… drove his father round the bend. Did he get in trouble? With the potion, I mean? Just detention. Again. It’s the third time this term, Brenda. Mrs. Davies called, sounding terribly concerned. She says he’s bright, but utterly lacks focus. It’s just… exhausting. All the constant monitoring, the phone checks, the arguments. And now this detention means he can’t go to Chloe’s party on Saturday. He’s absolutely furious. Poor love. Still, rules are rules, and detention's got to be served. Chloe’s parties are always a bit… lively, aren't they? Maybe it's a blessing in disguise. Though a furious teenager is never a fun thing to deal with. Is Emily alright, though? She seems a bit quiet lately when I see her bringing the post in. She’s… she’s coping. It’s still pretty raw, you know? Her grandma… it’s all happened so fast. The doctors finally confirmed it’s cancer, and they started chemo last week. She’s trying to be strong for everyone, but I can see it in her eyes. She’s exhausted, constantly worried. Oh, Sarah, that’s awful. Truly awful. Sending all my love to her, and to her mum too. Cancer’s a cruel thing. Is there anything I can do? Bring over a casserole? Maybe just sit with her for an hour while you pop to the building society? I know how stressful paperwork gets when things like this happen. Oh, Brenda, that’s incredibly kind of you. Actually, yes to the building society. I need to sort out a direct debit for the chemo costs. It’s a nightmare, trying to manage everything alongside work. I’m trying to cover for David while he's taking some emergency leave – his uncle’s poorly – and then Emily’s situation on top of everything. It's relentless. Work always finds a way to pile it on, doesn’t it?

… honestly, I’m beat. Double shift last night at The Mariner’s. Proper rammed, it was. Every student in Salford seemed to decide Friday night was the night to celebrate finishing essays. You wouldn't believe the state of the floor afterwards. Sticky carpets… the bane of my existence. Oh,  no . Sounds rough, Ella. I can almost smell the spilled cider from here. I’m just trying to wrestle with this reading list for History. It’s endless. Honestly, sometimes I think grappling with academic texts is harder than dealing with rowdy uni students. At least they're predictable in their chaos. Predictable chaos is a good way of putting it. You get to know the patterns, y'know? Like, 11pm, first big wave of freshers trying to order complicated cocktails they've seen on TikTok. Then midnight, the slightly more…refined crowd. And then after 1am it's just a blur of requests for Jägerbombs and desperate attempts to find a taxi. What are you reading about? Something exciting? It’s the social impact of the Industrial Revolution on Nottingham. Really fascinating, actually, when you get past the dense prose. It's making me think about my nan, really. She used to work at Player’s cigarette factory, and she’d tell me stories about it. It was  huge  in Nottingham, employed so many people. But the conditions... she never really went into detail, but you could tell it wasn’t easy. That sounds proper important, connecting it to your family like that. Makes it more real, doesn’t it? My grandad was a trawlerman out of Hull, spent his whole life at sea. I used to love hearing his stories. Rough life, though. And dangerous. Not like serving pints, even on a busy night, though I've had a few near misses with flying glasses! It’s funny, isn’t it? We're both surrounded by history, just in very different ways. You're uncovering it in books, and I'm…cleaning up after it. Cleaning up after it - that's a good way to look at it! Seriously though, I'm starting to think I need to get a part-time job. My student loan just…vanishes. Like a puff of smoke. It’s not enough to live on, especially now rent's gone up. Have you thought about anything different work wise? Anything using your degree? I have, yeah.

…and honestly, the all-inclusive thing is the only way to go with the kids. Otherwise, it’s just constant “Dad, I’m hungry!” “Dad, I’m bored!” “Dad, he’s looking at me!” It's exhausting. Though, Alicante wasn't exactly brimming with culture, was it? More…beige. Beige is a good word for it, Liam. My Stanley and I went to Skegness last year. Now  that  was beige. But cheap as chips, and the lad loved the arcades. He’s addicted to those grabber machines, absolutely hooked. Spent a fortune trying to win a stuffed penguin. Skegness, is it? Oh, the memories! Though, mine are a bit…dusty. Went there as a girl with my auntie Maureen. She won a goldfish. Named it Winston. It lasted all of three days. Poor Winston. Winston the goldfish. A tragic tale. Though, arguably, better than hearing about another beige holiday, Liam. I’m opting for something a bit more…vibrant this year. Thinking Morocco. Marrakech, maybe. Morocco? Seriously, David? That's a leap from Alicante. Brave. I tried to suggest something similar to my wife, she just said “Too much hassle." And then asked if we could go back to Bognor Regis. Bognor Regis? Oh, Liam, you poor man! That's where holidays go to  die . My grandma used to go there. She said the biggest excitement was watching the pigeons. Pigeons are dramatic creatures, mind you. I once saw two going at it hammer and tongs over a chip in Dublin. Proper feathery fight! It was like a tiny, winged boxing match. Now  that’s  a holiday story. More entertaining than anything I’ve heard so far. I’m hoping Marrakech will deliver a bit more…spice. I’m picturing vibrant markets, amazing food, maybe even a camel ride. Though, I'm not entirely sure about the camel ride. I've heard stories… Stories? Like what? Don't tell me they bite. My daughter's got it into her head that she wants to ride one. My cousin went to Egypt. Rode a camel. Said it smelled…distinctive. And was surprisingly wobbly. She ended up with a very sore bottom. Ah, camels. They're grand, truly. But they have opinions. And those opinions are usually expressed by spitting. My brother learned that the hard way in Tunisia. Spitting, you say? Well, that’s…useful information. Perhaps I’ll stick to the markets then.

Honestly, that was a  shocking  tackle. Absolutely shocking. Ref’s lost the plot completely. Never a yellow card, that should’ve been straight red. Come on, love, bit harsh, isn't it? He went in strong, yeah, but there wasn’t malicious intent. Bit clumsy, maybe. Though, I’ll grant you, the ref  has  been… inconsistent, to say the least. He let that offside go five minutes ago that was clear as day. Clumsy?! He nearly took the lad’s legs off! And inconsistent is putting it mildly. He's favouring them, pure and simple. Look at the free kicks they’re getting, every little nudge is a foul. It’s ridiculous. Proper biased. Makes you lose faith in the whole game, doesn't it? You say that every single time a decision goes against your team. You’re a walking, talking conspiracy theory when it comes to football. I swear. It's not a conspiracy, it's observation! Years of supporting Sunderland will teach you to be cynical. You’ve had an easy life supporting Aston Villa, you’ve not known true suffering. Hey! Don't bring Villa into this. We’ve had our moments of despair, thank you very much. Remember that 6-0 hammering by Liverpool a few years back? That was… humbling. But anyway, changing the subject, are you peckish? I was thinking of ordering something. All this yelling is making me hungry. Humbling is an understatement... They were a shambles. And yes, actually. I am. But not one of your healthy salads, mind. I need something proper. Comfort food. This game is stressing me out. Right, a proper comfort food situation. So, we’re talking… takeaway? What are we feeling? Pizza? Chinese? I’m open to suggestions. Though, I’m leaning towards a burger. A really,  really  good burger. Ooh, a burger does sound good. But not one of those fancy, posh burgers with the microgreens and truffle oil. I want a proper greasy burger. Like, a double cheeseburger with bacon and a mountain of chips. And garlic mayo. Don’t skimp on the garlic mayo. You’re a monster. A beautiful, burger-loving monster. Alright, alright, double cheeseburger, bacon, chips,  and  copious amounts of garlic mayo. I know a place down Mill Road that does a cracking one. "Burger Bliss", they call themselves. It's slightly pretentious, but the burgers are worth it. "Burger Bliss"?

…and honestly, the client just kept adding scope creep. It started as a simple website update, right? Now they want a fully integrated e-commerce platform with AI-powered product recommendations. Honestly, it’s madness. Another all-nighter looming, I reckon. AI-powered what-now, lad? Sounds like something out of one of those science fiction films they used to show at the Essoldo. Remember the Essoldo, Margaret? Proper sticky floors it had. Oh, don’t  start  on the Essoldo, Mum. You’ll be telling us about sneaking in with Arthur and getting told off by Old Man Hemmings again. And honestly, David, you need to learn to say 'no'. You’ll burn yourself out. You’re always taking on too much. Easy for you to say, you sales guru! You  thrive  on saying 'yes'. And yeah, I know, I know, I need boundaries. It’s just… difficult. They dangle the bonus carrot, you see. A carrot, is it? In my day, a good worker got a fair wage, not a carrot. Though, I did make a lovely carrot cake once. With walnuts, mind you. Not one of those fancy ones with cream cheese frosting. Just a plain, proper carrot cake. Mum, we’re talking about David’s stressful job, not your baking! Though, a slice of that carrot cake  would  be nice. Did you use the one from Mrs. Higginbottom’s recipe? She always swore by it. Heavens, no! Mrs. Higginbottom used lard in everything. Lard! I used butter, naturally. And a dash of nutmeg. That’s the secret, you see. A dash of nutmeg. Sounds delicious, Grandma. Though, to be honest, thinking about baking is a world away from spreadsheets and Gantt charts. Speaking of worlds away, did you two see that new Bond film? Apparently, it's… divisive. Divisive? What does that even  mean ? Is he still driving Aston Martins? That’s all I care about. A proper car, an Aston Martin. Not like those little boxes people drive around in now. Oh, the cars! Your grandfather had a lovely Austin Healey. Bright red, it was. He used to take me for drives down to Blackpool. We’d have fish and chips on the promenade. Those were the days. He kept that car spotless, always polishing it. Though he did manage to dent the wing once trying to park outside the Co-op. Blackpool! I haven't been to Blackpool since I was a kid.

Honestly, Leo, you've barely touched your pancake! It’s Pancake Day, for goodness sake. Do you  want  me to make you another one? And Elsie, slow down, you’ll get syrup everywhere! But it’s  really  good, Mummy. Can I have more sprinkles? Pleeeease? I don’t want another one. It’s too…flappy. “Flappy”? What on earth does that mean, darling? It just…flobs around on my plate. Like a sad fish. A sad fish, right. Well, a sad fish it is not going to win any prizes. Elsie, sprinkles in moderation. We need to think about brushing teeth after this sugary feast. Did you remember to tell your teacher you were a bit sniffly today? Yes! Miss Davies said I could have a tissue and she’d keep an extra eye on me. She said I was very brave for coming in with a little cough. That's lovely of her. Some of the little ones in my class are really struggling with being away from their parents, aren’t they? Little Thomas was  very  upset this morning. It breaks your heart. And you know, thinking about it, it makes you realise how lucky we are. Lucky? Why? Well, we have a warm house, and lots of food, and pancakes on Pancake Day. Some children don't have that, Leo. Some children don’t even have enough to eat, which is just…awful. Remember we talked about the food bank collection at school? Oh, yeah! I helped pack the pasta! You did, sweetheart, you were a star. Speaking of which, this is a bit of a food-related disaster, isn't it? Two nearly-full pancakes. We should have planned something different. Maybe we should go to the Science Museum this weekend? I saw they have a new exhibit on food production and sustainability. Ooh, the Science Museum! Can we see the robots? We can definitely try! It depends on how long this 'flappy pancake' situation takes to resolve itself. Although, maybe we should plan something a bit less…stimulating for Sunday? Grandma keeps hinting she wants to take us to the beach. The beach! With buckets and spades?! Buckets and spades, hopefully. Actually, I was looking at events at the Festival Hall for next month. They’re doing a storytelling performance of Green Knowe. Remember how much your father loved L.M. Boston? Green Knowe? Is that the spooky house one?

Honestly, this sweet and sour chicken is  chef’s kiss . Best takeaway we’ve had in ages. Though, it’s a bit…sticky, isn’t it? Like glue. Yeah, a bit. But I’m too hungry to care. Needed this after that…well, after everything with Old Man Hemmings’ funeral yesterday. It was a  long  day. Tell me about it. Ms. Hemmings was surprisingly stoic, though. I mean, they were married for sixty years. You'd expect more… histrionics, maybe? Not that I’m wishing for them, obviously. It just felt…contained. People grieve in different ways, don’t they? My granddad was the same. Very British, that one. Stiff upper lip and a quiet pint. Speaking of quiet, anyone see what happened with the cricket scores? England absolutely demolished them. Cricket? Really, now? We’re discussing funerals and you jump to cricket? You’re something else, Ben. Leave him alone, Amy. He’s processing. And yes, actually, I did see the score. Brilliant! Although, I barely understand the rules. It just seems to involve a lot of standing around and then someone hitting a thing. It’s more complicated than that, Liam. Much more. You should ask Ben to explain. He’ll happily talk about it for hours. Remember that time he tried to explain LBW to Sarah from accounts? She looked utterly bewildered. It's a subtle art! But back to more pressing matters - has anyone heard from Chloe? She said she was feeling a bit rough and might not make it to the film night on Friday. I texted her this morning. She said she’s still feeling awful. Think it’s just a bad cold, but she's definitely out for Friday. Such a shame, she was really looking forward to seeing that new sci-fi one. Right, we need a replacement then. Anyone got any suggestions? I'm open to anything, except maybe another superhero film. I'm superheroed-out. What about that French film, 'Amelie'? I’ve heard good things. It's supposed to be really charming. Ooh, good shout, Jess! That sounds perfect. Something a bit different. Although, it'll probably be a bit too sophisticated for Liam. He still thinks Bob the Builder is high art. Hey! Bob the Builder is a cultural icon! He taught me valuable lessons about teamwork and construction! And can we please not bring up my questionable viewing habits?

…and honestly, Mrs. Higgins practically  lived  in her garden. You wouldn’t believe the size of her marrows! She used to leave them on our doorstep, Dad, gigantic things. We had marrow chutney coming out of our ears for months. Do you remember?      Marrows, eh? Old Man Hemmings down the road in Wolverhampton grew prize-winning marrows. Used to boast about ‘em constantly. Said the secret was manure… well, you can imagine what  kind  of manure he meant! Though, I never had the patience for gardening myself. Numbers were more my thing. Neat, tidy columns. Unlike marrows, sprawled all over the place.      It’s funny, isn’t it, how people define themselves by their hobbies? Old Mr. Peterson, next door to my aunt in Taunton, was all about bicycles. He restored them, raced them, talked about them…even  dreamed  about bicycles, I think. Apparently, he had a shed full of them, meticulously organised. My aunt said it was like visiting a bicycle museum.      That sounds lovely, actually. A bit eccentric, perhaps, but lovely. It’s nice to be passionate about something. Speaking of slightly odd passions, remember Uncle George's obsession with Rice Krispy cakes? He’d eat them for breakfast, lunch  and  dinner if Mum hadn’t intervened.      George! Now  there  was a character. Always had his nose in a book, too. Languages, wasn't it? Tried to teach me a bit of French once. Utterly hopeless at it, I was. Couldn’t get my tongue around the pronunciations. Still, a good man, George. Always fair. Unlike young Timothy next door, used to steal apples from our tree.      Timothy! That’s a name I haven’t heard in years. Do you remember his mother, Mrs. Davies? She was always complaining about the supermarket scan-as-you-go machines. Said they were taking her job!      Oh, definitely! She was convinced they were plotting against shop assistants. It was a whole saga. I always felt a bit sorry for her, actually. Change can be frightening. Which reminds me, have you both seen the adverts for those driverless cars? Honestly, the thought of relinquishing control like that…terrifies me.      Driverless cars? Absolute poppycock! I’ve been driving for eighty years, young lady. Eighty years! And I can tell you, no machine can react to the road like a human being. The  feel  of the steering wheel, the judgment of distance… it’s all instinct.

…and honestly, the glitter is  everywhere . Honestly, Leo, you look like you’ve been hugged by a unicorn. It  was  a sparkly dragon, Mummy! A really, really sparkly dragon! Mine's got gold scales! And a long, long, long tail! It’s for Chinese New Year, right? That’s right, darling. It’s Chinese New Year this weekend. We’re celebrating on Sunday, remember? We're going to try and make some dumplings. Though, judging by the glitter situation, perhaps simpler crafts are best… Dumplings are good! Can we have spring rolls too? Those are yummy. And noodles! Long noodles for a long life! Grandma told me. Grandma's right! Long noodles it is. You two have been doing such lovely work on your dragons. Leo, yours is especially fierce. He looks like he could fly to… well, to another planet! He  can  fly to Saturn! It’s got rings! Miss Bell showed us pictures. I want to go to Jupiter! It’s all stripy! Is Jupiter made of noodles? That’s a fantastic question, Poppy. I’m pretty sure Jupiter isn’t made of noodles, sadly. It’s mostly gas. But maybe, in a different universe, it could be! You've been learning a lot about planets at school, haven't you? We made a model solar system! Mine had a really, really big sun. I bet it did! It's amazing how much you absorb. Speaking of absorbing things… Poppy, how’s piano going? Are you still practicing your scales? It’s hard. But Miss Evans said I’m getting better. I can almost play “Twinkle Twinkle Little Star” all the way through. That’s brilliant, sweetheart! Practice makes perfect. Leo, you’re still enjoying the drums, aren't you? Mr. Davies says you’ve got a good rhythm. Yeah! I can do a really loud boom! But Mummy gets cross. Mummy gets cross when the ‘really loud booms’ happen during dinner. A little quieter during mealtimes, please! And before I forget, Poppy, have you been practicing your aerial hoop? Yes! I can almost do a proper pull-up. It's really wobbly though. And Rosie was showing me a trick on Barbie and the Great Adventure... Oh? What trick? Do tell. Well, Barbie was stuck in a jungle and she had to swing on a vine to get away from the… the grumpy gorilla! She used her sparkly shoes for extra grip!

Honestly, this is… perfect. Just what I needed. Uni’s been a proper slog lately. Feels a million miles away from coursework deadlines, doesn’t it? And Rome… well, Rome's just Rome, innit? It really is. Though I’m already missing the smell of baking, weirdly. This heat makes me crave ice cream more than sourdough at the moment, though. How’s the AirBnB working out for you, Leo? You were a bit worried about it being further out, weren’t you? Yeah, that was me being a worrier. It's actually brilliant! Bit of a walk, granted, but the neighbourhood's proper authentic. Loads of little trattorias, and nobody trying to rip you off with tourist prices. Plus, the old lady who owns it brings me a little plate of biscuits every morning. Proper sweet. That sounds like Nonna Rosa levels of hospitality! I had an AirBnB nightmare in Naples once. Landlord kept trying to convince me my English accent meant I was loaded! This is much nicer to hear. So, dinner plans still up in the air then? I tried booking that place near the Trevi Fountain, but it's rammed. Yeah, Trevi’s a circus these days. Saw a bloke try to drink directly  from  the fountain. Security weren’t happy. I reckon we should find somewhere in Trastevere. Plenty of good eats over there, and a bit more… relaxed. Trastevere sounds good. I did a bit of research and found this tiny little pasta place, apparently the Nonna makes all the pasta fresh herself. Like,  all  of it. Sounds amazing. Sign me up for that! I need proper Italian carbs to fuel my sightseeing. Although, I’m starting to realise my Italian extends to ‘ciao’ and ‘grazie’. It’s embarrassing. I thought I'd picked up more from watching football. You and me both. My attempts at ordering coffee this morning resulted in me getting a cappuccino at 7pm. Bless the barista, she just smiled and gave me what I asked for. It's a different language, isn't it? Even just listening to people chat, it's so musical. It is. Makes my head spin trying to keep up, though. My Italian is limited to “Un altro birra, per favore,” which tends to get me pretty far, to be honest. Though I did try to ask for a table the other day, and accidentally asked the waiter if he was a horse.

…and honestly, the Pinterest boards are  terrifying . Like, glitter cannons AND a life drawing class? For Aunt Carol? I just… I don’t see it.      Oh, you are brave even attempting to plan this. Aunt Carol is… a character. Though the glitter cannon  does  sound vaguely magnificent, in a disaster-waiting-to-happen sort of way.      Disaster is putting it mildly. Remember her at Uncle David’s retirement do? The inflatable sumo suits? She nearly took out Brenda from accounts.      Oh god,  Brenda . And Carol was utterly convinced she won, despite clearly being assisted across the finish line by Graham. Anyway, back to the hen do. What's the actual brief? Has anyone actually asked Carol what  she  wants?      That's the problem! Mum keeps saying "Oh, she just wants something 'memorable'." Which, translated, means "something ridiculously embarrassing that will give us stories for years." I've suggested a nice spa day, or even a cocktail making class, but Mum's dismissive. “Too tame,” she said.      Tame is good! Especially with Carol. Honestly, I'm volunteering to hide during the “memorable” bits. But seriously, a spa day sounds lovely. And way less likely to end with someone needing A&E.      I’m with you on the spa day. I'm terrible at anything remotely crafty, everything ends up looking like a toddler made it, so forget anything involving sequins or flower arranging. And if there's cake decorating involved, someone needs to actively remove me from the vicinity of the icing.      Speaking of cake, I was thinking of offering to do the cake. I’ve been experimenting with some proper good recipes lately – a lemon and elderflower one is  amazing . But only if it’s not a themed monstrosity. No fondant Carol-shaped figures, promise me.      Oh, that would be incredible, actually! A proper, delicious cake would be a huge win. And absolutely no fondant Carol. I’m begging you. Mum was suggesting a cake in the shape of a… a toilet. Because Carol apparently has a funny story about a toilet.      A  toilet ?! Seriously?! That’s… next level.      Mum's definitely enjoying this too much. This is her opportunity for peak hen do shenanigans.      Right, intervention time. We need to collectively reign in the Mother of the Bride. I'm happy to be the voice of reason. And provide excellent cake. I’ve got some free time next week, I could do a trial run?

Right, so you reckon another knob of butter’s the answer? Honestly, this risotto is fighting me. It’s sticking like…well, like something really sticky. Another knob, yeah. Risotto's all about patience and butter, mate. You're rushing it. And you're not stirring  constantly . It needs love, this rice. It needs commitment. Commitment? It’s rice, not a relationship! I’ve been stirring for ages. My arm’s aching. And honestly, you make it look so effortless. You’re over there whipping up some sort of aromatic masterpiece and I’m battling a glutinous mass. It’s just a simple tomato and basil sauce. Relatively simple, anyway. And I’ve made this a  lot  since Uni, remember? All those student potlucks. You were usually out enjoying the ‘uni experience’ while I was stuck in the kitchen. Besides, you volunteered to make the risotto! Remember promising 'authentic Italian' after that trip to Rome? Don't remind me. Rome was… intense. And I was aiming for authentic, but I didn’t account for the fact that Italian Nonnas have generations of risotto-making wisdom coursing through their veins. Plus, I felt rough as a badger the whole time. Think I picked up some kind of lurgy. You did. You were coughing your lungs up on the Trevi Fountain. Honestly, you nearly got arrested for disturbing the peace. It wouldn't have been the first time. Speaking of feeling rough, are you still a bit under the weather? You look a bit peaky. Nah, that’s just concentration. And the stress of potentially ruining dinner. Just a bit of a lingering sniffle, I think. It’s probably the change in weather. It was roasting last week, proper summer vibes, now it's back to needing a jumper. Makes you wish you were still in Thailand, doesn't it? Oh god, Thailand. Don’t even. Remember that hotel in Bangkok? The one with the… questionable plumbing? And the rooster that decided 4am was a perfectly acceptable time for a concert? Don't. Just… don't. I still have nightmares. Although, the street food was incredible. And the beaches. That was worth the plumbing. Though I did spend a good hour scrubbing my hands raw after touching anything. Germaphobe tendencies kicking in. You're always a bit of a germaphobe. Remember when you refused to hold the handrail on the tube after that flu outbreak?

…and honestly, Doreen, I’m starting to think I need a list just to  remember  what I need to buy! It's not like the old days, popping down to Woolworths for everything. Everything’s spread out now. Right, let’s see…milk, definitely. And bread. Oh, and those little calendar fobs, the ones you hang on your keyring? I meant to get some last year, never did. Do you fancy a few? Oh, the calendar fobs! Good thinking, ANON. I do actually. Mine’s looking a bit battered from 2022 still, can you believe it? And yes, a list is essential. The brain isn’t what it used to be, is it? Though, speaking of remembering things… I was looking at birthday cards the other day, and honestly, the age ranges are ridiculous. '50-something', '60-something'… it takes all the fun out of it, doesn't it? Where's the specificity? Absolutely dreadful! It's like they’re afraid to actually  say  the number. It’s ageist, that's what it is! And it's completely unhelpful. I mean, I'm definitely in the 'older half' of the 50-somethings now, if you see what I mean. Though, it feels like yesterday we were complaining about the art and craft at St. John's. Remember Mrs. Higgins and her insistence on glitter  everywhere ? Oh, don’t remind me! Glitter for weeks afterwards. You'd find it in the packed lunches! And she was rather keen on potato printing, wasn’t she? I always thought it a rather messy affair. Though, thinking back to St. John’s… do you remember the hockey club? I was absolutely dreadful, but I enjoyed it. Though needing new boots every year was a nightmare for Mum! Dreadful, but utterly essential. My mum always said hockey boots were an investment. Though looking back, I suspect it was more about keeping us occupied and out of trouble. Anyway, hockey aside… I was chatting to young Emily the other day about what she's thinking of studying at university. She's completely torn. Oh? What’s she considering? Well, initially it was journalism, but she's now looking at sound recording. Apparently, they have a fantastic course at Sheffield. It's interesting, isn't it, how things have changed? When  we  were thinking about university, sound recording wasn't even on the radar! I ended up doing a postgrad in management, which feels a million miles away now.

…and honestly, the sheer  noise  of London just…vanished as soon as we hit the A303. It was bliss. Did you manage to get all the boxes unpacked, Dad? You looked a bit frazzled yesterday. Most of ‘em, love. Mostly. The study’s still a bit of a disaster zone, I’ll admit. Books everywhere. A chap’s got to have his books, you know. It’s a bit like being back in Southend, actually, having to sort through a lifetime of…accumulations. Though Southend never smelled of Devon wildflowers, that’s for sure. You’ll love the wildflowers. They're just coming into bloom now. Old Man Hemmings down the lane practically  lives  for them. He’s a bit of a character, though. Keeps a very close eye on everything that goes on. Oh, the 'Hemmings Watch'? I’ve heard whispers! Apparently, he knows the make and model of every car that drives past, and exactly what time Mrs. Peterson takes her bins out. Good Lord. Sounds like a right busybody. Still, a little neighbourhood watch isn't a bad thing, is it? Though I’m not sure my DIY skills are up to standard for keeping the place looking ship-shape, if he’s scrutinizing that too. I tried putting up a bird feeder yesterday and nearly took out a window. Oh, dear. Leave that to Mark, then. He's a dab hand at things like that. Much better than attempting it after a couple of pints at the Farmers Arms, I suspect. Have you been yet? Not yet. Sarah was insistent on getting me settled first. But yes, the Farmers Arms… sounds promising. A proper country pub, I presume? None of this gastropub nonsense. Oh, it's proper. And they do a fantastic ploughman’s. It’s where everyone seems to congregate. Apparently, there’s a local walking group that meets there after their hikes. You might enjoy that, Dad. Get you out and about, exploring the Moors. A walking group… hmmm. Tempting. I haven’t done much proper walking since…well, since retirement, to be honest. Mostly just pottering around the garden. Which reminds me, have you seen the state of the garden here? It’s a jungle! It needs a bit of tlc, definitely. But it’s a good size, and south-facing. You could grow anything you like. I found a little greenhouse tucked away at the back, too.

Honestly, this is ridiculous. Another 'limited time offer' on aftershave. Like I  need  more aftershave. It’s all just… algorithms trying to fleece ya, innit? You say that every time, Liam. And every time, you almost buy something. Remember that weird drone you were lookin' at last week? The one for deliverin' biscuits? That was research! Purely academic! I was investigatin’ the capabilities of modern logistics. Plus, imagine never havin' to get off the sofa for a digestive. Genius, truly. Right. And the inflatable T-Rex costume? Also 'research'? Okay, okay, I browse. Sue me. What else is there  to  do? Still no word back from that job at the chippy? Not yet. Old Man Hemmings said he’d ring if anything came up. He's probably still got half the town’s application forms piled up in his office. Honestly, the man runs a takeaway like it's a government department. Tell me about it. It’s not like I’m askin' for much, just a fryin' job. I can operate a fryer. I've, like,  observed  people operating fryers for twenty-odd years. Observing isn’t the same as doing, love. Though, to be fair, your observation skills are pretty sharp when it comes to identifying online deals. That's a valuable skill! Underrated, even. Speaking of tech, have you seen that new telly advert? The one with the colours that practically jump out the screen? The OLED one? Yeah, it's gorgeous. But also, three grand. We’re not gettin’ a three grand telly, Liam. Especially since you're… currently contributing zero pounds to the household income. Harsh, but fair. Still, imagine watchin’  Match of the Day  on that thing. The green of the pitch… it would be like bein'  there . You'd still be sat on this bed, complaining about the referee. A fancy telly won't change that. I'm actually tryin' to concentrate, you know? A-Levels aren’t gonna pass themselves. Sorry, sorry. Distractin’ ya, am I? I'm just… bored. Properly bored. This online job hunt is demoralisin'. It's all "five years experience required" for a position washin' dishes. Where am I supposed to  get  five years experience if no one will give me a start? I know, it’s frustrating. Have you tried that new employment agency in Cleator Moor? The one Ms. Davies at the library mentioned? Aye, sent 'em my CV.

…and honestly, the Aga is lovely, absolutely lovely, but it’s  always  on. It’s a heat monster! You'd think living in Devon we’d be used to a bit of warmth, but this is another level. Are you managing alright, David? You always feel the cold more than us. Managing? I’m thriving, actually! Though I will admit, it  is  a bit much. Reminds me of my nan’s kitchen back in Southend. Always red-hot, even in August. She used to say it kept the damp at bay. Still, I’m learning to live with it. We just have to open a window, even when it’s chucking it down, to avoid spontaneous combustion. What about lunch? Anything good brewing? I'm thinking a soup. It’s one of those grey days where something warm and substantial is needed. I was debating a quick cheddar and onion, or something with butternut squash. What do we reckon? Ooh, butternut squash sounds lovely, Sarah. Very autumnal. We could have some crusty bread with it. David, you okay with that? No strong feelings about squash? Squash is good. Anything is good when someone else is making it, to be honest. My days of sophisticated cooking are long gone. I used to attempt soufflés, you know. Disaster, every single time. Remember that one, Liz, with the…was it a collapsed chocolate one? Oh,  please . Don’t remind me! The kitchen looked like a bomb had hit it. And the dog got chocolate poisoning. A truly harrowing afternoon. It was rather dramatic! Right. Squash soup it is then. While that’s simmering, we should talk about your walk on Saturday, Liz. You were saying about the coastal path? Yes! I’m really looking forward to it. I was thinking of starting at Hartland Quay and walking towards Clovelly. It’s about eight miles, I think. Relatively flat, stunning views… Clovelly? Bit touristy, isn’t it? All those cobbled streets and gift shops. I’d rather walk into a brick wall. Oh, Dad! Don’t be such a grumpy old man. You don’t have to  go  into Clovelly. We can just walk  past  it. It’s the scenery I'm after. And a good blow to the cobwebs. It's lovely there, David. We could stop for a cream tea afterwards, if you’re feeling peckish. That might sweeten the deal? A cream tea… well, that  does  sound tempting.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of revisions on that grant proposal is doing my head in. It’s like, write a clear, concise argument, get it peer reviewed,  then  they come back with ‘needs more justification for the control group’ – which was already justified! It's infuriating. Pass the biscuits, would you? You sound properly stressed. That’s the bane of academic life, isn’t it? Always justifying, always needing ‘more evidence’ even when you  have  evidence. Honestly, sometimes I feel like my job is easier. At least with marking, the criteria are… relatively fixed. Though, don’t get me started on the appeals process. Relatively fixed is a generous description! I remember you telling me about that parent who argued their child deserved full marks because “they tried really hard”. Oh, don’t remind me. That was Brenda. Brenda is… a force of nature. But yeah, it’s different stress. Yours is the existential dread of your research being deemed unworthy, mine is Brenda. Though, lately, even the 'Brendas' are getting more complex with their arguments. The changes to the grading system are making everything so much more… nuanced. Nuanced is putting it politely. Sounds like you’re battling a whole new layer of bureaucracy. How’s your team coping? Are they feeling the strain? They are, actually. There’s a lot of anxiety over getting the data right, ensuring everything is standardized across the different schools we're working with. We had a really open team meeting yesterday, just checking in on everyone. Sarah was visibly struggling, mentioned feeling overwhelmed. I tried to reassure her, delegate a bit to lighten her load, but it’s hard when everyone’s already stretched thin. It makes you wonder if all the assessment  is  actually helping improve things, or just creating more pressure. That's a really good point. We get caught up in the methodology, the statistical significance, but sometimes forget to ask the fundamental question: is this actually  beneficial ? It’s the same with some of the health interventions I look at. Show a tiny reduction in anxiety scores, declare it a success, but ignore the fact it requires three hours of daily meditation and a complete lifestyle overhaul. Exactly! It's all about the metrics, isn't it? Remember Uncle George used to say "statistics are like bikinis, what they reveal is interesting, but what they conceal is vital"?

Honestly, this is lovely, isn't it? Mum, your roast potatoes are still the best. Though, I swear you use more butter every time. Don’t you start, Sarah. A little butter never hurt anyone. Besides, everyone raves about them. It’s a family tradition! Though, I  did  notice Dave eyeing up the gravy like a hawk. Cor, it  is  good gravy, Mary. Proper stuff. Not that watery nonsense you get in pubs these days. Reminds me of me nan's. She could make a feast out of nowt. Nan’s were always the best cooks, weren’t they? Mine used to make the most amazing apple crumble. Though, she always insisted on using lard. Said it was the secret. Thank you, Sarah. It is lovely, genuinely. And yes, the potatoes are divine, Mary. This is a proper treat after a shift. Honestly, some of the food in the hospital… let’s just say I appreciate a home-cooked meal. You wouldn't believe the things people try to sneak in, though. Old Mr. Henderson attempted to hide a whole tin of biscuits under his pillow last week! Oh, bless him! Always the rebel. Speaking of sneaky, did anyone see young Thomas trying to feed bits of his chicken to the dog under the table? I did. I told him, 'No, Thomas! Winston doesn't need your bones!' He's a growing boy himself, that dog. Eats like a horse as it is. Reminds me, did you ever finish looking into that dog training class, Sarah? Winston's getting a bit boisterous. I did, dear. Booked him in for next Saturday. Apparently, they focus a lot on recall, which is what we need. He's always trying to chase squirrels into next door’s garden. It’s a nightmare. Though, honestly, I think  I  might learn something too. He's a clever one. Squirrels, eh? Got a cheeky one in me garden, always nicking the bird food. Tried buildin’ a proper fortress around the feeder, didn't work. Little blighter just scaled the fence. Honestly, animals are so resourceful. It's amazing. I was reading an article recently about how crows can use tools. Like, they bend bits of wire into hooks to get food out of hard-to-reach places. That’s incredible! You learn something new every day. It’s amazing what they can do. It makes you think, doesn't it?

Aye, grandad, honestly, this rhubarb crumble is  divine . You wouldn’t believe how much better fresh rhubarb is than the stuff you get in the supermarket. It’s like, actually  tart , y’know? Not just sugary pink sticks. Tart, eh? Takes me back. Your grandmother, bless her, used to grow mountains of the stuff. Forced rhubarb, she called it. Had a proper hothouse in the garden for it. Said it was the only way to get a decent flavour. Though, truth be told, she’d add a good dollop of ginger beer to the crumble, that woman. Said it “lifted” it. Ginger beer in rhubarb crumble? That’s…unexpected. Sounds interesting actually. I’m a bit of a stickler for traditional recipes myself, but I’m always up for trying something new. See, I knew you’d be intrigued, Leo! Grandad’s stories are always full of little quirks like that. He’s a hidden culinary genius, he is. Though he’ll never admit it. Nonsense, lass. I just knew what tasted good. It wasn’t genius, it was common sense. Besides, back in my day, we didn’t have all these fancy food blogs and MasterChef contestants telling us how things  should  be done. You just used what you had and made it taste nice. Speaking of using what you had, did you two ever go to Italy? Italy? Yeah, I did a backpacking trip around the Amalfi Coast last year. Stunning scenery, incredible food, obviously. Though, I nearly got pickpocketed in Naples…that was a bit hairy. Naples, eh? That sounds…stressful. I’ve always wanted to go to Italy, but I’ve never quite got around to it. Been too busy with work and stuff. I did manage a week in Greece last summer, though. Santorini was amazing. All those white-washed buildings and the sunsets… Santorini… Now  that  I remember reading about. Your mother showed me some postcards. Said it was volcanic, all black sand and peculiar rocks. I never managed Italy myself, no. We went to Spain a couple of times, Benidorm mostly. Cheap and cheerful, that was. More my speed, I think. I wasn’t one for all that…cultural immersion. Give me a pint and a bit of sun, and I was happy. Benidorm? That's…very different from the Amalfi Coast! No offence, sir. It's just a different vibe entirely. I did Spain a few years ago – Barcelona.

…and honestly, the student feedback on the Baudrillard lecture was…sparse. Mostly just confused emojis. I think I lost them at ‘simulacra and simulation.’ It's just  too  dense for an introductory class, isn’t it? Dense is putting it mildly, love. Baudrillard is best served to postgraduates fuelled by copious amounts of coffee and existential dread. You were trying to get them to grapple with hyperreality on a Tuesday morning? Ambitious. I thought I could break it down! I really did. Simplify it. Relate it to social media… apparently not enough. I’m thinking of scrapping the whole thing and doing something on the ethics of AI instead. More relevant, potentially less… mind-bending. AI is good. Everyone's panicking about AI. Students will engage with panic. Plus, it lets you talk about surveillance capitalism, which, let's be honest, you find fascinating. What about your Thursday class? Still sticking with Derrida? Derrida’s sticking, thankfully. They seem to… tolerate him. It's not enthusiasm, but it’s not glazed-over eyes either. Although, I did get a question about whether deconstruction meant everything was just ‘made up.’ Oh, bless them. And what did you say? I tried to explain the instability of meaning, the reliance on difference… it probably just reinforced the ‘everything is made up’ idea. It's difficult, isn’t it? Trying to convey these ideas in a way that’s accessible without dumbing them down completely. It is. It's the constant tightrope walk of academia. You’re not just teaching content, you’re teaching  how  to think. That takes time. How about we look at your syllabus tonight, over proper Chinese food? I ordered some dan dan noodles, and I’m attempting aubergine in garlic sauce. Warning: It may be significantly less intellectual than Baudrillard. That sounds… wonderful. Honestly, I need the distraction. And dan dan noodles are  always  a good idea. You're getting remarkably good at Chinese cooking, by the way. It's a far cry from the burnt toast we lived on in our first year as lecturers! Practice makes perfect, and necessity is the mother of invention. Finding decent English sausages out here is… challenging. Honestly, sometimes I dream of a full English. Have you seen anything good on TV recently? I'm starting to think I need a new obsession other than perfecting my chilli oil recipe. I started watching that detective series, 'The Long Shadow'.

Honestly, this coffee machine is the bane of my existence. It either brews something akin to battery acid or lukewarm dishwater. There’s no in-between. And I  need  a decent cup now, after wrestling with those removal quotes. You and that coffee machine. It’s been a running battle for years, hasn’t it? What did the quotes say? Hopefully not too dreadful. We  do  need to get a lot of stuff into storage before the sale goes through. Dreadful is an understatement, I’d wager. Everything's gone up, hasn't it? Even breathing seems to have a surcharge attached these days. I saw a piece in here about the cost of living… utterly ridiculous. Ridiculous is putting it mildly! One company wanted nearly six hundred a month for a small container. Six hundred! For just  storing  things. That’s more than I used to spend on groceries for the whole month, and that was saying something. I think I’m going to have to drastically downsize what we keep. The antique dresser probably has to go. Six hundred a month? That  is  outrageous. Maybe we should look at self-storage? It’s more work, physically, but significantly cheaper. I'm happy to help with loading and unloading, though my back isn't what it used to be. Self-storage is an option, yes. Though you’ll regret it when you’re hauling boxes around. I remember doing that when we… well, never mind. It's all water under the bridge now. Speaking of regret, have you seen what’s happening with the Labour leadership? Another reshuffle, another mess. Oh, don't even get me  started  on politics. Honestly, I’m losing faith in anyone being able to fix anything. It’s all just…performative. Lots of shouting, very little substance. I used to think, you know, you could effect change. I spent years encouraging my students to be politically engaged. Now… It’s easy to become cynical, isn’t it? Especially after… well, everything. But I still think idealism has a place. You have to believe something can be better, or what’s the point? Though, agreeing on what “better”  is … that’s the hard part. This Labour lot seem to be circling the drain. They need someone with actual vision. Vision? They need someone who can actually string a coherent sentence together without contradicting themselves five minutes later.

Right, so you’re telling me “Brenda” is  actually  your aunt’s maiden name? That’s… wonderfully convoluted, Liv. Why not just use a normal pseudonym? Like, Sarah? Or… Fiona? Fiona's a bit basic, innit? And Brenda feels…solid. Like she's seen things. Plus, Auntie Maureen would be livid if I used her name for anything dodgy. Brenda’s safe. Besides, you’re one to talk, Alistair. Last time we did this, you were going by ‘Barnaby Finch, Antiquarian Book Dealer’. That was artistic license! I was researching a play! It demanded authenticity. Brenda just sounds…like someone who collects porcelain dolls. Right you two, less bickering, more carbs. Honestly, you’d think you were back at Uni. So, Kev, how’s the narrowboat life treating you? Still chugging up and down the Regent's Canal? Yeah, not bad, Rach. Actually, spent the weekend down the Lee Navigation. Beautiful stretch of water, surprisingly. Though navigating the Limehouse Basin is always a bit of a nightmare. Always someone trying to ‘shortcut’ and nearly causing a pile-up. Reminds me of Oxford Street on a Saturday. The Lee Navigation… isn’t that the one that gets really pongy near Stratford? I remember cycling along it once, the smell was…distinctive. That’s usually near the sewage works, love. Though, honestly, sometimes the canal water just  is  a bit whiffy. It’s all the decaying stuff at the bottom. People don’t realise it’s an ecosystem. Speaking of things people don’t realise… did you know there’s a kosher butcher near here? Seriously. Proper kosher. I was delivering a cake yesterday and the guy was explaining the whole process of  shechita … it’s intense. Absolutely fascinating, though. Right. Sounds…specific. I’m more interested in less specialist culinary preparation. Have either of you managed to get into that new Italian place on Roman Road? Heard good things about their pasta. I tried, booked a table, but they were completely rammed. Apparently, it's the place to be seen. Little bit pretentious for my liking, to be honest. Give me a good, simple trattoria any day. I've been. It's alright. A bit overpriced for what it is, but the tiramisu is divine. Though they don't do a proper side of chilli oil with the spaghetti  arrabiata.  A cardinal sin, if you ask me. Chilli oil on pasta? Rach, you're a monster.

Right, so I swiped right on this lad, yeah? Proper fit, looked like he actually  read  books, not just posed with ‘em for a photo. Turns out…he’s from Sheffield. Sheffield! Like, two hours away. What's the point, y'know? Oh, love, you've gone and done it again, haven’t ya? Always the long-distance potential. I swear, your Tinder algorithm is specifically designed to find men who live beyond reasonable travel distance. Two hours isn’t  that  bad, is it? I mean, I'm practically living on trains going back to Derby every other weekend. It’s just…part of uni life now, innit? Two hours is a commitment, Liv. Especially when you’ve barely committed to putting the washing out. Honestly, Elle, you need to filter by postcode. Aye, what Isla said. Postcode filter is your friend. Though, realistically, everyone on Tinder just lies about their height anyway. It’s a minefield. It  is  a minefield! And he was going on about how he's “career-focused” and “ambitious.” Sounds like a right bore already. I just want someone to go to the pub with, not someone planning their five-year plan. "Career-focused" is code for "doesn't have time for a proper relationship," darling. Trust me, I've decoded the Tinder lexicon. It's practically a second degree. How’s Ben, by the way? Still avoiding your calls? He “lost” his phone. Again. Honestly, I think he just enjoys the drama. I’m starting to suspect he’s secretly a professional phone loser. Oh, Ben. What a…character. Honestly, you deserve better. Speaking of deserving better, has anyone heard from Chloe about the house next year? She was looking at places near the canal, right? She mentioned something. Sounded pricey. And apparently, the landlord's a bit of a nightmare. Like, demanding viewings at 7am on a Sunday type of nightmare. Seven am?! That’s just cruel. We are  not  doing that. I’d rather live in a tent. This house is bad enough with Mark leaving his dirty socks everywhere. Seriously, it’s a biological hazard. Oh, Mark. The epitome of a student living situation. He thinks ‘tidying up’ involves piling everything into one corner. It's the classic student method. My flatmate last year used to build sculptures out of empty pizza boxes. It was…an experience. Do you guys think we  actually  want to live together again next year?

…and honestly, Arthur, I don’t know  why  they keep banging on about this Rwanda scheme. It’s utterly ridiculous, isn’t it? Costing a fortune and for what? Sending people off to… well, I don't even know  where  exactly. Sounds like something out of a bad novel. Aye, Derek, you're not wrong there. Costing a pretty penny, it is. Heard on the wireless this morning they reckon it’ll be over half a billion just for the first lot. Half a billion! Could fix a lot of potholes with that, eh? Seems a right waste when our own services are struggling. And the ethics of it all... sending folks away like that. It's appalling, the whole thing. And the way they talk about it, like these people are just… numbers. Like they don't have lives, families, stories. Makes my blood boil, it does. I saw a documentary last week, and it just highlighted how desperate these people are. Fleeing war, persecution... Exactly, Margaret! Desperate. And then  we're  expected to believe this is some sort of humanitarian solution? It’s political posturing, pure and simple. They’re trying to appeal to a certain…element. And it’s working, sadly. Saw old Mrs. Higgins down the shops yesterday, going on about “stopping the boats” like it’s that simple. Aye, the Higgins woman. She always has an opinion, doesn’t she? Doesn’t seem to think things through, though. Reminds me of my brother, bless him. Always believed everything he read in the  Daily Mail . Though, to be fair, most of us used to fall for that sort of thing when we were younger. Different times. It’s the simplifying of things that’s so frustrating. It's not ‘stopping the boats’, it’s addressing the reasons people are  on  the boats in the first place. And that requires international cooperation, aid, tackling climate change… all the things this government seems to be actively avoiding. And speaking of avoiding things, have you seen what they’re doing with the benefits system? Trying to push more people onto Universal Credit. Honestly, it's a nightmare for those who are already struggling. My niece, Sarah, she's having absolute hell with it. Kept having her payments delayed. Heard the same. Old man Peterson down the road – lost his housing benefit for a month, apparently. Said it was a simple error, but it nearly had him on the street.

Honestly, this shepherd’s pie feels like it’s taken all evening. And you wouldn’t believe the queue at the butchers. Everyone’s decided they want lamb tonight, apparently. Sounds… strenuous. Rough day at the shops then? Mine wasn’t much better, to be fair. Mrs. Higgins nearly had a fit when I told her the target’s gone up  again . Said she’s already rattling tins till her fingers bleed for the village hall roof. Rattling tins… exactly. It's always more from the people who have the least. Did you manage to explain the rationale? Or did you just get a barrage of complaints? A bit of both, actually. I tried to explain the rising costs, the increased need… you know the spiel. But she just kept pointing out that young Timmy’s football team still hasn’t got new kits. It’s difficult, isn't it? Making people part with their money, even for a good cause. It is. And it feels even harder when  you  don’t feel particularly valued for doing it. Speaking of things not being valued, how are things with Brenda at work? Still giving you the cold shoulder? Oh, Brenda. She's magnificent in her passive aggression, isn’t she? I think she's still smarting over me getting the lead on the Rotary Club appeal. Honestly, it’s just fund-raising, it's not conquering the world! Don’t let it get to you, love. You’re brilliant at what you do. You always have been. People just get competitive. It’s human nature. Easy for you to say, you’re not the one facing a frosty reception every morning. How was your day? Anything interesting happen at… well, whatever it is you  do  all day? You're always so vague! Vague is a perfectly acceptable operating mode. I had a rather lengthy debate with a student about the merits of post-structuralism. You'd have loved it. Or perhaps run screaming in the other direction. Sounds like a headache. I’m sticking to counting pennies, thank you very much. Though, I did overhear Mr. Davies talking about re-tiling the conservatory. Another fund-raising opportunity, perhaps? Potentially. Though with your luck, Brenda will swoop in and steal the glory. Have you seen that new detective series on Channel 4?  The Long Shadow ? It’s utterly gripping, but incredibly bleak. No, not yet.

Honestly, this Polish weather is…persistent. Grey, grey, grey. It’s been like this for weeks, hasn’t it? Makes you long for a proper English drizzle, strangely enough. At least you  know  where you are with drizzle. Tell me about it. It’s bleak. I’ve been showing my students pictures of the Lake District, trying to inspire some wanderlust, and even  I  feel depressed looking at the sunshine in the photos. Speaking of which… saw your mum’s obituary online. So sorry, truly. Is everything… are you managing? Oh, thank you, love. It’s… it’s been a lot. The funeral was last week. Cambridge was, well, Cambridge. All those old faces, all that politeness. It felt very… distant. Like I was observing someone else’s life. I haven’t really  lived  there, properly, for decades. It must be hard, going back to a place that feels so removed from your current reality. I struggle with that even going back to Bury. It's not  home  home anymore, you know? It’s just… where I  from . And seeing everyone settled, with their routines… it’s easy to feel a bit… adrift. Exactly! Adrift is the perfect word. I was thinking about it on the train. I’ve never really  had  a ‘home’ in the traditional sense. Not a place I’ve built a life in, anyway. Just places I’ve existed in. It's a bit pathetic when you say it out loud, I suppose. It’s not pathetic. It’s… nomadic. And lots of people feel that way, especially nowadays. I mean, I love my job here in Tarnow - the school’s brilliant, the students are lovely - but I don't know if I could put down roots  here  forever. I miss a proper Sunday roast, and having a real pub within walking distance. Silly things, maybe. Not silly at all. Those little things matter. I tried the Polish equivalent of a roast…let's just say it wasn’t the same. Though their pierogi are amazing. You know, I used to think being a TEFL teacher was a good fit for me. The flexibility, the travel. But after a while, it becomes… transient. You’re always explaining someone else’s culture, never truly  in  one. I get that. I actually really enjoyed my PGCE, the training to be a teacher. The classroom dynamic, the challenge of making complex ideas accessible…that was rewarding.

…and honestly, the brief was  wild . “Evoke the feeling of beige.” Beige! Like, how do you even  do  that? It’s a colour, not an emotion. They wanted it for…wait for it… industrial sealant. Industrial. Sealant. Oh my god, that’s brilliant. Beige industrial sealant. You’re kidding. Is that even a thing people get emotional about? Apparently! Mr. Henderson, the account manager, was very serious. He kept going on about “trustworthiness” and “dependability.” Apparently, beige equates to both in the sealant world. I ended up writing something about ‘unwavering protection, the colour of reliable foundations…’ It felt…overblown. It does. But hey, you’re a copywriter! You make the overblown sound…slightly less overblown. How’s the new job generally, though? Still enjoying being away from Ashford? It’s good, yeah. It’s a massive step up from waitressing through uni, that’s for sure. London is… a lot. Still trying to get my head around the tube map. And the prices! Honestly, going grocery shopping feels like a strategic military operation. Tell me about it. Even as a student, I wince at the supermarket bills. I went to Borough Market last week, thinking it would be a nice, atmospheric experience. It was atmospheric, alright – atmospherically expensive! Ended up just buying a single pear. A single pear?! Oh, that’s peak London. I tried to make a roast dinner last weekend. A  roast dinner . It cost me nearly forty quid! And that was using supermarket own brand everything. Forty quid?! That  is  insane. I stick to pasta most of the time. It's cheap and cheerful. Have you managed to see much of Chloe since you moved up? Not as much as I’d like, to be honest. She's still plugging away at her PhD. Said she's buried in research about… something to do with Victorian embroidery. It’s fascinating, apparently, but not exactly conducive to spontaneous pub trips. We did grab coffee a couple of weeks ago, though. She’s convinced she’s discovered a previously unknown pattern. Chloe and her embroidery! She's dedicated, that’s for sure. I saw Ben at a coding meetup last week. He's thriving, apparently. Landed a decent contract with some tech start-up. He asked after you. Said he misses our ridiculous game nights. Oh, good! Tell him I said hi. And yes, I miss those nights. We need to recreate them, even if it’s just over Zoom.

Honestly, I didn’t realise how  completely  wiped I was. Seven AM is far too early on a Saturday, even for a relatively peaceful one. What time is it now, actually? Seven-fifteen! And I made a picture for you, Mummy! It’s of a sparkly unicorn! Oh, darling, it’s  beautiful . Absolutely wonderful. You’re a very talented artist. Thank you. Where’s your brother? Still asleep? No! I’m awake. Just… comfy. Comfy is good. But comfy needs breakfast, doesn’t it? I was thinking pancakes. Sound good? Pancakes! With sprinkles?! Please, please, please! We can definitely do sprinkles. But first, a little tidy-up. We can’t make pancakes in a disaster zone. Your father’s already put the coffee on, which is a good sign. Do we  have  to tidy? Can’t we just eat? Just a quick one, love. Five minutes. Then pancakes. Deal? Fine. Deal. But I’m having loads of syrup. Me too! And blueberries! Blueberries for everyone. Now, what about today? I was thinking after breakfast, we could try those juggling balls I ordered? Remember? For learning circus skills? Circus skills?! Cool! Can I learn to be a trapeze artist? Maybe a little further down the line for the trapeze! Let’s start with juggling. And maybe some plate spinning if we’re feeling brave. I wanna be a clown! Can I wear funny shoes? We can definitely find some funny shoes. Perhaps your Father has some old ones we can borrow. Oh, and I nearly forgot! My friend, Chloe, just messaged. She's got tickets to that Neon Moon thing next month, the one with all the retro gaming and stuff. Do you think you'd both like to come? What's 'retro gaming'? Is it like Fortnite? Not exactly. It’s games from when  I  was a kid. Think Pac-Man and Space Invaders. Old-school. Ooh, sounds fun! Will there be flashing lights? Loads of flashing lights! It's all very 80s themed. Chloe was saying she met someone there last time who was a proper Aussie, and she was trying to teach her some phrases. She said it's all “no worries” and “chuck a sickie.” "Chuck a sickie"? What's that mean? Apparently, it means to pretend to be ill to get out of something. Not that  we  would ever do that, darling. No way! Exactly. Although, it does sound rather tempting sometimes...

Honestly, Rhys, you're gripping the steering wheel like you’re navigating rapids, not the M5. Relax! We’ve got hours yet. And honestly, all this talk about the latest Conservative policy… it just makes my blood boil. Another tax cut for the wealthy while the NHS is crumbling? It's utterly predictable. Now, now, Eleanor. Don't get yourself worked up. It  is  frustrating, I grant you. But getting agitated won’t change a thing. And I  am  relaxed, relatively. Just concentrating. This stretch is prone to lorries, you know. Besides, predictable doesn’t make it right, does it? It just makes it… inevitable, unless people actually  do  something. Can we maybe not 'do something' while we're on the motorway? My dissertation thanks you for keeping your eyes on the road, Professor. Though, I have to admit, Gran's rant on the radio yesterday about the state of the country was pretty compelling. She’s usually quite…moderate. Moderate? Your grandmother? Oh, she has opinions, alright. Very strong ones, usually concealed under a veneer of polite society. But she remembers things, you see. She lived through the post-war austerity, the miners’ strikes... she’s seen governments come and go and promises broken. It informs her worldview, naturally. She remembers the Bevan years fondly, your mother does. Says he understood what it meant to build a society  for  the people, not just  allowing  people to exist within a system designed to benefit the few. My own father, he worked in the mines, you know. Nantyglo. A tough life. He’d have had something scathing to say about this current lot, I assure you. I’ve heard stories about Nantyglo. It sounds… intense. All that community spirit, but also incredibly difficult. Gran always says your mum, Professor, was a force of nature, even then. Running the chapel choir and organizing protests simultaneously? Your grandmother exaggerates, but there’s truth to it. She was a remarkable woman. Had a fire in her belly. Used to say, "Rhys, a quiet life is a wasted life." I think I inherited some of that, though I try to channel it into academic papers rather than picket lines these days. It's less likely to get you arrested. Honestly, Rhys, your academic papers  are  your picket lines! All that challenging established thinking, questioning the norm… it’s just a more refined way of causing trouble.

…and then the badger, right, he’d built this  enormous  fortress out of jam jars and old wellington boots! But it wasn’t to keep people  out , it was to keep the glitter inside. He was obsessed with glitter. Glitter! Why? Well, he thought glitter was magic. He believed if he collected enough, he could wish for a never-ending supply of raspberry ripple ice cream. Raspberry ripple is the BEST! Better than chocolate. It  is  very good, isn't it? Though I have a soft spot for chocolate myself. But back to the badger… Anyway, the glitter kept escaping, obviously. Jam jars aren't exactly airtight. Did he get any raspberry ripple? Not yet! That's where  we  come in. We need to figure out how he can stop the glitter escaping. Any ideas? Put glue on all the jam jars! Loads and loads of glue! That’s… a very thorough solution, Leo. But maybe a little messy? And what about letting light in? Badgers need light, don’t they? Maybe he can use bubble wrap! Like when we send Grandma parcels. Glitter can’t get  through  bubble wrap! Oh, Maisie, that's brilliant! Bubble wrap fortress! That’s a much better idea. See, Leo? Sometimes gentler solutions are best. It's all about thinking creatively! We're really good at this story-making, aren't we? We are! It's better than playing Minecraft. Almost. Almost! That’s high praise indeed! Speaking of stories, has anyone been looking at the Linton Book Festival programme? It came through the school email today. What’s a… programme? It’s a list of all the authors who are coming to talk about their books. Lots of exciting events. I was thinking we might go on the Saturday. Are there any dinosaur books? I haven't checked yet. I was hoping we could look through it  together . There's usually someone doing dinosaur stuff. And, you know, other fun things. I saw Helen Moss is doing a reading. Helen Moss! The girl who finds shipwreck treasure? That’s the one! She writes amazing adventure stories. You two  loved  ‘The Mystery of the Pirate's Cove’ last year. I wanted a metal detector after that book. I remember. And you  did  spend a whole afternoon in the garden with a spoon pretending to be a treasure hunter. I found a button! It wasn't gold, though.

Honestly, this lentil shepherd’s pie is taking  ages . I swear, being vegetarian is so much more effort than just chucking some mince in. Oh, come on, El. It's not  that  much effort. And it smells amazing already. Besides, you know I'm firmly in the ‘animals are friends, not food’ camp. You're the one who occasionally caves and orders a cheeky Nando’s. Speaking of food… anyone want a pineapple? Found a decent one at the market. Also, the ethical debate continues, I see. Is anyone considering ‘shmeat’ as a solution? Cultured meat? Seems less… morally compromising than the whole abattoir situation. Shmeat? Seriously, Ben? It sounds like something out of a sci-fi film. And honestly, it still feels… weird. Like, growing meat in a lab? Is that even natural? It's arguably  more  natural than the conditions most farm animals live in, El. Think about it – cramped cages, pumped full of antibiotics… It’s a form of oppression, isn’t it? Plus, the environmental impact of livestock farming is insane. I know, I know, you’re right. It's just... I had a weird dream last night about a giant vat of chicken nuggets growing in a lab. It was deeply unsettling. And a bit orange. Right, well, stick to lentils then. But honestly, if it meant drastically reducing animal suffering, I’d give lab-grown steak a shot. It’s not ideal, but it’s a step towards something better. Though, I’d worry about the price initially. It’ll be extortionate. Exactly! It could democratise meat consumption, theoretically. Though, knowing capitalism, it’ll probably be a luxury item for a while. Speaking of luxury, and things I shouldn't be thinking about - did you guys see Larry David’s latest faux pas on Curb? He tried to return a half-eaten sandwich! Oh my god, no! That’s  classic  Larry! He’s a monster. Though, secretly, part of me understands the urge. Especially when they mess up your order. Like, I specifically asked for seeded bread, and they gave me white! The audacity! He's brilliant at exposing the ridiculousness of everyday social interactions. It's almost… cathartic. But back to food, and less important things. Have you been taking your B12, El? Being vegetarian, you need to supplement. Yes, Mum! I take my vitamins. Honestly, you lot treat me like I’m going to wither away from malnutrition.

Honestly, this washing machine is driving me round the bend. It’s making  that  noise again. The one that sounds like a strangled walrus. I swear, if it breaks down  now , just before New Year's, I’ll scream. We've got people coming, you know! A strangled walrus, eh? That's… descriptive, love. It probably just needs a good clean through. Remember what your Auntie Brenda said about putting vinegar in with the detergent? She swears by it. Though knowing Brenda, she probably uses it for everything – cleaning, cooking, hair conditioner… Oh, don’t even  start  on Brenda. She called the other day, rambling on about how young people don’t understand “proper English” anymore. Apparently, I was using too many ‘likes’ in a sentence.  Likes , Richard! Who even counts those? Oh god, Brenda’s language policing again? She does that to everyone. It’s exhausting. I had a call from her last week complaining I said “vibe check” to my cousin. A  vibe check ! She made it sound like I was performing a medical examination. She’s a character, that one. Always has been. Remember when she tried to convince us Welsh wasn’t a real language? Said it was just “a funny accent.” Oh, I remember! Poor Gareth nearly choked on his tea! Speaking of which, what  are  you making, Richard? Smells amazing. Is that the curry Auntie Sheila sent us? It is, actually. Though I’ve toned down the chilli a bit. Sheila thinks everyone needs to eat something that actively sets their mouth on fire. And, yes, it's intended to distract from the looming washing machine disaster. Anything to avoid looking at it. You’d think, with all the smart appliances out there, a washing machine wouldn’t be so… temperamental. I was reading an article today about AI-powered washing machines that adjust settings based on fabric type and dirt levels. Honestly? Sounds like overkill. I just want it to wash my clothes without sounding like a marine mammal in distress. Anyway, New Year's Eve… are we still on for a proper knees-up? I have ordered some prosecco. Absolutely! Though I’m not sure my knees are up to a ‘knees-up’ anymore. More of a gentle sway, perhaps. Your sister's coming, right? And young Harry? Yes, both of them. Harry’s already started asking about fireworks. And, predictably, a new phone.

…and honestly, the sheer audacity of asking for a  butterfly fork ! I mean, really? A butterfly fork? Like it’s going to magically make the peas easier to spear. What’s a butterfly fork? Sounds cool. Sounds…pointless. Like, a normal fork works fine. It  is  pointless, darling. It's a tiny, decorative fork shaped like a butterfly. Old Mrs. Higgins at the Historical Society requested one for the Victorian tea party. Said it was “authentically whimsical.” Authentically ridiculous, more like. It took me a good ten minutes to explain we don’t just  have  butterfly forks lying around. Did she get cross? Oh, terribly. A lot of huffing and puffing about standards slipping. It reminded me of Grandad when you tried to use a spoon for your cereal. Hey! I was six! And spoons are better for yogurt. That’s beside the point! Anyway, it led to a rather long discussion about the importance of historical accuracy. Honestly, you'd think we were recreating the Crimean War, not serving scones. Speaking of which, anyone want more? Yeah, please. This one’s good. Did you make the jam yourself? I did, actually. Plum. From the garden. It's rather tart. So, how was school today? Anything exciting happen? Miss Davies made us do two minutes of silence. Oh? Why’s that? Because Ben and Leo were messing around with paper aeroplanes. During history. About Russia. Russia?! What about Russia? Just…Russia. Miss Davies said it was disrespectful, considering everything that’s happening. And then she made  everyone  be quiet for two whole minutes. It was ages. That sounds…intense. Perhaps a slightly heavy-handed response, but I can understand the sentiment. It  is  a difficult time, with everything going on over there. Are you learning much about it in History? A bit. We talked about the Cold War. And Stalin. He sounds…bad. He was, very bad. It's important to learn about these things, you know.
